Introduction

How to Use This Book

Before you start

The editor compiled this book with a generative AI system (Claude). Each chapter was checked against the original papers several times, but errors may remain. Please confirm figures and quotations against the originals. The book will keep being revised; the edition and date you are reading are on the cover and in the colophon (edition 1.0-en, translated from Korean edition 1.0 of October 5, 2026).

To the extent the editor holds rights in it, this book is released under CC BY-NC 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International). You may adapt and share it for noncommercial purposes if you credit the author, name the license (with a link), and indicate any changes you made. You may not restrict others' use with legal terms or technological measures. This summary is for convenience; the license text governs. Tables, quotations and figures reproduced or redrawn from original works are not covered by this license and remain subject to the rights of their authors. If you hold rights in such material, tell us through the repository's issue tracker and we will correct or remove it.

This English edition is a translation of Korean edition 1.0 (October 5, 2026, including the correction of October 13, 2026). The editor made it with the same AI system and had it checked against the Korean text and, where a quotation was originally in English, against that original wording. The Korean edition counts its units as meetings of a study group; this edition calls them chapters, from Chapter 0 to Chapter 20. Sources that exist only in Korean, including some of the videos, are kept and marked "(in Korean)".

This edition keeps the Korean edition's Korean examples as they are. Very few arguments in this book rest on a Korean case, so this edition adds no boxes of comparable cases from other countries.

This is a self-study guide that Sunday AI, a study group, compiled to read papers on agentic AI for an hour each week. It is easier going if you have a grounding in probability, statistics, linear algebra and basic programming. If natural language processing and reinforcement learning are new to you, or it has been a while, you can review them first in Chapter 0 (preliminaries). You are welcome to run a study group the same way elsewhere, or to read it alone.

1. How a meeting runs

Each meeting was planned to take about an hour: roughly 50 minutes of presentation and 10 minutes of discussion. Each chapter has a "Presenter's guide" that points to the sections, figures and tables at the center of the paper and suggests how to divide the time. The presenter prepares from it. The other participants will find the presentation and discussion easier to follow if they read "The question this chapter answers" and "Building intuition" in advance.

Every chapter has the same structure.

Section What it contains Who uses it
The question this chapter answers One sentence Everyone
Links to the originals Links to the main paper's arXiv page, PDF, conference page and code, and to the relevant survey sections Everyone
Presenter's guide A 50-minute plan: must read, optional reading, what to cut from the presentation The presenter
Building intuition A bridge from what the reader already knows. The editor's analogies are marked with a box Everyone (before the meeting)
The paper in detail An account of the core paper, with tables reproduced from the original, equations and diagrams Everyone
Rereading with a statistician's eye A reanalysis using the numbers printed in the paper, or an exercise in designing a study that would test a claim. Folded solutions Readers interested in statistics
Limitations the paper states From the Limitations, Discussion and ethics statements The presenter
Side papers — how they differ from the main paper The remaining papers on the list, in three or four lines each: "what is different" The presenter (10 minutes)
Back to the surveys Where the paper sits among the categories of the two surveys in Part I Everyone
Common misreadings Things that are easy to get wrong in a presentation The presenter
Discussion questions 2–3 Discussion (10 minutes)
Videos · Further study · Sources Links Self-study

2. How many meetings? — Schedules

The bracket next to each chapter title gives its type and importance. Core chapters come from the list of papers first proposed in the study group; Optional chapters are supplements. ★★★ marks the backbone (leave it out and later chapters will not make sense), ★★ is recommended (later chapters still make sense without it, but one strand gets thin), and ★ can be skipped, with the side-paper notes elsewhere covering enough.

Plan Meetings What is included At one meeting a week
Full 20 All of Chapters 1–20 About 5 months
Basic 15 Core chapters only (1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17, 19, 20) About 3½ months
Minimum 13 The basic plan, with 8 + 10 and 19 + 20 combined About 3 months

If you add optional chapters, we suggest this order: 18 (statistics of evaluation) → 4 (CoT) → 14 (SWE-agent) → 5 (ToT) → 16 (alignment). Chapter 18 comes first because it suits readers with a statistics background best. Chapter 4 is directly needed to read the comparison in Chapter 6, because ReAct uses CoT as a baseline. If you leave out Chapter 4, as the 15-meeting basic plan does, fill the gap the way the item "If your group skipped Chapter 4" in Chapter 6's presenter's guide describes: spend the first 10 minutes of the Chapter 6 presentation introducing three figures from the CoT paper.

Whether to include optional chapters is up to the group. You can decide at the start or as you go. The chapter numbers in this book are fixed at 1 to 20, so skipped chapters do not make the others harder to find, and you can read a skipped chapter on your own. When you cover two chapters in one meeting, the reading range and time split are under "When combining chapters" in that chapter's presenter's guide.

3. The twenty chapters at a glance

Chapter Part The question this chapter answers Core reading Type Importance
1 I Overview How is an agent different from a workflow, and when should you not use one? Building effective agents Core ★★★
2 I Overview How do you separate "thinking", "acting" and "learning" within one frame? Agentic Reasoning survey (revised version) §2 Core ★★★
3 I Overview Why do systems built on the same model differ in performance and safety? Harness survey §1–2, §11 Core ★★★
4 II Thinking and Acting Why does having the model write intermediate steps raise accuracy, and when does it not? Chain-of-Thought Optional ★★
5 II Thinking and Acting What changes when you spread out several branches and choose among them, and what does it cost? Tree of Thoughts Optional ★
6 II Thinking and Acting When a model acts while observing the outside world, where does "thinking" come in? ReAct Core ★★★
7 III Tools How does a model know when to call a tool, and why did a standard protocol become necessary? Toolformer + MCP specification Core ★★★
8 IV Context What is the simplest probabilistic way to put knowledge that is not in the weights into an answer? RAG Core ★★★
9 IV Context Does the answer change with where the same information is placed? Lost in the Middle Core ★★★
10 IV Context Can the model itself judge whether to retrieve and how good the results are? Self-RAG Core ★★
11 V Verification How does fixing within the output differ from fixing on the next attempt? RARR + Reflexion Core ★★★
12 VI Memory When the window is fixed, who decides what stays and what is moved out? MemGPT Core ★★★
13 VII Collaboration Why do errors spread when agents are chained, and how do SOPs stop them? MetaGPT Core ★★
14 VIII Coding Agents Does performance change if you keep the model and change only the interface? SWE-agent Optional ★★
15 IX Security Why do sentences in a document an agent reads get executed as commands? Greshake et al. Core ★★★
16 IX Security How was the tendency to follow instructions well created, and what does it become in an agent? InstructGPT + Agentic misalignment Optional ★
17 X Evaluation and Operations What does agent evaluation measure, and how? Evaluation survey + GAIA Core ★★★
18 X Evaluation and Operations Is first place on the leaderboard really better? AI Agents That Matter + Error Bars Optional ★★
19 X Evaluation and Operations How do you tell whether a failure comes from the model or the harness, and how do you fix it? HarnessFix Core ★★
20 XI Synthesis If knowledge is compiled in advance, how are the parts seen so far rearranged? LLM Wiki (+ WikiSkill) Core ★★★

The principle of the order is "add parts to the augmented LLM one at a time". Thinking (4–5) comes before acting (6). That is because ReAct uses CoT as its point of comparison. Tools (7) come before context (8–10). In the broad sense, the retriever in RAG is one tool. Verification (11) follows context, and memory (12) follows verification. Reflexion's memory of reflections is the bridge to MemGPT's tiered memory. After single agents are covered come collaboration (13), then coding agents (14) as a real system with all the parts in place, and then security (15–16). The damage from indirect injection grows by passing through tools, retrieval, memory and code repositories, so it only makes sense once all the parts have been seen. Evaluation and operations (17–19) come after everything there is to evaluate has been covered, and synthesis (20) ends with LLM Wiki, where retrieval, memory, verification and governance come together again in one system.

How the twenty chapters are grouped into parts. The editor drew the diagram.

4. The two surveys of Part I — head and body

Every later chapter ends with "Back to the surveys", which returns to the two surveys of Part I. The Agentic Reasoning survey in Chapter 2 looks at the agent's head. It sorts how a model plans, uses tools and searches, and how it improves through feedback and memory, by "what is being optimized" (the reasoning trace z, the system state S, the parameters θ). The Harness survey in Chapter 3 looks at the agent's body and fence: everything outside the model, namely the execution environment, tool protocols, context management, orchestration, observability, verification and governance (ETCLOVG). The notation and layer names of the two surveys are fixed in Appendices I and II, and every chapter uses that notation.

5. Conventions

  • Video labels. [Author] marks a talk by the paper's authors or an official channel, [Review] a paper review by a lab or study group, and [Secondary] a third-party summary or what appears to be an automatically generated one. Watch [Secondary] videos alongside the original. The editor did not verify the content of the videos. Korean-language videos and other Korean-language materials are kept and marked "(in Korean)"; titles and channel names in Korean are given in English, translated or romanized by the editor.
  • Boxes. The Links to the originals box holds links, the A bridge from the editor box holds analogies, and the This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper box states the premises of a reanalysis.
  • Folded solutions. In the screen edition, click the "Solution" heading to open them. In the print edition they are all open.
  • Chapter references. Wherever "Chapter n" appears, it links to that chapter in the screen edition.
  • Notation. Appendix I. Terms are in Appendix II. Where the Korean edition paired a translated term with the original English at first use (for example, attribution, harness), this edition simply uses the English term.
  • Tables from the originals. The caption of each reproduced table gives the table number in the original. When you put numbers on presentation slides, look at the original table again, not this book.

6. What to know before you read

  1. Versions. Read the Agentic Reasoning survey in the revised TMLR version on OpenReview. The version on arXiv (2601.12538) differs from the revised version in its section and table numbers and in its categories. v2 only adds "Accepted by TMLR" on the arXiv abstract page; its body is the same as v1 (compared on October 5, 2026). For the other papers, the latest arXiv version and the official conference version are taken to have the same content, but page numbers may differ between versions.
  2. Peer review. Several of the 2026 sources are preprints (the Harness survey, HarnessFix, the position paper among the side papers of Chapter 18, and WikiSkill in Chapter 20). The Harness survey is posted on OpenReview, but as a direct archive upload, not after conference or journal review. Do not cite their claims and numbers as settled results.
  3. When the numbers date from. The performance numbers in the papers are for the models of their time (GPT-4, PaLM and so on). Do not use them to compare with today's models. When you carry a number over, give the sample and conditions with it.
  4. What company documents are. The posts by Anthropic, OpenAI, Manus and Chroma are prescriptions drawn from building their own products. The companies have an interest, and the posts were not peer reviewed. Read them as design guidance, not as generalized empirical evidence.
  5. Videos. Videos marked [Secondary] are third-party summaries or appear to be automatically generated. Watch them alongside the original.
  6. Distribution and copyright. Do not redistribute paper PDFs; share links (arXiv, OpenReview, conference pages). CC BY documents may be shared with attribution. Under its terms, the GAIA data may not be reshared outside its gated repository or published in a crawlable form.
  7. Security exercises. Do prompt-injection exercises only in an environment you own or in a public evaluation environment (AgentDojo and the like). Do not try them against real services or other people's accounts. Do not put internal company material or personal information into a practice agent.
  8. Terms. Terms follow the glossary in Appendix II.
  9. Telling analogy from claim. The "bridge" analogies (for example, reward model = a Bradley–Terry-type model) were laid down by the editor to aid understanding. Keep them apart from the papers' claims. Readings that differ from a paper are written as "can also be read as". They are points for discussion, not conclusions.
  10. Links. All links were checked on October 4, 2026. Blogs and videos may disappear or change address.
  11. "Rereading with a statistician's eye". This is a reanalysis the editor calculated using only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do such an analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. In chapters without numbers to work with, it is a study-design exercise that asks "how would you measure this to test the claim?"

7. For presenters

  • Do not put internal information from your organization in presentation materials.
  • When you write a number, give the model, task, metric and number of items with it. Not "ALFWorld 71%", but "PaLM-540B, 134 ALFWorld games, best of six prompts 71%, mean 57%".
  • You can prepare the 10 minutes on side papers from this book's "Side papers" section. For side papers you want to explore further, follow the links to the originals in that section.
  • If you show only one figure, the "Must read" item of each chapter names it.

Chapter 0 · not a meeting

Chapter 0. Preliminaries — Language Models, Tokens, In-Context Learning, and Reinforcement-Learning Terms

The question this chapter answers: what do you need to know to read a language model as a probability model, and which terms do the later chapters take for granted?

What this chapter is for. It is for readers who have never studied natural language processing or reinforcement learning, to read for an hour or two before the first meeting (or before Chapter 1, if you are reading alone). It is not presented. The later chapters use "token", "context window", "temperature", "a few examples", "episode" and "policy" without explanation; this chapter defines them and ties them to concepts you know from statistics. If you already know them, skip ahead and just do the "Self-check" at the end.

Links to the originals

Reading — GPT-3 paper §1–2 arXiv abstract · PDF · NeurIPS 2020 / InstructGPT Figure 2 arXiv abstract · PDF

Video — [Author] "[1hr Talk] Intro to Large Language Models" — Andrej Karpathy

One-paragraph summary. A language model is a probability model that outputs the conditional distribution of the next token, p(xt∣x<t), and training it is maximum likelihood estimation that reduces the negative log-likelihood. Tokens are word pieces cut by BPE, and there is an upper limit on how many tokens can serve as the condition (2,048 for GPT-3). Temperature flattens or sharpens the distribution; sending it to 0 gives greedy decoding. The GPT-3 paper used the name "in-context learning" for leaving the weights as they are and having the model solve a new task by putting an instruction and a few examples into the input. InstructGPT, which made that model follow instructions, went through three steps: demonstrations → reward model → reinforcement learning. The vocabulary of reinforcement learning (state, action, reward, policy, episode, trajectory, return, value function) is borrowed as is by the agent papers later in the book.

1. Reading a language model as a conditional distribution

One chain rule. The joint probability of a token sequence x1,x2,…,xn can be factored as follows for any distribution.

p(x1,…,xn)=∏t=1np(xt∣x<t),x<t=(x1,…,xt−1)

This is an identity, not an approximation. It just writes the chain rule in time order. When the GPT-3 paper calls its model an "autoregressive language model" (abstract), autoregressive means that the conditional distributions of this factorization are modeled with a single neural network that produces one token at a time from left to right. The substance of the model lies not in the factorization but in the family of functions used to approximate pθ(xt∣x<t) (for GPT-3, a transformer, §2.1) and in how far back it looks (the context window, below). An n-gram model is a Markov chain that cuts the past down to the last few tokens.

The training objective is the negative log-likelihood. Add up the log of the probability the model gave to the actual next token at each position, and flip the sign.

ℒ(θ)=−∑t=1nlogpθ(xt∣x<t)

Reducing this is maximum likelihood estimation, and it is the same as reducing the cross-entropy. If the model gave the actual next token a probability of 0.25, the loss at that position is ln4≈1.39. The average loss turned back through the exponential, exp(ℒ¯), is called perplexity, and it reads as "on average, how many candidates is the model choosing among?" In this example it is 4. Because the next token is itself the answer, no labels made by people are needed. All the GPT-3 models were trained on 300 billion tokens (Table 2.1 caption). On the other hand, this objective treats every token the same. §5 of the paper lists as a limitation that it cannot tell which predictions matter more.

What is a token? The unit the model sees is neither a character nor a word. GPT-3 says it uses GPT-2's tokenization as is (the "reversible tokenization" of §2.1), and it counts the size of its data in "byte-pair-encoded tokens" (§2.2: 570GB of filtered Common Crawl is roughly 400 billion tokens). BPE (byte-pair encoding) takes bytes as the initial vocabulary and repeatedly merges the pair that most often appears together into a new symbol until the vocabulary reaches a set size. Common words become one token and rare words are broken into pieces. The paper explains that one BPE token is on average about 0.7 words, so the letter-scrambling tasks require the model to pull apart the insides of tokens (§3.9.2), and it guesses that the unusually weak English→Romanian translation may be due to reusing GPT-2's BPE tokenizer, which was built from almost entirely English data (§3.3).

The context window. The past x<t used as the condition has an upper limit. All the GPT-3 models use a context window of nctx=2048 tokens (§2.1), and training always uses sequences filled to the full 2,048 tokens. Short documents are joined with an end-of-text token between them (Appendix B). Estimated at about 0.7 words per token, that is a little over 1,400 English words (the editor's calculation). This limit is also the limit of in-context learning. Examples go in as far as the window allows, usually 10 to 100 (§2). The "context" of the later chapters is all the tokens in this window, and it fills up as an agent piles up thoughts, actions and observations. That information is not used evenly even within the window, depending on its position, is the subject of Chapter 9; designs that keep memory outside the window are the subject of Chapter 12.

Three of the column names in the table below appear here for the first time. dmodel is the length of the vector that represents one token inside the transformer (§2.1 of the paper describes it as the number of units in each bottleneck layer). Attention is the computation by which each position weights the earlier positions by how much to consult them and mixes them; a head is a unit that splits that computation into several branches done in parallel. The head dimension dhead is the length of the vector one branch uses. The later chapters of this book do not use the inside of the transformer, so you can read the table only for "as the models grew, the layers and the width grew together" and move on.

Model Name nparams nlayers dmodel nheads × dhead
GPT-3 Small 125M 12 768 12 × 64
GPT-3 Medium 350M 24 1,024 16 × 64
GPT-3 Large 760M 24 1,536 16 × 96
GPT-3 XL 1.3B 24 2,048 24 × 128
GPT-3 2.7B 2.7B 32 2,560 32 × 80
GPT-3 6.7B 6.7B 32 4,096 32 × 128
GPT-3 13B 13.0B 40 5,140 40 × 128
GPT-3 175B or "GPT-3" 175.0B 96 12,288 96 × 128

Table 2.1 of the paper, with the batch-size and learning-rate columns removed. The context window is 2,048 for all eight models (§2.1). The comparison that follows is optional reading. The number of heads times the head dimension equals dmodel in six rows but not in XL (3,072 against 2,048) or 13B (5,120 against 5,140). Equality is not a required constraint and the paper does not explain it, so the original does not settle whether these are typos.

Sampling temperature and greedy decoding. For each token in the vocabulary V the model outputs a real-valued score zi (a logit), and the softmax turns these into probabilities. Temperature T>0 is the number the logits are divided by before that.

pT(i∣x<t)=exp(zi/T)∑j∈Vexp(zj/T)

At T=1 you get the distribution the model learned, unchanged. Raising T flattens the distribution; lowering it concentrates the mass on the largest logit. Here is the calculation for three tokens with logits (2,1,0) (the editor's calculation).

Temperature T First token Second token Third token
2.0 0.506 0.307 0.186
1.0 0.665 0.245 0.090
0.5 0.867 0.117 0.016
0.1 0.99995 0.00005 0.00000

If there is a single largest logit, the limit as T→0 gives that token probability 1. If two or more logits tie for the maximum, the limiting distribution is split evenly among them. So "temperature 0" means greedy decoding, which picks the most probable token at every position. With a rule fixed for ties, it is deterministic: the same input gives the same output. But picking the best token at each step does not maximize the probability of the whole sentence. Beam search, which carries several candidates along together, searches more widely for that. GPT-3 evaluated its free-form tasks with a beam width of 4 (§2.4). ReAct in Chapter 6 produces one trajectory by greedy decoding, while its comparison baseline CoT-SC samples 21 reasoning paths at temperature 0.7 and takes a majority vote (CoT-SC in ReAct §3.2; ReAct's greedy decoding in §3.3 footnote 4 and the Table 3 caption). Raise the temperature when you need varied samples, and lower it when you need one reproducible answer. Besides these there is top-k sampling, which draws only from the k highest tokens, and top-p sampling, which draws only from the tokens up to cumulative probability p (the poem samples in GPT-3 Appendix F use temperature 1 and P=0.9).

If you view next-token prediction as a multinomial logistic regression with tens of thousands of categories (the editor's analogy), the logits are the linear predictor, and dividing by the temperature is the same as sampling from a model with every coefficient multiplied by 1/T. Unlike regression, though, the token just drawn becomes an explanatory variable for the next prediction, so one token that goes astray can pull what follows along with it.

2. In-context learning — learning that does not change the weights

The GPT-3 paper's definition. §1 of the paper introduces in-context learning like this.

"… using the text input of a pretrained language model as a form of task specification: the model is conditioned on a natural language instruction and/or a few demonstrations of the task and is then expected to complete further instances of the task simply by predicting what comes next."

The task is specified in the input text. The model takes an instruction or a few examples as the condition and carries on the rest as if predicting the next token. The weights stay the same. In the language of section 1, the θ of the conditional distribution pθ(·∣x<t) is held fixed and only x<t changes.

Outer loop and inner loop — Figure 1.1. The paper places this within the frame of meta-learning. Changing the weights by SGD during pre-training is the outer loop, and what happens within the forward pass over a single sequence is the inner loop, that is, in-context learning. SGD (stochastic gradient descent) draws part of the data, computes the gradient of the loss, and moves the weights a little in the opposite direction. A forward pass computes the output distribution from the input with the current weights held as they are. In the inner loop no gradient is computed and no weight is moved. When the examples placed in front change, the output computed with the same weights simply changes. The sequences in the figure repeat additions such as 5 + 8 = 13, spelling corrections such as gaot => goat, and translations such as thanks => merci within one sequence.

Four settings — Figure 2.1. §2 sets out four settings side by side by how much task-specific data they use, and draws them with a single English→French translation example.

Setting What the model receives Weight updates
Fine-Tuning (FT) The prompt, after repeated training on thousands to hundreds of thousands of task examples A gradient update per example
Few-Shot (FS) Task description + K examples + prompt None
One-Shot (1S) Task description + 1 example + prompt None
Zero-Shot (0S) Task description + prompt None

Figure 2.1 and the definitions in §2 of the paper, arranged as a table. The heading of the fine-tuning panel on the right of the figure is "Traditional fine-tuning (not used for GPT-3)".

The input in the few-shot panel is these five lines.

Translate English to French:      ← task description
sea otter => loutre de mer        ← examples
peppermint => menthe poivrée
plush girafe => girafe peluche
cheese =>                         ← prompt

The few-shot panel of Figure 2.1 in the paper. The labels on the right are also in the figure, and "girafe" is spelled as in this panel (the fine-tuning panel has "giraffe").

All the model has to do is predict the token after cheese =>. The three example lines convey both the format and the task. In zero-shot, the one line of description has to do all of that. The paper writes that zero-shot is the most convenient but the hardest, and since even a person may find it hard to know the format without an example, as with a request to "make a table of world records for the 200m dash", it is in some cases "unfairly hard".

What does "shot" count? It is the number K of examples (demonstrations) given as the condition at inference time. It is neither the number of gradient updates nor the size of the training data. For each evaluation item, K examples are drawn afresh at random from that task's training set, and if there is a development set, several values of K are tried and the best is used (§2.4). This book says "give a few examples", and keeps the names zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot only for the settings.

Scores rise with the number of examples and the size of the model. Here are two sets of numbers that §1 gives directly in the text (GPT-3 175B). CoQA is a reading-comprehension task in which questions and answers about one passage follow one another like a conversation; the answers are free-form (§3.6, and Figure G.18 in Appendix G). The score is F1, which matches the model's answer against the correct answer word by word: the harmonic mean of precision and recall, written on a scale of 0 to 100 (the definition of F1 is the editor's general explanation; the GPT-3 paper does not give it). TriviaQA is a set of quiz-style factual questions. The "closed-book" setting is the condition in which only the question is given, without retrieving and attaching related documents (§3.2). The score is the share of questions answered correctly.

Task (metric) zero-shot one-shot few-shot
CoQA (F1) 81.5 84.0 85.0
TriviaQA (accuracy %, closed-book) 64.3 68.0 71.2

Numbers from the text of §1 of the GPT-3 paper. The paper writes that the few-shot TriviaQA score of 71.2 was the best result at the time, above fine-tuned models in the same closed-book setting.

The paper sees a tendency for the gap between zero-, one- and few-shot to widen as the model grows, and interprets it as a sign that larger models may be better meta-learners (§1, Figures 1.2 and 1.3). The values read off the figures' axes are not carried over here. The sentence the paper stresses is this one.

"We emphasize that these 'learning' curves involve no gradient updates or fine-tuning, just increasing numbers of demonstrations given as conditioning."

How do the examples work? — what the paper says. The paper does not explain the mechanism; it deliberately leaves it open. Footnote 1 says that the names zero-, one- and few-shot "are intended to remain agnostic on the question of whether the model learns new tasks from scratch at inference time or simply recognizes patterns seen during training". §5 lays out that question as a spectrum. The model may already have seen examples from the same distribution during training, or the same task in a different format, or it may really be learning a new skill, and where on that spectrum it falls differs from task to task. The paper's guess is that artificial tasks such as letter scrambling are learned from scratch, while translation was learned in pre-training. As evidence, §3.9.2 points to the results that on the scrambling tasks the one-shot score drops to half or less of the few-shot score and that the model can rarely do them zero-shot, while adding the caveat that this cannot be confirmed with certainty.

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

In statistics, "learning" usually means estimating parameters: you look at data and revise θ^. Fine-tuning and GPT-3's pre-training (the outer loop) are of this kind. To people who use Bayesian models, another sense is familiar too. When you compute the posterior predictive distribution p(ynew∣xnew,D), the model stays as it is and you only put the data D into the condition, yet the prediction adapts to that data. In-context learning looks like this from the outside. The K examples take the place of D, and what changes is the condition, not the model.

There are places where the analogy fails. In a Bayesian model the prior and likelihood are explicit, so the result of conditioning can be worked out by calculation. What a language model computes when it receives examples is not known, and the paper stays neutral on that question (footnote 1, §5).

How this connects to later chapters. CoT in Chapter 4, ToT in Chapter 5 and ReAct in Chapter 6 all sit on top of this setting. A model with frozen weights is shown a few worked examples written by people and made to follow their format (ReAct's HotpotQA prompt has 6 examples and its FEVER prompt has 3). The first optimization target the survey in Chapter 2 names, "in-context reasoning", belongs to this line: the parameters θ are held fixed and only the reasoning trace z changes (Appendix I, section 4).

3. How models that follow instructions were made

GPT-3 was trained to guess the next token, not to follow instructions. §1 of the InstructGPT paper points to this gap. Predicting the next token on a webpage from the internet is a different objective from "follow the user's instructions helpfully and safely", so the paper says the language modeling objective is "misaligned", that is, not aligned. §5 of the GPT-3 paper also writes that useful language systems might be better thought of as taking goal-directed actions rather than just making predictions, and it names learning an objective function from humans and fine-tuning with reinforcement learning as directions for future work. Linking the two papers this way is this book's reading. InstructGPT's starting point is GPT-3 (§3.5).

The three steps of Figure 2 in the InstructGPT paper, redrawn. The wording of each step follows the figure and §3.1, the numbers of prompts follow §3.2, and the range of K follows §3.5. The example prompt for step 3 in the original figure is "Write a story about frogs". The editor drew the diagram.

Step 1 — supervised learning on demonstrations (SFT). For a sampled prompt, a labeler writes the desired answer by hand. The example in the figure is the prompt "Explain the moon landing to a 6 year old" with an answer that begins "Some people went to the moon..." GPT-3 is fine-tuned on these demonstrations with supervised learning (supervised fine-tuning). The original says only "supervised learning" and does not give the loss. Reading it as the negative log-likelihood of section 1 applied to the labelers' answers is the editor's explanation.

Step 2 — a reward model from comparisons (RM). For one prompt, 4 to 9 model outputs are sampled and a labeler ranks them, and all (K2) pairs that come out of one ranking are used in training (§3.5). The reward model takes a prompt and an answer and outputs one scalar score (the paper used only the 6B size). The loss (Eq. 1 in the paper) models the probability that the preferred answer gets the higher score with a logistic function, and Chapter 16 reads it again as a paired-comparison model.

Step 3 — reinforcement learning against the reward model (PPO). A policy that starts from the SFT model writes answers to new prompts, the reward model scores them, and PPO updates the policy with those scores as the reward. To keep the policy from chasing the reward model alone and writing nonsense, a penalty for how far it has moved from the SFT model (the KL divergence) is subtracted at each token (§3.5). The prompts in this step carry no human labels. Human judgment has already gone into the reward model in step 2. Steps 2 and 3 can be repeated, but in practice most of the comparison data came from outputs of the SFT policy (§3.1).

The result in one line. Outputs from the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT were preferred in human evaluations to those of the 175B GPT-3 (abstract). The win rates in Figure 1 would have to be read off the axes, so they are not carried over. The details and the evaluation are covered in Chapter 16; from this chapter take only the flow and the words needed to read step 3 (policy, reward, episode).

4. Reinforcement-learning terms — episode, reward, policy, value

Reflexion in Chapter 11 has "Verbal Reinforcement Learning" in its very title, and DeepSeek-R1, among the side papers of Chapter 4, draws out reasoning ability with reinforcement learning, as its title says. The scoreboard in Chapter 6 includes imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning baselines. This section sets out, at textbook level, the words these papers use without defining them, with notation matched to Appendix I. At each time t the agent looks at the state of the environment (or observes only part of it) and chooses an action; the environment moves to the next state and gives a reward. This repeats until the end.

Term Symbol Meaning Example in this book
state st (an element of X in Appendix I) The situation the environment is in now. The agent may not see all of it Where things in an ALFWorld house actually are
observation ot The information the agent actually receives An environment response such as "Nothing happens."
action at What the agent sends out to the environment go to coffeetable 1, search[entity]
reward rt A numeric signal the environment gives after an action 1 for task success, 0 for failure
policy π(at∣·) The rule (a probability distribution) that chooses an action from the information so far A language model given a prompt
episode — One round from the starting state to termination One ALFWorld game, one WebShop instruction
trajectory τ The record of observations, actions and rewards from one episode ReAct's log of thoughts, actions and observations
return Gt The discounted sum of rewards after time t —
value function Vπ(s) The expected return from state s when following policy π InstructGPT's value function (initialized from the reward model, §3.5)

Return and discounting. The return is the sum of the rewards received after time t, discounted by the discount factor γ∈(0,1).

Gt=∑k≥0γkrt+k

If the agent succeeds and receives a reward of 1 only after its third action, then with γ=0.9 the return at the first time step is G0=0.92=0.81. After the tenth action it would be 0.99≈0.39. Discounting rates policies that succeed quickly more highly. The value function is the expected return Vπ(s)=𝔼π[Gt∣st=s], and Qπ(s,a), which also fixes the action, is the action-value function. Reinforcement learning looks for the policy that maximizes the expected return. When the policy is determined by parameters θ, this becomes the objective in Appendix I.

J(θ)=𝔼τ~πθ[∑t≥0γtrt]

The survey in Chapter 2 writes the environment as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), E=⟨X,O,A,T,Ω,R,γ⟩ (latent state space, observation space, action space, transition kernel, observation kernel, reward, discount factor). The terms in the table above each fill one of these slots.

Episode and trajectory. An episode is an event, one attempt at a task from start to finish; a trajectory is the record of that event, the data. The ReAct paper defines the WebShop success rate as the "percentage of episodes where the chosen product satisfies all requirements" (§4). Success is counted per episode, and the log of thoughts, actions and observations read in Chapter 6 is a trajectory. Reflexion calls one attempt a "trial" and writes that each trial produces a trajectory τt (§3, Algorithm 1).

Episode length also differs from task to task. One ALFWorld game runs to dozens of actions. Step 3 of InstructGPT is a bandit environment that ends in a single step: it presents one customer prompt, receives an answer, gives the reward set by the reward model, and ends the episode (§3.5). Reinforcement learning ran for 256,000 episodes, over about 31,000 distinct prompts (Appendix C.4). The same appendix states that no discount was applied in estimating the advantage.

What are the policy and the reward? In a language-model agent, the policy is the language model given a prompt. ReAct §2 writes the policy as π(at∣ct), where the context ct is the text of the observations and actions so far, joined together. Even under the same πθ, what θ refers to differs from paper to paper. In Appendix I and in InstructGPT it is the weights, but Reflexion's Algorithm 1 sets θ={Ma,mem}, the actor model bundled with the memory of reflections. The paper writes that it parameterizes a policy "as an agent's memory encoding paired with a choice of LLM parameters" (§1), and states that it reinforces through verbal feedback without updating weights (abstract). The same goes for the reward. Reflexion's evaluator takes a trajectory and outputs a scalar reward rt=Me(τt) (§3), while InstructGPT's reward comes from a reward model learned from human comparisons. Who assigns the reward is the definition of "what counts as having done well", so this touches the evaluation problems of Chapter 17.

Imitation learning against reinforcement learning. Imitation learning trains by supervised learning to copy the actions in expert trajectories. It needs demonstrations and no reward. Reinforcement learning revises the policy with the rewards received from interacting with an environment. It needs a reward and an environment, and no demonstrations. The baselines in ReAct §4 show both.

Baseline Training method Data used Source
BUTLER (ALFWorld) Imitation learning 105 expert trajectories per task type ReAct §4
IL (WebShop) Imitation learning 1,012 human-annotated trajectories ReAct §4, Table 4
IL+RL (WebShop) Imitation learning, then reinforcement learning On top of the above, 10,587 training instructions ReAct §4, Table 4
ReAct (both tasks) No training (in-context learning) Example trajectories in the prompt (1 for WebShop, 2 for ALFWorld) ReAct §4

The account in the text of ReAct §4, arranged as a table. ReAct's Table 4 states that the IL and IL+RL figures come from the original WebShop paper (Yao et al. 2022).

Notice that what IL+RL added was not trajectories but "instructions". Reinforcement learning does not need records of people solving the task. You give it the task, let it solve it directly, and then give a reward. In this book's reading, InstructGPT has the same structure. Step 1, SFT, has the form of imitation learning, copying demonstrations, and step 3 is reinforcement learning that gives only prompts and revises with rewards. The policy-update algorithm that step 3 used is PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, Schulman et al. 2017). In this book you only need to know the name.

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

If you have worked with state-space models, you already know half of a POMDP. A latent state moves according to a transition distribution, and we see only the observation ot. That is the X, T and Ω of E. Add an action at that changes the transition and a reward rt, and you have a sequential decision problem. In the language of statistical decision theory, a policy is a decision rule, a function that sends observations to actions, and the value function is that rule's expected utility (with the sign flipped, its risk). Stop at estimating the state with a Kalman filter and you have a state-space model; go on to decide what to do with the estimated state and you have sequential decision-making.

There are places where the analogy fails. In the textbook problems of decision theory, the data come first and the decision is made once. In reinforcement learning, actions change the data you will see next, so you have to decide whether to take the gains where you know them or to explore where you do not. Rewards come late and rarely. Which of the earlier actions to credit for the final reward is the credit assignment problem.

5. The notation and words this book uses

The notation is in Appendix I, and the terms are in Appendix II. Let us fix just five words first.

  • thought. Intermediate reasoning written out in words before an action. It does not go out to the environment; it only accumulates in the context. Symbol zt.
  • action. Output that goes out to the environment: a tool call, a search, a final answer. Symbol at.
  • observation. What the environment returns in response to an action. Usually text. Symbol ot.
  • reasoning trace. Another name for thought. The survey in Chapter 2 treats its space Z as either latent plans or thoughts written out in words.
  • harness. Everything outside the model that runs the model: the execution environment, tool protocols, context management, orchestration, observability, verification and governance. It is the subject of Chapter 3.

Where the symbols overlap. This chapter has used some letters in two senses.

Letter Meaning in section 1 of this chapter Meaning in Appendix I (from Chapter 2 on)
xt The t-th token (capital X) The latent environment state space
T Sampling temperature The transition kernel
K The number of examples put in the prompt (GPT-3), the number of outputs ranked (InstructGPT) The upper limit on the number of episodes (k=1,…,K, Eq. 5). The (K2) in Chapter 16 keeps InstructGPT's meaning
Gt Return (section 4, textbook notation) (capital G) The agent tuple ⟨Z,M,πreason,πexec,U⟩, and the group size in GRPO
st State (section 4, textbook notation) Not used. Written with the observation ot and the history ht

Self-check

Answer each question in a line or two. The answers are collected in the folded solution at the bottom.

  1. What does "temperature 0" mean? You cannot put 0 into the formula, so why is it called that?
  2. Run the same prompt twice at temperature 1 and the answers can differ. How did the CoT-SC baseline in the ReAct paper use this property?
  3. Under what assumption does the autoregressive factorization p(x1,…,xn)=∏tp(xt∣x<t) hold as an approximation?
  4. What is the negative log-likelihood at a position where the next token was given probability 0.5? If that value kept coming up, what would the perplexity be?
  5. Can a document of 2,000 English words fit in a model with a 2,048-token context window? What do you estimate it with?
  6. What does the "shot" in few-shot count? How many times are GPT-3's weights updated in the few-shot setting?
  7. How do an episode and a trajectory differ? What is the unit counted in WebShop's success rate?
  8. How many steps make up one episode in step 3 of InstructGPT? Why is the discount factor not an issue?
  9. How does the training data of imitation learning differ from that of reinforcement learning? What data did WebShop's IL+RL add to IL?
  10. A reward of 1 comes only after the fourth action, and γ=0.9. What is the return G0 at the first time step? What does θ in Reflexion's policy πθ refer to?
SolutionSolution
  1. It is greedy decoding, which picks the token with the largest logit at every position. If there is a single largest logit, the limit as T→0 gives that token probability 1, hence the name. With a rule for ties it is deterministic, but it does not maximize the probability of the whole sentence.
  2. It sampled 21 CoT paths at temperature 0.7 and took the majority vote over the answers (ReAct §3.2).
  3. It is not an approximation; it is an identity that holds for any joint distribution. Approximation enters when the conditional distributions are modeled with a neural network and the past is cut to the length of the window.
  4. ln2≈0.69, and the perplexity is 2.
  5. No. Estimated at about 0.7 words per token (GPT-3 §3.9.2), it is about 2,900 tokens. You have to measure in tokens, not words, and the number of tokens depends on the tokenizer and the language.
  6. The number K of examples given as the condition at inference time. The weights are updated 0 times (§1).
  7. An episode is the event of one round; a trajectory is its record. WebShop's success rate is the share of episodes that met all the requirements (ReAct §4).
  8. One step. It is a bandit environment that ends with one answer and one reward for one prompt (InstructGPT §3.5). There is no future reward to discount, and the paper did not apply discounting either (Appendix C.4).
  9. Imitation learning needs demonstrations; reinforcement learning needs a reward and an environment. IL+RL used 10,587 training instructions on top of the 1,012 human trajectories (ReAct §4). What it added was instructions, not trajectories.
  10. The reward comes at time 3 (the fourth action, counting from t=0), so G0=0.93=0.729. Reflexion's θ is the bundle {Ma,mem} of the actor model and the memory of reflections (Algorithm 1).

Chapter 1 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 1. What Is an Agent? — A Practitioner's Map

The question this chapter answers: is every LLM with tools attached an agent? When should you not use an agent?

Core reading. Erik S. and Barry Zhang (Anthropic), "Building effective agents", Anthropic Engineering blog, December 19, 2024. This is a practical guide, not a paper. About 1,900 words of main text and about 2,700 with the two appendices (8 to 9 pages printed).

Links to the originals

Main reading — Original post (Anthropic Engineering)

Side papers — Weng, "LLM Powered Autonomous Agents" · OpenAI, "A practical guide to building agents" (PDF)

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §2.3, §2.4 and Table 5, §3.1.1, §5.2.1 · Harness survey §1, §2.1, §2.2 and Figure 1

One-paragraph summary. The post distills what Anthropic learned from working with dozens of teams across industries and from building its own agents. A workflow ties LLMs and tools together through code paths fixed in advance; an agent is an LLM that directs its own process and tool use; together they are called agentic systems. The prescription fits in one line. Look for the simplest solution first, and raise complexity only when results actually improve. The post holds that for many applications a single LLM call with retrieval and examples is enough. It then lines up, in order of complexity, the augmented LLM, five workflows (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer) and agents. It has no measurements. You can read the papers in later chapters by placing them in the cells of this map.
