Building intuition

Two definitions — who decides the next step

"Agent" can mean a fully autonomous system that runs on its own for a long time and uses many tools to get complex work done, or a more prescriptive implementation that follows a predefined workflow. The post calls both agentic systems, but draws one structural line.

Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths.

Agents, on the other hand, are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks.

The two sentences differ in one thing: who decides the next step. In a workflow, code the developer wrote decides, and the LLM is one of the functions that code calls. In an agent, the LLM decides, and the code steps back to running the tool the LLM picked and returning the result. Ask whether what happens next is written in an if statement in the code or in the model's output. One caveat: the question is about the structure of the steps. Inside a workflow, too, the model can make judgments such as classifying an input or splitting a task. If those judgments happen inside branches and steps the code opened in advance, it is a workflow; if the model also decides the kinds of steps and their order, it is an agent. The patterns that sit on the boundary come back in section 5 of "The paper in detail".

Tools are not the criterion. An LLM with retrieval and tools attached is only the basic building block (the augmented LLM). Call that block in an order set by code and you have a workflow; let it choose its own next call and you have an agent. The post's answer to "is every LLM with tools attached an agent?" is no.

The statements in "When (and when not) to use agents" and in the opening of "Building blocks, workflows, and agents", set out as a ladder. This is not a figure from the post; the editor drew the diagram.

The editor's bridge — parsimony in model selection

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

When we choose a regression model, we check whether out-of-sample prediction improves enough to justify each added explanatory variable. AIC and BIC put a penalty on every parameter, writing "complexity is not free" as a formula. The prescription of L21 has the same shape. One augmented-LLM call is the base model, and workflows and agents are extended models. Accept an extension only when evaluation shows an improvement; what plays the role of the penalty term is latency, cost, compounding errors and the difficulty of debugging.

For developers or database administrators, you can also put it as a batch job against an interactive analyst. A workflow is a nightly batch with fixed steps and branches, so the log tells you where it failed. An agent is an analyst who looks at the result and decides the next query on their own, strong on questions never seen before but not following the same path every time.

The analogy also breaks down. An information criterion states its penalty exactly as a count of parameters, but in agent design it is not even settled what to count as complexity (the number of calls, of branches, of actions available to choose from). And an agent's "improvement" is visible only through evaluations that depend on a sample of tasks and on the randomness of repeated runs. How to design that evaluation is the subject of "Rereading with a statistician's eye".

The post's own analogies are two. It likens evaluator-optimizer to the way a person polishes a piece of writing, and it says to invest as much effort in the agent-computer interface (ACI) as goes into human-computer interfaces (HCI) (Appendix 2).

The paper in detail

1. What is an agent? — definition and scope (What are agents?)

A short section. Beyond the two definitions, two things deserve attention. First, it draws the scope wide. Fully autonomous systems and prescriptive workflows are all agentic systems, so instead of "agent or not" you get a continuous axis: how many decisions are handed to the model. The rest of the post moves along this axis. Second, the criterion for the distinction is architecture ("an important architectural distinction"). With the same model and the same tools you can build either a workflow or an agent.

2. When to use agents and when not to (When (and when not) to use agents)

Read the two paragraphs sentence by sentence.

When building applications with LLMs, we recommend finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed. This might mean not building agentic systems at all.

The prescription opens with "This might mean not building agentic systems at all." A post that teaches you how to build agents starts with a sentence telling you not to build one.

Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and you should consider when this tradeoff makes sense.

What you pay is latency and cost; what you buy is task performance. The post says only "often" and gives no size. Anthropic's own numbers for the size appear in a post half a year later (Side papers).

When more complexity is warranted, workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks, whereas agents are the better option when flexibility and model-driven decision-making are needed at scale. For many applications, however, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough.

Three levels come out here. In summary:

Level When What you gain What you pay
Single LLM call (refined with retrieval and examples) For many applications this is enough Simplicity A ceiling on performance
Workflow When the task is well defined Predictability, consistency Latency and cost, a fixed path
Agent When flexibility and the model's judgment are needed at scale Flexibility Latency and cost, lower predictability

The editor put the two paragraphs of the post into a table. "A ceiling on performance" and "lower predictability" are the editor's reading of the flip side of the advantages the post names.

"Summary" says the same thing again about success: "It's about building the right system for your needs. Start with simple prompts, optimize them with comprehensive evaluation, and add multi-step agentic systems only when simpler solutions fall short." The last sentence of "Combining and customizing these patterns" says it too: "To repeat: you should consider adding complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes." The same recommendation appears three times, and the later two ("Summary" and "Combining") attach a condition of measurement ("comprehensive evaluation", "measuring performance", "demonstrably"). The first, in "When (and when not) to use agents", does not. So the real content of the recommendation can also be read as "do not raise complexity without evaluation". Read that way, the post lays down the evaluation problems of Chapter 17 and Chapter 18 already in Chapter 1.

On frameworks (cut from the presentation). Frameworks make low-level tasks easy, but their layers of abstraction hide the prompts and responses, which makes debugging harder, and they make it tempting to add unnecessary complexity. So the post says to use LLM APIs directly first, and, if you do use a framework, to understand the code underneath. The ground for this is the observation that incorrect assumptions about what is under the hood are a common source of customer error.

3. The building block — the augmented LLM (Building block: The augmented LLM)

The material of every pattern is a single LLM augmented with retrieval, tools and memory. The model writes its own search queries, chooses tools and decides what to keep. What to attend to is tailoring these capabilities to the use case and giving the LLM an easy, well-documented interface. As one route to implementation, the post names the Model Context Protocol, released 24 days before the post (November 25, 2024). We read MCP as a specification in Chapter 7.

The last sentence of the section is the key to reading the rest: "For the remainder of this post, we'll assume each LLM call has access to these augmented capabilities." Since every LLM call in a workflow can already use tools, one branch of a routing workflow or one worker may itself be a small agent that uses tools several times. The post does not take up this overlap. In the editor's reading, the distinction between workflow and agent is made for one layer of the control flow, not for the system as a whole. Also, planning, which Weng counts as one of the three components of an agent, is absent from L21's augmented LLM. Planning moves to the question of how the blocks are put together, that is, workflow or agent.

4. Five workflows (Workflow: Prompt chaining to Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer)

The post lays out the patterns it has seen in production, from the simplest up. Each pattern gets a definition, a "When to use this workflow" paragraph and examples. The post has a diagram for each pattern; here they are summarized in a table instead.

Pattern What it does When to use it (gist of the post's "When to use") The post's examples In this book
Prompt chaining Splits the task into steps and feeds each call's output into the next. Code gates in between When the task splits cleanly into fixed subtasks Writing marketing copy, then translating it. Checking an outline, then writing the document The SOPs of Chapter 13
Routing Classifies the input and sends it to a specialized follow-up task When there are distinct categories to handle separately and classification is accurate Customer queries into general, refund and technical support. Easy questions to a small model —
Parallelization Sectioning runs independent subtasks at once; voting runs the same task several times. Code aggregates the outputs When subtasks can be split for speed or several perspectives or attempts are needed Guardrails that split the response from screening inappropriate requests. Reviewing code for vulnerabilities with several prompts Self-consistency in Chapter 4
Orchestrator-workers A central LLM breaks the task down dynamically, hands it to workers and synthesizes the results When you cannot predict the subtasks needed Coding products that change several files. Search that gathers several sources Chapter 13
Evaluator-optimizer One call produces an answer and another evaluates it and gives feedback, in a loop When evaluation criteria are clear and iterative refinement gives measurable value Literary translation. Search in which the evaluator decides whether to search further Chapter 11

The editor summarized the five workflow sections of the post in a table. The links in the last column are this book's reading.

The gates in chaining. A gate is one of the "programmatic checks", a check written in code. At each intermediate step it confirms that the process is still on track. Chaining makes each call an easier task, paying latency to buy accuracy.

The rationale for routing. Without routing, a prompt tuned for one kind of input can hurt performance on other inputs. This is separation of concerns. The classification can be done by an LLM or by a traditional classification model. Even when an LLM makes the judgment, if the branches are written into the code in advance, it is a workflow.

The two variations of parallelization. A rule of thumb comes attached: for tasks with several considerations, calling a separate LLM for each consideration usually works better. Splitting guardrails from the core response, instead of handing both to one call, "tends to perform better", but no size is given. Voting resembles self-consistency in Chapter 4. But self-consistency samples several reasoning paths from the same prompt and picks by majority vote, while the post's voting examples balance false positives and false negatives with different prompts or different vote thresholds. This is a matter of tuning a decision rule's sensitivity and specificity through its threshold.

How orchestrator-workers differs from parallelization. The post itself admits the two are "topographically similar". The difference is flexibility. In parallelization the subtasks are defined in advance; in orchestrator-workers the orchestrator decides them after seeing the input. The example given is coding, where you cannot know how many files need changing, or how, before you see the task.

The two signs of good fit for evaluator-optimizer. That a response improves noticeably when a person states feedback in words, and that an LLM can give such feedback. Without the second, the generator may faithfully follow off-target feedback and get worse (this is the editor's inference, reading the two signs in reverse). It comes back in Chapter 11.

"Combining and customizing these patterns" adds that these blocks are not prescriptions but common patterns, to be combined, with performance measured and implementations iterated.

5. Agents (Agents)

The post writes that agents are emerging in production as four capabilities mature (understanding complex inputs, reasoning and planning, using tools reliably and recovering from errors), and sketches an agent's life. It starts with a command from a person or a discussion; once the task is clear, it plans and acts on its own, at each step gaining "ground truth" from the environment (the results of tool calls or code execution) to judge its progress. At checkpoints or when it hits a blocker, it waits for human feedback, and it ends when the task is done, though stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations are also common. The gist is these two sentences.

Agents can handle sophisticated tasks, but their implementation is often straightforward. They are typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop.

This is the thought-action-observation loop of ReAct, which we read in Chapter 6 (the post does not cite ReAct). Because the skeleton of the loop is simple, the post moves straight to saying that what counts is designing the toolset and its documentation clearly and thoughtfully, and hands off to Appendix 2. Its judgment is that success or failure is decided outside the loop, and the concept of the harness in Chapter 3 can be read as turning this into a system.

When to use them, what they cost. Use them for open-ended problems where you cannot predict the number of steps needed and cannot hard-code the path. You "must have some level of trust in its decision-making", and agents are suited to scaling tasks in "trusted environments." What happens when the documents an agent reads cannot be trusted is the question of Chapter 15. The price is higher cost and compounding errors, so the post recommends extensive testing in sandboxes and appropriate guardrails. Its examples are Anthropic's own SWE-bench coding agent and its computer use reference implementation.

Getting a feel for compounding errors in numbers. The post does not give sizes. The editor calculates the simplest model. If each step succeeds independently with probability p and a single failure fails the whole task, the probability that a k-step task succeeds is pk.

Step success rate p 5 steps 10 steps 20 steps 50 steps
0.99 0.951 0.904 0.818 0.605
0.95 0.774 0.599 0.358 0.077
0.90 0.590 0.349 0.122 0.005

Values the editor calculated as pk. A simple model that assumes independence between steps and "one failure ends it".

A real agent does better than this when it looks at the ground truth and fixes failures from earlier steps, and worse when an earlier error contaminates the next input. Still, the table shows that the longer the task, the more steeply the demand on per-step reliability rises. The pass^k metric in Chapter 17 looks at the same multiplicative structure from the side of repeated trials.

The editor's formalization — where the function that sets the path lives. Write the two definitions in the notation of Chapter 2. The post has no formulas.

In a workflow, a function g written by the developer decides the next call. It looks at the current step ℓt and the output yt that the step's LLM call just produced, and chooses the next step (ℓ and y are symbols the editor introduced and are not in the notation appendix. yt gets a different letter because it is the output of an LLM inside the workflow, not an observation ot from the environment).

ℓt+1=g(ℓt,yt)

For routing, yt is the classification result and g is a table that turns it into a branch number. The LLM's output affects the path, but the set of possible paths was enumerated in advance by whoever wrote g.

In an agent, the next action comes from the model's execution policy.

at~πexec(at∣ht,zt),at∈A=Atool∪{finish}

The developer sets the tool list Atool, but the model decides what to use, how many times, in what order and when to end with finish. The harness only sets outside limits such as a maximum number of iterations.

Written this way, two patterns in L21's own classification turn out to sit on the boundary. Orchestrator-workers is a workflow, yet its subtasks "aren't pre-defined". In the search example of evaluator-optimizer, the evaluator decides whether to search further, so the number of iterations is open. Read "predefined code paths" as "the skeleton of the calls is in the code", and the two statements fit together. In orchestrator-workers, the code holds the skeleton "decompose → execute → synthesize" and the model fills in only the number and content; an agent has no skeleton for the order in which to solve the task. An agent too has a skeleton — the loop that repeats "call → run the tool → return the result" and a cap on iterations — but that is the skeleton of the layer that wraps execution (the harness), not of the order in which the task is carried out. You can also read the two as joined by a continuous band rather than a line.

6. Appendix 1 — customer support and coding agents (Appendix 1: Agents in practice)

Appendix 1 names two applications that were especially promising in work with customers. Its first paragraph states what the two have in common. Agents add the most value for tasks that have these four features:

  • They need both conversation and action.
  • They have clear success criteria.
  • They allow feedback loops.
  • Meaningful human oversight can be attached.

A. Customer support. A chatbot interface with tools attached. It follows a conversation flow yet needs outside information and actions; tools that pull customer data and order history and actions such as refunds and ticket updates can be attached; and success can be measured through "user-defined resolutions." As evidence of viability, the post notes that several companies use pricing models that charge only for resolved cases, but it gives no company names or figures.

B. Coding agents. Solutions are verified by automated tests, the agent can iterate using test results as feedback, the problem space is structured and quality can be measured objectively. The post writes that its own implementation can solve real GitHub issues in SWE-bench Verified from the pull request description alone, but it gives no resolve rate. And it adds the caveat that whether a solution fits broader system requirements still needs human review.

In both cases, agents do well where the environment tells you "what success is". This observation pairs with the point in the previous section that agents gain "ground truth" from the environment.

7. Appendix 2 — prompt engineering for tools too (Appendix 2: Prompt engineering your tools)

This comes back in Chapter 7, so look only at the gist: give tool definitions as much prompt-engineering attention as the overall prompt. A file edit can be specified as a diff or as a rewrite of the whole file, and structured output as markdown or as JSON. To a person these are cosmetic differences that convert losslessly, but some formats are harder for an LLM. A diff requires knowing how many lines change before the new code is written, and code inside JSON requires escaping every newline and quote. So the post says to give the model enough tokens to "think", to keep the format close to what it would have seen naturally in text on the internet and to remove formatting overhead such as counting lines or escaping. As tips for the ACI it lists putting yourself in the model's shoes, writing parameter names and descriptions like a docstring for a junior developer, testing with many inputs to find mistakes and poka-yoke, changing the arguments so that mistakes are structurally harder.

The anecdote at the end goes like this. When building its SWE-bench agent, Anthropic spent more time optimizing its tools than the overall prompt. When the model made mistakes with relative paths after moving out of the root directory, the tool was changed to always require absolute paths, and the model used this method "flawlessly." How many times this was tested is not stated.

8. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

The post has no numbers to reanalyze. Instead we pick one claim and ask "what would we measure, and how, to test this empirically?" The post did not run such an experiment, and the aim is not to overturn its recommendations. The sample sizes are calculated from numbers the editor assumed. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18.

The recommendation of "finding the simplest solution possible" rests on two empirical claims: that there is a trade in which agentic systems pay latency and cost to buy performance, and that in many applications the trade does not pay off. The post gives the size of neither. A post from the same company half a year later (How we built our multi-agent research system) put token multiples of about 4× and 15× on the cost side ("In our data"), but it does not say how many cases were measured or how widely they scatter. The performance side will differ by task, so to test the recommendation you would have the same tasks solved by a single call, a workflow and an agent, and compare them in pairs.

Exercise — turning the advice to start simple into an experiment. Suppose your organization has a set of recurring tasks (for example, drafting replies to customer queries, answering questions about internal rules, small code fixes). You want to have the same tasks solved by (W) a workflow built from prompt chaining or routing and (A) an agent using the same tools, and compare success rate, cost and variance. (a) How would you set up treatment and control? What must be held the same? (b) Choose three or more outcome measures. Variance of what? (c) What is the sampling unit, and how many do you need? Estimate under the assumption of a 70% success rate for the workflow and 78% for the agent. (d) Name confounders that would contaminate the results. (e) What can this design still not answer?

SolutionSolution

(a) Treatment and control. The treatment is the control structure alone, and everything else is held fixed: the same model snapshot (record version and date), the same tools and tool descriptions, the same search index, the same token and time caps. Add one more control arm: (S) a single call with retrieval and examples. The recommendation itself says such a call "is usually enough", so leaving S out tests only half of it. If you design it as a within-task comparison in which every task is solved by all three arms, differences in difficulty cancel, and success becomes binary data paired by task. Randomize the order of runs.

(b) Outcome measures.

  • Success rate: a grader fixed before the runs (passing tests for code, a scoring rubric for documents).
  • Cost: tokens and money per task. The right tail is long, so look at the per-task log difference logcA−logcW and read the exponential of its mean as the geometric-mean cost multiple.
  • Latency: median and 90th percentile.
  • Two kinds of variance: how much success wobbles when the same task is run k times (the per-task success probability pi and pi(1−pi), or the share in which all k runs succeed), and the scatter of cost per task. The first measures the "predictability and consistency" that L21 names as the advantage of workflows.

(c) Sampling unit and size. The unit is the task, not the run. The paired comparison of success rates is the McNemar test, and the information comes only from tasks on which the two arms disagree. Let p01 be the share where W fails and A succeeds and p10 the reverse, and set ψ=p01+p10, δ=p01−p10. The normal approximation for the number of tasks needed at a two-sided significance level of 5% and power of 80% is as follows. zq is the q quantile of the standard normal distribution (z0.975≈1.96, z0.8≈0.84); change the significance level or the target power and all the numbers below change.

n≈(z0.975ψ+z0.8ψ−δ2)2δ2

For 70% against 78%, plugging in p01=0.15 and p10=0.07 gives about 268. Simulating the exact McNemar test gave a power of 0.64 at 200 tasks and 0.82 at 300. The more the two arms succeed and fail together on the same tasks, the fewer you need: with p01=0.10 and p10=0.02, about 145. Comparing on different task sets without pairing takes about 471 per arm.

When the effect is large, a small sample is enough. The multi-agent post cited above writes that early on, when one prompt change can raise the success rate from 30% to 80%, a few cases are enough to see a change, and that it started with about 20 queries. Assuming 30% against 80% on 20 tasks (both succeed 28%, only before 2%, only after 52%, both fail 18%), the power of the exact McNemar test is about 0.93, and the Wilson 95% intervals for 6 against 16 cases, [14.5%, 51.9%] and [58.4%, 91.9%], also separate. "Start small" and "you need hundreds to detect 8 percentage points" are both right, because the effect sizes differ.

Repeated runs are not independent. With k=5 runs per task and an intraclass correlation of ρ=0.6, the design effect is 1+(k−1)ρ=3.4, so 500 runs carry the information of about 147 independent samples. For the cost multiple, assuming a standard deviation of 0.8 for the log difference, (1.96×0.8/ln1.2)2≈74 tasks pin it down to within ±20%.

(d) Confounders.

  • The designer's effort. The workflow was built for this set of tasks, so split the tasks into development and evaluation sets and do not open the evaluation set until the design is finished.
  • Token budget. If the agent won but used five times the tokens, you cannot tell whether the effect is the structure's or the compute's. Table 5 of the revised AR survey also warns, of multi-agent comparisons, that "Reported comparisons are confounded by backbone and token budget" (the "Multiple specialized roles" row, Section 5.2.2). Holding that the same confound applies to single-agent comparisons is the editor's extension. Run both a condition with equal caps and a condition with no cap.
  • The grader. An LLM grader may favor longer answers, so hide which arm produced each output, and have people regrade a portion to measure agreement.
  • Model drift. Alternate the arms and record the time of each run.

(e) What it cannot answer. This experiment answers for "this task set, this model, this point in time". Flexibility when unfamiliar task types creep in (the post's "at scale") needs a separate design that deliberately shifts the task distribution, and maintenance costs that pile up over months are not captured. Whether a development process that "starts simple and steps up when needed" beats one that "goes to an agent from the start" can be answered only by an experiment with teams as the unit, and teams are hard to assign at random, so it easily becomes an observational study with team skill left as a confounder.

Takeaway. To test the advice to start simple, put the simple option (S) in the comparison too. Detecting a small effect takes hundreds of tasks, and the cheapest way to cut that number is to pair on the same tasks.

9. Limitations the paper states

This is not a paper, so it has no Limitations section. Here are the caveats and reservations scattered through it.

  • The trade. Agentic systems often pay latency and cost to buy performance, and whether the trade makes sense is for the builder to judge.
  • The price of autonomy. Agents cost more and errors can compound, so the post says to test in sandboxes and set guardrails.
  • The premise of trust. You must be able to trust the agent's judgment, and agents suit trusted environments. Untrusted environments are not discussed.
  • Human review. Even for coding agents, fit with broader requirements needs human review (Appendix 1).
  • Shelf life. The note at the top of the current page says the tooling has changed a great deal since December 2024 ("Which version").

There are also things the post does not state. Its basis is that "We've worked with dozens of teams", but it does not say how it judged "the most successful implementations". If you pull common features out of the successes, the simple implementations that failed stay invisible, so the post alone can also be read as leaving unsettled whether "the simple implementations succeeded" means "simple means success". Still, the prescription itself is "justify any added complexity with measurement", so it does not collapse under this weakness.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

The side papers for this chapter are Weng's post and the OpenAI guide. We add one later post from the same company and three papers, by pattern, that we will meet in later chapters.

LLM Powered Autonomous Agents (Weng 2023 · supporting material for this chapter). A personal blog post from June 23, 2023. It puts the LLM as the brain, supported by three components: planning (breaking into subgoals, reflection and refinement), memory (short-term as in-context learning, long-term as an external vector store) and tool use. Weng divides by what an agent is made of, and L21 by who sets the path. So Weng's map has no distinction between workflow and agent. HuggingGPT, which Weng gives as a tool-use case, has four fixed stages — task planning, model selection, task execution and response generation — and what it decides after seeing the input is the task list and the model assigned to each task, so in L21's terms it is close to an orchestrator-workers workflow (this book's reading). Of the three challenges at the end, the reliability of the natural language interface (much of the demo code goes into parsing model output) points to the same place as L21's Appendix 2.

A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI 2025). A 34-page PDF in which another company covers the same subject (no publication date given; the PDF was created on April 7, 2025). It uses the same word in a different sense. In this guide, "A workflow is a sequence of steps that must be executed to meet the user's goal," that is, the work itself, and an agent is a system that carries out that work on your behalf with a high degree of independence (p. 4). It says that applications that integrate LLMs but do not use them to control workflow execution are not agents, so L21's workflows would mostly fall outside this definition of an agent. Its prescriptions to maximize a single agent's capabilities first (p. 16) and that a deterministic solution may suffice (p. 6) overlap with L21's advice to find "the simplest solution possible". Only the guide takes up model choice. It says to set a baseline with the most capable model and then try swapping in smaller models (p. 8). L21's "simplicity" is the simplicity of the system's structure, not advice to start with a small model. In L21, model size appears only in the routing example (easy queries to a small model, hard ones to a large model). The manager pattern and the decentralized (handoff) pattern resemble, in shape, L21's orchestrator-workers and routing respectively. The text on p. 31 explains that the preceding example uses the math_homework_tripwire guardrail, but the guardrail in the code on pp. 28–30 is churn_detection_tripwire.

How we built our multi-agent research system (Hadfield et al. 2025). A post in which Anthropic, half a year later, says it built its Research feature on an "orchestrator-worker pattern". The workers are subagents that use tools several times on their own, so the "agent inside a block" of section 3 of "The paper in detail" actually appears, and there are numbers. A Claude Opus 4 lead agent with Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval (the number of items and the definition of the metric are not given); on BrowseComp, token usage by itself explained 80% of the variance in performance; and agents use about 4× more tokens than chat, multi-agent systems about 15×. It also adds the caveat that most coding tasks, with little to parallelize, are not yet a good fit.

Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book). It stretches evaluator-optimizer across trials. An Actor produces a trajectory, an Evaluator scores it (with exact match, heuristics or another LLM) and a Self-Reflection model turns that into a written reflection stored in memory (§3). L21's loop polishes one answer and leaves nothing behind when it ends. Table 4 of the revised AR survey writes this difference in symbols. Self-Refine, which corrects within one answer, is z; Reflexion, which carries its reflection over to the next attempt, is S.

MetaGPT (Hong et al. 2024 · Chapter 13 of this book). The problem its abstract aims at is "cascading hallucinations caused by naively chaining LLMs", that is, the failure of prompt chaining without gates. Its answer is to encode standard operating procedures (SOPs) into prompt sequences and to have roles such as product manager, architect and engineer exchange structured outputs through a shared message pool (publish–subscribe) and check intermediate results (§3). Roles and order are fixed by the SOP, so on L21's map it is close to chaining with gates, and in that it hands out work, it also overlaps with orchestrator-workers. §5.2.1 of the revised AR survey classifies it under Manually Crafted Pipelines.

SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024 · Chapter 14 of this book). A paper that measures, with ablations, the agent-computer interface (ACI) that L21's Appendix 2 discussed through anecdote and advice (arXiv, May 2024; L21 does not cite it). SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo solved 12.47% (286) of the 2,294 SWE-bench tasks and 18.00% (54) of the 300-task SWE-bench Lite (§5). In Table 3, which changes the interface one piece at a time on Lite, removing the edit command dropped 18.0 to 10.3, showing the whole file dropped it to 12.7, and iterative search, which pages through results one at a time (12.0), was lower even than having no search tool (15.7). It is a measurement showing that the advice to give tool design as much attention as the prompt shows up as differences of several percentage points with the same model.

Back to the surveys

Open the two surveys and you can see where L21's distinction sits in each.

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version — "what does it optimize?" and "who sets the path?"

§2.3 — the axes the survey rejected. The revised version names three classification axes it rejected: capability lists, architectural composition (single-agent / tool-based / multi-agent) and learning-paradigm-first. It rejected the composition axis because it is orthogonal to adaptation, leaving self-evolution no natural home, and the axis it chose is environmental dynamics × optimization target (z, S, θ). L21's axis (who holds the control flow) coincides exactly with neither. §2.1 writes that two systems with the same composition are separated when one searches z and the other updates θ. Put the other way round, L21's workflows and agents can fall into the same cell in the survey.

§3.1.1 and Figure 2 — the workflow is a layer, not an alternative. The revised version has Workflow Design as one branch of in-context planning: approaches that structure the planning process into stages such as perception, reasoning, execution and verification. And it writes:

This reactive workflow view unifies scripted stage design with online adaptation: the workflow provides interpretable structure and interfaces (what is done when), while the reactive loop supplies closed-loop grounding and error recovery (how it is done in context).

L21 sets workflows and agents up as things to choose between (two rungs of a ladder); the revised version sets them up as two layers of one system. It is the same picture as the reading in section 5 of "The paper in detail", where orchestrator-workers was reconciled as "skeleton in code, content from the model". The caption of Figure 2 groups workflow design with the families of the system state S, not z, and §2.2 warns that calling work that optimizes prompts, workflows and communication graphs without touching weights "post-training" conflates two regimes. The work of L21's developer, revising a workflow's code and prompts while watching evaluations, can be read in this frame as optimizing S by hand (the editor's interpretation).

§5.2.1 — pipelines crafted by people and pipelines built by LLMs. In-context collaboration among multiple agents is split into two lines. Manually Crafted Pipelines fix agent roles, execution order and communication rules before execution (MetaGPT); LLM-Driven Pipelines have an LLM orchestrator decompose a goal, route the pieces to specialized agents or tools and refine the workflow from intermediate feedback (Magentic-One and others). The survey judges that the former offer interpretability and simple execution but are rigid and hard to adapt to ambiguous tasks. Apart from its scope being multi-agent, this is where L21's distinction is most closely reproduced in the survey.

§2.4 and Table 5 — which mode, and when. A design guide the revised version added during review.

Constraint Reach for Why Watch out for
No training budget; one-off or low-volume tasks z Zero marginal setup cost; deployable against any frozen API model Brittle across domains; cost recurs on every call and grows with search width
Repeated tasks in a fixed domain; no GPU access S Cost amortizes across episodes; the state is inspectable, editable, and auditable Stale or wrong entries accumulate; an eviction and validation policy is required, not optional
Known task distribution; serving latency matters θ Moves cost from serving to training and yields the shortest traces Expensive; degrades off-distribution; cannot be patched without retraining
Long-horizon, feedback-rich deployment S first, then θ S gives fast, reversible adaptation and generates the trajectories that θ later needs Credit assignment over long horizons remains open (Section 8.2)
Multiple specialized roles S (prompt/topology) Far cheaper than multi-agent RL and currently competitive with it Reported comparisons are confounded by backbone and token budget (Section 5.2.2)
Auditability or regulatory review required S The artifact that changed is a readable object rather than a weight delta Persistent state creates its own audit problem: the write that caused a failure may be many episodes old

Table 5 of the revised AR survey (§2.4), reproduced from the original.

Table 5 asks "what to optimize", and L21 asks "how much control to hand to the model". Still, they overlap. Everything L21 covers lies within the two weight-frozen rows, z and S, and fine-tuning is never mentioned. The first rung of the ladder is the starting point on the same ground as the z row's "Zero marginal setup cost", and the cost that workflows and agents pay is written in the z row as "cost recurs on every call". The revised version itself stresses that the table gives "readings of a fast-moving and often confounded literature rather than settled results". Neither L21, an account of experience, nor the survey, which organizes 866 bibliography entries (§1.1), offers its design guidance as a measured law.

Notation table. Linking L21's terms to the survey's symbols. The correspondence is the editor's reading.

L21's term AR survey, revised version
A single call refined with retrieval and examples θ fixed, z mode (first row of Table 5)
A workflow's code paths and prompts Part of the system state S (§2.2, Figure 2 caption)
An agent's loop at chosen by πexec; "ReAct-style interleaving" in Table 3
Ground truth gained from the environment Observation ot, feedback Fk
Evaluator-optimizer (within one answer / across trials) Self-Refine z / Reflexion S (Table 4)
Orchestrator-workers §5.2.1 LLM-Driven Pipelines
Stopping conditions, sandboxes, guardrails Outside the formalism; the harness's job (Chapter 3)

Harness survey — inside one box of harness engineering

§1 — where it is cited. The survey cites L21 once (Anthropic, 2024a). It contrasts academic work, which studies planning, memory and tool use as separate capabilities, with production-oriented accounts, which describe tool contracts, retries, handoffs and permission boundaries, and gives L21 as one of the latter.

§2.1 — its place in the timeline. The timeline has three entries, "Reasoning–action (ReAct) loops (2022)", "Tool integration and multi-agent coordination (2023)" and "The harness turn (2025)", and no slot for 2024. L21 (December 2024) falls between the second and the third. The first entry notes that early systems ran on "a while loop, a prompt template, and a small tool-dispatch table", the same observation as L21's "their implementation is often straightforward." The third entry writes that by early 2026, practitioner reports increasingly attributed agent reliability to the design of the surrounding infrastructure as well as to model capability. L21's Appendix 2, which says to design tools and their documentation carefully, can be read as a paragraph that pointed to this shift ahead of time.

§2.2 and Figure 1 — three scopes. The survey places prompt engineering, context engineering and harness engineering as progressively broader scopes. The three pillars of Figure 1 (p. 1 of the PDF) are these.

Scope Heading in Figure 1 Boxes
Prompt engineering Single-call Optimization — Optimize the model input Instruction & Role, Example & Format, Prompt Iteration
Context engineering Multi-step Context Optimization — Optimize what the model sees Retrieval & Loading, Memory & State, Compression & Filtering
Harness engineering System-level Optimization — Optimize how the model runs Tools & Environment, Orchestration, Verification & Evaluation, Governance & Security

The text of Figure 1 of the Harness survey, set out as a table. In the figure, the description under the Example & Format box is printed exactly the same as the box above it: "Define task, persona and constraints".

L21's content spans all three pillars. The single call refined with retrieval and examples is prompt engineering and Retrieval & Loading; the memory of the augmented LLM is Memory & State; the ACI of Appendix 2 is Tools & Environment; sandboxes and guardrails are Governance & Security; and measuring performance and iterating is Verification & Evaluation. The workflow–agent distinction that gives the post its name goes into one box of the harness pillar, Orchestration ("Plan, act, verify, retry, or delegate"). §2.3, too, defines the Lifecycle/Orchestration (L) layer as the layer that organizes control flow, "from single-agent loops to multi-agent and issue-to-pull-request workflows." L21's distinction is a design choice within the L layer, one of seven layers.

§11.2 — the trade between capability and control. The more authority you give, the larger the control problem. Wider tool menus increase selection error and the prompt-injection surface, and permissive sandboxes enlarge the blast radius of misaligned actions. This can be read as the harness side restating the conditions L21 set for agents: "you must have some level of trust in its decision-making" and "trusted environments."

The AR survey has received only an "Accept as is" from its TMLR action editor; its OpenReview status is still "Decision pending" and there is no final published version. The Harness survey is a preprint that has not gone through conference or journal review. We do not cite the classifications of either survey as settled conclusions.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "An LLM with tools attached is an agent." In L21, an LLM with retrieval, tools and memory attached is only the basic building block (the augmented LLM). Call that block in an order set by code and it is a workflow; it is an agent only when the LLM directs its own process and tool use ("What are agents?"). The OpenAI guide also writes that applications that do not use an LLM to control workflow execution are not agents (p. 4).

Misreading 2. "Agents are a more advanced stage than workflows, so in the end you should go to agents." L21 divides the two by use, not by stage of development. For well-defined tasks a predictable and consistent workflow is better; when flexibility is needed at scale an agent is better; and for many applications a single call is enough ("When (and when not) to use agents").

Misreading 3. "Orchestrator-workers is another name for parallelization." The post itself admits the shapes are similar. The difference is who decides the subtasks, and when. Parallelization runs subtasks defined in advance at the same time; in orchestrator-workers, the orchestrator creates them on the spot after seeing the input ("Workflow: Orchestrator-workers").

Misreading 4. "The workflow of the OpenAI guide and the workflow of this post are the same word." L21's workflow is a system in which code sets the path; the OpenAI guide's workflow is a sequence of steps that reaches a goal, that is, the work itself (guide, p. 4). In the guide, agents are what "perform the same workflows" on the users' behalf. Quote the two together and the same sentence reads the opposite way.

Misreading 5. "The post's recommendations are results confirmed by experiment." The basis is experience from "dozens of teams" and the company's own implementations, and there are no measurements. The token multiples (about 4× and 15×) and the improvement (90.2%) that the same company published half a year later also come without task counts or scatter. The design guide of the revised AR survey (Table 5) also states that it is not a settled result. Read corporate documents as design guidance, not as generalized empirical findings.

Misreading 6. "To build an agent, you must first pick a framework." The post recommends using LLM APIs directly first, and, if you do use a framework, understanding the code underneath ("When and how to use frameworks"). The framework names in that section changed after publication, so take the logic, not the names.

Misreading 7. "Attach an evaluator-optimizer loop and the output always gets better." The evaluation criteria must be clear, a response must improve when a person gives feedback in words and an LLM must be able to give such feedback ("Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer"). Without these conditions the loop only adds cost. What the evaluator should be is taken up again in Chapter 11.

Discussion questions

  1. Put your own task on the ladder. Where would you place one recurring task from your work: single call, workflow or agent? Is your reason whether the task is well defined, whether you know the number of steps in advance or what you lose if it fails? How would you show that moving up one rung made things better?

  2. Parsimony in two directions. L21 says to build the structure up from the simple; the OpenAI guide says to bring the model down from the most capable. Do the two prescriptions conflict, or are they different axes you can use together? Just as forward selection and backward elimination do not always reach the same model, can the two directions arrive at different systems?

  3. What is a trusted environment? L21 writes that agents are suited to scaling tasks in trusted environments. Of the documents, emails and web pages an agent would read in your organization, how far does "trusted" extend? Think ahead to indirect prompt injection in Chapter 15 and the governance layer in Chapter 3.
