The pk table in section 5 of "The paper in detail", the sample sizes in the statistics section (normal-approximation formula), the power of the exact McNemar test (multinomial simulation, 10,000 to 20,000 runs), the Wilson intervals and the design effect were calculated by the editor in Python (numpy and scipy) from assumed values.

Chapter 2 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 2. The Agent's Head — Thinking, Acting, and Learning in One Frame

The question this chapter answers: how do we separate "thinking", "acting" and "learning" within one probability model?

Core reading. Tianxin Wei et al., "Agentic Reasoning for Large Language Models: A Survey", under review at TMLR (action editor "Accept as is" on September 15, 2026; OpenReview "Decision pending"). This book reads the revised post-review version posted on OpenReview (an anonymized review copy). Of its 146 pages, this chapter reads §1–§2.4, a little over 16 pages of the main text.

Links to the originals

Main paper — OpenReview, revised version (with public reviews) · arXiv abstract (the arXiv version — section and table numbers differ) · arXiv PDF (the arXiv version — section and table numbers differ) · Paper-list repository

Surveys — In this chapter the survey itself is the subject. The counterpart to compare it with is the Harness survey §1, §2.2–2.5 (PDF)

One-paragraph summary. The survey tries to set hundreds of papers on agents on top of one probability model. It writes the environment as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and the agent as a separate tuple. It writes the agent's policy as the product of a part that produces "thoughts" and a part that produces "actions", and the survey itself states that this factorization (Eq. 1) is only the chain rule, the content lying in three assumptions, A0, A1 and A2. It then divides every method by "what does it optimize?" Does it search the reasoning trace z on the spot (in-context reasoning), revise a system state S that persists across episodes (system-level optimization) or change the model parameters θ (post-training)? It crosses these three modes with three layers set by how dynamic the environment is (foundational, self-evolving, collective) to make a 3×3 grid, and summarizes in one table (Table 5) which mode to choose under which deployment conditions. The papers of Chapter 4 through Chapter 13 of this book all sit in some cell of this grid.

Presenter's guide

A 50-minute plan. The 10 minutes after the presentation are for discussion.

Time Content In the paper
0–5 min The question and the map: three layers, and LLM reasoning against agentic reasoning Figure 1, Table 1 (p. 2, p. 9)
5–10 min How this survey differs from its neighbors §2.1, Table 2 (pp. 9–11)
10–25 min Formalization: the two tuples, Eq. 1, assumptions A0, A1 and A2 First half of §2.2 (pp. 11–12)
25–33 min The three optimization targets z, S, θ and Eq. 5 Second half of §2.2 (pp. 12–14)
33–41 min The 3 layers × 3 modes grid and its boundaries §2.3, Table 3, Table 4 (pp. 14–16)
41–46 min The design guide: which mode under which conditions §2.4, Table 5 (p. 16)
46–50 min Head and body: the contrast with the Harness survey "Back to the surveys" in this chapter

Must read. §2.2 Preliminaries. It is the center of this chapter and runs a little over 4 pages. In the post-training paragraph, though, only the first two sentences, which say that θ is optimized to align the policy with long-horizon rewards, are required; Eqs. 3 and 4 and the details of GRPO go to the optional reading below. Next come Table 3 in §2.3 and Table 5 in §2.4. If you show only one figure, show Table 3, not Figure 1. Every paper in the later chapters comes back to one of its nine cells.

Optional reading. §1.1 Survey Methodology (p. 5, for those interested in statistics). The makeup of the 866 entries by year and by category is printed in numbers, and section 8 of this chapter practices on those numbers. The post-training paragraph of §2.2 (Eqs. 3 and 4, GRPO) is recommended for readers familiar with reinforcement learning or who want to know more. This book does not go deep into post-training.

What to cut from the presentation. The detailed subsections of §3–§5 are read in the later chapters (Chapter 5, Chapter 7, Chapter 8, Chapter 11, Chapter 12, Chapter 13), §6 in Chapter 14, §7 in Chapter 17 and Chapter 18, and §8–§9 in Chapter 20. Skip the guide to the organization on p. 6 and the table of contents on pp. 7–8.

Do not skip or combine this chapter. The "Back to the surveys" sections of Chapter 4 through Chapter 13 all presuppose this chapter's notation and grid. If your group skipped Chapter 1, introduce in the first 3 minutes only the distinction that "a workflow calls the model along fixed code paths, while an agent sets its own path". Point out that this distinction (who sets the path) and this chapter's (what is optimized) answer different questions.

When you quote the numbers. This survey has almost no performance figures. The numbers to carry over are about the makeup of the corpus (§1.1) and the row counts of tables, and those describe the literature the authors chose, not a sample of the whole field. Give the denominator, as in "of the 866 bibliography entries in this survey", and name the version (the revised version on OpenReview).

Building intuition

What to divide the "head" by

Chapter 1 looked at agents through control flow (who decides the next step), and Chapter 3 looks at the execution infrastructure that wraps the model. This chapter looks at what lies between: how the model thinks, acts and learns.

The survey uses a single question: "what does it optimize?" (§1). Agents that are "good at making plans" can search on the spot with prompts, revise a store of past plans or change their weights with reinforcement learning. Divide by a list of capabilities and the three go into one cell; divide by optimization target and they go into three. The survey chooses the latter.

The editor's bridge — from hidden Markov models to POMDPs

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

Think of a hidden Markov model (HMM). An unobserved state moves according to transition probabilities, and at each time an observation ot comes out according to emission probabilities. A state-space model (the Kalman filter) puts a continuous state on the same skeleton. The survey's environment tuple E=⟨X,O,A,T,Ω,R,γ⟩ is a POMDP: this skeleton plus actions at (the transition T also depends on the action), a reward R and a discount factor γ. Ω corresponds to the HMM's emission probability.

A joint distribution can always be written as p(z,a)=p(z)p(a∣z), and this identity assumes nothing. A model gains content when you posit conditional independences. The survey's Eq. 1 and assumptions A0–A2 stand in exactly this relation. In the language of path analysis, assumption A2 is a full-mediation assumption: all of the history ht's effect on the action at passes through the thought zt.

Sufficient statistics make a bridge too. Just as you lose nothing by holding only the sample mean when estimating the mean of a normal distribution, assumption A1 says you lose nothing in producing the next thought by holding only a summarized memory mt instead of the history ht. It is the same idea as carrying the posterior distribution of the hidden state (the belief state) instead of the history in a POMDP.

The analogy also breaks down. A sufficient statistic in statistics is defined with respect to information about a parameter, while A1 is defined with respect to the distribution of the next thought zt. And the memory mt is not something an analyst estimates but something a designer builds. The survey, too, writes of A1 that it "is an assumption made by systems, not a property of the setting" (§2.2).

Instead of analogies, the survey states in the first paragraph of §2.2 that it will unify the capabilities of the three layers "under a single control-theoretic framework."

The paper in detail

1. Scope and question — Figure 1 and Table 1 (§1, §2)

Figure 1. The figure on p. 2 has four tiers. The top band is a flow in which a User proposes (Propose) a Task, an Agentic Reasoning System solves it (Solve), and the experience generalizes (Generalize) to Future Tasks. The second band, under the title "LLM Reasoning → Agentic Reasoning (▷§Section 2)", draws three pairs of transitions. Paradigm goes from Static Input to Dynamic Context, Compute from Passive to Interactive and Learning from Pre-trained to Evolving. "And More …" is attached at the right end. The four panels below are the body: Foundational (Complex Planning · Tool Use · Web Search, §3), Self-evolving (Feedback Loop · Agentic Memory · Self-Evolving, §4), Collective Multi-agent (Role Assigning · Collaboration · Co-evolving, §5) and Applications and Benchmarks (§6 and §7; healthcare, finance, legal, education, robotics, science, software, gaming and web).

The caption says the three layers are arranged "in order of increasing environmental dynamics": stable environments (foundational), environments with feedback and accumulated state (self-evolving) and environments shared by several agents (collective). This is the survey's first axis.

Table 1 — LLM reasoning against agentic reasoning. The opening of §2 contrasts the two: traditional LLM reasoning raises performance by "scaling test-time computation," while agentic reasoning emphasizes "scaling test-time interaction."

Dimension LLM Reasoning Agentic Reasoning
Paradigm passive / static input interactive / dynamic context
Computation single pass / internal compute multi step / with feedback
Statefulness context window / no persistence external memory / state tracking
Learning offline pretraining / fixed knowledge continual improvement / self evolving
Goal Orientation prompt based / reactive explicit goal / planning

Table 1 of the paper. The original links each of the two pairs in a dimension with "↔".

Do not read "single pass" as meaning that the network's forward computation runs only once. Even while generating one answer, the forward computation repeats for every token (Chapter 0, section 1), and methods that scale test-time computation make exactly that generation longer. What the table separates is whether feedback from the environment arrives in the middle of generation. If the model takes the input and goes all the way to an answer with no response from outside, it is a single pass; if it emits an action, receives an observation and continues generating, it is multi-step (this gloss is the editor's reading).

The right-hand cell of the "Learning" row does not mean only retraining the weights. A good part of this survey's self-evolution leaves the weights alone and revises memory or tool libraries (four of the six representative families in Table 4 change S. Counting the 56 rows of Tables 9 and 10, the method tables of the self-evolving layer, gives S 25 rows, θ 20 and z 11 — section 5 of this chapter). The "learning" in this chapter's title has that broad sense too.

2. How it differs from neighboring surveys (§2.1, Table 2)

The survey compares itself with nine closely related surveys in one table, Table 2. The columns are Formalisation, Planning, Tool use, Retrieval/RAG, Feedback, Memory, MAS, MAS training, Applications, Benchmarks and, last, "Per-system optim. target". There are three marks: • (substantive treatment, a dedicated section or more), ◦ (partial treatment) and – (not covered). In the last column, only this survey gets a •; three of the nine (Lin et al. 2025c, Fang et al. 2025a, Gao et al. 2026) get ◦ and the other six get –. This column is where the authors claim the biggest difference. The caption states that "each mark is our reading of the survey's own section structure."

§2.1 treats the table carefully as the authors' own judgment. Of Ke et al. (2025a), it writes itself that since that survey already takes interactive settings as one of its axes, "it would be inaccurate to characterize this literature as confined to single-forward-pass reasoning", and it states the differences narrowly ("we state them rather than overclaiming"). Of Zhang et al. (2025f), whose coverage overlaps most, it concedes that it already treats parameter-level multi-agent training in depth. It also gives a reason for each of the three ◦ marks in the last column. For example, Gao et al. (2026) did tabulate a per-method "what evolves" matrix, but only over 24 representative methods, and its axes do not separate the reasoning trace from the surrounding context. The differences among the three surveys come back in "Side papers" in this chapter. Note, though, that the marks in Table 2 were assigned by the authors, who are a party to the comparison, not reassigned by a third party on the same criteria.

3. Two tuples — separating the environment from the agent (§2.2)

The first paragraph of §2.2 is headed "Formalizing Agentic Reasoning: A Latent-Space View." The problem is stated in one sentence: "Standard approaches often conflate the agent's context with the environment state." So the survey keeps the two syntactically separate and writes them as two tuples.

The environment.

E=⟨X,O,A,T,Ω,R,γ⟩

X is the latent state space the agent cannot observe, O the observation space (user queries, API returns and so on), A the external action space (tool invocations, final answers and so on), T and Ω the transition and observation kernels, R the reward and γ∈(0,1) the discount factor.

The agent.

G=⟨Z,M,πreason,πexec,U⟩

Z is the reasoning trace space. The survey's wording is "latent plans, optionally verbalized as chain-of-thought". M is the agent's internal memory/context space, πreason and πexec are the reasoning and execution policies, and U is the system-update operator that appears later in Eq. 5.

Why separate them. Z and M are design choices of the agent. The environment neither observes them nor is changed by them, so two agents with different Z or M face the same E. The survey's answer is that folding them into the environment tuple obscures the very distinction the survey is organized around.

Put in the language of experimental design, the environment is the subject population and the agent is the treatment. If you write the treatment down as an attribute of the subjects, it no longer makes sense to say you are comparing two treatments on the same population (this rendering is the editor's reading).

The two tuples and assumption A0 from §2.2 of the revised AR survey, redrawn. The editor drew the diagram.

History and memory. At time t the agent conditions on the history ht=(o≤t,z<t,a<t). The inequality signs give the order: observe ot, emit zt, emit at. The history can be summarized by an internal memory state mt∈M.

4. Eq. 1 and the three assumptions (§2.2)

The policy is factored like this.

πθ(zt,at∣ht)=πreason(zt∣ht)⏟Internal Thought·πexec(at∣ht,zt)⏟External Action(Eq. 1)

The very next sentence takes the weight off the equation itself.

Eq. 1 is an application of the chain rule and carries no content on its own; it holds for any joint distribution over (zt,at).

Eq. 1 is p(z,a∣h)=p(z∣h)p(a∣h,z), and it holds for any joint distribution. The survey says the content lies not in this equation but in the modeling commitments that accompany it, and that it states them explicitly because different families of systems accept different subsets of them.

Assumption Formula What the survey says
A0 Ordering and externality zt is generated before at and is not emitted to the environment: T and Ω are functions of at alone It is this assumption, not the factorization itself, that separates agentic reasoning from a single forward pass. Every system the survey covers assumes it
A1 Memory sufficiency πreason(zt∣ht)=πreason(zt∣mt), i.e., mt is a sufficient statistic for ht An assumption made by systems, not a property of the setting. The mechanisms of §4.2 try to make it hold approximately, and failures on long-horizon tasks are failures of A1
A2 Execution sufficiency πexec(at∣ht,zt)=πexec(at∣zt) Not generally assumed. It holds for plan-then-execute architectures (§3) and fails for interleaved architectures such as ReAct, where the action is conditioned on the raw observation as well

The three assumptions of §2.2, set out as a table.

A0's "T and Ω are functions of at alone" is the original sentence ("T and Ω are functions of at alone") carried over as it stands, but read literally it says that transitions and observations do not depend on the state either, which does not fit the POMDP defined just before. The transition still sets the next state from the current latent state and the action, and observations still come out according to the state. What the sentence rules out is a path by which, of what comes from the agent's side, the thought zt, rather than the action at, affects the environment directly. For example, if you write the transition as T(xt+1∣xt,at), zt does not enter the conditioning (the editor introduced this notation; the original has no equation of this form).

Rewrite the three assumptions in the language of conditional independence and you can see what is at stake.

  • A1 is zt⟂ht∣mt. Every system that summarizes an old conversation and puts the summary into the context relies on it. It breaks when the summary leaves out something the next thought needs. This is the subject of Chapter 12.
  • A2 is at⟂ht∣zt. All the information the action needs passes through the thought. As Chapter 6 shows, ReAct puts the object number from an observation into an action without passing it through a thought, so A2 does not hold.
  • A0 is not a conditional independence but an assumption of ordering and blocking. The thought does not reach the environment, and of what the agent emits, the environment sees only the action.

That A2 is "not generally assumed" shows what the formalization is good for. Under the same Eq. 1, structures that accept A2 part ways with those that do not, and the difference lines up with differences in design. The survey names ReAct as an example where A2 breaks, but for the side where it holds it writes only "plan-then-execute architectures (Section 3)". A good example of the side where it holds is ReWOO in §3.1.1 (which separates the observation module from the reasoning module). When A2 holds, observation text cannot reach an action without passing through the plan, which connects it to security as well (Chapter 15). Both connections are the editor's reading.

The last line of the formalization is maximizing the expected discounted return J(θ)=𝔼τ[∑t≥0γtrt].

This formalization and the review process

In the public reviews on the OpenReview forum, reviewer 8QGv (July 27, 2026) pointed out that Eq. 1 in the manuscript before revision was "the chain rule presented as a finding" and that the assumptions that would make it substantive ("a independent of h given z", "m_t is a sufficient statistic for h_t") were never stated, and reviewer sncv (August 6, 2026) wrote that the formalism in §2.2 was not mapped back onto §3–5, making it "decorative rather than load-bearing". The authors' response (September 2, 2026) says they identified Eq. 1 as the chain rule, stated the three assumptions and changed the optimization axis to the three modes z, S and θ. The action editor's decision is "Accept as is" (September 15, 2026). The revised version's list of contributions includes "stating the assumptions under which the think–act factorization is substantive" (§1, Contributions).

5. The three optimization targets — z, S, θ (§2.2)

§2.2 writes four paragraphs in this order: in-context reasoning, post-training, collective intelligence and self-evolution. Three of them produce the three modes. In-context reasoning optimizes z, post-training θ and self-evolution S. Collective intelligence is about the scope over which those three modes are applied to several agents. This chapter looks at the three modes in a row first and puts collective intelligence at the end.

In-context reasoning — search at inference time. The parameters θ are frozen. The agent searches over Z and picks a reasoning trajectory that maximizes a heuristic value function v^(ht,z). Inference is modeled as selecting a trajectory τ=(h0,z0,a0,h1,z1,a1,…). ReAct is greedy decoding over alternating thoughts z and actions a. Tree of Thoughts (ToT) and the MCTS (Monte Carlo tree search) family treat partial thoughts as nodes u. The survey says these families do not share an objective and states them separately rather than collapsing them into one expression. Below, v^ϕ is a value estimator that scores nodes or steps, and ϕ is that estimator's parameter (it may be an LLM prompted to give scores or a trained verifier).

ToT-style search with pruning keeps, under a node budget B, only the children whose value satisfies v^ϕ(u)≥κ, and returns the highest-scoring leaf (argmaxu∈LHv^ϕ(u)) among the set LH of leaves reachable at depth at most H. It is not a sum along the path. MCTS estimates values by repeating rollouts (the original says simulation) that play out from a node to the end. The sum of the results of the rollouts that passed through the branch from node u to child u′ is W(u,u′), the number of times that branch was passed is N(u,u′), and the next branch is chosen by an upper-confidence rule that adds to their mean Q(u,u′)=W(u,u′)/N(u,u′) a bonus that grows for less-visited branches. A path sum is the right object only for process-reward and step-verifier aggregation.

τ⋆∈argmaxτ∈ΓH∑tv^ϕ(ut)(Eq. 2)

ΓH is the set of feasible trajectories of depth at most H (a different symbol from the transition kernel T), and v^ϕ is a step-level verifier or process reward model. The survey explains that maximizing without constraint makes the sum unbounded, so the problem is well posed only when restricted to ΓH. In statistical terms, ToT is an optimization that picks a leaf by heuristic scores, and MCTS is sequential decision-making that picks while estimating values by repeated sampling. Chapter 5 looks at this in detail.

Post-training — policy optimization. θ is revised to fit long-horizon rewards rt such as correctness or safety. Examples are reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 and systems like Search-R1 that learn to search with reinforcement learning. PPO is the standard, and methods in the GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) family are widely used for reasoning tasks. GRPO standardizes the rewards of G outputs for the same prompt within the group to make the advantage A^i=(ri−μ)/(σ+δ) (Eq. 4). μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of those G rewards, and δ>0 is a small constant that keeps the division from blowing up when σ is 0. The advantage is a value that says how much better this output is than a baseline: if it is positive, the probability of producing that output goes up, and if negative, down. The key is what to take as the baseline. PPO separately trains a value network (a neural-network approximation of the value function in section 4 of Chapter 0) that predicts the expected return for each state, and uses it as the baseline. GRPO drops that value network and takes the mean of sibling answers to the same problem as the baseline. In statistical terms, it is a standard score within the group. In this book, post-training comes up in Chapter 7, Chapter 10 and Chapter 16.

Self-evolution — the meta-learning loop. Self-evolving agents optimize the system itself across episodes k=1,…,K. Let Sk be the evolvable system state (explicit memories, tool libraries, code and so on); the generic meta-update rule is this.

Sk+1←U(Sk,τk,Fk)(Eq. 5)

τk is the trajectory of episode k, and Fk is environmental feedback (rewards, execution errors). The survey divides self-evolution into three branches by the content of S.

Branch Content of S The survey's example
Verbal Evolution Textual reflections or guidelines Reflexion — synthesizes error logs into linguistic cues
Procedural Evolution A library of executable tools or skills Voyager — expands the action space A permanently with new skills
Structural Evolution The agent's source code or architecture itself AlphaEvolve — searches over code using an LLM as a mutation operator

The "Self-Evolving Agents" paragraph of §2.2, set out as a table.

To a reader familiar with statistics, Eq. 5 reads as the general form of sequential updating. Just as Bayesian updating makes a posterior from a prior and data, U makes the next state from the current state, a new trajectory and feedback. The difference is that S is not a probability distribution but a document or code a person can read (this comparison is the editor's).

Collective intelligence — widening the three modes to multiple agents. This paragraph does not add a fourth mode; it widens the scope over which the three modes apply. It extends the single-agent formulation to a decentralized partially observable setting (Dec-POMDP). Agent i's observation oti includes messages ct−1−i its peers produced at the previous time step, through a communication channel C. The survey stresses that communication is not merely signal transmission but an extension of reasoning: one agent's external action becomes a prompt that triggers another agent's internal reasoning. The three modes split here too. AutoGen and CAMEL are static role-playing with fixed policies; GPTSwarm and MaAS optimize the coordination structure with θ frozen; and agents trained with PPO or GRPO update θ. Chapter 13 picks up this paragraph.

Summed up as three modes. The three optimization variables that emerge this way are the axis that divides the whole survey. The survey stresses that this is not a binary in-context/post-training split.

Mode What changes What is fixed What persists Cost
z: in-context reasoning The reasoning trace (searched at inference time) θ Nothing. The same query issued twice receives the same treatment Paid per call
S: system-level optimization The system state of Eq. 5 — explicit memories, tool and skill libraries, prompts, communication topologies, the agent's own code θ Persists across episodes. The state can be inspected and edited Amortized over episodes
θ: post-training Model parameters (supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning) — Strategies are internalized into the forward pass Paid once at training and amortized at serving, at the price of reduced editability

The "Three Optimization Modes" paragraph of §2.2, set out as a table.

Why separate S from θ at all. The abstract, §1 and §2.2 repeat the claim. Research that optimizes prompts, workflows and communication graphs without touching weights is growing fast, and putting it under "post-training" because it has an optimization loop mixes two regimes with different cost profiles, deployment requirements and failure modes. The abstract's phrase is "otherwise misfiled as post-training."

Differences between versions arise here too. A Korean-language post that introduced the arXiv manuscript (AI Native Insight by Lee Seung-hyun, in Korean) presents the survey as "three layers × two optimization modes (in-context versus post-training)" (our translation) and explains Reflexion on the in-context side. In the revised version there are three modes, and Reflexion is classified as S (Table 4, Table 9). Keep this difference in mind when you look at material that covers the pre-review manuscript (including the two secondary videos for this chapter). The authors' affiliations also differ from the title of the same post: of 29 authors, 22 are at UIUC, with 2 at Meta, 2 at Amazon, 1 at Google DeepMind, 1 at UCSD and 1 at Yale (the revised PDF is anonymized, so these were counted from the affiliations on p. 1 of the arXiv manuscript).

6. The 3 layers × 3 modes grid (§2.3, Table 3, Table 4)

§2.3 begins "A taxonomy is a choice, not a discovery," and writes that a survey owes the reader the alternatives it rejected and the cost of the one it kept.

Three rejected alternatives.

  • Capability lists (planning / tool use / memory / …). Easy to look things up in, but they say nothing about how a capability is obtained. Prompted planning and planning learned by reinforcement learning sit side by side.
  • Architectural composition (single-agent / tool-based / multi-agent). Orthogonal to adaptation, so self-evolution has no place in it.
  • Learning-paradigm-first (prompting / SFT / reinforcement learning). It loses the environmental-dynamics dimension, so single-agent and multi-agent reinforcement learning fall into one bucket.

The chosen axis. "Environmental dynamics × optimization target". It separates where the difficulty comes from from what is spent to address it (z, S, θ).

Table 3 — the grid.

Environmental dynamics In-context (z) System-level (S) Post-training (θ)
Foundational (§3) Prompted and search-based planning; ReAct-style interleaving; tree/graph search (§3) Tool libraries and orchestration (§3.2.3); structured retrieval substrates (§3.3.2) RL/SFT for planning (§3.1.2), tool use (§3.2.2), and search (§3.3.3)
Self-evolving (§4) Within-episode self-critique and validator retries (§4.1) Reflective note stores, episodic and semantic memory, skill libraries (§4.2); tool and skill creation (§4.3.2) Parametric adaptation from feedback (§4.1); RL-controlled memory (§4.2.3). – tool creation: gap (i)
Collective (§5) Debate, role-play, and static pipelines (§5.2.1) Prompt, workflow, and topology optimization (§5.2.2); shared and distributed memory (§5) Multi-agent RL and preference-based co-training (§5.2.3). – shared memory: gap (ii)

Table 3 of the paper. "–" marks a family the grid predicts but for which no established literature was found.

Two gaps. Saying that "an absence of work is itself a finding", the survey marks two empty cells.

  • Gap (i), self-evolving × θ, tool creation. The authors are aware of no established line of work that updates θ to make a model better at "writing new tools". Tool "selection" is a different problem and is covered under foundational × θ (§3.2.2).
  • Gap (ii), collective × θ, shared memory. Multi-agent memory is optimized almost exclusively at the system level, and the authors are aware of no established work that post-trains agents to read and write a shared store (§5.3.2).

Boundary cases. The three layers are not disjoint. A planner that retrieves past plans is foundational in capability but self-evolving in mechanism. Tool creation is a foundational capability and also a permanent expansion of A, that is, Procedural Evolution. The survey does not force such intersections into one cell; it labels them as intersections.

Table 4 — the three vocabularies of self-evolution. The content of S (verbal, procedural, structural) is the primary cut, and mechanism (§4) and temporal scope (intra-test-time versus inter-test-time, the terminology of Gao et al. 2026) are cross-cuts.

Primary: content of S (§2.2) Cross-cut: mechanism (§4) Cross-cut: temporal scope (§5) Representative Optim.
Verbal Evolution Feedback (§4.1) intra-test-time Reflexion S
none (trace only) Feedback (§4.1) intra-test-time Self-Refine, SelfCheckGPT z
Verbal Evolution Memory (§4.2) inter-test-time MemGPT, A-Mem, Reasoning Bank S
Procedural Evolution Evolving capabilities (§4) inter-test-time Voyager, LATM, CREATOR S
Structural Evolution Multi-agent evolution (§5) inter-test-time AlphaEvolve, GPTSwarm, AFlow S
(orthogonal: not a form of S) Parametric adaptation (§4.1) inter-test-time AgentTuning, ReST, Memory-R1 θ

Table 4 of the paper. According to the caption, Reflexion's critique store persists across trials of one task, which makes it S under the primary cut but intra-test-time under the temporal one.

Set the first and second rows side by side and you can see where the three-mode distinction does its work. Self-Refine and Reflexion are both "generate–critique–revise" loops. Self-Refine revises only the trace and leaves nothing behind, so it is z; Reflexion writes its critiques to notes that persist across episodes, so it is S (§4.1.1). §3.1.2 applies the same distinction to Reflexion and Reflect-then-Plan (which refines only a belief state within an episode, z) and writes: "both are 'reflection', and only one of them accumulates".

7. The design guide — which mode under which conditions (§2.4, Table 5)

§2.4 opens by saying that the optimization axis is useful only if it answers a question a system designer actually faces, and gives in one table, for each deployment constraint, the mode the current evidence favors and what to watch for. It also attaches the caveat that these are readings of a fast-moving and often confounded literature rather than settled results.

Constraint Reach for Why Watch out for
No training budget; one-off or low-volume tasks z Zero marginal setup cost; deployable against any frozen API model Brittle across domains; cost recurs on every call and grows with search width
Repeated tasks in a fixed domain; no GPU access S Cost amortizes across episodes; the state is inspectable, editable, and auditable Stale or wrong entries accumulate; an eviction and validation policy is required, not optional
Known task distribution; serving latency matters θ Moves cost from serving to training and yields the shortest traces Expensive; degrades off-distribution; cannot be patched without retraining
Long-horizon, feedback-rich deployment S first, then θ S gives fast, reversible adaptation and generates the trajectories that θ later needs Credit assignment over long horizons remains open (Section 8.2)
Multiple specialized roles S (prompt/topology) Far cheaper than multi-agent RL and currently competitive with it Reported comparisons are confounded by backbone and token budget (Section 5.2.2)
Auditability or regulatory review required S The artifact that changed is a readable object rather than a weight delta Persistent state creates its own audit problem: the write that caused a failure may be many episodes old

Table 5 of the paper.

Four of the six rows recommend S. The warning in the last row (the write that caused a failure may be many episodes old) comes back in Chapter 19, when we trace the cause of a failure backward, and in Chapter 20, when wiki pages written in advance go stale. A concrete case of the second row's "an eviction and validation policy is required" is Chapter 12.

The "Why" column is mostly the logic of cost and operations, with no performance comparisons in numbers. Reading this table as a checklist for design judgment rather than as a prescription confirmed by experiment fits the survey's own caveat better.

8. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

The calculations use only the numbers printed in the survey and row counts the editor made from the survey's tables. The survey did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18.

The corpus in §1.1 is printed in numbers. The survey states that it was not built from a single systematic query, so it reports the process actually followed rather than reconstructing a PRISMA-style protocol after the fact. It monitored five arXiv listings, the ACL Anthology, OpenReview and the proceedings of major conferences, closed at a primary cutoff in January 2026, and repeated citation-chaining until new candidates were mostly already in the set. The inclusion criteria are work that treats reasoning as unfolding through interaction and reports a method or an evaluation artifact; the exclusion criteria are single-forward-pass prompting without external interaction, pure long-context modeling and position papers.

Year (earliest public version) Entries Category (first substantive appearance) Entries
2022 or earlier 36 Planning 111
2023 124 Tool use 70
2024 264 Agentic search 21
2025 386 Feedback 27
2026 56 Memory and self-evolution 61
Multi-agent 118
Applications 262
Benchmarks 145
Open problems 30
Cited only in the abstract, introduction or positioning of §2 21
Total 866 Total 866

The numbers in "Corpus profile" of §1.1, set out as a table. The editor added up the totals to check them.

Both columns add up to 866. Applications and benchmarks together come to 407 entries, 47.0% of the total. This is the number the survey calls "roughly half", and the survey reads it as reflecting how quickly the evaluation layer is growing rather than as a bias in its search.

The year column grows steeply: 2.13 times from 2023 to 2024 and 1.46 times from 2024 to 2025. The 56 entries for 2026 combine the primary cutoff (January 2026) with a small number of later additions, so they are left out of this comparison. One sentence in the definition of years is open to more than one reading. It says that for entries with no peer-reviewed venue the year was taken from the arXiv identifier, and that "the four entries that do carry one keep their venue's year." Yet the bibliography shows several entries with venues, such as CoT (NeurIPS 2022) and Toolformer and Reflexion (NeurIPS 2023). What "the four entries" refers to cannot be settled from the text alone.

The relation between the inclusion criteria and the 866 entries is also worth noting. The 866 are the whole bibliography. By the exclusion criteria, prompting without external interaction is not under review, yet CoT, its leading example, is cited in §1 and §3.2.1 and is among the 866. This chapter reads the 866 as "the citation list", not as "the works under review that passed the inclusion criteria".

Exercise 1 — count the "optimization target" column of the method tables. The survey's list of contributions says "the framing is used: every method table records which of the three a system optimizes." Counting the last column of Tables 6–11 gives the following (the editor counted row by row from the PDF text).

Table Topic Layer z S θ Rows
Table 6 Planning Foundational 14 5 4 23
Table 7 Tool use Foundational 5 6 6 17
Table 8 Agentic search Foundational 3 4 10 17
Table 9 Feedback Self-evolving 11 3 12 26
Table 10 Memory Self-evolving 0 22 8 30
Table 11 Multi-agent collaboration Collective 5 12 12 29
Total 38 52 52 142

(a) Combine by layer into a 3×3 contingency table and find the shares of the three modes in each layer. (b) Run a chi-square test of the null hypothesis "layer and mode are independent". Run the same test at the level of tables (6×3). Why do the two results differ? (c) Some systems, such as ReAct (Tables 7, 8 and 9), appear in more than one table. Does removing duplicates within the same layer change the conclusion? (d) What is the p value of this test a statement about?

SolutionSolution

(a) The layer totals are foundational (22,15,20), self-evolving (11,25,20) and collective (5,12,12). As shares, foundational is z 38.6% · S 26.3% · θ 35.1%, self-evolving 19.6% · 44.6% · 35.7% and collective 17.2% · 41.4% · 41.4%. In the foundational layer z is the most common, and in the two layers above it S grows. This reads as pointing in the direction that the more the environment moves, the more persistent state gets used (this reading is the editor's).

(b) The Pearson chi-square for the 3×3 table is χ2=8.07, 4 degrees of freedom, p≈0.089. At the level of tables (6×3), χ2=46.1, 10 degrees of freedom, p≈1.4×10−6 (some cells have expected counts below 5, so the approximation is rough; the smallest expected count is about 4.5). The two tests differ from the null hypothesis on. The 3×3 tests "layer and mode are independent", and the 6×3 tests "table (subtopic) and mode are independent". The reason only the 6×3 rejects strongly is heterogeneity within a layer. In the self-evolving layer, feedback (Table 9) has z 11 · S 3 and memory (Table 10) z 0 · S 22, exact opposites, and a 2×3 test of these two tables alone gives χ2≈26.1, p≈2×10−6. Combine them into a layer and this contrast cancels out.

(c) Five rows overlap within the same layer (ReAct, Toolformer, Tool-Planner and ReSearch in the foundational layer, MemGPT in the self-evolving layer). Removing them leaves 137 rows, with χ2=7.86, p≈0.097, almost unchanged. Removing duplicates across layers as well (ReAct, Reflexion, WebGPT) leaves 134 distinct systems. The seven systems that appear in more than one table are all recorded with the same optimization target in every table. The consistency of the record is confirmed.

(d) These 142 rows are not a probability sample but a list the authors chose as "representative". The p value is not evidence about association in the field as a whole; it only describes how hard it would be for random assignment to explain the differences in makeup by layer in the chosen list. To say something about the field, you would need data assigning an optimization target to all 866 entries (or to a random sample). The survey says its repository will include the paper collection (§1.1, Artifact), so once it is released this can be tried.

Takeaway. Test results change with the level at which you combine a contingency table. Changing the level of combination changes the null hypothesis too, so it is less that the conclusion to one question flipped than that a different question got a different answer. Remember separately, though, that combining into layers lets contrasts within a layer cancel and disappear from view. And a test on a curated list is a statement about the choices of whoever made the list.

Exercise 2 — can you divide the rows of a table by the number of corpus entries? Set the number of corpus entries by category beside the number of rows in the method tables: planning 23/111, tools 17/70, search 17/21, feedback 26/27, memory 30/61, multi-agent 29/118. (a) Find each ratio. (b) Can you say "96% of feedback papers made it into the table"? Answer by comparing how the numerator and denominator are defined.

SolutionSolution

(a) Planning 20.7%, tools 24.3%, search 81.0%, feedback 96.3%, memory 49.2%, multi-agent 24.6%.

(b) You cannot. The denominator (the category counts of §1.1) counts each work only once, "at its first substantive appearance," while the numerator (the rows of a table) also includes works whose first appearance is in another category. ReAct in Table 9 (feedback) is already cited in §1 and also appears in Tables 7 and 8. WebGPT, MemGPT and Voyager are also works that probably appeared first elsewhere. The numerator is not a subset of the denominator, so this ratio is not an "inclusion rate", and for the same reason the 81% for search is not to be read at face value either.

Takeaway. Even under the same category names, you cannot divide if the counting rules differ. Before you form a ratio, check first whether the numerator is a subset of the denominator.

9. Limitations the paper states

  • Known coverage gaps (§1.1). It names four: non-English literature; industrial systems without public write-ups; reinforcement-learning infrastructure and systems papers (cited only where they change what an agent can do); and the game-playing and negotiation literature.
  • The scope boundary of agentic search (§1.1). Much of the RAG literature lies outside the inclusion criteria. When you read Chapter 8, remember that this survey does not cover RAG as a whole.
  • The cost of the taxonomy (§2.3). Methods that adapt structure and parameters together must be assigned to the dominant mechanism, and reasonable people can disagree about that judgment. The survey writes that this is a real limitation of its axis, one a capability-list taxonomy does not have.
  • The status of the design guide (§2.4). It states that Table 5 is a reading of a fast-moving and often confounded literature, not a settled result.
  • Anonymized review copy. The address of the companion repository (paper collection, Tables 2–5, benchmark inventory, citation-audit log) is omitted for anonymous review and is to be included in the camera-ready version (§1.1, footnote 1). The authors' paper-list repository, to which p. 1 of the arXiv version points, is the likely candidate, but as of October 5, 2026 it holds only lists of papers and benchmarks and one PDF of presentation slides, not Tables 2–5 or the citation-audit log.

If we add one limitation the paper does not state, it is that assumptions A0–A2 are not used again outside §2.2. The names "A0", "A1" and "A2" could not be found outside their definitions in §2.2 (the editor searched the PDF text). The body of §4.2 does not discuss long-horizon failures under the name of A1 either. By contrast, the optimization targets z, S and θ are recorded in every row of Tables 6–11. It can also be read that in this survey, the formalization that bears load is the three optimization targets rather than the three assumptions. Discussion question 1 takes this up.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

The list first proposed in the study group has no side papers for this chapter. Instead, we contrast three neighboring surveys that this survey compares itself with in Table 2, and three core papers from other chapters of this book that each illustrate one of the three modes. All descriptions are limited to what this survey writes about that literature.

A Survey of Frontiers in LLM Reasoning (Ke et al. 2025). The survey gives this as an example of a survey of LLM reasoning that reaches into interactive settings. It is organized as the product of reasoning regime (inference scaling versus learning to reason) and system architecture (standalone LLM / single-agent / multi-agent). The difference is the axis. Ke et al. divide by architecture, this survey by optimization target. The survey notes that Ke et al. has no memory section, and explains separately that not covering benchmarks is a scope decision Ke et al. themselves state (§2.1).

The Landscape of Agentic Reinforcement Learning for LLMs (Zhang et al. 2025). The work the survey admits overlaps most in coverage. It divides by the product of a capability axis and a task-domain axis, and as its formalization sets the single-step MDP of conventional LLM reinforcement learning against the POMDP of agentic reinforcement learning. Its per-system tables record the backbone model, the reward type and the reinforcement-learning algorithm. This survey records "what does it optimize?" in the same place. That is why the two part ways in the last column of Table 2.

LLM-based Agentic Reasoning Frameworks: A Survey from Methods to Scenarios (Zhao et al. 2025). Another work the survey counts as close. It puts forward a unified formal description of the reasoning process and divides into single-agent / tool-based / multi-agent. There are two differences. Its axis is architectural composition, so two systems of the same composition go into the same cell even if one searches z and the other changes θ. And it restricts itself to training-free frameworks, leaving SFT and reinforcement learning out of its classification. In terms of this survey's grid, the whole θ column is missing.

Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al. 2022 · Chapter 4 of this book) — the prototype of z. Defining Z, the survey writes "optionally verbalized as chain-of-thought". At the same time it distinguishes CoT from agentic reasoning: CoT assumes a static context and a short horizon (§1) and works in a closed world confined to the model's internal knowledge (§3.2.1). CoT itself does not appear as a row in Tables 6–11. In this book's reading, CoT is a z whose only external action is the final answer, the closest neighbor of the "single forward pass" that A0 separates off.

Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book) — the representative of S. The survey gives Reflexion as the first example of Verbal Evolution (§2.2). In Table 6 and in Table 9 (self-reflective, I-a) alike, its optimization target is S, contrasted with Self-Refine (z), the same generate–critique–revise loop (§4.1.1). Compare this with the post that introduced the pre-review manuscript and explained Reflexion on the in-context side, and you can see where the three-mode distinction does its work.

Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023 · Chapter 7 of this book) — the representative of θ. The survey lists Toolformer in Table 7 (training method "Self-sup. + SFT") and Table 8, as θ in both. §3.2.2 explains that it generates, verifies and retains useful API calls within unlabeled text and fine-tunes on the filtered data. Among "agents that use tools", ReAct (first row of Table 7, z) and Toolformer sit in different columns. The "same cell by capability list, different cells by optimization target" of section 6 is these two rows.

Back to the surveys

Since the survey itself is the subject of this chapter, this section serves as a place to contrast it with the Harness survey of Chapter 3 (H for short; this survey is AR). AR looks at the agent's head: how the model plans, uses tools and improves through feedback and memory. H looks at the body and the fence: the execution environment, tool contracts, context management, orchestration, observability, verification and governance outside the model.

What is taken as the unit of analysis

The first sentence of H's abstract says that reliable task execution depends on the infrastructure that surrounds the underlying model, the harness, as well as on the model itself. §2.4 defines the harness as "the engineered wrapper that turns model calls into bounded, stateful, tool-mediated task execution", and makes clear that the unit of analysis is "not the foundation model or prompt alone."

Set the scope statements of the two surveys side by side.

Agentic Reasoning survey (§1.1) Harness survey (§1, §2.4–2.5)
What it collects Method and evaluation work on reasoning that unfolds through interaction. 866 bibliography entries More than 170 open-source projects that provide reusable harness mechanisms
What it excludes Single-forward-pass prompting without external interaction, pure long-context modeling, position papers Foundation-model training and standalone prompting methods
Post-training Included as one of the three modes (θ) Foundation-model training is out of scope, except where it directly determines a harness interface or mechanism (§1); §4.3 has a section on tool-augmented training
Collection procedure States that it does not reconstruct a PRISMA-style protocol after the fact States that it followed the reporting discipline of systematic reviews (Page et al. 2021) and describes four collection streams and a coding protocol
Organizing axis Environmental dynamics (3 layers) × optimization target (3 modes) Seven layers, ETCLOVG (§2.3)

The editor set the scope statements of the two surveys side by side.

Both exclude standalone prompting techniques, and they part ways on post-training. The side that looks at the head takes research that changes weights as one axis; the side that looks at the body puts foundation-model training out of scope, keeping only training that meshes directly with harness mechanisms.

Overlap seen through the tables of contents

Put the tables of contents against each other and the overlaps are tools (AR §3.2 against H §4), memory (AR §4.2 against H §5.4–5.5), multi-agent (AR §5 against H §6.3) and evaluation (AR §7 against H §8). Even on the same topic they ask different things. Take tools: AR asks how tool use is learned, H how tools are connected. For memory, this book reads the classification from AR (Table 10) and the implementation layers from H (Chapter 12). The places with no overlap at all tell you more. The execution environment and sandbox (H §3) and observability (H §7) have no section in AR, and the distinction of optimization modes, assumptions A0–A2 and the search objectives are absent from H.

Laying the two maps over each other

In the editor's reading, the two surveys meet at S. The examples of S the survey gives — explicit memories, tool and skill libraries, prompts, communication topologies and the agent's own code — become, carried over to the layers of the Harness survey, objects of context (C), tools (T) and orchestration (L) respectively. What is "learned state" on the head side becomes "infrastructure to design and operate" on the body side. The warning in the last row of Table 5 (persistent state creates its own audit problem) can also be read as saying that this state is, on the harness side, an object of observability (O) and governance (G). Neither survey writes this correspondence out directly. Laying S over each layer of ETCLOVG in Chapter 3 makes good review.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "Eq. 1 is this survey's key finding." The survey itself writes that Eq. 1 is an application of the chain rule and carries no content on its own (§2.2). It holds for any joint distribution. The content lies in assumptions A0–A2 and in the three modes, set by what is optimized.

Misreading 2. "In an agent, the action is decided by looking only at the thought (A2)." A2 is not generally assumed (§2.2). It holds only for plan-then-execute architectures, and breaks in interleaved architectures such as ReAct, where the action is conditioned on the raw observation as well. What the survey states is "assumed by every system we survey" is A0, and judging from the phrase "Unlike A0 and A1" in the A2 entry, it places A1 on the generally assumed side too. A2 is the only one not generally assumed.

Misreading 3. "If the weights do not change, it is all prompting, that is, in-context reasoning." Correcting this is the point of the revised version. Revising memory, tool libraries, prompts or communication topologies across episodes with the weights frozen is the S mode (§2.2, Three Optimization Modes). Whether anything persists is what separates z from S. Self-Refine is z, Reflexion S (Table 4).

Misreading 4. "If there is an optimization loop, it is post-training." This is the classification the survey opposes most strongly. It writes that putting research that optimizes prompts or communication graphs under "post-training" conflates regimes with entirely different cost profiles, deployment requirements and failure modes (abstract, §1, §2.2). Conversely, Self-RAG, often introduced as a prompting technique, fine-tunes its generator on a corpus with reflection tokens, so it is θ (§3.3.3, Table 8).

Misreading 5. "The 866 entries are a sample of the field, and since applications and benchmarks are half, so is the field." The survey itself states that it did not dress up a PRISMA-style protocol after the fact (§1.1). The 866 are the whole bibliography cited in the body, and the inclusion criteria put much of the RAG literature out of scope. This is the makeup of this survey's citations, not a sample of the whole field.

Misreading 6. "Table 5 is a prescription verified by experiment." The survey writes that Table 5 is a reading of a fast-moving and often confounded literature, not a settled result (§2.4). It has no performance figures, and the multiple-roles row directly warns that reported comparisons are confounded.

Discussion questions

  1. Is the formalization decoration, or does it bear load? Eq. 1 is the chain rule, and assumptions A0–A2 are not used again by name outside §2.2. By contrast, z, S and θ are recorded in every method table. If you were a reviewer, how would you ask the authors to show that this formalization bears load? Design an experiment that compares a structure where A2 holds with one where it breaks, on the same model and the same task, and measures how much the action wobbles when a sentence irrelevant to the observation is inserted (treatment, outcome measures, sampling unit, confounders). We use it again in Chapter 6 and Chapter 15.

  2. To whom is this classification useful? If you brought an agent into your work, which row of Table 5 would apply? Put the recommendation of S when "Auditability or regulatory review required" together with the warning "the write that caused a failure may be many episodes old". How would you manage the records that pile up in S? This connects to wiki maintenance in Chapter 20.

  3. Where is the boundary between head and body? The same memory store is the optimized state S in this survey and an object of implementation in the context layer (C) in the Harness survey. How does the answer to "what to fix when performance gets worse" change with the point of view? Check your answer in Chapter 3 and Chapter 19.

Chapter 3 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 3. The Agent's Body and Fence — The Harness

The question this chapter answers: why do performance and safety differ from system to system when the model is the same?

Core reading. Junjie Li et al., "Agent Harness Engineering: A Survey", 2026, unpublished preprint (uploaded directly to the OpenReview archive; it has not been through conference or journal review). 51 pages of main text, 71 with the references and appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper — Project page · PDF · OpenReview · Copy of the survey PDF (Hugging Face) · Repository (awesome-agent-harness)

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §1.1, §2.2–2.4, §8.7, §9 · Harness survey (the subject of this chapter) §1–2, §10–11

One-paragraph summary. As agents came to work for long stretches in repositories, browsers and terminals, the success of a task stopped being decided by the model's responses alone. This survey calls the operational infrastructure around the model a harness and sets it up as an engineering object in its own right: the infrastructure that feeds in context, calls tools through stable interfaces, preserves state, recovers from failures, verifies results and keeps the agent inside its permissions. The framework is a seven-layer taxonomy, ETCLOVG (Execution, Tooling, Context, Lifecycle/Orchestration, Observability, Verification, Governance). The authors place more than 170 public repositories on these layers to draw a map, then gather three tradeoffs between layers. It is a map, not an experimental paper. The evidence that harnesses change performance comes from other people's reports, and the authors themselves say that this evidence is concentrated on coding agents.

Presenter's guide

A 50-minute plan. The 10 minutes after the presentation are for discussion.

Time Content In the paper
0–5 min The question and the intuition: same model, different scores §1, second paragraph
5–12 min The timeline and the three kinds of engineering: from a single loop to infrastructure §2.1 and Figure 2, §2.2 and Figure 1
12–27 min The seven ETCLOVG layers and their boundaries §2.3, Figure 3, Figure 4
27–33 min How the corpus was collected and what it cannot say §2.4–2.9, Appendix A Table S1
33–41 min Tradeoffs between layers: the trilemma, capability against control, coupling §10, §11
41–45 min Side papers: one company's harness (S21) and the interface ablation (SWE-agent Table 3) "Side papers" in this chapter
45–50 min Back to the surveys: set against the revised AR survey — head and body "Back to the surveys" in this chapter

Must read. All of §1 (under three pages), §2.1–2.3, §10–11 (two pages together) and §13 (one paragraph). If you show only one figure, make it Figure 3. Four layers are pillars, one looks down from above, one supports from below and one surrounds the whole.

Optional reading (for those interested in statistics). §2.4–2.9 (scope, collection procedure, inclusion criteria, coding protocol, limitations of the corpus and aggregate analysis, two pages together) and Table S1 in Appendix A. The reanalysis in section 7 uses these. Table S2 in Appendix B (which layers each of six reference implementations covers) is half a page.

What to cut from the presentation. The layer-by-layer chapters, §3–§9, are read one at a time in the later chapters (the table in section 4). Also skip the references (pages 52–66) and the body of the project list in Appendix A.

If your group will not hold Chapter 14. Put SWE-agent's Table 3 (the ablation of the agent-computer interface) from "Side papers" into the presentation. It is the table that shows, as a controlled experiment, the "fix the model and change only the harness" that the survey speaks of only through other people's reports.

When you quote the numbers. Most of the performance figures in the survey were not measured by the survey. They were carried over from blogs and technical reports. When you write a number, give the model, the benchmark and the original report with it, and say that the survey itself is a preprint that has not been peer-reviewed. The ecosystem figures are a snapshot of May 8, 2026.

Building intuition

Same model, different scores

At the outset the survey gives three cases in which the model's weights stayed fixed and only the surroundings changed (§1).

Report What changed Result as carried over by the survey
Bölük (2026, blog) The format of the edit tool and the tool harness around it, across 15 models Large gains on coding benchmarks, up to 10× for one model
Trivedy (2026, LangChain blog) Restructuring the system prompt, injecting context through middleware, adding self-verification hooks GPT-5.2-Codex fixed, 52.8% → 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0
Meta-Harness (Lee et al. 2026) Automatically optimizing part of the harness Showed that parts of the harness can be optimized automatically

§1 of the Harness survey put into a table. The survey does not give the sample sizes or the number of repetitions of the original reports.

§1 immediately adds a cautious sentence. "The strongest controlled evidence currently comes from coding-agent benchmarks, and these results do not establish that the harness matters more than the model in every setting." Performance depends jointly on the model and its execution system. How to divide up and name what lies outside the model is the work of this survey.

The editor's bridge — the controlled conditions and measuring instruments of an experiment

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

In a clinical trial the treatment is the drug. Even for the same drug, the effect estimate changes if the dosing interval, the prohibited concomitant drugs, the rule for handling dropouts or the test equipment differ. If the model is the drug, the harness is the trial protocol and the measuring instruments put together. The tools that may be used (permitted concomitant use), the condition for stopping (the stopping rule), the records kept (the case report form) and the judgment of success (the endpoint) all sit in the harness.

Developers can think of a DBMS. Even with the same query engine, if the isolation level, the permission scheme, the log and audit settings, or the backup and recovery policy differ, the same query produces different results and different incidents. Place the seven layers around a DBMS and E is close to the server and its isolation, T to the drivers and API conventions, C to the buffer pool, L to the transaction manager, O to monitoring and the slow query log, V to regression tests, and G to permissions and the audit log.

The analogy also breaks down. A measuring instrument ideally leaves the object untouched, but a harness changes, inside the loop, what the model sees and what it can do. Treatment and measurement mix. And transactions have a formal contract such as ACID, whereas §12.4 of the survey writes that the layers of a harness do not yet have such a contract ("cross-layer handoff contract").

The survey's own framework is closer to control theory. §11.3 writes that changing a context policy, tool schema, verifier or recovery loop changes the closed-loop controller CH and therefore the measured behavior of the same model (citing Zhang et al. 2026c). The model is the plant; the harness is the controller.

The paper in detail

1. What a harness is — definition and boundary (§1, §2.4)

Definition. §1 lists seven things an agent must do to accomplish a task and calls the surrounding operational infrastructure that provides them the agent harness.

An agent must receive relevant context, invoke tools through stable interfaces, preserve state, recover from failures, expose its actions for inspection, verify outcomes, and operate within defined permissions. We refer to the surrounding operational infrastructure that provides these functions as the agent harness.

Harness engineering is the work of designing and integrating these mechanisms so that model capabilities can support reliable execution.

Boundary. §2.4 narrows the definition on purpose. A harness is not "any software around an LLM" but "the engineered wrapper that turns model calls into bounded, stateful, tool-mediated task execution". The line is drawn by function, not by product category. Frameworks that expose reusable mechanisms such as stateful orchestration, tool routing, policy hooks or trace collection are in scope. Thin API wrappers, prompt collections, static datasets, general-purpose containers, vector databases, APM dashboards and content filters are out of scope unless they have been adapted to agent execution. The vector-database retriever of Chapter 8 is not, by itself, a harness either.

Three questions. §1 names three questions that earlier work found hard to answer: where the harness begins and ends, how its interacting mechanisms are organized, and which parts of the design space are well covered. Academia studies planning, memory, tools, verification and safety separately, while practitioners talk about context pipelines, tool contracts, retries and permission boundaries, so the same problem goes by different names. That is the survey's diagnosis.

The contributions are numbered in two ways within the document. The abstract goes ① establishing the harness as a distinct engineering object ② ETCLOVG ③ the ecosystem map, while the list in §1 goes ① ETCLOVG ② the ecosystem map ③ the cross-layer synthesis. The "Claim 1, 2 and 3" of the body (the start of §3, §10) follow the order of the abstract. When you refer to them by number in a presentation, say which list you mean.

2. The timeline — from a single loop to infrastructure (§2.1, Figure 2)

§2.1 divides the change in agent systems into three periods, as changes of architecture and infrastructure.

  • Reasoning–action loops (2022). ReAct popularized the loop that alternates reasoning, action and observation. The early infrastructure was a single while loop, one prompt template and a small tool dispatch table. When AutoGPT and BabyAGI widened the pattern with task queues, memory and broader tool use, the need for explicit termination, context control, state recovery and monitoring came into view.
  • Tool integration and multi-agent coordination (2023). Gorilla, ToolLLM and Toolformer showed tool use as an ability that can be learned or elicited, and CAMEL, ChatDev and MetaGPT put forward coordination patterns. The evaluation infrastructure grew with SWE-bench, AgentBench, WebArena and GAIA, and MCP and A2A pushed standard interfaces.
  • The harness turn (2025). Reports attributing reliability to the design of the surroundings increased. OpenAI used the term "harness engineering" for Codex-style work, Meta-Harness outperformed hand-built scaffolds through automatic optimization, and the 52.8% → 66.5% report above appeared. The survey sums up that harness design has become "a measurable experimental factor rather than a fixed implementation detail." The subheading says 2025, but the text begins "By early 2026," and all the examples are from 2026.

Reading Figure 2. The figure places 51 representative systems on a timeline and colors them by the seven ETCLOVG layers. Enlarged and counted, it gives the following.

Layer Entries Entries that overlap with this book
E Execution environment 8 OpenHands, SWE-ReX (SWE-agent's execution backend)
T Tools 8 Toolformer, Gorilla, Model Context Protocol
C Context 8 Generative Agents, Lost in the Middle, MemGPT, Context Rot
L Lifecycle and orchestration 6 ReAct, Claude Code, OpenCode
O Observability 8 —
V Verification 8 WebArena, AgentBench, SWE-bench, GAIA
G Governance 5 Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL, a side paper in Chapter 15)

The editor counted the entries of Figure 2 of the Harness survey by layer.

By year there are 1 entry in 2022, 18 in 2023, 12 in 2024, 16 in 2025 and 4 in 2026. All five entries colored G date from January 2025 or later. The picture fits §2.9's statement that governance matured late, but the 51 are "representative" systems chosen by the authors, not a sample, so it is not read as a trend. That "Beyond Permission Prompts" (Oct 2025), which deals with permissions, is colored E rather than G can also be read as a sign that permissions sit where the boundary between G and E blurs.

3. Three kinds of engineering — prompt, context, harness (§2.2, Figure 1)

§2.2 divides the engineering around LLM systems into three expanding scopes.

Object of design What it decides What it cannot decide
Prompt engineering The instructions that go into one call Instructions, examples, output format, reasoning templates How information is kept across steps and how outputs become controlled actions
Context engineering The whole information state available to the model at each step Which documents, memories and earlier interactions to include, and how to order, filter and summarize them Where actions run, what permissions apply, and how failures are found and recovered from
Harness engineering The closed-loop system around the model call How outputs become actions, how results return as feedback, when to stop, and which operations need constraints or human approval —

The three paragraphs of §2.2 of the Harness survey put into a table.

Figure 1 sets the three columns from left to right and gives them the subtitles "Optimize the model input" (Instruction & Role, Example & Format, Prompt Iteration), "Optimize what the model sees" (Retrieval & Loading, Memory & State, Compression & Filtering) and "Optimize how the model runs" (Tools & Environment, Orchestration, Verification & Evaluation, Governance & Security), each with its items. The last paragraph of §2.2 writes that harness engineering does not replace the other two but integrates them into a broader operational process. The caption says that this three-part distinction was articulated early in a February 2026 blog post (MadPlay 2026) and that similar formulations followed (OpenAI 2026c, Meng et al. 2026). S22, a supplementary source for this chapter, is OpenAI 2026c.

Scope or era? The caption of Figure 1 compares the three kinds of engineering as "progressively broader scopes", while §13 calls the same thing a "three-phase engineering evolution". The word "phase" by itself makes the earlier ones sound like eras that have passed, but the last paragraph of §2.2 writes that harness engineering integrates the earlier two rather than replacing them (Misreading 2). So the two descriptions are not an either-or. Read them as saying that the emphasis of engineering moved outward from period to period while the earlier kinds remain as inner concentric circles, and the two fit together.

4. ETCLOVG — the seven layers (§2.3, Figure 3, Figure 4)

The names in §2.3 are Execution, Tooling, Context, Lifecycle, Observability, Verification and Governance (the abstract and §1 use slightly longer names: Execution environment, Tool interface, Context management, Lifecycle/Orchestration, …). The first four are the structural core, and the last three are the control plane around it.

The layout of Figure 3 of the Harness survey and the sub-items in each box. O reaches down to the four pillars, V reaches up to them, and G is the outer border. The editor drew the diagram.

Here is what each of the seven layers is responsible for and where this book meets that layer again, gathered in one table.

Layer Its job as defined in §2.3 Where we meet it again
E Execution environment Where agent code runs and which sandbox constraints bind it Chapter 14 · §3
T Tools How external capabilities are described, discovered and invoked Chapter 7 · §4
C Context What the model sees over three time horizons: short-term, session and persistent Chapter 9 · §5.1–5.3, §5.6–5.7, Chapter 12 · §5.4–5.5
L Lifecycle and orchestration The control flow that reads and writes that state, from single loops to multi-agent work and from issue to pull request Chapter 6 · §6.2, Chapter 13 · §6.3
O Observability Captures trace, cost, failure and reliability signals Chapter 19 · §7
V Verification Turns tasks and traces into evaluation, failure attribution and regression feedback Chapter 17 · §8.1–8.2, Chapter 18 · §11.1, Chapter 19 · §8.5
G Governance Constrains behavior through permission, identity, policy, hardening, audit and human oversight Chapter 15 · §9, §3.3

The definitions of §2.3. The subcategories of each layer are in Figure 4. "Where we meet it again" is this book's arrangement, and Chapter 20 maps all seven layers onto the parts of the LLM Wiki.

Three choices that differ from earlier taxonomies. The survey contrasts its taxonomy with Meng et al. (2026), who described one harness as six components: an execution loop, tool registry, context manager, state store, lifecycle hooks and evaluation interface. ① It divides by engineering surface rather than by minimal runtime role, so that it can map an ecosystem that mixes complete harnesses, protocols, sandboxes, memory systems, observability tools and evaluation frameworks. ② It raises observability (O) to an independent layer. The reason is that practice has dedicated tools (Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, OpenLLMetry) and its own routines (OpenTelemetry instrumentation, cost attribution). ③ It makes governance (G) a first-class layer that holds model-level defenses, system-level permissions and gateways, and organization-level audit and human approval.

As a result, state management goes into L together with the execution flow that reads and writes state, while lifecycle hooks and policy enforcement go into G. The C box in the figure also has "session state", which makes this easy to confuse. The split is this. C is about what the model sees at each step, that is, choosing the content of state and putting it in. State management in L is the control flow that creates, updates and resumes state during execution (§1 writes "where state is created, updated, resumed, and consumed during execution", and §6.1 lists remaining subtasks, tool results, session persistence and resuming from checkpoints). Summarizing a long conversation and putting it into the next call is C; restarting an interrupted task from a checkpoint is L. Apply this taxonomy and even the hooks familiar to readers who have used Claude Code become parts of G.

5. The corpus — how the 170-odd entries were collected (§2.4–2.9, Appendix A)

Collection (§2.5). The authors write that they built the corpus as a systematic mapping of harness artifacts with public documentation, and that, following the reporting discipline of systematic reviews (PRISMA 2020, Page et al. 2021), they made their sources, search strategy and screening process visible. Candidates came from four streams: earlier surveys and benchmark papers, GitHub searches run reproducibly, curated lists and package registries, and corporate engineering blogs and release notes. The search terms were combinations such as agent harness, coding agent, MCP server and agent observability, and the metadata was frozen on May 8, 2026. Figure 5 draws this as three stages: candidate collection (through deduplication) → inclusion criteria → boundary checks and layer assignment. Note that this flow diagram has no counts per stage. The heart of a PRISMA flow diagram is recording how many records came in at each stage and how many were dropped and why.

Inclusion and exclusion (§2.6). An artifact was included if it had public documentation, implemented or specified a concrete harness-level mechanism, and gave grounds for assigning at least one layer. Chatbot demos, prompt collections, thin client wrappers, datasets and leaderboards without a runtime, and product pages whose behavior could not be confirmed from public documentation were excluded. Boundary cases were decided by mechanism, not by label.

Coding (§2.7). Coding was multi-label, based on public artifacts (READMEs, documentation, papers, examples, release notes), and the most central mechanism was marked as the primary layer. Then comes this sentence.

The current snapshot uses a single-primary-coder protocol with author audit rather than a formal multi-coder agreement study, so we do not report Cohen's kappa or a comparable inter-annotator statistic.

One coder did the coding and the authors audited it; agreement between coders was not measured. Where the public evidence was unclear, the layer assignment was withheld.

Limitations (§2.8). The corpus is not a census but "a map of the visible agent-harness ecosystem" (the biases are in section 8). Absence from a layer means "not publicly evidenced" rather than "not implemented".

Aggregation (§2.9). All of the body's judgments about the ecosystem are qualitative. Execution environments, tool interfaces, lifecycle orchestration and verification are densest; context and memory are buried inside large frameworks; observability and governance are thin in open source. The body has no numbers behind these judgments.

The numbers are in the appendix. Appendix A gives the scale of the May 8, 2026 snapshot as 171 public entries, 146 GitHub entries, 142 GitHub entries in project categories and 0 broken URLs. Table S1, which excludes reading lists, ecosystem maps, list repositories and tutorials, gives each artifact one primary layer and its GitHub star count.
