The entry counts are taken from the category header lines of Table S1 in Appendix A of the Harness survey ("20 entries; primary layer: E" and so on), and counting the rows of the table directly gave the same numbers. The shares, medians and counts of "10k stars or more" were calculated by the editor from the star counts printed in the table.

Two things stand out. First, "170+" and the 138 of Table S1 differ. The table does not say how many of the missing 33 came from which categories. Second, L accounts for more than one in three. As the name of the L category, "Harness Architecture & Orchestration", suggests, this can be read as the result of complete harnesses with several layers, such as Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex CLI, landing in L when one primary layer had to be chosen. Six of the ten entries with the most stars are L. Table 2 in §6 also gives star counts, but its reference date (May 12, 2026) is different and so are its values, so do not mix the two.

6. Between the layers — the trilemma, capability against control, coupling (§10, §11)

The diagnosis of §10 is that many failures in practice arise at the interfaces between surfaces. The execution environment (E) constrains which orchestration strategies (L) are practical, context management (C) affects the reproducibility of evaluation (V), and governance (G) imposes identity, permission and audit constraints on every layer. A harness design should therefore "be read as a dependency structure, not as a checklist of separable components." The gaps that keep appearing at the boundaries are interoperability between tools, cost attribution, failure recovery, coordination across several repositories, and handoff between humans and agents.

The abstract and §1 introduce the problems that cut across layers as three, but the opening of §11 speaks of "five system-level effects" and adds 11.4 (from frameworks to platforms) and 11.5 (the research agenda). The last two are closer to trends and agenda. Read the three as the core.

Section Tradeoff Examples in the paper
11.1 The cost–quality–speed trilemma Stronger controls cost more and run slower Strong sandboxes raise safety and reproducibility but add startup latency and cost. Rich memory policies add token and retrieval overhead; deep evaluation and observability add iteration latency and storage costs
11.2 The capability–control tradeoff The more authority granted, the larger the control problem Larger tool menus increase selection errors and the prompt-injection surface, persistent memory brings provenance, staleness and privacy risks, and permissive sandboxes enlarge the blast radius of wrong actions
11.3 The harness coupling problem Layers interlock, so local optimizations break easily The execution environment changes evaluation results through packages, initialization and latency, tool descriptions eat into the context budget, and traces become governance evidence only when identity and permission state are recorded in the same unit

§11.1–11.3 of the Harness survey put into a table.

The conclusion of 11.1 is that quality cannot be treated as a single scalar objective. It is the same picture as the balance among sample size, measurement precision and survey cost.

11.3 answers this chapter's question most directly. A harness change has to be tested as a system change. A component that is beneficial on its own can make the whole worse once combined with the rest of the control loop. So a score cannot be cleanly attributed to the model without specifying the surrounding controller. §8.1 puts it this way: "A harness-aware evaluation should treat the reported score as a property of the model–harness pair, not of the model alone." Evaluation should either lock the harness across models or vary it as an explicit experimental factor.

When models improve (§12.5). Each wrapper, reset, verifier, memory rule and permission gate encodes an assumption about "what the model cannot do reliably on its own." When the model changes, the effect of the intervention has to be estimated again. The survey writes that a factorial model × harness evaluation can reveal whether an intervention helps all models, helps only certain families or reverses the rankings (citing Zhang et al. 2026c), and it passes on Anthropic's report that context resets which had been useful for one model became unnecessary with a stronger model, and removing them cut cost with no loss of quality. It also warns that a harness that optimizes itself against a narrow benchmark can become brittle.

The strength of the conclusion (§13). §13 sums up the survey with the "binding-constraint thesis": "infrastructure quality, not model capability alone, sets the ceiling on real-world agent reliability." It is a stronger statement than the cautious sentence in §1. With the qualifier "not … alone" it is not a contradiction, but the survey contains no comparative experiment to support "sets the ceiling".

7. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

The calculations use only numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can also be read through the eyes of statistics. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (Can We Trust the Scores?).

This survey has no scoreboard to put confidence intervals on. Instead, the results of its coding are printed in the appendix (the 138 rows of Table S1). So this chapter takes the reanalysis form. The material is the entry counts and star counts by layer, and SWE-agent's table, which measured "same model, different harness" under control.

There is no inter-coder agreement. There was one coder, and no kappa was reported (§2.7). This means the reliability of the measurement called layer assignment is unknown. Choosing one primary layer is easy to dispute in boundary cases, especially whether to put a complete harness in L.

L alone makes the distribution. A goodness-of-fit test against the null hypothesis that the seven layers are equally represented gives χ2=49.5 (6 degrees of freedom), p≈6×10−9. The distribution is not even. But run the same test on the other six layers alone (91 entries), leaving out L, and you get χ2=7.04 (5 degrees of freedom), p=0.22. This is a reference calculation that assumes a multinomial model in which entries fall into layers independently and evenly, and since the corpus is not a probability sample this p is not read as an inference about a population (Exercise 1(c)). Under that assumption, all one can say is that the differences among the six layers do not exceed the fluctuation that even assignment would produce. §2.9 writes that E, T, L and V are densest and O and G thin, but by primary layer T has 12 entries, sixth of the seven layers and fewer than O (15) or G (14). The judgment in §2.9 may refer to "coverage" that includes secondary layers assigned through multi-label coding, but the secondary-layer assignments are not printed anywhere. How to reconcile the two statements remains open.

Stars are even more skewed. Of the roughly 2.25 million stars across the 138 entries, 56.3% sit in L. The median for L is 13.9k; for the other 91 entries it is 4.0k. A Kruskal–Wallis test of the null hypothesis that the distributions are the same across layers gives H=29.2 (6 degrees of freedom), p≈5.6×10−5. Attention goes to complete harnesses, and the components of V and E, with a median of 1.8k, get the least. Star counts are a proxy for attention, not for use, and they are a one-day snapshot.

Exercise 1 — how far can the layer distribution in Table S1 be trusted? (a) Find the 95% Wilson confidence intervals for the shares of L (47/138) and T (12/138), and Goodman simultaneous confidence intervals for all seven shares. A Goodman interval is the Wilson interval formula with z2 replaced by A=χ1,1−0.05/72≈7.24 (the critical value from splitting a familywise error rate of 5% across 7 categories, A≈2.69). That is, for a category with ni entries the interval is {A+2ni±A[A+4ni(n−ni)/n]}/{2(n+A)}. (b) Reproduce the two goodness-of-fit tests above. (c) What population are these intervals about? Answer on the basis of §2.5 and §2.8. (d) If ten boundary cases moved between L and other layers, how would the conclusions change? What should the next edition report so that this question can be answered?

SolutionSolution

(a) L is 34.1%, Wilson 95% interval [26.7%, 42.3%]. T is 8.7%, [5.0%, 14.6%]. The Goodman simultaneous intervals are wider: L [24.2%, 45.5%], T [4.1%, 17.4%], C [2.8%, 14.6%], E [8.2%, 24.3%]. The intervals of the six layers other than L all overlap one another.

(b) With expected frequency 138/7≈19.7, χ2=49.5, 6 degrees of freedom, p≈6.0×10−9. Without L, with expected frequency 91/6≈15.2, χ2=7.04, 5 degrees of freedom, p=0.22.

(c) It is not a probability sample. The sources are search terms, lists and blogs chosen by the authors (§2.5), and the corpus is skewed toward English, GitHub, open source and coding agents (§2.8). The intervals in (a) have a coverage probability of 95% only under a hypothetical sampling model in which 138 entries were drawn at random from the "visible ecosystem". The actual collection was not random sampling and there is no sampling mechanism that would fix inclusion probabilities, so the probability that these intervals contain the true value is unknown. There is no basis for reading them as a "lower bound" on the uncertainty either. Selection bias is an error with a direction, and widening the interval does not solve it. Narrowing the population to something like "repositories findable on GitHub with these search terms as of May 8, 2026" makes clear what the sampling frame is, but the authors did not draw at random from that frame either, so the situation is the same. These intervals are a reference value: "had this been a random sample of this size, the share would fluctuate this much".

(d) If the ten moved from L and scattered across the six layers, the conclusion that L is largest would hold, but rankings such as "T has fewer than O or G" would flip after a few reassignments. Have a second coder independently code a random subsample (say 30 to 40 entries) and report kappa and a confusion matrix by layer, and print the coverage counts by layer including secondary layers; then the judgment in §2.9 could be checked.

Takeaway. The distribution in a taxonomy survey is a product of the measuring instrument (the coding protocol) and the sampling frame (the collection procedure). Read those two before the numbers.

Exercise 2 — same model, different harness: how large must a difference be to show? The SWE-agent paper (Yang et al. 2024) fixed the model, changed only the interface and measured the results on the 300 items of SWE-bench Lite (Table 1, Table 3; reproduced in "Side papers"). (a) Convert Shell-only's 11.00% and SWE-agent's 18.00% into counts and compare them as if they were independent samples. (b) With item-level results not published, what range can the p value of an exact McNemar test take? (c) If each of the eight ablations in Table 3 is compared with the default configuration, how many survive multiple comparisons? (d) How many tasks per harness would be needed to detect the 52.8% → 66.5% cited in §1 at a 5% significance level with 80% power? With a paired design?

SolutionSolution

(a) 11.00% is 33/300 and 18.00% is 54/300 (the paper's text writes "18.00% (54/300)"). The Wilson 95% intervals are [7.9%, 15.0%] and [14.1%, 22.7%]. The standard error of the difference in an independent-sample comparison is 0.11×0.89/300+0.18×0.82/300≈0.0286; the difference of 7.0 percentage points is 2.45 standard errors, two-sided p≈0.014.

(b) In a paired comparison the information lies only in the items solved by one side (the discordant pairs). If SWE-agent solved all 33 items that Shell-only solved, the discordant pairs are 21 solved only by SWE-agent against 0 the other way, and the two-sided p of the exact McNemar test is ≈9.5×10−7. If the items the two systems solved did not overlap at all, the discordant pairs are 54 against 33 and p≈0.031. The true value lies somewhere between. The advantage of a design that compared on the same items can be used only once item-level results are published.

(c) With the independent-sample approximation the p values are: no edit 0.0067, iterative search 0.039, full file 0.069, 30 lines 0.22, editing without linting 0.32, full history 0.32, no search 0.45, no demonstration 0.59. The Bonferroni threshold 0.05/8=0.00625 is narrowly missed even by the smallest, "No edit". A paired analysis could make them smaller, but that needs item-level results. This calculation does not deny the direction the paper presents together with its case analysis (editing and search interfaces matter), but it is too early to read each cell as an established effect.

(d) For an independent comparison, about 200 tasks per harness are needed. The survey does not give the number of tasks or repetitions for Terminal-Bench 2.0, so the power of that report is not judged here. For a paired design, about 81 tasks are needed if the two harnesses disagree on 20% of tasks, and about 123 if they disagree on 30% (normal approximation of the McNemar test).

Takeaway. When you see a report that "changing only the harness raised the score by so many percentage points", look first for the number of tasks, the number of repetitions and whether the comparison was paired. §12.3 of the survey also cites Bjarnason et al. (2026) to say that the pass rate of a single run can hide large variance. Chapter 18 extends this exercise.

8. Limitations the paper states

  • The evidence is concentrated on coding agents. It does not show that the harness matters more in every setting (§1).
  • Bias of the corpus. It is skewed toward English, GitHub, open source and coding agents, and commercial systems are underrepresented (§2.8). The conclusion also names extending the analysis to closed systems and beyond coding as future work (§13).
  • No inter-coder agreement. The coding was done by one coder with author audit (§2.7).
  • The taxonomy is descriptive. Turning it into a normative framework that guides design decisions is the next step (§13).
  • Unsolved problems. Context drift, in which behavior gradually degrades over long interactions, is the hardest open problem of the C layer (§5.7), and a self-optimizing harness risks overfitting to benchmarks (§12.5).

Two things the survey does not state are noted here as well. One is that the survey is a preprint that has not been peer-reviewed and did not measure the figures for harness effects itself. The other is that all six authors of Zhang et al. (2026c), which the survey cites in §5.7, §8.1, §11.3 and §12.5 as the basis for treating the harness as an experimental factor, are on the author list of this survey. Self-citation is common, but it is worth pointing out before reading that claim as an independently confirmed result. This remark is this book's reading.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

Effective harnesses for long-running agents (Justin Young 2025, Anthropic). The post the survey cites several times as "Anthropic 2025e". The problem is long-running work that spans several context windows. A new session starts with no memory of the previous one, and compaction alone was not enough. The failures were trying to do everything at once and running out of context midway, and a later session declaring the work finished. The remedy is for an initializer agent in the first session to create init.sh, a progress file, a first git commit and a JSON list of more than 200 features all marked "failing", after which a coding agent implements just one feature per session, tests it end to end through the browser, then leaves a commit and a progress note. A footnote says the two "agents" differ only in their initial user prompt and share the same harness. What differs from the survey is that this is one company's design case rather than a map, and it reports the effect in words without numbers. The progress file sits in C, git in L, the feature list and browser tests in V, and init.sh in E (this mapping is this book's reading).

SWE-agent's ablation of the agent-computer interface (Yang et al. 2024 · Chapter 14 of this book). Most of the reports the survey offers as evidence are blogs whose comparison conditions are not published. SWE-agent fixed the model, changed the interface components one at a time and measured on the 300 items of SWE-bench Lite. Table S2 in Appendix B of the survey also sees SWE-agent's key contribution as the agent-computer interface (ACI) and writes that commands, observations, editing, tests and execution backends become "part of the measured harness".

Component Configuration % Resolved
Editor edit action 15.0 (↓3.0)
w/ linting (default) 18.0
No edit 10.3 (↓7.7)
Search Summarized (default) 18.0
Iterative 12.0 (↓6.0)
No search 15.7 (↓2.3)
File Viewer 30 lines 14.3 (↓3.7)
100 lines (default) 18.0
Full file 12.7 (↓5.3)
Context Last 5 Obs. (default) 18.0
Full history 15.0 (↓3.0)
w/o demo. 16.3 (↓1.7)

Table 3 of the SWE-agent paper. Resolution rates on SWE-bench Lite (300 items). "Default" marks the default configuration that the original indicates with an icon; the numbers in parentheses are the drops given in the original. §5.1 of the text calls the configuration for this ablation "SWE-agent w/ GPT-4", and Table 1 gives the same 18.00% as "GPT-4 Turbo".

In Table 1 of the same paper, with the same model (GPT-4 Turbo), the Shell-only agent scored 11.00% and SWE-agent 18.00%, and the paper calls this a 64% relative increase due to the ACI. The result that iterative search does worse than no search command at all (12.0 against 15.7) is put down to agents paging through results one by one until they exhaust their budget, and it shows that an interface built for people may not suit agents. How statistically solid the cells are was calculated in Exercise 2 of section 7. L21 in Chapter 1 also advises putting as much effort into the ACI as into the HCI.

Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world (Ryan Lopopolo 2026, OpenAI · Original · Korean edition (in Korean)). The post the survey cites as "OpenAI 2026c" across §1, §2, §6.4 and §12.5. It is a five-month report from a team that built an internal beta product with Codex alone, without people writing a single line of code by hand. Starting from an empty repository in late August 2025, it reached about a million lines of code and about 1,500 merged PRs, and each of the three engineers on the team at first produced an average of 3.5 PRs per day. That it took one-tenth of the time hand-written code would have is the authors' estimate. The post writes that the people's work moved from writing code to designing environments, specifying intent and building feedback loops.

Its devices hang on nearly all of the survey's layers (the mapping is this book's reading). Each worktree boots the app with a disposable observability stack for logs, metrics and traces per task (E, O). The agent handles the screen directly through Chrome DevTools Protocol and skills for DOM snapshots and screenshots (T). An AGENTS.md of about 100 lines serves as a table of contents rather than an encyclopedia, and docs/ is treated as the system of record, disclosed only as needed (C). Execution plans are committed to the repository along with progress and decision logs (L). The direction of dependencies between layers is enforced mechanically by custom linters and structural tests, and the lint error messages carry instructions for fixing the problem into the agent's context (V, G). A "doc-gardening" agent that scans the documentation and background jobs that look for violations of "golden principles" open cleanup PRs (V, L).

It parts ways with the survey in three places. First, the name. "Harness engineering" appears only in the title and is not defined in the body. Neither the three-stage distinction among prompt, context and harness engineering nor the term "task runner" is in the body. The statement in §2.1 that OpenAI adopted the term is supported by the title. But when the caption of Figure 1 and §2.2 lean on this post for the three-stage distinction, they are reading its content through the survey's framework. In content, the passage that goes from one prompt through bug reproduction, the fix, a demo video, a PR and the merge fits the task runner of §6.4 well. Second, §12.5. The survey writes that OpenAI sees harness engineering not simply as adding more scaffolding but as aligning human attention, repository state and agent execution (OpenAI 2026c;d). The statement that human time and attention are the one truly scarce resource, and the statement that the repository serves as the system of record, are in the body. But the contrast with scaffolding is not in this post; on the contrary, its conclusion says "the discipline shows up more in the scaffolding rather than the code." Nor is the contrast in 2026d, cited alongside it. 2026d is Michael Bolin's post that unrolls the agent loop of Codex CLI ("Unrolling the Codex agent loop", January 23, 2026). It calls the agent a "harness" and explains how the prompt is assembled as a list of items, the prompt cache that hits only when the prefix matches exactly, requests that keep no state, and conversation compaction. It does not deal with scaffolding, human attention or what happens as models improve. The contrast in §12.5 should be seen as the survey's synthesis from reading the two posts together. Third, the nature of the evidence. The figures are one team's self-report with no comparison condition. The post itself says that this autonomy depends heavily on the structure and tooling of this repository and should not be assumed to generalize without similar investment, and it writes that it does not know how this system will change as models improve. If the SWE-agent ablation above showed the effect of the harness through a controlled comparison, this post backs the same claim with operational experience. Its last reservation is the same question as §12.5's demand that "harness interventions should be re-estimated" as models improve.

Agent Harness for Large Language Model Agents: A Survey (Qianyu Meng et al. 2026, Preprints). The earlier synthesis that the survey sets directly against its own taxonomy (Preprints 202604.0428. The nine authors in the survey's references match v1 and v2 (April 7 and April 9, 2026); v3 of April 28, 2026 has eleven authors). If this one is an anatomy chart that describes one harness as six components, the Harness survey is a map that sorts many projects into seven boxes (section 4 of "The paper in detail"). There is also a different survey with a similar name (Guo et al., "From Question Answering to Task Completion: A Survey on Agent System and Harness Design"), so do not mix up the bibliographic details when searching.

Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness (Yunbei Zhang et al. 2026 · Chapter 18 of this book). The position-paper preprint the survey cites as "Zhang et al. 2026c". What the survey passes on is that a score is a property of the model–harness pair (§8.1), that the harness is the closed-loop controller CH (§11.3), and that a factorial model × harness experiment can reveal reversals of ranking (§12.5). Where the survey places this idea as one conclusion of an ecosystem map, this paper sets it up as a demand on evaluation practice. The problem with comparisons that do not disclose the harness is taken up again in the side papers of Chapter 18.

Building effective agents (Erik S. and Barry Zhang 2024, Anthropic · Chapter 1 of this book). Chapter 1 separated workflows (LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths) from agents (the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use), and advised starting from the simplest solution. If Chapter 1 asks what to build, this chapter asks what to wrap it in. The parsimony principle of Chapter 1 meets §12.5's demand that harness interventions be re-estimated as models improve.

Back to the surveys

The subject of this chapter is the Harness survey itself, so this section reads it against the revised version of the Agentic Reasoning survey of Chapter 2 (the revised AR survey below). The two cover the same object in the same year, yet barely overlap.

Head and body — the questions the two surveys ask

The revised AR survey asks of every method "what does it optimize?", divides methods into in-context search over the reasoning trace z, updating the system state S and post-training of the parameters θ, then crosses these with the dynamics of the environment (foundational, self-evolving, collective) to form a 3 × 3 grid (§1, §2.2, Table 3). It is a survey that looks at the agent's head. The Harness survey asks which surface outside the model is responsible for what. Body and fence.

The revised AR survey does not use "harness" as a concept. Search its 146 pages and the word appears only in three reference titles ("Harnessing …"). Conversely, the Harness survey has no formalization such as z, S and θ. One draws the same agent as a probabilistic model, the other as a system diagram.

Comparing the tables of contents

Topic Revised AR survey (146 pages) Harness survey (71 pages) In this book

Formalization and taxonomy §2.2 (tuples E and G, Eq. 1, assumptions A0–A2, Eq. 5), §2.3, Table 3 §2.3, Figures 3–4 Chapter 2 / Chapter 3
Design guidance §2.4, Table 5 §10, §11 Chapter 2 / Chapter 3

Context management none §5.1–5.3, §5.6–5.7 Chapter 9
Memory §4.2, Table 10 §5.4–5.5 Chapter 12

The editor set the tables of contents of the two surveys side by side. "None" means that the table of contents has no section on that topic.

The three topics without a section in the revised AR survey — context management, execution environment and observability — are exactly the ones the Harness survey set up as independent layers.

Placing it in the formalization — where in the tuple is the harness?

§2.2 of the revised AR survey deliberately separates the environment E=⟨X,O,A,T,Ω,R,γ⟩ from the agent G=⟨Z,M,πreason,πexec,U⟩. Where does the harness go? The mapping below is this book's reading; neither survey makes this mapping.

ETCLOVG layer Symbol in §2.2 of the revised AR survey Grounds and caveats
T Tools External action space A Tool schemas define the set of actions. §2.3 of the revised AR survey also calls tool creation "a permanent expansion of A"
E Execution environment Transition and observation kernels T, Ω The next state and observation depend on what the sandbox allows and returns
C Context Memory space M, summary mt A function that reduces the history ht to mt. Whether assumption A1 (sufficiency of memory) holds is the quality of the C layer
L Lifecycle and orchestration The loop itself, the stopping time, the communication channel C among multiple agents Decides how many times and until when Eq. 1 runs
O Observability, V Verification Mostly outside the tuple — the side that measures the trajectory τ and the reward R The Harness survey puts the measuring instruments inside the system. But if the verifier's judgment defines the reward (as when passing tests is the reward), V also corresponds to R inside the tuple
G Governance Restrictions on A, human approval Agent-level governance in §8.7 of the revised AR survey includes "restriction of the action space A"

The editor's mapping, not a claim of either survey.

In Chapter 2, the revised AR survey wrote that "two agents with different Z or M face the same E." Placed as above, when a harness change touches tool permissions or the execution environment, A and T change along with M. In that case even the same model (θ fixed) in effect faces a different environment. Conversely, a harness change that touches only the context policy (C) or the observability instruments (O) counts as a case where only M or the measuring side differs within the same E. This is one formal answer to "why does performance differ when the model is the same?"

The S of the revised AR survey is memory, tool libraries, prompts, communication topology and the agent's own code, and it overlaps a great deal with the parts list of a harness. The difference is that S is updated across episodes (Eq. 5, Sk+1←U(Sk,τk,Fk)), while a harness is usually designed by people and held fixed. Meta-Harness, which optimizes the harness automatically, and the HarnessFix of Chapter 19, which fixes harness defects from failed trajectories, become cases of the S mode in the language of the revised AR survey.

Comparing methods — how did the two surveys disclose their corpora?

Revised AR survey §1.1 Harness survey §2.5–2.8
Unit Papers (reference entries) Public artifacts (repositories, protocols, platforms)
Scale 866 entries, all cited in the text "170+", 138 rows in Appendix Table S1
PRISMA States that "it was not built from a single systematic query, so we report the process we actually followed rather than reconstructing a PRISMA-style protocol after the fact" Cites the reporting discipline of PRISMA 2020 as followed, but gives no counts per stage
Counts by category Printed in the text (e.g., planning 111, multi-agent 118, applications 262, benchmarks 145) Only in the category header lines of Appendix Table S1
Gaps acknowledged Non-English literature, industrial systems without public write-ups, RL infrastructure, games and negotiation Skew toward English, what GitHub does not show, commercial systems, overrepresentation of coding agents

The editor set §1.1 of the revised AR survey against §2.5–2.8 and Appendix A of the Harness survey.

Their attitudes toward PRISMA are opposite. The revised AR survey says it did not follow it and prints the counts in the text. The Harness survey says it followed it, but its flow diagram has no counts. The gaps they acknowledge are alike. Industrial systems that are not public show up poorly on either map.

Design guidance and governance

Table 5 of the revised AR survey recommends which mode to choose for each deployment condition: z for one-off tasks without a training budget, S for repeated tasks in a fixed domain, θ when the task distribution is known and serving latency matters. §11 of the Harness survey records tradeoffs between layers rather than a prescription table. One asks which one to choose; the other asks whatever you choose, what you must accept.

On governance the two surveys arrive at the same structure. §8.7 of the revised AR survey divides governance into the model level (alignment), the agent level (tool permissions, sandboxing, restriction of the action space, human confirmation) and the ecosystem level (responsibility among agents run by different principals), and writes that the engineering controls at the agent level are "currently underspecified relative to how widely agents are deployed." The G layer of the Harness survey holds model-level defenses, system-level permissions and gateways, and organization-level audit and human approval. The agent level that the revised AR survey calls underspecified becomes, in the Harness survey, the content of two layers, E and G. Likewise, §8.7 of the revised AR survey requires provenance for every write to S, and §12.2 of the Harness survey requires provenance and staleness markers for remembered facts. A survey that started from the head and one that started from the body meet at auditability.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "The harness matters more than the model." The survey does not claim this. §1 writes that the strongest evidence comes from coding-agent benchmarks and does not show that the harness matters more in every setting. The "sets the ceiling" of the conclusion also carries the qualifier "not model capability alone". The video title "Why The Harness Matters More Than The Model" is not a sentence of the survey.

Misreading 2. "Harness engineering is the next stage that replaced prompt and context engineering." §2.2 writes that harness engineering integrates the two rather than replacing them. Writing prompts well is still needed inside a harness.

Misreading 3. "ETCLOVG is the order in which to build a harness and a design guide." §13 writes that the taxonomy is descriptive and that turning it into a normative framework is the next step. The seven layers are boxes for sorting what exists, not a process for building upward. The table closer to "what to choose" is Table 5 of the revised AR survey.

Misreading 4. "The layer distribution of the 170-odd projects is the shape of the ecosystem." §2.8 says to read the corpus as a map of the visible ecosystem. Table S1 gives 138 entries one primary layer each, and agreement between coders was not measured. Leave out L, and the differences between layers are not pronounced even in a reference calculation that assumes even assignment (section 7). That the corpus is not a probability sample comes first.

Misreading 5. "This survey showed the effect of harnesses experimentally." The survey ran no experiments. Its figures on harness effects are carried over from blogs and other studies, and their sample sizes and numbers of repetitions are not given. An example of a controlled comparison is SWE-agent's Table 3 in "Side papers".

Misreading 6. "Observability (O) and verification (V) are the same job." §2.3 sets them up separately. O captures signals; V turns them into evaluation, failure attribution and regression feedback. §12.3 cites LangChain's 2026 survey that 89% of teams use observability tools while 52.4% run offline evaluations, and reads this as a state in which teams see what agents did but do not systematically judge whether it was right.

Misreading 7. "Harnesses are a story about coding agents." Coding agents are overrepresented because they leave many public traces (§2.8). The conclusion names extending the map beyond coding as future work. The LLM Wiki of Chapter 20 is a case of meeting the seven layers again outside coding.

Discussion questions

  1. The harness as a control variable. If you have compared two models, did you hold the prompts, tools, retry rules and evaluation scripts fixed? If not, what could you have attributed to the difference between the models? Of the two options in §8.1 (lock the harness or vary it as a factor), which is realistic for you? Check your answer in Chapter 18.

  2. Capability against control: where to draw the line. Just as you decide how far to give developers write access to a production database, you have to draw a line when giving an agent file-system, shell or external-API permissions. Of the devices for reducing the blast radius in §11.2, which would you put in first, and what would you give up in exchange? Think ahead to Chapter 15.

  3. Should the harness shrink as models improve? §12.5 says that each device of a harness is an assumption about "what the model cannot do reliably on its own." What could be removed a year from now? What experiment would show whether it is safe to remove? We ask again in Chapter 19 and Chapter 20.

How this was checked. On October 5, 2026 the section, figure and table numbers, the figures and the quotations were checked against the Harness survey PDF (71 pages), the revised AR survey PDF (146 pages, anonymized review copy) and the SWE-agent PDF. Authors, publication status and links follow the bibliographic details in Appendix III, checked on October 4, 2026. S21 was read as text downloaded from the original at the link above, and S22 was read as text downloaded from the English original page on October 5, 2026 and checked against every place the survey cites it (§1, §2.1, 2.2, 2.4 and 2.5, Figures 1 and 9, §6.4, §12.5). The 138 rows of Table S1 were parsed and confirmed to match the entry counts in the category header lines, and Wilson intervals, Goodman simultaneous intervals, chi-square goodness-of-fit tests, a Kruskal–Wallis test and binomial tests were calculated. The SWE-agent comparisons used a normal-approximation test of two proportions, the two extremes of the exact McNemar test and the Bonferroni correction; sample sizes were found from the normal-approximation formulas for comparing two proportions and for the McNemar test.

Chapter 4 · Optional · ★★

Chapter 4. Getting the Model to Write Out Its Thinking — Chain-of-Thought

The question this chapter answers: why does accuracy go up when the model is made to write intermediate steps before answering, and when does it not?

Core reading. Jason Wei et al., "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models", NeurIPS 2022. 9 pages of main text, 43 with the appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · NeurIPS 2022 paper page · There is no official code repository

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §2.2, §3.1, §3.2.1, §4.1.1 · The Harness survey has no section corresponding to this chapter

One-paragraph summary. A language model with frozen weights is shown eight examples, and in each example a worked solution written by a person is inserted between the question and the answer. The model then also writes a solution first for a new question and gives its answer. This is chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. On GSM8K, a benchmark of grade-school arithmetic word problems, the accuracy of PaLM 540B rose from 17.9% to 56.9%. The effect appeared only once models grew to around 100 billion parameters, and in small models accuracy actually fell. On GSM8K the effect disappeared when the model was made to write only an equation, to write dots as long as the solution, or to write the solution after the answer. The authors read this as evidence that the effect comes from writing a natural-language solution before the answer. It is the starting point of the "thought" that the later chapters of this book talk about.

Presenter's guide

A 50-minute plan. The 10 minutes after the presentation are for discussion.

Time Content In the paper
0–5 min The question and the intuition: one problem, two prompts Figure 1
5–12 min The definition and four properties §1–2 (a little over 2 pages)
12–25 min Arithmetic reasoning: setup, effect by scale, the scoreboard §3.1–3.2, Figure 4, Appendix Table 2
25–33 min Ablations: where does the effect come from? §3.3, Figure 5, Appendix Table 6
33–38 min Robustness: does it work whoever writes the examples? §3.4, Figure 6, Appendix A.2
38–43 min Commonsense and symbolic reasoning and length generalization — use coin flip alone to compare in-domain and out-of-domain, and leave the other tasks and Table 4 as advance reading §5, Appendix Table 5 (§4 and Figure 3 as advance reading)
43–50 min Side papers and surveys: from one path to many, from prompting to training "Side papers" in this chapter, revised AR survey §2.2

Must read. All of §1–2 (including Figure 1), §3.1–3.4 and the §6 Discussion. If you show only two figures, make them Figure 1 and Figure 4. Figure 1 shows what the method is, Figure 4 when it works. Read the numbers for Figure 4 from Table 2 in Appendix B rather than from the figure.

Optional reading. Appendix A (FAQ), especially A.1 (why the model has to be large) and A.2 (the role of prompt engineering). Appendices D.1 and D.2 (people reading and classifying 100 solutions written by LaMDA 137B) are short as well.

What to cut from the presentation. The "Side papers" section of this chapter stands in for §7, Related Work, and Appendix C (extended related work). Of Appendices F (input–output examples) and G (full prompts), skim only Table 20 (the eight examples for arithmetic word problems). Skip Appendix E (reproducibility, resources and licenses).

If you skip this chapter. Introduce only Figure 1 and Figure 4 in the first 10 minutes of the Chapter 6 presentation (the first subsection of "Building intuition" in this chapter and the table of gains by scale in section 3 of "The paper in detail"). Chapter 6 uses this paper's CoT and the follow-up self-consistency (CoT-SC) as baselines, and Chapter 5 widens this chapter's single-line reasoning path into a tree. To read those two chapters you need only this: "put solutions in the examples so that the model writes a solution first, and greedily draw a single path".

When you quote the numbers. The scores in this paper are results from 2022 models given a few examples and sampled once with greedy decoding. The arithmetic benchmarks use eight examples (four for AQuA), and the commonsense and symbolic tasks differ by task (the first 10 items of the evaluation set for the two BIG-bench tasks, 6 for SayCan, 4 for last-letter concatenation — §4 and §5 and Appendix G). Only LaMDA is averaged over five orderings of the examples; the others use one ordering (§3.1). Give the model and its size, and the benchmark and its number of items, with every number, and since the same value differs from table to table in places (sections 3 and 4 of "The paper in detail"), also say which table you took it from.

Building intuition

Figure 1 — one problem, two prompts

Figure 1 sets standard prompting on the left beside CoT prompting on the right. The upper panel is the input given to the model and the lower panel is the model's output.

Standard Prompting
  Model Input
    Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls. He buys 2 more cans of tennis balls. Each can
       has 3 tennis balls. How many tennis balls does he have now?
    A: The answer is 11.
    Q: The cafeteria had 23 apples. If they used 20 to make lunch and bought 6
       more, how many apples do they have?
  Model Output
    A: The answer is 27.                                         (wrong)

Chain-of-Thought Prompting
  Model Input
    Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls. He buys 2 more cans of tennis balls. Each can
       has 3 tennis balls. How many tennis balls does he have now?
    A: Roger started with 5 balls. 2 cans of 3 tennis balls each is 6 tennis
       balls. 5 + 6 = 11. The answer is 11.
    Q: The cafeteria had 23 apples. If they used 20 to make lunch and bought 6
       more, how many apples do they have?
  Model Output
    A: The cafeteria had 23 apples originally. They used 20 to make lunch. So
       they had 23 - 20 = 3. They bought 6 more apples, so they have 3 + 6 = 9.
       The answer is 9.                                          (correct)

Figure 1 of the CoT paper. The original figure highlights the solution parts of the example and output on the right in color and puts wrong and correct marks beside the outputs. The marks in parentheses render those in words.

The only difference between the two inputs is one line in the example answer. The example on the right first writes out the solution that leads to "5 + 6 = 11", and the model follows that format, writing 23 − 20 = 3 and then 3 + 6 = 9 to get the right answer. The model on the left gives only an answer and gets it wrong with 27. The figure shows just one example, but the actual prompt contained eight (§3.1, Appendix Table 20), and the figure does not say which model produced the output. It is a diagram that shows the method, not an experimental result.

The editor's bridge — marginalizing a latent variable

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

Let the question be x, the final answer y and the solution between them r. The distribution of the answer can be written as a mixture model with the solution as a latent variable.

p(y∣x)=∑rp(r∣x)p(y∣x,r)

There is something to be careful about here. The distribution depends on the examples in the prompt. Standard prompting draws one answer directly from p(y∣x,D) under examples D that carry only answers. CoT first writes one solution r under examples D′ that carry solutions and reads the answer off its end, so each term of the formula above is conditioned on D′, and its marginal distribution p(y∣x,D′) is not the same distribution as p(y∣x,D). The mixture formula above and the rest of the formulas in this box are distributions under the CoT prompt, written with D′ left out. Once the solution is finished the answer is nearly settled, so p(y∣x,r) is in effect concentrated on one point. CoT, which greedily draws a single solution, looks at only one term of this sum.

Self-consistency, a side paper, samples several solutions and picks the answer by majority vote. For readers familiar with statistics it is a Monte Carlo approximation. Draw m solutions ri~p(r∣x) and the vote share of each answer, 1m∑i1[ans(ri)=y], becomes an estimate of the marginal distribution p(y∣x,D′) under the CoT prompt; the majority vote picks the mode of that estimate. The abstract of the self-consistency paper calls this procedure "marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths."

The analogy also breaks down. Changing the sampling temperature makes the distribution of ri differ from the model's original p(r∣x), so the vote share is not a strict estimate of the marginal probability. And whether a "distribution of solutions" really exists inside the model, and whether a solution shows the model's actual computation, the paper leaves as open questions (the second property in §2, §6).

The paper's own analogy is the way people solve problems (§2). When solving a multi-step word problem, people break it into intermediate steps, solve each, and then give the answer: "After Jane gives 2 flowers to her mom she has 10 . . . then after she gives 3 to her dad she will have 7 . . . so the answer is 7." The authors grant that such a solution is no different from a worked solution, but because a worked solution usually comes after the answer, they call it a "chain of thought" in the sense that it imitates the thought process leading to the answer. This insistence on order comes back in the ablations of section 4 of "The paper in detail".

The paper in detail

1. The definition and four properties (§1–2)

It combines two lines of thought (§1). One is research that trains models from scratch (Ling et al. 2017) or fine-tunes them (Cobbe et al. 2021) to generate natural-language rationales that lead to an answer. The other is the in-context learning that GPT-3 demonstrated. The first is expensive because it needs a large amount of data annotated with rationales; the second performs poorly on reasoning tasks and does not improve much as models grow. The paper combines the two and puts in examples that are triples of three elements: ⟨input, chain of thought, output⟩.

The definition is one sentence: "A chain of thought is a series of intermediate natural language reasoning steps that lead to the final output" (§1). It is a series of intermediate reasoning steps in natural language that lead to the answer.

In formulas, it looks like this. Let the set of examples be D. The examples of standard prompting are D={(xi,yi)}, and the model generates y for a new question x. The examples of CoT are D′={(xi,ci,yi)}, and the model generates the chain c first and then y.

pθ(c,y∣x,D′)=pθ(c∣x,D′)·pθ(y∣x,c,D′)

The parameters θ are fixed. Only the examples in the prompt change. This formula is the editor's rendering of the paper's description; the paper has no formula.

The structure of standard prompting and CoT prompting. In both cases the weights are fixed and only the format of the examples differs. The dashed arrows mean that the examples set the format of generation. The editor drew the diagram from the descriptions in §1–2 and §3.1 of the paper.

Four properties (§2). The paper gives four reasons why CoT is attractive.

  1. It can break a multi-step problem into intermediate steps. So more computation can be allocated to problems that need more reasoning steps.
  2. It gives a window for looking into how the model arrived at an answer and for finding where the reasoning went wrong. In parentheses, though, it adds the caveat that fully characterizing the computation behind an answer remains an open question.
  3. In principle it can be used for any task that people can solve through language, such as arithmetic word problems, commonsense reasoning and symbolic manipulation.
  4. In a sufficiently large off-the-shelf model it can be elicited just by putting chains into the examples.

The first property is tested by "variable compute only" in section 4 of "The paper in detail", and the caveat of the second comes up again in "Common misreadings".

2. Arithmetic reasoning — the experimental setup (§3.1)

Five benchmarks. The numbers of items are in Appendix Table 12.

Benchmark Character Evaluation items
GSM8K Grade-school arithmetic word problems, multi-step 1,319
SVAMP Arithmetic word problems with varied structure 1,000
ASDiv Arithmetic word problems of diverse types 2,096
AQuA Algebraic word problems, five-way multiple choice 254
MAWPS Four subsets: SingleOp, SingleEq, AddSub, MultiArith 562 · 508 · 395 · 600

Only the numbers of items are taken from Appendix Table 12 of the paper.

Examples. Most datasets have only an evaluation split, so the authors wrote eight examples with chains themselves (Appendix Table 20) and used the same ones for every arithmetic benchmark except AQuA. For AQuA, which is multiple choice, they used four examples and solutions from the training set (Appendix Table 21). The authors say these examples did not undergo prompt engineering.

Models. There are five families.

  • GPT-3: text-ada-001, text-babbage-001, text-curie-001, text-davinci-002. The paper writes that these "presumably" correspond to InstructGPT models of 350M, 1.3B, 6.7B and 175B parameters. The sizes are guesses.
  • LaMDA: 422M, 2B, 8B, 68B, 137B. Appendix Table 2 gives the smallest model as 420M.
  • PaLM: 8B, 62B, 540B.
  • UL2 20B and Codex (code-davinci-002). According to the version record in Appendix E, these were added in v5. That the abstract still says "three large language models" can be read as a trace of the earlier version.

Decoding. Every model samples once with greedy decoding. In parentheses the authors note that follow-up work improves results by sampling several times and taking a majority vote, citing the self-consistency paper (Wang et al. 2022a) (§3.1). That paper is a side paper of this chapter.

3. Results — it appears only with scale (§3.2, Figure 4, Appendix Table 2)

The authors draw three things from the results.

First, CoT is an emergent ability of model scale. Small models gain nothing; gains appear only at around 100 billion parameters. Smaller models are said to have written chains that were fluent but illogical. Read the GSM8K column family by family and the pattern is clear. The gains (CoT − standard) are as follows.

Family Gain by size (percentage points)
LaMDA 420M −2.2 · 2B −1.7 · 8B −1.6 · 68B +2.5 · 137B +7.8

Below 10B the gains are negative in all three families. Appendix A.1 also writes that "chain of thought actually hurts performance for most models smaller than 10B parameters." The AQuA column moves differently: even at 10B and above, CoT is lower for PaLM 62B (25.6 → 22.4), LaMDA 68B (22.3 → 20.2) and LaMDA 137B (25.5 → 20.6). With five choices, guessing alone gives 20%, so the AQuA standard scores of the models below 10B (12.6–23.5%) are close to chance.

Second, the more complex the problem, the larger the gain. On GSM8K, where the baseline score is lowest, the scores of the largest GPT and PaLM more than doubled. On MAWPS SingleOp, which one step solves, the gain was negative or very small (Appendix Table 3). Here is the PaLM 540B row.

MAWPS subset Character PaLM 540B standard → CoT
SingleOp one step 94.1 → 94.1
SingleEq one or two steps 86.5 → 92.3
AddSub one or two steps 93.9 → 91.9
MultiArith (not stated separately in the original) 42.2 → 94.7

The PaLM 540B row of Appendix Table 3 of the paper. The characters of the subsets follow the descriptions in §3.2, Appendix A.3 and the caption of Table 3. The original groups SingleOp, SingleEq and AddSub together as easy problems solved in one or two steps.

Third, it rivals task-specific fine-tuned models. PaLM 540B exceeded the prior state of the art on GSM8K, SVAMP and MAWPS (on SVAMP standard prompting had already exceeded it), and came within 2% on AQuA and ASDiv. The prior state of the art on GSM8K is the 55% of Cobbe et al. (2021), who fine-tuned GPT-3 and added a verifier, and "surpassing even finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier" in the abstract is this comparison. Whether this difference exceeds the margin of chance is calculated in "Rereading with a statistician's eye".

An external calculator. Because there are cases where the solution is right but only the arithmetic is wrong, Appendix B also tried post-processing that recomputes the equations in the solution with Python eval and puts the results back. In the GSM8K column of Appendix Table 1, CoT rose from 14.3 → 17.8 for LaMDA 137B, 46.9 → 49.6 for GPT-3 175B and 56.9 → 58.6 for PaLM 540B.

People read the solutions. The authors randomly chose 50 correct and 50 incorrect solutions written by LaMDA 137B on GSM8K and read them. According to the main text (§3.2), all 50 correct ones had correct logic and arithmetic except two that got the right answer by coincidence. Of the 50 incorrect ones, 46% were almost-correct solutions with only minor mistakes, and 54% had major errors of semantic understanding or coherence. The breakdown in Appendix D.2 is calculator error only 8%, symbol mapping error 16%, one step missing 22% and needing major changes 54% (27 cases); the first three add up to 46%.

Two numbers disagree. The main text says "two" solutions were correct by coincidence, while Appendix D.1 says "only one". D.1 then lists six by adding five with minor imperfections, and the table also shows six examples, yet the caption of Table 9 says there were 7 imperfect cases and 43 others. D.2 also says that with the external calculator LaMDA 137B's GSM8K score went "from 14.3% to 17.3%", pointing to Table 2, but the calculator results are in Table 1 and the value is 17.8. Which is right cannot be settled from the original.

Errors fixed by scale (Appendix A.1). When the 45 items PaLM 62B got wrong were classified by hand, 540B fixed 6 of the 20 semantic understanding errors, 12 of the 18 one-step-missing errors and 4 of the 7 other errors (hallucination, repetition, symbol mapping errors). The authors see this as consistent with the hypothesis that larger models acquire semantic understanding and logical reasoning ability, while adding the caveat that scale is confounded with factors such as training compute.

4. Ablations — where does the effect come from? (§3.3, Figure 5, Appendix Tables 6 and 7)

If CoT has an effect, there could be several causes. The authors test three plausible explanations one at a time. Equation only has the model write only an equation before the answer. Variable compute only has it write dots (. . .) as many as the characters of the equation the solution needs. Reasoning after answer has it give the answer first and write the solution afterward. They target, respectively, the explanations that the effect comes from producing equations, from spending more intermediate tokens (computation), and from activating knowledge acquired in pretraining.

Figure 5 shows bars for five conditions (standard, the three variants and CoT) for LaMDA 137B and PaLM 540B on GSM8K. LaMDA's numbers are in Appendix Table 6. The paper gives no table of PaLM 540B's numbers by variant, so this chapter does not carry them.

Condition (LaMDA 137B) GSM8K SVAMP ASDiv MAWPS
Standard prompting 6.5 ±0.4 29.5 ±0.6 40.1 ±0.6 43.2 ±0.9
Chain of thought prompting 14.3 ±0.4 36.7 ±0.4 46.6 ±0.7 57.9 ±1.5
equation only 5.4 ±0.2 35.1 ±0.4 45.9 ±0.6 50.1 ±1.0
variable compute only 6.4 ±0.3 28.0 ±0.6 39.4 ±0.4 41.3 ±1.1
reasoning after answer 6.1 ±0.4 30.7 ±0.9 38.6 ±0.6 43.6 ±1.0

The first part of Appendix Table 6 of the paper. The ± values are the standard deviations of runs with five different orderings of the examples (caption).

Equation only does not help on GSM8K. At 5.4 it is even lower than standard (6.5). The authors' interpretation is that the meaning of GSM8K items is too semantically challenging to translate straight into one equation without natural-language reasoning steps. On SVAMP, ASDiv and MAWPS, which have many one- or two-step problems, writing only an equation does raise the score (29.5 → 35.1, 40.1 → 45.9, 43.2 → 50.1). Appendix A.4 gives one example from LaMDA 137B.

QUESTION: Mike plays ping pong for 40 minutes. In the first 20 minutes, he scores
4 points. In the second 20 minutes, he scores 25% more points. How many total
points did he score?

EQUATION ONLY (WRONG ANSWER): (4 + 20 * 0.25) = 6. The answer is 6.

CHAIN OF THOUGHT (CORRECT): Mike played ping pong for 40 minutes. In the first 20
minutes, he scored 4 points. In the second 20 minutes, he scored 25% more points.
So he scored 25% more in the second 20 minutes. 4 x 1.25 = 5. So he scored 5
points in the second 20 minutes. So he scored 9 points in total. The answer is 9.

The equation-only side cannot decide what "25% more" is 25% of, and drags in the number 20. The side that writes a chain first establishes in a sentence the intermediate fact that the second 20 minutes gave 1.25 times 4 points. The authors' reading is that the step written as a sentence does the work of pinning down the meaning.

Increasing computation alone does not help. Writing only dots gives 6.4, about the same as standard. In this setting (LaMDA 137B, GSM8K), increasing the number of intermediate tokens alone did not explain the effect of CoT. The experiment tests the first of the four properties (the problem can be broken up and more computation allocated), and the result fits the authors' reading that natural-language steps matter. But it tested only one variant, dot tokens, so it does not go as far as showing the necessary condition that the computation must be expressed in natural language.

Writing the solution after the answer does not help. At 6.1 it is about the same as standard. If the solution sentences only had the effect of activating knowledge, they should help even when written after the answer. Since they do not, the authors conclude that the sequential reasoning contained in the chain is useful for reasons beyond knowledge activation. This result can be read alongside assumption A0 from Chapter 2 (the reasoning trace zt is generated before the action at). Reverse the order and the effect disappears. This connection is this book's reading.

Appendix Table 7 repeats the same ablations on five commonsense and symbolic tasks (Table 7 has no equation-only row). Variable compute only and reasoning after answer both stay near standard on date understanding, sports understanding, last-letter concatenation and coin flip. Only SayCan is an exception: reasoning after answer (83.3) is slightly higher than standard (80.8), and variable compute only (74.2) is lower than standard.

One number disagrees. The LaMDA 137B CoT SVAMP value in Table 6 is 36.7, while the same cell in Appendix Tables 2 and 1 is 37.5. GSM8K (14.3), ASDiv (46.6) and MAWPS (57.9) agree across the three tables, so only the SVAMP cell differs. The paper does not explain the difference.

5. Robustness — does it work whoever writes the examples? (§3.4, Figure 6, Appendix A.2)

Prompting is sensitive to examples. The authors open this section with the earlier finding (Zhao et al. 2021) that on GPT-3, merely changing the order of the examples moved SST-2 accuracy from 54.3% to 93.4%, and then try changing only the chains while keeping the questions of the examples.

  • Annotators B and C. The chains in the main experiment were written by annotator A. Two co-authors independently wrote chains for the same examples (Appendix H). They were given no instructions on how to write them.
  • Concise style. Annotator A rewrote the chains more briefly, following the style of the solutions in Cobbe et al. (2021).
  • Examples α, β and γ from the GSM8K training set. Three sets of eight were randomly drawn from GSM8K training items that came with crowd workers' solutions. To fit the input window, items of 60 tokens or fewer were chosen, and to compare fairly with the examples the authors wrote, items of two steps or fewer (footnote 2).
Chain (LaMDA 137B) GSM8K SVAMP ASDiv MAWPS
Standard prompting 6.5 ±0.4 29.5 ±0.6 40.1 ±0.6 43.2 ±0.9
Chain of thought prompting (annotator A, main experiment) 14.3 ±0.4 36.7 ±0.4 46.6 ±0.7 57.9 ±1.5
different annotator (B) 15.5 ±0.6 35.2 ±0.4 46.5 ±0.4 58.2 ±1.0
different annotator (C) 17.6 ±1.0 37.5 ±2.0 48.7 ±0.7 60.1 ±2.0
intentionally concise style 11.1 ±0.3 38.7 ±0.8 48.0 ±0.3 59.6 ±0.7
exemplars from GSM8K (α) 12.6 ±0.6 32.8 ±1.1 44.1 ±0.9 53.9 ±1.1
exemplars from GSM8K (β) 12.7 ±0.5 34.8 ±1.1 46.9 ±0.6 60.9 ±0.8

The second part (Robustness) of Appendix Table 6 of the paper. The standard and annotator A rows are taken from the first part of the same table.

The authors write that every variant beats standard "by a large margin" on the four benchmarks (§3.4, Appendix A.2). Look at Table 6 and some cells show small differences. On SVAMP, variant α is 32.8 against 29.5, a difference of 3.3 percentage points, and annotator B a difference of 5.7. The authors read this to mean that the success of CoT does not depend on a particular style, and that since the GSM8K examples also worked on other benchmarks, the examples need not come from the same distribution as the test items (Appendix A.2).

Prompt engineering still matters (Appendix A.2). This is a caveat the authors add themselves. On coin flip, annotator A's chains scored 99.6% and annotator C's 71.4% (Appendix Table 7). There is also the anecdote that on a task of reversing the order of five items, two co-authors could not write chains that worked, and a third co-author wrote chains that solved it perfectly.

The rest of the checks in A.2 are summarized briefly. Except for coin flip, the standard deviation across orderings of the examples was small. Changing the number of examples generally kept the gain (Figure 11). The number of examples was fixed at 8 because the input length was limited to 1,024 tokens (Appendix D.3). A.2 writes that when the same prompts were used across models, only GPT-3's CSQA and StrategyQA showed no gain, and the authors record this as a limitation. But in Table 1, which A.2 points to as its basis, LaMDA 137B's AQuA also goes down from 25.5 to 20.6 (section 3 of "The paper in detail"). The "only" of A.2 leaves that cell uncounted. A.2 gives the standard prompting value for coin flip as "50.0%", while Table 7, which it points to, gives 49.0 ±2.1.
