In-domain, PaLM 540B's CoT is nearly 100%. The authors themselves stress that these are toy tasks in which the structure of the solution is already in the examples and the same steps just have to be repeated with new symbols, and yet they note that small models failed. Out of domain, standard prompting fails on both tasks and CoT rises with scale. This is length generalization to inputs longer than the examples. On coin flip, PaLM 540B's standard prompting alone gets 98.1% in-domain, so that cell is weak evidence for the effect of CoT.

7. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

The calculations use only numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can also be read through the eyes of statistics. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (Can We Trust the Scores?).

This paper prints the numbers of items. That is the difference from ReAct's Table 1 in Chapter 6 (Appendix Table 12). So a binomial standard error can be attached to each accuracy. On GSM8K (1,319 items), the standard error near an accuracy of 14.3% is 0.143×0.857/1319≈0.0096, or about 1.0 percentage points, and near 56.9% it is about 1.4 percentage points. The ± values in the GSM8K column of Appendix Table 6 (0.2–1.0 percentage points) are a different quantity. They are the fluctuation when only the order of the examples changes on the same items, so they do not include the uncertainty from sampling items. Read these ± values as confidence intervals and you understate the uncertainty.

Reading the "emergence" of scale as a threshold model. Treat the table of gains by scale in section 3 of "The paper in detail" as a regression. With x the base-10 logarithm of the number of parameters, the hinge model Δ(x)=β0+β1max(0,x−x0) with the constraints β0=0 and β1>0 is a rendering of the statement "no effect below the threshold x0 and a growing one above it". Left unconstrained, it is a model that allows a constant effect β0 below the threshold as well. The problem is the data. Each family has three to five points, and the points above the threshold are two for PaLM, two for LaMDA and one for GPT. With these one cannot tell a broken line from a smoothly bending curve, and the threshold can only be pinned down as an interval such as "between 8B and 62B for PaLM". Appendix A.1 uses emergence in the sense that "its success cannot be predicted only by extrapolating the performance of small scale models," but the failure of an extrapolation depends on which extrapolation model was used. It was later argued that with discontinuous metrics such as exact-match accuracy, even smooth change can look like a jump (Schaeffer et al. 2023). The negative gains of small models are seen with the same eye. LaMDA 420M's −2.2 percentage points is larger than the item sampling error (about 0.5 percentage points), but Appendix A.1 writes that small models often produced output that could not be parsed because they repeated themselves or did not reach a conclusion. Part of the negative gain can also be read as a product of measurement, namely failures of answer extraction.

Checking the numbers in the tables. With the numbers of items you can also run checks. Two things come up. First, the MAWPS column of Appendix Table 2 matches the simple average of the subset accuracies, not the accuracy over the 2,065 items of the four subsets combined. The four Table 3 values for PaLM 540B standard prompting (94.1, 86.5, 93.9, 42.2) have a simple average of 79.2, the same as Table 2, while the average weighted by the numbers of items (562, 508, 395, 600) is 77.1. The six other rows the editor checked (UL2 20B, GPT-3 175B, Codex, PaLM 8B and 62B, LaMDA 137B) also match the simple average within rounding. The paper does not state how it aggregated. Second, the accuracies of models that used only one ordering of the examples (all but LaMDA) should be "integer ÷ number of items" rounded, but four values in the SingleEq (508 items) column (UL2 20B's 18.0 and 20.2, PaLM 8B's 28.2, PaLM 540B's 86.5) cannot arise from 508 items. For example, 439/508 = 86.42% and 440/508 = 86.61%, so no integer gives 86.5. Why this happens cannot be learned from the paper. AQuA (254 items) and the other MAWPS subsets pass this check, and the benchmarks with 1,000 items or more (SVAMP 1,000, GSM8K 1,319, ASDiv 2,096) realize every 0.1-percentage-point value with some integer, so this check cannot catch anything there.

Exercise 1 — measuring differences on the 1,319 GSM8K items. (a) How many items are PaLM 540B's 17.9% (standard) and 56.9% (CoT)? Find the Wilson 95% confidence interval for each. (b) The two methods were compared on the same 1,319 items. Treated as independent samples, what is the standard error of the difference of 39.0 percentage points? Since the item-level results are unknown, also estimate the range the standard error of a paired comparison could take. (c) The abstract writes that PaLM 540B + CoT (56.9%) beat fine-tuned GPT-3 + verifier (55%) to set a new state of the art. Test this difference the same way. What about the 58.6% with the external calculator? (d) In the ablations, may LaMDA 137B's standard 6.5% and "reasoning after answer" 6.1% be read as "about the same"?

SolutionSolution

(a) The only integer that gives 17.9% is 236 (236/1319 = 17.89%). 56.9% is 750 or 751. The Wilson intervals are [15.9%, 20.1%] for 236 items and [54.2%, 59.5%] for 750 items (with 751 the upper limit is 59.6%).

(b) Calculated with 750 items, the difference is 39.0 percentage points, the independent-sample standard error is 0.179×0.821/1319+0.569×0.431/1319≈0.0172, or 1.7 percentage points, and the 95% interval is [35.6, 42.3] percentage points. In a paired comparison the number of items on which the two methods disagree matters. Let b be the items only standard got right and c the items only CoT got right; then c−b=514 is fixed and b can range from 0 to 236. The standard error of the paired difference, [(b+c)/N−((c−b)/N)2]/N, is 1.3 percentage points at b=0 and 2.1 percentage points at b=236. Either way the difference is more than 18 standard errors. The p value of the exact McNemar test is below 10−60 even under the least favorable assumption, b=236. This difference is not a matter of noise.

(c) Treated as independent samples, the difference of 1.9 percentage points has a standard error of 1.93 percentage points, z≈0.98, two-sided p≈0.33, 95% interval [−1.9, 5.7] percentage points. The 58.6% with the external calculator also gives z≈1.87, p≈0.06. Pairing the item-level results could reduce the standard error, but neither paper has that data, and 55 is printed as an integer, so there is rounding slack as well. "A new state of the art" is right as a ranking of point estimates, but it is hard to say that it is distinguishable from the prior state of the art with 1,319 items. The contribution of this paper lies not in that ranking but in the 39-percentage-point difference from standard prompting.

(d) Treated as independent samples, the difference of 0.4 percentage points between 6.5% and 6.1% is smaller than the standard error of about 0.95 percentage points, and the 95% interval of the difference is [−1.5, 2.3] percentage points. What can be said here goes only as far as "no difference was detected". Non-significance is not evidence of equivalence. To judge them "about the same" you must first fix the margin of difference you will tolerate. If, say, you had decided to count anything within ±3 percentage points as the same, the interval falls inside it and you can call them equivalent; if you had set ±1 percentage point, this data cannot decide. In the same table the gain from CoT is 7.8 percentage points, so this interval is much narrower than that. The LaMDA values are averages over five orderings of the examples, so this standard error is approximate.

Takeaway. With the numbers of items you can tell a "large difference" from a "ranking". Within the same table, a difference of 39 percentage points is overwhelming, and a state of the art set by 1.9 percentage points cannot be distinguished from chance.

Exercise 2 — fluctuation by who wrote the chains. The GSM8K column of the table in section 5 of "The paper in detail" has seven CoT variants (annotators A, B and C, concise style, GSM8K examples α, β and γ). (a) Find the mean and standard deviation of the seven values, and compare them with the ± in the table (the standard deviation over orderings of the examples) and with the binomial standard error (about 1.0 percentage points). (b) If the authors had picked the best of the seven to report, how much higher than the mean would the score be expected to come out? Assume the seven values came independently from the same normal distribution (if the distribution is not normal, the expected value of the maximum changes). The expected maximum of seven standard normal draws can be found with a short simulation (for example, draw 100,000 batches of 7 normal random numbers and average the maxima). Where does annotator A's value, the one actually reported, sit? (c) Annotators A, B and C on coin flip (Appendix Table 7) score 99.6 ±0.3, 77.5 ±7.9 and 71.4 ±11.1. Can "robust to different annotators" be said for this task too? (d) To report the score of "the method called CoT" as one number, what is better to write, and how?

SolutionSolution

(a) The seven values (14.3, 15.5, 17.6, 11.1, 12.6, 12.7, 12.6) have a mean of 13.8%, a standard deviation of 2.2 percentage points and a range of 6.5 percentage points. That is two to seven times the standard deviation over orderings of the examples (0.3–1.0 percentage points) and larger than the item sampling error (about 1.0 percentage points) too. The largest source of uncertainty is who wrote the chains and how.

(b) The expected maximum of seven independent draws from a standard normal distribution is about 1.35 by simulation (1.351 over 1 million batches). So picking the best to report would be expected to come out about 1.35×2.2≈3.0 percentage points above the mean. The actual maximum is annotator C's 17.6 (mean +3.8 percentage points). Annotator A of the main experiment (14.3) sits close to the mean, so the representative score has almost no best-of selection bias. But the concise style is annotator A's rewrite and α, β and γ were drawn from the same source, so the seven values are not independent. The expected value above is approximate.

(c) All three chains score above standard (49.0%), so robustness in the sense of "better than standard" holds. But the scores differ by more than 28 percentage points, and annotator C's chains have a standard deviation of 11.1 percentage points just from changing the order of the examples. Robustness in the sense of "about the same whoever writes them" does not hold for this task. That one must first decide in which sense "robust" is being used is the same structure as the ALFWorld results in Chapter 6.

(d) Treat the chains as a random effect. The mean of annotators A, B and C is 15.8% with a standard deviation of 1.67 percentage points, and from annotator variation alone the standard error of the mean is 1.67/3≈0.96 percentage points. Item sampling error is added on top. "The mean of three annotators, 15.8% (standard deviation between annotators 1.7 percentage points, 3 annotators, 1,319 items)" is a more honest statement about the method than "14.3% with annotator A". Three annotators are a small sample, so this standard deviation is itself uncertain.

Takeaway. First check what fluctuation the ± in a prompting paper refers to. The order of the examples, the choice of examples, the person who wrote the chains and the sample of items are different sources of uncertainty, and the reported ± often captures only one of them.

8. Limitations the paper states

  • Does the model really "reason"? That CoT imitates the human thought process does not answer whether the neural network actually reasons. It is left as an open question (§6).
  • Annotation cost. Adding chains to a few examples costs little, but large-scale annotation for fine-tuning could be expensive; the paper notes that this might be overcome with synthetic data generation or zero-shot generalization (§6). DeepSeek-R1 and Zero-shot CoT among the side papers touch these two directions respectively (this book's reading).
  • Correct reasoning paths are not guaranteed. Wrong paths lead both to wrong answers and to answers that happen to be right (§6, Appendix D.2), and on multiple-choice and binary classification tasks it is much more likely to get the right answer through a wrong path (Appendix D.1). The NeurIPS checklist adds that the authors do not suggest using the generated chains in a factual manner or in any real-world scenario.
  • It appears only in large models. That makes it expensive to use in real services. Research on eliciting reasoning in small models is left as future work (§6).
  • Gains that do not carry over between models. The same prompts produced no gain on GPT-3's CSQA and StrategyQA (Appendix A.2).
  • Scale confounded with other factors. Model scale is confounded with factors such as training compute, and the paper writes that what makes reasoning possible must be studied separately through pretraining data, architecture and objective functions (Appendix A.1).

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

Three side papers (Zero-shot CoT, self-consistency, DeepSeek-R1) are treated only within the scope of their abstracts, and one earlier work the main paper compares itself with directly is added, along with the next two chapters of this book.

Zero-shot CoT (Kojima et al. 2022 · NeurIPS 2022). With no examples, it simply adds the one sentence "Let's think step by step" before each answer. According to the abstract, on text-davinci-002 GSM8K rose from 10.4% to 40.7% and MultiArith from 17.7% to 78.7%, with similar results on PaLM 540B. The main paper gives eight examples with chains written by people for each task, while Kojima et al. get the same thing done with one sentence unrelated to the task. The baselines differ (answering with no examples against standard prompting with examples), so the numbers of the two papers are not set against each other. The "zero-shot generalization" that §6 of the main paper names as a way past annotation cost is this direction.

Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022 · ICLR 2023 · the CoT-SC of Chapter 6 of this book). The abstract proposes replacing CoT's "naive greedy decoding". It samples several reasoning paths and picks the most consistent answer by "marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths." The improvements the abstract reports are GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%, StrategyQA +6.4% and ARC-challenge +3.9% (the abstract does not say for which model). It is the paper that §3.1 of the main paper cites as follow-up work, from the same group with the first and second authors swapped. The difference is the number of paths (one against many), and the cost grows with the number of samples.

DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI 2025 · Nature, vol. 645). The abstract starts from the point that the success of CoT is heavily contingent on human-annotated demonstrations, and claims to have elicited reasoning ability through pure reinforcement learning alone, "obviating the need for human-labeled reasoning trajectories." It says that patterns such as self-reflection, verification and strategy switching emerged during training, and that it outperformed supervised models on verifiable tasks such as mathematics and coding. The main paper holds the parameters θ fixed and elicits chains through examples; R1 changes θ to build the habit of writing chains into the model. In the language of Chapter 2, it is the z mode against the θ mode.

GSM8K and verifiers (Cobbe et al. 2021, bibliographic details checked against the main paper's reference list). The source of GSM8K and the opponent the main paper compared itself with as the prior state of the art (55%). According to the abstract, it built GSM8K from 8,500 arithmetic word problems and trained a verifier that judges whether a solution is correct, then picks from many candidate solutions the one ranked highest. Unlike the main paper it changes the parameters, and it does "generate many, then choose", but the choosing device is a trained verifier rather than a majority vote. Appendix D.2 of the main paper also names this method as a way to improve decoding, with the caveat that a verifier has to be trained.

Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023 · Chapter 5 of this book). The ToT abstract diagnoses that language models' reasoning is confined to "token-level, left-to-right" decision-making. CoT's chain is also written once from left to right and does not go back. ToT spreads out several branches, evaluates them itself and backtracks. As an example in the abstract, on the Game of 24 GPT-4 + CoT scored 4% and ToT 74%. The difference is whether there is search.

ReAct (Yao et al. 2022 · Chapter 6 of this book). It uses the main paper's CoT as a baseline while calling CoT "a static black box". It generates thoughts only from internal representations and is not grounded outside, so facts get made up and errors spread. On HotpotQA (PaLM-540B, EM), CoT scored 29.4, CoT-SC 33.4 and ReAct 27.4 (ReAct Table 1). The difference is what the chain is conditioned on. CoT's chain is conditioned only on the question and the earlier chain; ReAct's thoughts are conditioned on the environment's observations as well.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §2.2 — CoT is z

We bring back the notation of Chapter 2. In the agent tuple G=⟨Z,M,πreason,πexec,U⟩, the survey defines Z as "a reasoning trace space (e.g., latent plans, optionally verbalized as chain-of-thought)". It names this paper's chain directly as an example of a reasoning trace space. Mapped onto the main paper's notation, it looks like this (the mapping was made by the editor).

CoT paper Revised AR survey §2.2
Question x and examples D′ History ht (the observation o0 of a one-step episode)
Chain c Reasoning trace zt∈Z
Final answer y External action at∈A — the survey names the final answer as an example of A
The chain is written before the answer Assumption A0: zt is generated before at
Weights fixed, only examples changed The z mode (in-context reasoning): θ fixed, nothing persists across episodes
One path by greedy decoding The simplest case, with no search over Z

Two points are added. First, assumption A0 also says that zt is not emitted to the environment. CoT's chain is mixed into the output and visible to people, but if one regards only the parsed answer as passed to the grader (the environment), it fits A0. Second, "reasoning after answer" in section 4 of "The paper in detail" is a treatment that reverses A0's order, and the effect disappeared then. What this ablation shows goes only as far as the effect being present when the solution comes before the answer. It points in the same direction as the order A0 describes, so the two can be read together, but the experiment does not prove what the survey makes of A0, namely the line it draws between a single forward pass and agentic reasoning. What counts as agentic reasoning is a separate judgment. This connection is this book's reading, and the survey does not cite this experiment.

The three side papers sit on the same axis. Apply the survey's definitions and Zero-shot CoT (only the prompt changes) and self-consistency (several z are sampled) are the z mode. DeepSeek-R1 is the model that the post-training paragraph of the survey's §2.2 names directly as an example of the θ mode. One path, many paths and learned parameters: these three boxes show the z-against-θ distinction of Chapter 2.

Where CoT sits in the survey

  • §1, the introduction, and the start of §2. The survey puts CoT at the starting point. Techniques that make intermediate reasoning explicit improved performance but assume "static contexts and short-horizon reasoning" (§1), and conventional language models remain passive sequence predictors within fixed prompts (§2).
  • §3.1, planning reasoning, and Table 6. Table 6 (representative planning systems) has no CoT row, and the text of §3.1.1 does not cite Wei et al. (2022) by name either. The closest things are the ToT row (structure: tree, representation: natural language, tools: none, optimization target: z) and the mention of structured prompting and "X-of-Thought" in the "workflow design" paragraph. In the Table 3 grid, "Prompted and search-based planning" in the foundational × in-context (z) cell holds this line of work.
  • §3.2.1, in-context tool integration. CoT appears by name again: "The foundation of in-context agentic reasoning lies in augmenting the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process with the ability to take action." The same paragraph writes that CoT "operates in a closed world, limited by the model's internal knowledge." It is the same diagnosis as ReAct's "static black box".
  • §4.1.1, reflective feedback. Self-consistency (cited as Wang et al. 2023d) is grouped with ToT under "Search-based reasoning strategies" in the paragraph on the I-a self-reflection type. It generates several candidate paths and picks by voting, scoring or an evaluator, with all the signals produced by the model itself. It is the counterpart to the externally grounded type (I-b) of Chapter 11.
  • §6.5.1, web agents. Zero-shot CoT (Kojima et al. 2022) is cited once, for the observation that a language model becomes a zero-shot reasoner when made to write out intermediate steps.

In the design guidance (§2.4 Table 5, §3.4). Table 5 recommends the z mode for tasks with no training budget that are one-off or low in volume, warning that it is brittle when the domain shifts and costs something on every call. Section 5 of "The paper in detail" meets this warning. The gain did not carry over to GPT-3's CSQA and StrategyQA, and coin flip varied by more than 28 percentage points depending on who wrote the chains. §3.4 sums up that z search wins when the task is hard but the environment is stable and verification is cheap.

Harness survey — not applicable

There is no corresponding section of the Harness survey for this chapter. The Harness survey has no section that cites or discusses this paper. The phrase "chain of thought" appears only twice in passing, in sentences introducing other papers (the discussion of formal verification and the discussion of token budgets in §5), and the CoT paper, self-consistency and DeepSeek-R1 do not appear. Still, this paper's experimental devices, such as "parse only the answer and pass it to the grader" and "fit eight examples into a 1,024-token window", could be seen as a small harness (Chapter 3).

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "CoT raises accuracy on any model." In the GSM8K column of Appendix Table 2, CoT is lower for models below 10B in all three families (LaMDA 420M 2.6 → 0.4, GPT 350M 2.2 → 0.5, PaLM 8B 4.9 → 4.1). Appendix A.1 writes that CoT hurts performance for most models smaller than 10B. The effect appeared only at around 100 billion parameters (§3.2).

Misreading 2. "The source of the effect is that a long solution spends more computation." The "variable compute only" ablation tested this explanation. When the model wrote dots as long as the solution, LaMDA 137B's GSM8K score was 6.4%, the same as standard (6.5%) (Appendix Table 6). The authors read the effect as coming from expressing the intermediate steps in natural language (§3.3).

Misreading 3. "The chain the model writes is the process by which the model actually reached the answer." The paper says the chain becomes a window onto the model's behavior, while adding the caveat that fully characterizing the computation is an open question (§2, §6). Even among chains that produced correct answers, some were right by coincidence (§3.2, Appendix D.1). What the "reasoning after answer" ablation showed is that the position of the chain affects the answer, not that the chain faithfully reports the computation.

Misreading 4. "CoT is a method for training models to reason." No model in this paper was fine-tuned (§6, Appendix E.2). Every result comes from prompting off-the-shelf models with examples. Changing the parameters to make the model write chains belongs to DeepSeek-R1 among the side papers.

Misreading 5. "The effect is large whether the task is hard or easy." On one-step SingleOp, PaLM 540B stayed at 94.1 → 94.1 (Appendix Table 3), and the gain on CSQA was also small (§4). Appendix A.3 names three conditions under which CoT helps most: the task requires multi-step reasoning, the model is large, and the scaling curve of standard prompting is relatively flat.

Misreading 6. "This paper sampled several solutions and took a majority vote." Every main experiment sampled once with greedy decoding (§3.1). Majority voting is the method of the follow-up work, self-consistency, which the main paper only cites in parentheses. CoT and CoT-SC in Table 1 of Chapter 6 correspond to the two papers respectively.

Discussion questions

  1. What changes when the model writes out a solution? "Equation only" helped on one- or two-step problems and was useless on GSM8K. In your own work, which errors does a form that asks only for conclusions reduce or increase, compared with a form that asks for the intermediate grounds? How would you measure the difference?

  2. Is "emergence" a property of the model or of the measurement? Look again at the table of gains by scale. If the metric were changed from exact-match accuracy to the log probability of the correct tokens or to partial credit, how might the picture change? What more would be needed to claim a threshold in the PaLM family, which has only three points? We continue in Chapter 18.

  3. One path, many paths, training. With the same compute budget, which would you choose: greedy CoT on a large model, self-consistency on a mid-sized model, or a small model that learned to reason through reinforcement learning? Weigh the costs and benefits of the z mode, which costs something on every call, against the θ mode, which costs once at training time, in light of Table 5 of the AR survey and the discussion of cost in Chapter 5.

Chapter 5 · Optional · ★

Chapter 5. Planning and Search — Tree of Thoughts

The question this chapter answers: what changes when the model spreads out several branches and chooses among them instead of thinking in a single line, and what does it cost?

Core reading. Shunyu Yao et al., "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models", NeurIPS 2023. 9 pages of main text, 14 with the appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · NeurIPS 2023 paper page · Code, prompts and trajectories

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §2.2, §3.1, Figure 2, Table 6 · the Harness survey has no section that overlaps with this chapter

One-paragraph summary. GPT-4, with its weights frozen, is made to write out its solution in units of "thoughts". At each step it produces several candidates for the next thought (the thought generator), the same model is asked whether each candidate has a chance of reaching the answer (the state evaluator), and breadth-first search (BFS) or depth-first search (DFS) carries on only the promising branches. The authors built three new tasks that GPT-4 also finds hard (Game of 24, Creative Writing and 5×5 Mini Crosswords) and tested on them. On the 100 hard Game of 24 problems, CoT solved 4.0% and ToT (breadth 5) solved 74%. The price is tokens. According to Appendix B.3, ToT spends 5.5k generated tokens per problem, close to what 100 CoT samples use (6.7k), and its cost per problem is higher, at USD 0.74. Today this framework is grouped, together with the MCTS family, under the heading of inference-time search.

What to cut from the presentation. The "Side papers" section of this chapter stands in for §5, Related Work. If time is short, skip the prompt strings in Appendix B.1 and the crossword details in Figure 6.

If you skip this chapter. This chapter has one ★ in this book. If you skip it, put the following paragraph into "Side papers" in Chapter 4 (or Chapter 6). "ToT (Yao et al. 2023) spreads CoT's single-line solution into a tree. It cuts the solution into units of 'thoughts,' produces several candidates at each step, has the same model evaluate their promise, and prunes branches with BFS or DFS. On the 100 hard Game of 24 problems, success rose from 4.0% with CoT to 74% with ToT (GPT-4, May 2023), but the generated tokens per problem match those of 100 CoT samples (Appendix B.3). Where CoT-SC picks among several finished solutions by majority vote, ToT picks and discards in the middle of solving".

If your group skipped Chapter 4. In the first 5 minutes of the presentation, read §2 of this paper. It formalizes IO, CoT and CoT-SC in one notation, which sums up the core of Chapter 4. In exchange, shorten the CoT entry under "Side papers".

When you quote the numbers. The scores in this paper come from GPT-4 in Chat Completion mode at temperature 0.7, run between May 5 and May 16, 2023 (footnote 1). Game of 24 has 100 problems and the crosswords 20 games. The IO and CoT cells are averages over 100 samples per problem (10 for the crosswords); for the ToT cells no number of repetitions is given (with no mention of an average, they read as the result of a single search). Give the model, the task, the metric and the number of problems together.

Building intuition

The four schematics of Figure 1

Figure 1 draws four ways of solving a problem in the same symbols. The ovals are the input and the output, and each gray rectangle is a "thought". In IO, a single arrow runs straight down from input to output. In CoT, thought rectangles run in a line between them. In CoT-SC, three strands split and each runs to the end, and the three ovals at the ends (two green, one pink) pass through "Majority vote" to become the output. In ToT, branches split at every node, some rectangles are green and some pink, and one path of dark green arrows reaches the output.

The legend does not explain the colors. The editor reads green as thoughts that passed evaluation and pink as discarded thoughts. The panel labels are (a) IO, (c) CoT, (c) CoT-SC and (d) ToT: there is no (b), and (c) appears twice. §3 of the text refers to ToT as "Figure 1(c)", but in the figure ToT is (d). In the presentation, call the panels by name from left to right to avoid confusion.

The differences among the four schematics come from two axes: how many candidates are produced (one or several), and when the choice is made (after writing or during writing). The table is the editor's arrangement.

Choose after writing Choose and discard while writing
One solution IO, CoT — nothing to choose —
Several solutions CoT-SC — majority vote over finished answers ToT — evaluates partial solutions and prunes branches

In the paper's words, existing methods have two shortcomings (§3). Locally, they do not explore different continuations within a thought process, that is, the branches of the tree. Globally, they have no planning, lookahead or backtracking.

One scene from Game of 24

Figure 2 shows what actually happens. The input is the four numbers 4 9 10 13, and the task is to make 24 with the four arithmetic operations. One thought is one line of equation.

(a) Propose Prompt
    {one example}
    Input: 4 9 10 13
    Possible next steps:
  → Thought Generation
    4 + 9 = 13 (left: 10 13 13)
    10 - 4 = 6 (left: 6 9 13)
    {...more lines...}

(b) Value Prompt
    Evaluate if given numbers can reach 24 (sure/likely/impossible)
    10 14: 10 + 14 = 24. sure
    {more examples}
    10 13 13
  → Thought Evaluation
    (13 - 10) * 13 = 3 * 13 = 39
    10 + 13 + 13 = 36 There is no way to obtain 24 with these big numbers. impossible

The two prompts and the model outputs in Figure 2 of the ToT paper. The braces and ellipses are in the original figure.

The propose prompt (a) gives one example and the remaining numbers, ends with "Possible next steps:", and gets back several lines. The value prompt (b) gives only the remaining numbers and asks for one of three answers on whether they can reach 24. The model in the figure tries two calculations on the 10, 13 and 13 left after 4 + 9 = 13 and answers impossible. In the tree on the left of the figure this branch is red, and the branch 10-4=6 → 13-9=4 → 4*6=24 is green. The evaluation rests on lookahead by trying a few calculations and on commonsense such as "1 2 3 are too small to reach 24," and the paper notes that "Such valuations do not need to be perfect, and only need to be approximately helpful for decision making" (§3).

The editor's bridge — search trees and the maximum of a sample

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

For developers, the closest thing is a sudoku solver. List the numbers that could go in one empty cell (generation), check whether putting one in breaks a rule (evaluation), and if it does, discard that branch and go back to the previous cell (pruning and backtracking). This is the DFS of Algorithm 2. The BFS of Algorithm 1 is closer to beam search. At each step it keeps only the b highest-scoring candidates and forgets the rest. A database administrator can think of a query optimizer, which estimates candidate join orders with a cost model and cuts them off early. ToT's state evaluator sits where that cost model sits.

For readers at home with statistics, the bridge is "draw several times and pick the best". The expected maximum of k draws is larger than the mean (order statistics). The "best of 100" in Table 2 picks with an oracle that knows the answer, while ToT picks with the model's own estimate. So the questions become: how accurate is the yardstick used to choose, and what does choosing cost?

The analogy also breaks down. A sudoku rule check and a cost model are deterministic and cheap. ToT's evaluator is a sampled language-model call, so its verdict can change each time it is called (which is why the evaluation is sampled three times), and its cost is of the same kind as generation. It also differs in that the evaluator and the generator are the same model. Nothing guarantees that it knows at evaluation time what it did not know at generation time.

The paper's own analogies are two. One is the dual-process model of human thinking (§1). A language model that decides token by token from left to right resembles the fast, automatic "System 1", so the idea is to augment it with the planning process of a deliberate "System 2". The other is the problem space of Newell, Shaw and Simon: search through a tree whose nodes are partial solutions and whose branches are operators. The opening of §3 carries a sentence from Newell et al. as its epigraph.

"A genuine problem-solving process involves the repeated use of available information to initiate exploration, which discloses, in turn, more information until a way to attain the solution is finally discovered."

The paper in detail

1. Formalizing existing methods — IO, CoT and CoT-SC (§2)

The paper writes language sequences with lowercase x,y,z,s and collections of sequences with uppercase S. The pretrained language model is pθ, and the conditional distribution wrapped in a prompt is abbreviated as pθprompt(output∣input)=pθ(output∣prompt(input)).

IO prompting. Wrap the input in task instructions and input-output examples and draw the output directly.

y~pθIO(y∣x)

CoT prompting. Place a chain of thoughts z1,…,zn between input and output. Each zi is a meaningful intermediate step toward the solution (for a math problem, an intermediate equation).

zi~pθCoT(zi∣x,z1⋯i−1),y~pθCoT(y∣x,z1⋯n)

The paper points out that in practice [z1⋯n,y] is sampled as one continuous language sequence, and where to cut a thought (a phrase, a sentence or a paragraph) is left ambiguous. This is the first point ToT sets out to fix.

CoT-SC. Sample k i.i.d. chains of thought and pick the most frequent answer.

[z1⋯n(i),y(i)]~pθCoT(z1⋯n,y∣x) (i=1,…,k),y^=argmaxy#{i∣y(i)=y}

The same problem generally has several thought processes (different ways to prove the same theorem), so exploring a richer set of thoughts makes the answer more faithful. In the paper's view, though, there are two limits. Within one chain there is no local exploration of different thought steps. And the "most frequent" heuristic only applies when the output space is limited (as in multiple-choice QA). To take the editor's example, majority vote does not work for creative writing, where the same passage will never come out twice.

2. ToT's four questions (§3)

ToT treats a problem as search over a tree. Each node of the tree is a state s=[x,z1⋯i], a partial solution made of the input and the thoughts so far. To build a specific ToT, you have to answer four questions.

① What unit to cut thoughts into (thought decomposition). CoT writes thoughts on without explicit decomposition. ToT designs its thought steps to fit the properties of the problem. The principle is one sentence: "a thought should be 'small' enough so that LMs can generate promising and diverse samples (e.g. generating a whole book is usually too 'big' to be coherent), yet 'big' enough so that LMs can evaluate its prospect toward problem solving (e.g. generating one token is usually too 'small' to evaluate)."

Game of 24 Creative Writing 5x5 Crosswords
Input 4 numbers (4 9 10 13) 4 random sentences 10 clues (h1. presented;..)
Output An equation to reach 24 (13-9)*(10-4)=24 A passage of 4 paragraphs ending in the 4 sentences 5x5 letters: SHOWN; WIRRA; AVAIL; ...
Thoughts 3 intermediate equations (13-9=4 (left 4,4,10); 10-4=6 (left 4,6); 4*6=24) A short writing plan (1. Introduce a book that connects...) Words to fill in for clues: (h1. shown; v5. naled; ...)
#ToT steps 3 1 5-10 (variable)

Table 1 of the paper. The cell text is the original's.

② How to generate thoughts (thought generator G(pθ,s,k)). There are two ways to produce k candidates for the next thought from a state s.

  • (a) Sample them independently from a CoT prompt: z(j)~pθCoT(zi+1∣s) (j=1,…,k). This works better when the thought space is rich (when one thought is a paragraph), because independent samples give diversity. Creative Writing works this way.
  • (b) Have a single "propose prompt" put out the candidates in sequence, all at once: [z(1),…,z(k)]~pθpropose(zi+1(1⋯k)∣s). This works better when the thought space is constrained (one word, one line of equation). Asking for several in the same context avoids duplicates. Game of 24 and the crosswords work this way.

③ How to evaluate states (state evaluator V(pθ,S)). This is the heuristic that decides which states the search algorithm continues from and in what order. Heuristics are usually programmed (DeepBlue) or learned (AlphaGo); the paper takes a third path and has the language model reason deliberately about the states. The authors' claim is that this can be more flexible than programmed rules and more sample-efficient than learned models.

  • (a) Value each state independently: V(pθ,S)(s)~pθvalue(v∣s). The value is a scalar such as 1–10 or a classification such as sure / likely / impossible, and a classification is turned heuristically into a value.
  • (b) Vote across states: V(pθ,S)(s)=1[s=s*], where s*~pθvote(s*∣S). This is used when it is hard to value directly, as with the coherence of a passage. The paper likens it to "a 'step-wise' self-consistency strategy". With either method, asking several times and aggregating gives a more reliable heuristic at greater cost.

④ Which search algorithm to use. The paper uses only two relatively simple ones and leaves advanced algorithms such as A* and MCTS for future work.

Algorithm 1  ToT-BFS(x, pθ, G, k, V, T, b)
Require: Input x, LM pθ, thought generator G() & size limit k,
         states evaluator V(), step limit T, breadth limit b.
S0 ← {x}
for t = 1, ..., T do
    S't ← {[s, z] | s ∈ S(t-1), zt ∈ G(pθ, s, k)}
    Vt  ← V(pθ, S't)
    St  ← argmax over S ⊂ S't with |S| = b of  Σ_{s∈S} Vt(s)
end for
return G(pθ, argmax_{s∈ST} VT(s), 1)

Algorithm 2  ToT-DFS(s, t, pθ, G, k, V, T, vth)
Require: Current state s, step t, LM pθ, thought generator G() and size limit k,
         states evaluator V(), step limit T, threshold vth
if t > T then record output G(pθ, s, 1)
end if
for s' ∈ G(pθ, s, k) do                      ▷ sorted candidates
    if V(pθ, {s'})(s) > vthres then          ▷ pruning
        DFS(s', t + 1)
    end if
end for

Algorithms 1 and 2 from §3 of the paper. Subscripts are written out as plain text.

BFS keeps the b most promising states at each step. It generates candidates from each state, evaluates all the candidates and picks the subset of b with the largest sum of values. At the last step it produces the output from the state with the highest value. It is used for Game of 24 and Creative Writing, where the tree is shallow (T≤3) and the early steps can be pruned to a small set (b≤5). DFS digs into the most promising state first, all the way down; when it reaches the output (t>T) or the evaluator judges that the problem cannot be solved from this state (V≤vth), it prunes the subtree below and backtracks to the parent state. It is used for the crosswords.

The pseudocode of Algorithm 2 has two places where the symbols do not match. The input argument is vth but the condition uses vthres, and the condition evaluates the candidate s′ while the argument outside the parentheses is s. Read together with the text (§3, 4(b)), it means "descend if the value of candidate s′ clears the threshold". The control flow also has one gap. The original t>T branch ends after recording the output, with no line that returns, so followed literally the search would enter the for loop below and continue even past the depth limit. The reproduction above leaves the original as it is. To match "until the final output is reached (t>T)" in the text, read it as returning from that call right after recording the output.

The four parts of one ToT step. The example values come from Figure 2 and §4.1 of the paper; the editor drew the diagram.

Four benefits the paper claims (§3). (1) Generality. IO, CoT, CoT-SC and self-refinement can be seen as special cases of ToT with limited depth and breadth. (2) Modularity. The model and the decomposition, generation, evaluation and search procedures can each be varied independently. (3) Adaptability. It can be fitted to the problem, the model's capability and resource constraints. (4) Convenience. No extra training is needed; one pretrained model is enough.

3. Game of 24 (§4.1)

Task. Make 24 from four numbers and the four arithmetic operations. Given the input "4 9 10 13", one solution is "(10 - 4) * (13 - 9) = 24". The authors took 1,362 games from 4nums.com. They are sorted from easy to hard by the time people take to solve them, and the 100 relatively hard games indexed 901–1,000 are used for testing. An output counts as a success if it is a valid equation that equals 24 and uses each input number exactly once. The metric is the success rate over the 100 games.

Baselines. All use the same GPT-4.

  • IO: five input-output examples.
  • CoT: the same examples with three intermediate equations added, for example "13 - 9 = 4 (left: 4 4 10); 10 - 4 = 6 (left: 4 6); 4 * 6 = 24 (left: 24)".
  • IO and CoT are sampled 100 times per game for the average score.
  • CoT-SC: the majority answer of 100 CoT samples.
  • IO + Refine: starts from one IO sample and revises it at most 10 times. If the equation is wrong, the model sees the whole history and is told to "reflect on your mistakes and generate a refined answer". It uses a ground-truth signal: whether the equation is correct.

ToT setup. The thoughts are split into three steps, three lines of intermediate equations. At each node the remaining numbers are extracted and the propose prompt asks for candidates for the next step (Figure 2(a)). The same propose prompt is used for all three steps, and that prompt has only one example with four numbers. The search is BFS, keeping the best b=5 candidates at each step. For evaluation, each candidate is rated sure / maybe / impossible on whether it can reach 24, and the value is sampled three times. The text says "maybe" while Figure 2 and §3 say "likely". They read as the same grade.

Scoreboard — Table 2 (GPT-4, 100 hard games)

Method Success
IO prompt 7.3%
CoT prompt 4.0%
CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%
ToT (ours) (b=1) 45%
ToT (ours) (b=5) 74%
IO + Refine (k=10) 27%
IO (best of 100) 33%
CoT (best of 100) 49%

Table 2 of the paper. The last three rows are set off by a rule in the original. IO + Refine uses a ground-truth signal, and best of 100 is an oracle setup that counts a success if any one of 100 samples is right (§4.1, Results).

Read the table in this order.

  1. CoT is lower than IO (4.0% against 7.3%). Asking for intermediate equations made it worse. The error analysis below gives a clue to why.
  2. ToT with breadth 1 already reaches 45%. It keeps only one candidate per step, so it is a solution that "goes in a single line while passing through evaluation", yet it scores five times CoT-SC. This is the combined effect of the propose prompt's format and step-by-step evaluation, and this table alone cannot separate the two.
  3. Widening the breadth to 5 gives 74%.
  4. It beats even the oracle. CoT best of 100, which knows the answer and picks a correct one among 100, reaches 49%.

Sample count and success rate — Figure 3(a). IO and CoT best of k (1≤k≤100) are treated as visiting k nodes, and ToT (b=1,…,5) is plotted by the number of nodes visited per game against success rate. The paper notes that CoT scales better than IO and that CoT best of 100 reaches 49%, but that it is still much worse than ToT with b>1. This chapter does not reproduce values read off the gridlines. The paper describes the horizontal axis only as "tree nodes visited per task" and does not say whether it counts the evaluation calls ToT makes three times per thought (the word "nodes" suggests they are left out). The same horizontal position does not mean the same amount of computation. For computation, see the token tables in section 6.

Error analysis — Figure 3(b). A bar chart broken down by the step at which a sample failed. For CoT the thought at that step, and for ToT all b remaining thoughts, being invalid or unable to reach 24 counts as failure. The horizontal axis is 1, 2, 3, 4, Correct. The text points out one thing. About 60% of CoT samples had already failed after writing the first step, that is, the first three words (such as "4 + 9"). The authors read this as a problem with direct left-to-right decoding. Once the first move is wrong, there is no way back. The paper does not explain what the fourth position on the horizontal axis is.

4. Creative Writing (§4.2)

Task. Given four random sentences, write a coherent passage of four paragraphs, each ending in one of the four sentences. It is an open-ended and exploratory task that calls for creative thinking and high-level planning at once. The 100 inputs were made from sentences drawn from randomwordgenerator.com. There is no ground-truth passage. GPT-4 follows the input constraints most of the time, so the evaluation focuses on the coherence (coherency) of the passage and measures it in two ways.

  • A zero-shot GPT-4 prompt gives a score from 1 to 10. Five scores are sampled per output and averaged. The five scores were usually consistent, with a standard deviation of around 0.56 per output on average.
  • People pair a CoT passage with a ToT passage and pick the more coherent one. A subset of the authors judged in a blind study, and the order of the two passages was flipped at random over the 100 inputs.

Baselines. Both IO and CoT are zero-shot, with instructions only. CoT first makes a short plan and then writes the passage; the plan is the intermediate thought. Ten samples are drawn per task. IO + Refine starts from one random IO sample and, at most five times, decides whether the passage is already "perfectly coherent" and, if not, writes a refined one.

ToT setup. Depth 2, with only one intermediate thought step. It makes k=5 plans and picks one by vote, then makes five passages from that plan and again picks one by vote. Only one is kept per step, so the breadth is b=1. Five votes are sampled at each step. Generation is (a) independent sampling from the previous section, and evaluation is (b) voting.

Figure 4 shows the first step of one task picked at random.

(a) Input
Write a coherent passage of 4 short paragraphs. The end sentence of each paragraph must be:
1. It isn't difficult to do a handstand if you just stand on your hands.
2. It caught him off guard that space smelled of seared steak.
3. When she didn't like a guy who was trying to pick her up, she started using sign language.
4. Each person who knows you has a different perception of who you are.

(b) Plans
Plan 1: 1. Introduce and explain the technique of doing a handstand 2. Switch to a story
        about an astronaut's first time in space …                              [0/5 votes]
Plan 2: 1. Introduction to an unusual self-help book, mentioning a handstand as a metaphor
        for embracing challenges. 2. Discuss the unexpected things learned from astronauts,
        including the smell of space. …                                        [3/5 votes]

(c) Votes
… Choice 2 offers an interesting perspective by using the required end sentences to present
a self-help book's content. … The best choice is 2.

From Figure 4 of the ToT paper. The editor shortened the plans and the vote (the ellipses " … " are the editor's omissions, though some of the omissions in the (c) vote panel are the "{...}" marks in the original figure).

Plan 1 only goes through the four sentences in turn. Plan 2 uses one "self-help book" as a frame to tie the four sentences to one theme, and gets 3 of 5 votes. When a thought is a one-paragraph plan, the evaluator can judge the prospect of coherence without the whole passage.

Results — Figure 5. The average GPT-4 score over the 100 tasks is 6.19 for IO, 6.93 for CoT and 7.56 for ToT (panel (a) is a box plot; the means are taken from the text). In the human comparison, of 100 pairs ToT was preferred in 41, CoT in 21, and 38 were similar (the numbers are printed on the bars in panel (b)). The paper says the human judgments make up for the noise of the automatic metric and confirm the same direction.

IO + Refine raised the IO score from 6.19 to 7.67, and refinement added on top of ToT raised the ToT score from 7.56 to 7.91. IO + Refine alone beat ToT (7.56). The authors grant that iterative refinement is more effective on this task, and suggest that producing new thoughts by refining old ones can be seen as a third way of generating thoughts.

5. Mini Crosswords (§4.3)

Why this task. In the first two tasks, ToT is a shallow tree with at most three thought steps. Crosswords are a deeper search problem. The authors write that the goal is not just to solve the task but to see the limits of a language model as a general problem solver.

Setup. Of the 156 games on GooBix, adjacent games have similar clues, so the 20 games indexed 1, 6, …, 91, 96 are used for testing and games 136, 141, 146, 151 and 156 for prompting. The input is five horizontal and five vertical clues, and the output is a board of 25 letters. Success is measured at three levels: the share of correct letters (25 per game), the share of correct words (10 per game) and the share of games solved.

Baselines. The IO prompt gives five input-output examples, and the CoT prompt adds intermediate words in the order h1..5 then v1..5. Each is sampled 10 times and averaged.

ToT setup. DFS (Algorithm 2). It keeps filling the most promising next clue, and when a state stops being promising it goes back to the parent state and explores another thought. To keep the search tractable, later thoughts may not change any word or letter already filled in, so the depth of a path (the number of clues filled) is at most 10. For generation, the thoughts so far are turned into letter constraints for the remaining clues (as in v1.To heap: tm_s_) and the propose prompt is called five times; the model is also asked to give a confidence level for each thought, and these are aggregated across proposals into a sorted list ("h4. salon (sure)", "v5. srdry (low)" and "v3. string (high)" in Figure 6(a)). For evaluation, the model is asked for each remaining clue whether it can be filled under the current constraints, and if even one is "impossible", the subtree below is pruned and the search backtracks (Figure 6(b)). DFS stops after 100 search steps ("We limit DFS search steps to 100") and takes the deepest explored state (the first explored one if there are several) as the output. A depth of 10 and 100 steps are different quantities. The first is the number of clues filled along one path; the second reads as the total number of times states were visited and expanded, backtracking included (the original says only "search steps").

Scoreboard — Table 3 (GPT-4, 20 games, success rate %)

Method Letter Word Game
IO 38.7 14 0
CoT 40.6 15.6 1
ToT (ours) 78 60 20
+best state 82.4 67.5 35
-prune 65.4 41.5 5
-backtrack 54.6 20 5

Table 3 of the paper. The last three rows are the oracle and the ablations. The game-level success rates of IO and CoT are averages over 10 samples, so they do not come to whole numbers of games.

  • ToT reached 60% at the word level and solved 4 of the 20 games. IO and CoT stay below 16% at the word level. The paper says this is not surprising, since IO and CoT have no mechanism to try different clues, change decisions or backtrack.
  • +best state. If the output is the state that is actually best among the states DFS passed through (an oracle), rather than the one picked by the heuristic, it solves 7/20 games. There is a lot of room to improve the output rule (the deepest state).
  • -prune. Stopping the evaluator from pruning makes results generally worse. Yet even in this setting the search reached the correct state in 4/20 games (only 1 game through the heuristic output), and 3 of those were games that ToT with pruning could not solve within 100 search steps. That means the evaluator sometimes cut off the right branch. The example in footnote 2 shows one cause: "agend" is an obsolete form of "agendum", but GPT-4 judged it a typo for "agenda". 5×5 crosswords contain rare or obsolete words by design. The authors add that external retrieval or web interaction could help when knowledge is uncertain.
  • -backtrack. With no backtracking, the search keeps filling the most promising clue for at most 20 steps, with overwriting allowed. This is similar to a "greedy" BFS with breadth 1, and it reaches only 20% at the word level.

6. Cost, efficiency and easier tasks (Appendix B)

Appendix B is short, but it is where the paper answers this chapter's question (what does it cost?) directly.

Applied to easier tasks — B.1, Table 4. The same generic zero-shot ToT-BFS as for Creative Writing (sample 5 strategies → vote → 5 solutions from that strategy → vote) was applied to GSM8K and StrategyQA, 100 random questions each (the GSM8K test set and the StrategyQA dev set).

GSM8K StrategyQA
IO 51 73
CoT 86 82
ToT 90 83

Table 4 of the paper. GPT-4, zero-shot prompts, accuracy (%).

The paper itself says "only slightly". The explanation is that GPT-4 + CoT already does well on these tasks and that StrategyQA's bottleneck is external knowledge. Given the cost, it recommends smaller models + ToT for traditional tasks.

Switching to a weaker model — B.2, Tables 5 and 6.

Game of 24 (GPT-4) Game of 24 (GPT-3.5) Creative Writing (GPT-4) Creative Writing (GPT-3.5)
IO 7.3% 6% 6.19 4.47
CoT 4.0% 3% 6.93 5.16
ToT 74% 19% 7.56 6.62

Table 5 (Game of 24 success rate) and Table 6 (Creative Writing GPT-4 scores) of the paper combined into one table. GPT-3.5 is gpt-3.5-turbo, and B.2 notes that on Game of 24 the propose prompt had to be changed from 1-shot to 3-shot to make it work.

The text says that "ToT > CoT > IO" still holds for GPT-3.5 on both tasks. On Creative Writing it does. On Game of 24 the table itself puts CoT (3%) below IO (6%) (as with GPT-4, 4.0% against 7.3%), so the sentence is right only in the sense that ToT is highest. There is also an experiment that separates generation from evaluation. Generating with GPT-4 and evaluating with GPT-3.5 gives 64%; the reverse gives 31%. The authors read this as saying the bottleneck is thought generation. The number of runs is not given.

Cost — B.3, Tables 7 and 8. ToT uses far more computation than IO or CoT.

CoT 0.9k / 0.4k $0.07
ToT 4k / 2.9k $0.32

Table 8 of the paper. The original caption is "Cost analysis on Game of 24", but the text introduces this table as the cost for Creative Writing, and the table header is also "Creative Writing". The caption appears to be a slip.

The paper reads them this way. On Game of 24, ToT spends 5.5k generated tokens per problem, close to 100 CoT trials (6.7k), but performs better than the best of 100 independent CoT trials. On Creative Writing, generated tokens and cost are about 5 times higher, and Appendix B.3 explains this as "intuitive as b=5 and most tokens are generated passages." But §4.2 gives the breadth limit as b=1 and the number of candidates as k=5 (section 4 of this chapter), so the b=5 in B.3 appears to refer to k=5. The paper puts the cost of the two main experiments at 0.74×100+0.32×100=106 dollars and says the crossword DFS experiments should also be within USD 100. ToT can need 5 to 100 times more generated tokens than CoT. The authors recommend using it on tasks where CoT struggles, matching cost by changing the beam size, the number of votes or the model, and they name stopping BFS early once a solution is found as one way to improve efficiency. The original wording is a recommendation, not "use it only on": "We recommend using ToT on tasks requiring deliberate reasoning, on which CoT struggles."

Do the numbers in the tables agree with each other? Five rows of Tables 7 and 8 (IO and CoT best of 100, and the three Creative Writing rows) are reproduced within ±USD 0.01 by a single pair of unit prices: about USD 0.062 per 1k generated tokens and about USD 0.024 per 1k prompt tokens. Computing ToT's Game of 24 row (5.5k / 1.4k) with the same prices gives about USD 0.38, roughly half of the USD 0.74 in the table. For USD 0.74, the prompt tokens would have to be a little over 16k, not 1.4k. The unit prices were not taken from outside the paper; they were back-calculated from the other rows of the tables. The paper alone cannot settle which number is wrong, but with a design that calls the evaluator three times per thought, there is reason to suspect the prompt column. When you quote the cost, say that the numbers disagree.

7. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

Game of 24 states its number of problems. It is 100 games. The Wilson 95% confidence intervals are [64.6%, 81.6%] for ToT (b=5) at 74%, [35.6%, 54.8%] for ToT (b=1) at 45%, [39.4%, 58.7%] for CoT best of 100 at 49%, and [4.8%, 16.2%] for CoT-SC at 9%. CoT's 4.0% is an average over 100 samples per game, so it is not "4 games", but if you roughly set it at 4/100 and run Fisher's exact test, the two-sided p value against 74/100 is about 7.9×10−27, and even against CoT-SC (9/100), which gives one answer per game, it is about 5.5×10−22. There is no doubt about this difference. What needs checking lies elsewhere.

The differences on easier tasks cannot be told apart. For GSM8K in Table 4, on the same 100 questions, CoT scores 86 and ToT 90. With the same questions, a paired comparison (McNemar) is the right one. Even on the most favorable assumption, that ToT got right all 86 questions CoT got right, the exact two-sided p value for all 4 discordant questions falling on ToT's side is 2×0.54=0.125. However the pairs are arranged, no difference can be claimed at the 5% level, and StrategyQA (82 against 83) has even less to say.

Creative Writing: the judge and the people. The human judgments are 41 for ToT, 21 for CoT and 38 ties. Dropping the tied pairs, a sign test gives a two-sided p≈0.015, and ToT's share of wins among the untied pairs is 66% (Wilson [53.7%, 76.7%]). But the judges, though blind to order, were the authors, who knew the hypothesis. The agreement between the GPT-4 scores and the human judgments cannot be computed. Without GPT-4 scores for each pair, no cross-tabulation can be made; all that can be confirmed is that the means point the same way. And ToT chose coherent plans and passages by GPT-4 votes, while the evaluation also has GPT-4 score coherence. The yardstick for choosing and the yardstick for measuring are the same, so part of the score gain can also be read as fitting the judge's taste. That is why the human judgments matter. With a standard deviation of 0.56 among the five scores per output, the standard error of one mean score is about 0.56/5≈0.25, but without the variance across tasks, the standard error of 7.56 against 6.93 cannot be found.

The rest is left for exercises.

Exercise 1 — bounding paired data with only the margins. The methods in Table 2 were compared on the same 100 games, but the paper does not give per-game results. (a) Treat ToT (b=5) at 74% and CoT best of 100 at 49% as independent samples and run Fisher's exact test. (b) Since the games are the same, the McNemar test is the right one. Knowing only the margins 74 and 49, construct the most favorable and least favorable cases for the discordant cells, and find the exact p value for each. (c) Do the same calculation for ToT with b=1 (45%) and b=5 (74%).

SolutionSolution

(a) The two-sided p value of Fisher's exact test is about 4.5×10−4.

(b) The discordant cells are "only ToT succeeds" (n10) and "only CoT best of 100 succeeds" (n01). The margins are fixed, so n10−n01=74−49=25. The most favorable case is when ToT solves all 49 games CoT solved, (n10,n01)=(25,0), with exact p≈6.0×10−8. The least favorable case is when the games both solve are the smallest possible number, 74+49−100=23, giving (51,26) with exact p≈0.0059. Either way, the difference is significant at the 5% level.

(c) Fisher's exact test gives p≈4.8×10−5. The range for the paired comparison runs from p≈3.7×10−9 at (29,0) to p≈0.0017 at (55,26).

Takeaway. When a design is paired but the paired results are not reported, readers can know the p value only as a range, not as a point. In this paper the differences are large enough that the whole range is significant, but for comparisons with small differences nothing can be said without per-question results.

Exercise 2 — best of 100 and a fair denominator for cost. (a) If a single CoT sample had the same 4.0% chance of success on every game, what should the best-of-100 success rate be? And for IO (7.3%)? Compare with the actual values, 49% and 33%. (b) Model the games as a two-point mixture in which a share π of games has success probability r and the rest have 0, and find the π and r that match the mean and the best of 100. (c) From Table 7, find the cost and the generated tokens "per game solved". (d) Without knowing the answer, what you can do with the same 100 CoT samples is CoT-SC (9%). Assuming CoT-SC costs the same as CoT best of 100, find its cost per game solved.

SolutionSolution

(a) 1−0.96100≈98.3%, and for IO 1−0.927100≈99.95%. The actual values are 49% and 33%. That means the chance of being solved differs greatly from game to game.

(b) Solving πr=m and π{1−(1−r)100}=best gives π≈0.49, r≈0.082 for CoT and π≈0.33, r≈0.22 for IO. A little over half the games are hardly ever solved even with 100 draws. If instead the success probability follows a beta distribution fitted to the same two conditions, CoT gets Beta(0.22, 5.27), with a median of 0.6% and 56% of games below 1%. This distribution predicts CoT best of 10, 20 and 50 at 21.7%, 30.0% and 41.2%. Best of k measures "how many games can be solved eventually" more than average skill. The pass@k of Chapter 17 is the same calculation.

(c) The cost per game solved is 0.13/0.33≈ USD 0.39 for IO best of 100, 0.47/0.49≈ USD 0.96 for CoT best of 100 and 0.74/0.74= USD 1.00 for ToT. The generated tokens per game solved are 5.5k, 13.7k and 7.4k. ToT pays USD 0.27 more than CoT best of 100 and gains 25 more percentage points, about USD 0.011 per percentage point. Compared with one CoT sample (about 67 tokens), that is about (5,500−67)/(74−4.0)≈78 generated tokens per percentage point.

(d) 0.47/0.09≈ USD 5.2. Among methods that can be used without an oracle, ToT (USD 1.00) is about five times cheaper per game solved than CoT-SC on the same budget (an assumption made because Table 7 has no CoT-SC row).

Takeaway. Cost efficiency changes with the denominator. Per problem, ToT is the most expensive; per game solved, it is about the same as the oracle best of 100; and among methods usable without the answer, it is the cheapest.

8. Limitations the paper states

  • Many tasks do not need it. Deliberate search like ToT may not be necessary for existing tasks that GPT-4 already does well (§6, Appendix B.1). This work covered only three relatively simple tasks that challenge GPT-4.
  • It takes more resources. Search uses more resources (GPT-4 API cost and the like) than sampling. The authors expect that modularity lets users tune the performance–cost trade-off and that open models will bring costs down (§6, Appendix B.3).
  • Only off-the-shelf models were used. The path of fine-tuning models with ToT-style counterfactual decision making, such as deliberating over candidates for the next paragraph instead of predicting the next token, is left open (§6).
  • The evaluator can be wrong. In the crosswords, the evaluator sometimes prunes words of a game that has actually been solved as "impossible", and the authors guess the cause is rare or obsolete words (§4.3 — the original hedges with "might" and "possibly").
  • Interaction with the outside world. The current tasks are limited to reasoning and search, but applications that interact with external environments or people could make harmful uses easier. On the other hand, the paper says, decisions remain in readable, high-level language, which improves interpretability and the opportunity for human alignment (Broader Impact).

The three tasks were built by the authors to be hard for GPT-4, and the paper says so (§6 "three relatively simple tasks that challenges GPT-4"; the opening of Appendix B "three hard tasks invented to challenge it"). The implication the editor draws is this. It is safer to read the distance between 74% and 4% as the gain "when you have chosen a task that needs search"; on general tasks, Table 4 points the other way.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

Planning survey (Huang et al. 2024). Written from the abstract only. A preprint that divides research on planning by LLM agents into five strands: Task Decomposition, Plan Selection, External Module, Reflection and Memory. The abstract does not say where ToT belongs. As the editor sees it, ToT, which produces several candidates and picks among them, touches Plan Selection, and its first question, choosing the unit of thought, touches Task Decomposition. If the survey is a map of planning methods as a whole, ToT is one item on it: tree search over units of thought within a single problem.

CoT and CoT-SC (CoT paper · Self-Consistency paper · Chapter 4 of this book). They are the three schematics on the left of Figure 1 and the baselines of Table 2. The CoT paper itself experimented with greedy decoding and mentions in parentheses the follow-up work showing that a majority vote over several samples raises scores. The difference is when the choice is made. CoT-SC picks among solutions written to the end by the frequency of their answers; ToT evaluates and discards partial solutions while writing. That is why ToT can be used for creative writing, where answers do not converge, and why the gap is largest on Game of 24, where about 60% of CoT samples fail at the first step.

ReAct (Yao et al. 2023 · Chapter 6 of this book). Same first author, and §5 of the ToT paper cites it as planning research. ReAct is a single path that chains thoughts and actions greedily, one at a time; in footnote 4 it suspects greedy decoding as the cause of repetitive loops and lists decoding such as beam search as future work. ToT went in that direction but does not look outside. Its three tasks have no actions and no observations, and footnote 2 and the Broader Impact statement leave external retrieval and interaction with environments for later. The contrast of ReAct as "a single line, looking outside" and ToT as "many branches, inside" is this book's reading.

Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book). §5 of the ToT paper cites it as an example of self-reflection (the reference list gives it under its old title). The difference is the time scale and what is kept. ToT prunes branches within one problem and keeps nothing when it is done. Reflexion writes a reflection into memory after an attempt ends and carries it to the next attempt. Table 6 of the revised AR survey also lists ToT as z and Reflexion as S. Among ToT's baselines, IO + Refine, which revises on a ground-truth signal, is closer to Reflexion.

RAP and the MCTS family (Hao et al. 2023). §5 of the ToT paper names it as concurrent work. It treats language-model reasoning as planning with an internal world model and proposes an MCTS-based method similar to ToT. The ToT authors judge that RAP's tasks are simpler and that its framework lacks the modularity to swap in different search algorithms (this is the authors' assessment). The revised AR survey lists Hao et al. (2023a) under the MCTS family and world-model-based planning in §3.1.1.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §2.2 — search objectives are not all the same

Of the three optimization targets in Chapter 2, ToT belongs to the first, in-context reasoning. It fixes the parameters θ and searches over the space Z of reasoning traces to raise a heuristic value v^(ht,z). The survey goes one step further and states separately that the search families within this regime do not share a single objective (survey §2.2, "In-Context Reasoning: Inference-Time Search." Section 4 of Appendix I in this book reproduces the formulas).

  • ReAct. Greedy decoding over alternating thoughts z and actions a.
  • ToT (best-first, BFS and DFS with value-based pruning). It expands a frontier under a node budget B, keeps a child u only when its value satisfies v^ϕ(u)≥κ, and returns the highest-scoring leaf at depth at most H. The objective is argmaxu∈LHv^ϕ(u) over the set LH of reachable leaves, not a sum along the path.
  • MCTS. It selects by an upper-confidence rule over the backed-up value Q(u,u′)=W(u,u′)/N(u,u′) accumulated by simulation, and follows the most-visited (or highest-Q) child from the root. What it maximizes is an estimate backed up from rollouts. (Optional reading) The survey does not explain the symbols. Read by MCTS convention, N is the number of simulations that passed through that branch (the visit count) and W is the sum of rewards those simulations obtained at the end, so Q is the mean reward. One cycle goes like this: starting from the root, descend by choosing branches with a score that adds to Q "a bonus that is larger for less-visited branches" (the upper-confidence rule), roll out roughly to the end from a leaf (the rollout), and add the reward obtained to the W and N of the branches passed through.
  • Process reward and step verifiers. Only here is a path sum the right object: τ⋆∈argmaxτ∈ΓH∑tv^ϕ(ut) (Eq. 2).

All of these methods plan within Z without updating the policy parameters. Placing the ToT paper's notation in this frame gives the following.

ToT paper §2–3 AR survey, revised version §2.2
Input x First observation o0 (the question)
Thought zi, state s=[x,z1⋯i] Reasoning trace z, node u∈U (a representation built from (ht,zt))
Thought generator G(pθ,s,k) The expansion operator that produces the trajectory set ΓH
State evaluator V(pθ,S) v^ϕ — in ToT, the same pθ given a value prompt
Step limit T Depth H (ToT's T is a different symbol from the environment's transition kernel T)
DFS threshold vth κ
Cap on DFS search steps (100 for the crosswords) Node budget B
Collection of states S No counterpart (a different symbol from the survey's system state S)
GPT-4 with frozen weights θ fixed, the z mode

Lining up the correspondence brings out three places where the survey's one-line formalization and the paper do not match. First, ToT's BFS does not keep the children above a threshold κ; it keeps the b with the largest sum of values (Algorithm 1). The threshold belongs to DFS. The survey's sentence reads as BFS and DFS folded into one line. Second, the crossword DFS outputs not the highest-scoring leaf but "the deepest explored state" (§4.3). Third, the survey's v^ϕ is written as if the value function had its own parameters ϕ, but ToT uses the same model as the generator, through a prompt, as its evaluator. The evaluator can be swapped for a different model, as in Appendix B.2. These mismatches arise when several papers are bundled under one notation, and they are why the originals need to be read alongside.

§3.1, Figure 2, Table 6 — where ToT sits

  • Figure 2. A figure that groups planning reasoning by optimization target. Under "In-context Planning (z)", the Tree Search box holds Traversal (BFS, DFS, MCTS) and Heuristic (A* search, Beam), with Process Formalization and Decomposition beside it. "System-level Planning (S)" has Workflow Design and Tool Use, and "Post-training Planning (θ)" has Reward Design. ToT belongs in the Tree Search box.
  • §3.1.1 Tree Search / Algorithm Simulation. It says tree search has become prominent as an interpretable planning scaffold, and gives Yao et al. (2023a) as the first example of work that explores thought trees with breadth- or depth-first strategies.
  • Table 6. The ToT row in the language-agents group has plan structure Tree, representation Natural Language, tool None and optimization target z. The foundational layer × in-context cell of Table 3 (§2.3) also contains "tree/graph search".
  • §4.1.1 (I-a). ToT also appears once in the feedback section. It says that the gains of search-based reasoning strategies (Yao et al. 2023a and others) come not from revising a single trajectory but from comparison across alternatives, and that every signal this group uses is generated by the model itself. The sentence points out that ToT's evaluator does not see the answer.

On the cost side. The §3.4 discussion says that searching z dominates when the task is hard, the environment is stable and the verifier is cheap, and points out that the three modes have almost never been compared at matched compute: "In-context search buys accuracy with tokens". Table 5 in §2.4 also warns that the cost of the z mode recurs with every call and grows with the breadth of search. ToT's Table 7 is a rare table that measures that cost, and as Exercise 2 showed, how it reads depends on the denominator.

Harness survey

The Harness survey has no section corresponding to this chapter and does not discuss ToT in its text. One line is added as this book's reading. The breadth b, the three evaluation samples, the cap of 100 DFS search steps and the output rule are all control flow set outside the model, so in the terms of Chapter 3 this is the same GPT-4 wearing a harness called search. The crosswords' +best state (20% → 35%) can be read as the upper bound (an oracle) on what can be gained by fixing the output rule.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "ToT is a method for training the model further." It leaves the weights as they are. One of the four benefits the paper claims is convenience: no extra training is needed (§3). The generator and the evaluator are both the same GPT-4 given different prompts. Training is left as future work in §6.

Misreading 2. "ToT is 18 times more accurate than CoT." 4.0% against 74% comes from the 100 hard Game of 24 games, chosen to be hard for GPT-4. On GSM8K it is 86 against 90 (Table 4), and that difference cannot be told apart statistically however the pairs are arranged (section 7).

Misreading 3. "ToT uses fewer tokens than running CoT 100 times, so it is cheaper." It uses fewer generated tokens, 5.5k against 6.7k, but costs more per problem, USD 0.74 against USD 0.47 (Table 7). What is more, that USD 0.74 does not match the unit prices back-calculated from the other rows of the table (section 6). Per game solved, ToT and CoT best of 100 are about the same.

Misreading 4. "CoT best of 100 is a fair baseline to set against ToT." It is an oracle setup that knows the answer and picks a correct one among 100 (§4.1). The method you could actually use on the same budget is CoT-SC, and its success rate is 9%.

Misreading 5. "ToT's evaluator judges by looking at the answer." It does not. The same model judges by looking only at the remaining numbers or the letter constraints. The baseline that uses a ground-truth signal is IO + Refine. The evaluator also makes mistakes: in the crosswords, turning pruning off reached the correct state in 3 games that ToT with pruning missed (§4.3).

Misreading 6. "ToT chooses thoughts with Monte Carlo tree search." The paper uses only BFS and DFS and leaves A* and MCTS for future work (§3). The revised AR survey also states the search objectives of ToT and MCTS separately.

Discussion questions

  1. The same model produces and the same model evaluates. In Appendix B.2, generating with GPT-4 and evaluating with GPT-3.5 gave 64%, and the reverse 31%. In your own work, what gets missed when the person (or model) who made a draft is also the one who screens it? Think ahead to the distinction between self-reflective and externally grounded feedback in Chapter 11.

  2. On the same budget, what would you buy? You could spend USD 0.74 per problem on search, or pool that money for fine-tuning or calls to a larger model. If you designed a fair comparison experiment, what would you use as the denominator (number of calls, tokens, money, latency)? Chapter 18 returns to this.

  3. Search before actions that cannot be undone. ToT's backtracking is a simulation in the head, so there is no cost of undoing what was done outside (the tokens and latency of producing and evaluating new candidates are still spent). What does backtracking mean for an agent that deletes files or makes payments (Chapter 6, Chapter 14)? §3.1.1 of the AR survey says that tree-search planning lets an agent backtrack and verify before committing to irreversible actions. How would you divide search before acting from correction after acting?
