Chapter 6 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 6. Thinking and Acting in Turn — ReAct

The question this chapter answers: for a language model to act while observing the outside world, where should "thinking" come in?

Core reading. Shunyu Yao et al., "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models", ICLR 2023. 10 pages of main text, 33 with the appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · ICLR 2023 presentation page · Project page · Code

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §2.2 · Harness survey §2.1, §6.2

One-paragraph summary. A language model with frozen weights (PaLM-540B) is shown one to six worked examples written by people and asked to write thoughts (Thought) and actions (Action) in turn. Actions go out to an environment such as the Wikipedia API or a text game, and the observation (Observation) the environment returns becomes material for the next thought. On the knowledge tasks, failures from made-up facts went down and failures of reasoning went up. On the decision-making tasks, the success rate beat imitation- and reinforcement-learning baselines trained on 103 to 105 examples. The basic loop of today's coding agents has this structure.

Presenter's guide

A 50-minute plan. The 10 minutes after the presentation are for discussion.

Time Content In the paper
0–5 min The question and the intuition: put the four prompting methods in a 2×2 table Figure 1(1)
5–15 min Formalization: adding language to the action space §2 (a little over a page)
15–27 min Knowledge tasks: the scoreboard and the success and failure modes §3.1–3.3, Table 1, Table 2, Figure 2
27–35 min Decision-making tasks — first show which thoughts were removed in the ALFWorld pepper-shaker trajectory (Figure 1(2)), then use the Act, ReAct and ReAct-IM comparison to point out "kinds of thought". Cut WebShop down to the metrics and one line of Table 4 results §4 ALFWorld paragraphs, Table 3, Figure 1(2) (WebShop and Table 4 as advance reading)
35–45 min Side papers: how CoT, Inner Monologue and Reflexion differ "Side papers" in this chapter
45–50 min Back to the surveys: where assumption A2 breaks AR survey, revised version §2.2

Must read. §1 (especially Figure 1), all of §2, §3.1–3.3, and the ALFWorld paragraphs of §4 with Table 3 and Table 4. If you show only one figure, make it Figure 1. Set the four panels of (1) beside the two panels of (2) and most of what the paper claims is visible.

Optional reading. Appendix A.3 and Figure 5 (a person edits two lines of thought and turns a trajectory that would have failed into a success), Appendix A.1 and Table 5 (the results rerun with GPT-3), Appendix A.2 and Figure 4 (an example where the dataset's answer had gone out of date).

What to cut from the presentation. Look at only one of the full prompts in Appendix C. The first ReAct example for HotpotQA in C.1 (Colorado orogeny) is enough. The "Side papers" section of this chapter stands in for §5, Related Work. Skip Appendix B (details of fine-tuning and ReAct-IM) and Appendix D (collected trajectories).

If your group skipped Chapter 4. In the first 10 minutes, introduce three figures from the CoT paper (Wei et al. 2022): Figure 1 (standard prompting against CoT on one arithmetic word problem), Figure 3 (examples for arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning) and Figure 4 (the effect appears only as the model grows). Cut the side papers to 5 minutes.

When you quote the numbers. The main ReAct prompting experiments in this paper (Tables 1–4) come from the 2022 PaLM-540B given a few examples. The fine-tuned PaLM-8B and 62B (Figure 3), the GPT-3 rerun (Appendix Table 5) and the outside baselines taken from other papers (supervised state of the art, BUTLER, IL and IL+RL) were run under different conditions, so report them separately. When you put a number on a slide, give the model, the task and the metric (EM, accuracy or success rate) with it.

Building intuition

Putting Figure 1 in a 2×2 table

The paper built its three baselines by deleting parts of ReAct trajectories (§3.2, Baselines). Delete the thoughts, actions and observations and you get Standard; delete the actions and observations and you get CoT; delete only the thoughts and you get Act. Treated as two factors, this makes a 2×2 table. The table is the editor's arrangement, and reading it like a factorial experiment shows the paper's comparison design at a glance.

Does not ask the outside world Asks the outside world
Does not write thoughts Standard — answers at once Act — only searches
Writes thoughts CoT — reasons from memory alone ReAct — reasons while searching

The question in Figure 1(1) is this: "Aside from the Apple Remote, what other device can control the program Apple Remote was originally designed to interact with?" The three baselines each go wrong in a different way, and ReAct reaches the right answer.

  • Standard answers "iPod".
  • CoT starts from a wrong fact ("Apple Remote was originally designed to interact with Apple TV.") and arrives at "iPhone, iPad, iPod Touch". The form of the reasoning is fine. The fact it started from was wrong.
  • Act searches three times and gets as far as finding that Front Row is discontinued media center software. Then it ends with Finish[yes]. The paper's diagnosis is that choosing the last action required complex reasoning over the whole trajectory, and Act could not do it (§2). In the editor's words, it forgot what it was looking for.
  • ReAct reaches "keyboard function keys" by the trajectory below.
Thought 1: I need to search Apple Remote and find the program it was originally
           designed to interact with.
Act 1:     Search[Apple Remote]
Obs 1:     The Apple Remote is a remote control introduced in October 2005 by Apple
           … originally designed to control the Front Row media center program …
Thought 2: Apple Remote was originally designed to control the Front Row media center
           program. I need to search Front Row next and find what other device can
           control it.
Act 2:     Search[Front Row]
Obs 2:     Could not find [Front Row]. Similar: ['Front Row Seat to Earth',
           'Front Row Motorsports', 'Front Row (software)', …]
Thought 3: Front Row is not found. I need to search Front Row (software).
Act 3:     Search[Front Row (software)]
Obs 3:     Front Row is a discontinued media center software …
Thought 4: Front Row (software) is controlled by an Apple Remote or the keyboard
           function keys. So the answer is keyboard function keys.
Act 4:     Finish[keyboard function keys]

The trajectory in Figure 1(1d) of the ReAct paper. The ellipses are in the original figure.

Each of the four thoughts does a different job. Thought 1 splits the question into two steps. Thought 2 pulls out only the needed fact from the observation and decides the next search term. Thought 3 recovers from a failed search. Thought 4 pulls the answer out of the observation and concludes. These lines are the very examples the paper gives when §2 lists the uses of thoughts (goal decomposition in thought 1, extracting from observations in thoughts 2 and 4, handling exceptions in thought 3).

The editor's bridge — sequential experimental design

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

In a sequential experimental design, where to take the next observation is decided by looking at the data gathered so far. In between, the researcher runs an interim analysis and writes down what is known so far, what is still missing and therefore what to measure next. ReAct's thought corresponds to this interim-analysis record, its action to the choice of the next observation point, and its observation to the newly arrived data.

Seen this way, the baselines' failures read as a researcher's failures. Act is a researcher who chooses observation points but keeps no interim analysis. After the third observation it loses the original question. CoT is a researcher who writes the conclusion from memory without collecting more data. Developers can think of an interactive SQL session. You send a query, look at the result, add a one-line comment and write the next query. Chain queries with no comments, and by about the fifth one you forget why you were looking at this table.

The analogy also breaks down. A sequential design fixes its stopping rule and error rate in advance. In ReAct the model decides when to stop (Finish), and from outside only a cap on the number of steps is set.

The paper's own analogy is the kitchen (§1). A cook thinks in words between two actions: "now that everything is cut, I should heat up the pot of water"; "I don't have salt, so let me use soy sauce and pepper instead"; "how do I prepare dough? Let me search on the Internet". The authors explain this by drawing on the cognitive-science literature on inner speech and working memory.

The paper in detail

1. Formalization — adding "words" to the action space (§2)

At time t the agent receives an observation ot∈𝒪 from the environment and chooses an action at∈𝒜 according to a policy π(at∣ct). The context ct is the observations and actions so far, strung together.

ct=(o1,a1,…,ot−1,at−1,ot)

The problem the paper points to is that when the mapping ct↦at is highly implicit and needs a lot of computation, the policy is hard to learn. Examples are the Act agent in Figure 1(1c), which got the last action wrong, and the Act agent in Figure 1(2a), which did not notice that there was no pepper shaker at the sink and repeated the same action.

ReAct's idea fits in one line. Add the language space ℒ to the action space.

𝒜^=𝒜∪ℒ

The paper calls an action a^t in ℒ a thought or a reasoning trace. A thought does not change the environment, so no observation comes back. Instead it extends the context.

ct+1=(ct,a^t)

The ALFWorld trajectory implements this formalization literally. The first action in Figure 1(2b) is Act 1: Think[First I need to find a pepper shaker...]. The thought appears as an action named Think[…].

One cycle of ReAct. The thought on the left only accumulates in the context, and only the action in the middle goes out to the environment. The editor drew the diagram from the formalization in §2 of the paper.

Uses of thoughts. The paper does not fix the kinds of thought. It gives examples of their uses instead (§2, §3.2).

Use Example in the paper
Decompose the goal and make a plan "I need to search x, find y, then find z"
Extract what is needed from an observation "x was started in 1844", "The paragraph does not tell x"
Reason with commonsense or arithmetic "x is not y, so z must instead be...", "1844 < 1989"
Reformulate the search "maybe I can search/look up x instead"
Track progress and move on to the next subgoal "Now I find a pepper shaker 1. Next, I need to put it in/on drawer 1." (Figure 1(2b), Act 8)
Synthesize the answer "...so the answer is x"

Why prompting. ℒ is an unbounded space, so learning a policy from scratch in this augmented action space is hard. It needs strong language priors. So the paper mainly uses a setting in which a frozen PaLM-540B is shown a few trajectories written by people as examples. Each example is a record of the actions, thoughts and observations a person left while solving the task (Appendix C).

Density of thoughts. How thoughts are inserted depends on the task.

  • On reasoning-heavy tasks (HotpotQA and FEVER), thought, action and observation alternate at every step. The paper calls this dense thought.
  • On action-heavy decision-making tasks (ALFWorld and WebShop), thoughts appear only sparsely, at the places in the trajectory where they are needed. The model decides when to think.

Four properties the paper claims (§2). A) It is easy to design. Annotators only type their thoughts on top of their actions, and the paper says it made no ad-hoc choices of format or examples. B) It works across tasks with different action spaces and reasoning needs. C) With only one to six examples it consistently beats baselines that only think or only act, and it is robust to the choice of prompt (§4). Set beside the tables, these two claims can also be read differently. On HotpotQA, ReAct scored below CoT, which only thinks (Table 1), and the ALFWorld success rate ranged from 48% to 71% depending on the prompt (Table 3). D) People can read and correct the trajectories. Figure 5 in Appendix A.3 shows this last property.

2. Knowledge tasks — HotpotQA and FEVER (§3)

Tasks. HotpotQA is multi-hop question answering, where the answer requires passing through two or more Wikipedia passages; the metric is exact match (EM). FEVER is fact verification, judging a claim as one of SUPPORTS, REFUTES or NOT ENOUGH INFO; the metric is accuracy. In both tasks the model gets only the question or claim, not the supporting passages. It has to rely on its internal knowledge or fetch knowledge by interacting with the environment.

Action space. The Wikipedia API accepts only three actions.

Action What it returns
search[entity] The first 5 sentences of the page with that name if it exists, otherwise the top 5 similar entities from the Wikipedia search engine
lookup[string] The next sentence in the current page that contains the string (like Ctrl+F in a browser)
finish[answer] Submits the answer and ends the task

The API was made weak on purpose. You need the exact page name, and it returns only a small part of a passage at a time. The paper itself notes that it is significantly weaker than state-of-the-art lexical or neural retrievers. The aim is to mimic how people use Wikipedia and to force the model to retrieve only through explicit reasoning in language.

Prompts. From the training set, 6 cases for HotpotQA and 3 for FEVER were chosen at random, and people wrote ReAct-format trajectories for them. Adding more examples did not improve performance (footnote 2).

Baselines.

  • Standard: question–answer examples with all thoughts, actions and observations deleted from the trajectories.
  • CoT: examples with actions and observations deleted, keeping only the thoughts.
  • CoT-SC (self-consistency): sample 21 CoT trajectories at temperature 0.7 and pick the answer by majority vote.
  • Act: examples with only the thoughts deleted. The paper notes that this loosely resembles how WebGPT uses the internet.

Combining the two methods. The paper judges that ReAct is more factual and grounded while CoT is better at structuring its reasoning, and it made two rules for switching between them.

  • ReAct → CoT-SC: if ReAct does not return an answer within a fixed number of steps, fall back to CoT-SC. The step caps are 7 for HotpotQA and 5 for FEVER. Among trajectories that reached the right answer, those that went to 7 steps (HotpotQA) or 5 steps (FEVER) were only 0.84% and 1.33% (footnote 3).
  • CoT-SC → ReAct: if the majority answer appears fewer than n/2 times among n CoT-SC samples — that is, if the internal knowledge looks unsure — switch to ReAct.

Readers with a statistics background will recognize the second rule. It uses the share of the modal answer among the sampled answers as a proxy for confidence.

Scoreboard — Table 1 (PaLM-540B, prompting)

Method HotpotQA (EM) FEVER (accuracy)
Standard 28.7 57.1
CoT 29.4 56.3
CoT-SC 33.4 60.4
Act 25.7 58.9
ReAct 27.4 60.9
CoT-SC → ReAct 34.2 64.6
ReAct → CoT-SC 35.1 62.0
Supervised SoTA 67.5 89.5

Table 1 of the paper. According to its footnote, the HotpotQA EM reported in another paper (Wang et al. 2022b) is 27.1 for Standard, 28.9 for CoT and 33.8 for CoT-SC. The FEVER supervised state of the art, 89.5, is cited from Lewis et al. 2020 (RAG, Chapter 8), but that paper's 89.5 is a two-way (FEVER-2) score; RAG's score on the three-way task ReAct solves is 72.5. Keep this in mind when you read the two papers side by side.

Read the table in this order.

  1. ReAct beats Act on both tasks (27.4 against 25.7, 60.9 against 58.9). This is the comparison the paper puts forward as evidence that thoughts help guide actions.
  2. ReAct and CoT split by task. On FEVER, ReAct is higher (60.9 against 56.3); on HotpotQA, slightly lower (27.4 against 29.4). The paper's explanation: "Fever claims for SUPPORTS/REFUTES might only differ by a slight amount (see Appendix D.1), so acting to retrieve accurate and up-to-date knowledge is vital."
  3. The combinations do best. On HotpotQA, ReAct → CoT-SC (35.1); on FEVER, CoT-SC → ReAct (64.6).
  4. Even so, all of them fall far short of the supervised state of the art.

Success and failure modes — Table 2. The scoreboard alone does not show how ReAct and CoT go wrong differently. The authors drew at random 50 trajectories with correct answers and 50 with incorrect answers (judged by EM) from each of ReAct and CoT on HotpotQA, 200 in all, and labeled the modes by hand.

Type Definition ReAct CoT
Success True positive Correct reasoning trace and facts 94% 86%
Success False positive Hallucinated reasoning trace or facts 6% 14%
Failure Reasoning error Wrong reasoning trace (including failing to recover from repetitive steps) 47% 16%
Failure Search result error Search return empty or does not contain useful information 23% —
Failure Hallucination Hallucinated reasoning trace or facts 0% 56%
Failure Label ambiguity Right prediction but did not match the label precisely 29% 28%

Table 2 of the paper. The caption says only that these are percentages in randomly selected examples studied by humans. From the layout of the table, they read as shares within the 50 successes and within the 50 failures (the editor's reading).

The paper draws three observations from this table.

  • Hallucination is CoT's biggest problem. Hallucination accounts for 56% of its failures, and even among correct answers 14% rest on made-up facts.
  • ReAct gained grounding and lost flexibility. The structural constraint of interleaving thought, action and observation keeps it from formulating reasoning steps freely, and reasoning errors went up (47% against 16%). A frequent failure was repeating the previous thoughts and actions and never getting out of the loop. The authors suspect greedy decoding as the cause and note that better decoding such as beam search might help (footnote 4).
  • ReAct lives or dies by useful search. Non-informative search results account for 23% of the errors. Once it goes off track, it has a hard time recovering and reformulating its thoughts.

The authors call this "perhaps an expected trade-off between factuality and flexibility" and use it to justify the combined methods above.

How efficiently the combinations use samples — Figure 2. The horizontal axis of this figure is the number of CoT-SC samples. Both combined methods are above CoT-SC at every sample count, and with only 3 to 5 samples they reach the performance of CoT-SC with 21. Mixing in outside knowledge gets the same accuracy with fewer samples.

Fine-tuning — Figure 3. Writing reasoning traces by hand at scale is hard. So small models (PaLM-8B and 62B) were fine-tuned on 3,000 trajectories with correct answers produced by ReAct (and by each baseline). This is bootstrapping similar to STaR (Zelikman et al. 2022), which retrains a model on the correct solutions it generated itself.

  • With prompting alone, at 8B and 62B ReAct is the worst of the four methods. Learning to reason and act together from a few examples is hard for a small model.
  • Fine-tuned on 3,000 trajectories, ReAct becomes the best. The fine-tuned 8B ReAct beats every prompting method at 62B, and the fine-tuned 62B ReAct beats every prompting method at 540B.
  • The paper's interpretation: fine-tuning Standard or CoT teaches the model to memorize (possibly made-up) facts, while fine-tuning ReAct or Act teaches it how to fetch information from Wikipedia, and the latter generalizes better.

This chapter does not reproduce values read off the figure's gridlines. The paper does not give the numbers in Figure 3 as a table either.

When the answer is out of date — Appendix A.2. The question in Figure 4 asks for the number of rooms in the hotel where a certain show is performed. The room count went up after the dataset was built, so the dataset's answer is out of date and the current value ReAct retrieved is actually correct. In this case EM counts a right answer as wrong. This is a case to bring back in Chapter 17 when we discuss the validity of evaluations.

3. Decision-making tasks — ALFWorld and WebShop (§4)

ALFWorld. A text game built to match the embodied benchmark ALFRED. There are six task types. The agent receives a high-level goal such as "examine paper under desklamp" and moves around a simulated house with text actions such as go to coffeetable 1 and take paper 2. One task can have more than 50 locations, and an expert policy can take more than 50 steps. It needs commonsense, for example that a lamp is usually on a desk or a shelf, so this is an environment where a language model's prior knowledge helps.

  • Prompts: for each task type, three trajectories were chosen from the training set and annotated with sparse thoughts. The thoughts decompose the goal, track subgoal completion, decide the next subgoal and reason by commonsense about where an object is likely to be.
  • Evaluation: 134 unseen games.
  • Robustness check: choosing two of the three annotated trajectories with order taken into account gives 3×2=6 prompts. All six were run for each task type.
  • Controlled comparison: the Act prompts delete only the thoughts from the same trajectories. The paper's explanation is that the example tasks were chosen at random from the training set, so this is a controlled comparison that favors neither side.
  • Outside baseline: BUTLER, an imitation-learning agent trained on 105 expert trajectories per task type.

Scoreboard — Table 3 (success rate by task type, %)

Method Pick Clean Heat Cool Look Pick 2 All
Act (best of 6) 88 42 74 67 72 41 45
ReAct (avg) 65 39 83 76 55 24 57
ReAct (best of 6) 92 58 96 86 78 41 71
ReAct-IM (avg) 55 59 60 55 23 24 48
ReAct-IM (best of 6) 62 68 87 57 39 33 53
BUTLERg (best of 8) 33 26 70 76 17 12 22
BUTLER (best of 8) 46 39 74 100 22 24 37

Table 3 of the paper. The BUTLER figures come from Table 4 of the original ALFWorld paper (Shridhar et al. 2020b). Only BUTLER uses beam search; the others use greedy decoding.

  • The best ReAct run, at 71%, beats the best Act (45%) and BUTLER (37%). Even the worst ReAct run (48%) is above the best runs of both.
  • ReAct beat Act in all six controlled runs, with relative gains from 33% to 90%, 62% on average.
  • Qualitatively, Act without thoughts fails to decompose the goal into subgoals or loses track of the environment's current state. In Figure 1(2a), Act tries Take peppershaker 1 from sinkbasin 1 twice at a sink with no pepper shaker and gets "Nothing happens." both times.

The ablation against Inner Monologue. The closest prior work is Inner Monologue (IM, Huang et al. 2022b). It guides an embodied agent's actions with feedback injected from the environment — the "inner monologue". The authors judge that IM's monologue is limited to observations of the environment's state and what remains to be done for the goal, and they built ReAct-IM by re-annotating the same expert trajectories with only IM-style dense external-feedback thoughts (Appendix B.2). ReAct-IM has no thoughts that judge when a subgoal is finished, what the next subgoal is or where an object is likely to be. Appendix B.2 says that ReAct-IM does think about decomposing the current goal, while the body of §4 gives "a lack of high-level goal decomposition" as a cause of ReAct-IM's failures. How to reconcile the two statements is an open question and worth raising in the presentation.

The result is 71 against 53 (all task types, best of 6), and the paper says ReAct comes out ahead on five of the six types. The exception in the table is Clean (58 against 68 on best of 6). ReAct-IM often misjudged whether a subgoal was finished and what to do next, and failed to work out where an object was likely to be. The result says the problem is the kind of thought, not the amount.

WebShop. An online shopping environment built from 1.18 million real products scraped from Amazon and 12,000 purchase instructions written by people. The agent receives an instruction such as "I am looking for a nightstand with drawers. It should have a nickel finish, and priced lower than $140" and searches, picks a product, picks options and buys. Evaluation uses 500 test instructions. There are two metrics. The average score is the average percentage of desired attributes the chosen product has, and the success rate (SR) is the share of episodes that satisfy every requirement.

Method Score Success rate
Act 62.3 30.1
ReAct 66.6 40.0
IL (imitation learning on 1,012 human trajectories) 59.9 29.1
IL+RL (plus reinforcement learning on 10,587 training instructions) 62.4 28.7
Human expert 82.1 59.6

Table 4 of the paper. IL and IL+RL are the figures from the original WebShop paper (Yao et al. 2022).

Act, given a single example, is already on par with IL and IL+RL. ReAct, which adds sparse thoughts, is about 10 percentage points above the previous best success rate in absolute terms (40.0 against 29.1). The abstract's absolute gains of 34% (ALFWorld) and 10% (WebShop) refer to 71 − 37 and to this difference. The gap to human experts is still large. The paper points out that people browse far more products and rewrite their queries more often.

Does it work with another model — Appendix A.1. The results rerun with GPT-3 (text-davinci-002, greedy decoding).

PaLM-540B GPT-3
HotpotQA (EM, 500 questions sampled at random from the validation set) 29.4 30.8
ALFWorld (success rate %, all 134 unseen tasks, best prompt according to PaLM) 70.9 78.4

Table 5 of the paper.

The PaLM-540B HotpotQA value here, 29.4, differs from ReAct's 27.4 in Table 1. The difference seems to come from a different set of questions, but the paper does not explain it. Do not mix the numbers of the two tables.

4. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

Table 1 has no question count and no uncertainty. Nowhere in the main text or the appendices is the number of evaluation questions behind Table 1 given (only the GPT-3 comparison in Appendix Table 5 says it uses a 500-question subset). Without the question count you cannot judge whether a difference lies within the range of chance. Make one assumption. If there were 500 questions, the standard error near an EM of 28% would be 0.28×0.72/500≈0.020. That means a half-width of about 4 percentage points for the 95% interval. The 2.0-point difference between ReAct's 27.4 and CoT's 29.4 then falls inside it. The two methods were compared on the same questions, so a paired analysis by question could narrow this, but that needs per-question results. The 500 is only an assumption.

The WebShop difference holds up. The 500 test instructions are stated. With no per-question results, treat ReAct's success rate of 40.0% and Act's 30.1% as independent samples: the standard error of the difference is about 3.0 percentage points, and the 9.9-point difference is 3.3 times that. Because the two methods were compared on the same 500 instructions, a positive correlation between their successes and failures would make the paired standard error smaller, and this approximation would then be conservative. A negative correlation would do the opposite, but there is little reason for one on the same items. Not every difference is noise.

The other two are left for you to calculate as exercises.

Exercise 1 — each cell of Table 2 rests on 50 cases. (a) 56% of CoT's failures are hallucinations, against 0% for ReAct. How many cases is each? Find the 95% confidence interval for each proportion and the exact-test p value for the null hypothesis that the two proportions are equal. (b) Do the same for the false positives among successes, 6% (ReAct) and 14% (CoT). (c) What do 47%, 23%, 0% and 29% in ReAct's failure column come to in cases out of 50? (d) These 200 cases are a stratified sample with 50 correct and 50 incorrect answers fixed in advance. Using the EM in Table 1 as the stratum weights, estimate for ReAct and for CoT the share of all answers that contain made-up facts.

SolutionSolution

(a) 56% is 28 of 50 cases and 0% is 0 cases. The Wilson 95% confidence intervals are [42.3%, 68.8%] and [0%, 7.1%], and the two-sided p value of Fisher's exact test is about 3.6×10−11. Fifty cases are enough to separate them.

(b) 6% is 3 cases and 14% is 7. The Wilson intervals, [2.1%, 16.2%] and [7.0%, 26.2%], overlap widely, and the two-sided p value of Fisher's exact test is about 0.32. The impression that "CoT's false positives are more than double ReAct's" cannot be told apart from chance at this sample size.

(c) They come to 23.5, 11.5, 0 and 14.5 cases, which are not whole numbers, and the sum is 99%. The paper does not say whether this is rounding, more than one mode assigned to a trajectory or a denominator other than 50. CoT's failure column in the same table (16%, 56%, 28%) comes out exactly at 8, 28 and 14 cases.

(d) The percentages in the table are shares "given failure" or "given success". To turn them back into overall shares, weight each stratum and add. Assuming the EM in Table 1 can be used as the weight of success,

CoT:(1−0.294)×0.56+0.294×0.14≈0.395+0.041=0.437

ReAct:(1−0.274)×0+0.274×0.06≈0.016

The estimate is that a little over 40% of CoT's answers contain made-up facts, against about 2% for ReAct. The strata were split by EM, so using Table 1's EM as stratum weights is natural. But the paper does not say whether the 200 cases were drawn from the same evaluation set as Table 1, so this is only a rough estimate.

Takeaway. Within the same table, some differences (0 against 28 cases) hold up and others (3 against 7) do not. And do not read conditional shares as if they were overall shares.

Exercise 2 — what does "best of 6" inflate? On ALFWorld, ReAct's average over the six prompts is 57% and its best is 71%. (a) If the six prompts truly performed the same and each estimate were independent, how much higher than the average would you expect the maximum of the six to come out? Calculate with a success rate of 57% and 134 games. (b) What can you say when you compare this with the actual difference of 14 percentage points? (c) What is the fairest comparison in this table?

SolutionSolution

(a) The standard error of one prompt's success-rate estimate is 0.57×0.43/134≈0.043, or 4.3 percentage points. The expected maximum of 6 independent draws from a standard normal distribution is about 1.27. So even if all the prompts performed the same, you would expect the maximum to come out 1.27×4.3≈5.4 percentage points above the average. A maximum picked on the evaluation set is biased upward by that much.

(b) 5.4 percentage points is only the expected value of "maximum − average" under the null model; a judgment needs the upper tail of that distribution. Simulating under the same assumptions (success probability 57%, 134 games, six independent runs; 200,000 repetitions), the 95th percentile of "maximum − average" is 9.3 percentage points, the 99th percentile is 11.3, and the probability of 14 or more is about 0.1%. The actual 14 points clear these thresholds, so a model in which all six prompts perform the same has trouble explaining it. It is more natural to conclude that the prompts really differ in performance. In addition, the six runs use the same 134 games, so the estimates may be positively correlated. If so, the null distribution narrows and the conclusion gets stronger. The sign and size of that correlation, though, are a separate assumption, not something checked against data. That the choice of prompt moves performance this much is itself a weakness of the method and something to report.

(c) Average against average is fair, but the table has no average for Act. Two things the paper states separately in the text are fairer comparisons. One is the result of pairing ReAct and Act within each of the six controlled runs (relative gains of 33% to 90%, 62% on average), which is a paired comparison. The other is that ReAct's worst (48%) is above Act's best (45%), a comparison that hands the side with selection bias to the opponent.

Takeaway. When you see a number reported as "best of k", look first for k and the standard error. Read BUTLER's "best of 8" the same way.

5. Limitations the paper states

  • Reasoning errors and repetitive loops. The largest failure mode of ReAct on the knowledge tasks. The paper suspects greedy decoding as the cause (footnote 4).
  • Dependence on search quality. Non-informative search is 23% of the errors.
  • Small models and context length. Small models do not learn ReAct from prompting alone. Complex tasks with large action spaces need more examples, which easily exceeds the input-length limit of in-context learning (§6). The authors see fine-tuning on high-quality human-written data as the next step.
  • Risks of acting. The ethics statement notes that connecting a language model to an action space carries the risk of looking up inappropriate or private information or taking harmful actions. The experiments were limited to Wikipedia and WebShop, which hold no private information, and dangerous actions were removed from the action spaces. In WebShop you cannot actually buy anything, and you cannot edit Wikipedia. Chapter 15, on indirect prompt injection, starts from this paragraph.

Optional reading — fixing actions by fixing thoughts (Appendix A.3). The ALFWorld task in Figure 5 is to put two keychains in a safe. The original trajectory fails because of one hallucinated sentence in the thought at Act 17. A person deletes that sentence and adds a small hint to the thought at Act 23, and the trajectory turns into a success. From the person's side, instead of entering dozens of actions, you edit just two lines of thought. The authors judge that such on-the-fly correction is hard with Act or with existing reinforcement-learning methods, because a person cannot change the model's parameters, and changing a few actions may not make the remaining actions change with them.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

The side papers in this chapter are the works this paper compares itself with and the works covered in the chapters before and after this one.

CoT and CoT-SC (CoT paper · Self-Consistency paper · Chapter 4 of this book). These are the paper's baselines themselves. CoT has the model write its thinking but does not look outside. In the paper's words, it is "a static black box, in that the model uses its own internal representations to generate thoughts and is not grounded in the external world". CoT-SC samples several such paths of thought and picks by majority vote. The difference from ReAct is what the thoughts are conditioned on. CoT's thoughts are conditioned only on the question and earlier thoughts; ReAct's are conditioned on observations as well.

Inner Monologue (Huang et al. 2022). How the content of the monologue differs, and the ReAct-IM ablation, are in section 3 of "The paper in detail". Two points are added here. The paper credits IM as the first work to demonstrate a closed-loop system and says ReAct builds on it, yet it goes as far as to argue "that Inner Monologue does not truly comprise of inner thoughts". And the comparison in Table 3 that supports this argument is an ablation that swaps only the thoughts on the same expert trajectories, not a run of the original IM system.

WebGPT (Nakano et al. 2021). A language model that answers questions by operating a browser. The Act baseline loosely resembles its way of interacting. The differences are how it is trained and whether reasoning is made explicit. WebGPT is trained with imitation learning and reinforcement learning from human feedback and does not model thoughts explicitly. ReAct uses only prompting and leaves its thoughts in writing.

Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book). It uses ReAct as its actor unchanged. On the 134 ALFWorld environments it uses the example trajectories of Yao et al. with GPT-3, but treats a run as failed when the same action gets the same response more than three times or when an environment takes more than 30 actions, and then writes its own reflection. Its memory keeps only the three most recent reflections. As a result, over 12 consecutive trials it solved 130 of the 134 cumulatively. The difference is the time scale of correction. ReAct corrects the next action within one episode by looking at observations. Reflexion leaves a reflection after an episode ends and corrects the next attempt. Reflexion's repetition-detection rule can also be read as a device aimed at the repetitive loops of ReAct's Table 2 (this connection is this book's reading). In addition, Reflexion's appendix reports that on WebShop, ReAct + Reflexion was not significantly better than ReAct.

Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023 · Chapter 7 of this book). The model learns, in a self-supervised way, which API to call, when and with what arguments. ReAct leaves the weights alone and draws out tool use with examples. In the notation of Chapter 2, Toolformer works on θ and ReAct on z.

Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023 · Chapter 5 of this book). Same first author as ReAct. According to §2.2 of the revised AR survey, ToT treats partial thoughts as nodes of a search tree and prunes branches with value estimates. ReAct is a single path that chains thoughts and actions greedily, one at a time.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §2.2 — where assumption A2 breaks

Bring back the formalization from Chapter 2. The environment is a POMDP E=⟨X,O,A,T,Ω,R,γ⟩, and the agent is a separate tuple G=⟨Z,M,πreason,πexec,U⟩. The history at time t is ht=(o≤t,z<t,a<t), and the policy factors as follows.

πθ(zt,at∣ht)=πreason(zt∣ht)·πexec(at∣ht,zt)(Eq. 1)

The survey itself says that Eq. 1 is only an application of the chain rule and carries no content on its own, and that the content lies in the assumptions made with it. Placed in this frame, ReAct maps as follows.

ReAct paper, §2 AR survey, revised version, §2.2
Context ct History ht (or a memory mt that summarizes it)
Thought a^t∈ℒ Reasoning trace zt∈Z
Action at∈𝒜 External action at∈A
A thought does not change the environment, and no observation comes back Assumption A0: zt is generated before at and is not emitted to the environment. T and Ω are functions of at alone
Examples given to a frozen PaLM-540B θ fixed, searching over z at inference time
The fine-tuning experiment of §3.3 The θ mode

Assumption A2 (sufficiency of execution) is πexec(at∣ht,zt)=πexec(at∣zt): given the thought, the action is conditionally independent of the history. The survey notes that, unlike A0 and A1, A2 is not generally assumed. It holds in structures that fix a plan first and then execute it, and it breaks in interleaved structures like ReAct. In ReAct the action is conditioned on the raw observation as well as on the thought.

Assumption A2 from §2.2 of the revised AR survey, drawn as a graph. The editor drew the diagram.

Look at Figure 1(2b) and this arrow becomes visible. After the observation at Act 6 ("On the countertop 3, you see a apple 1, a bread 1, ...... a pepper shaker 1, and a vase 3."), Act 7, Take pepper shaker 1 from countertop 3, follows at once with no thought. The object number and location number in the action came from the observation, not from a thought. In a trajectory like ALFWorld's, where thoughts appear sparsely, many steps have no thought, and the action at those steps can only rely on the history. To fit ReAct's sparse thoughts into the survey's frame, treat zt at those steps as an empty string. This mapping is the editor's interpretation.

As an instance of in-context reasoning. The survey gives ReAct as an example of in-context reasoning, which fixes θ and searches over Z, and says that methods like ReAct "perform greedy decoding over alternating thoughts z and actions a." In the same place it formalizes ToT and the MCTS family separately, as searches with different objective functions. Read together with the fact that footnote 4 of the ReAct paper suspected greedy decoding as the cause of repetitive loops, the search in Chapter 5 can be seen as one response to this weakness.

Where ReAct sits in the tables. The revised version puts ReAct in four tables and lists its optimization target as z in all four.

Table Cell Description
Table 3 (3 layers × 3 modes grid) Foundational layer × in-context (z) "ReAct-style interleaving"
Table 7 (tool use) Optimization regime I, in-context integration Interleaving reasoning and acting, prompting
Table 8 (agentic search) Optimization regime I, in-context search Natural language + actions, search API
Table 9 (feedback) I-b, externally grounded feedback The feedback source is the result of the action

In Table 9, ReAct is classified as a feedback technique. §4.1.1 gives ReAct as the first example of externally grounded feedback, explaining that ReAct "interleaves reasoning with actions so that the environment's response, rather than the model's own judgment, determines whether a step succeeded." When Chapter 11 separates the self-reflective type (I-a) from the externally grounded type (I-b), this sentence is the reference point.

In the design guidance. Table 5 in §2.4 recommends the z mode for tasks with no training budget that are one-off or low in volume. The reasons given are that there is no extra setup cost and that it can be attached to any frozen API model. As cautions it lists that it breaks easily when the domain shifts and that its cost recurs with every call and grows with the breadth of search. ReAct's results can be looked at again in light of this warning. The ALFWorld success rate ranged from 48% to 71% depending on the prompt (Exercise 2 above). The paper reads the fact that ReAct beat Act under all six prompts as robustness to prompt choice. The same numbers can also be read as saying that the score swings widely with the prompt. The judgment turns on whether "robust" means always better than the competing method or means that the score varies little. That generating thoughts costs extra tokens on every call points the same way, but the paper did not measure cost.

Harness survey — today's agent loop

  • §2.1 timeline. The first entry is "Reasoning–action (ReAct) loops (2022)". The content of the timeline is given in section 2 of "The paper in detail" in Chapter 3. The thread is that ReAct popularized the loop and that, as later systems widened it, termination, context management, state recovery and monitoring became necessary.
  • §6.2 the inner loop of a single agent. The survey says that a single-agent loop conceptually follows the ReAct paradigm. At the same time it stresses that such a system's behavior is set not by the model alone but together with the harness that builds the prompt, calls tools, manages control flow and returns tool output to the next step. The survey's Table 2 groups OpenCode, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Aider and SWE-agent all under the "Single loop" type. It also notes that such systems suffer from context fragmentation, error accumulation and weak task decomposition on long tasks.

There is a harness inside the ReAct paper too. The step caps (7 and 5), the rule for falling back to CoT-SC, the grammar of actions (search[…]) and an API that cuts observations to the first 5 sentences were all set outside the model. Apply the definition of a harness from Chapter 3 to this paper, and the two combination rows of Table 1 can also be read as the same model wearing different harnesses. The paper does not explain them in these terms.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "ReAct is more accurate than CoT." It depends on the task. On HotpotQA, ReAct's EM was lower than CoT's (27.4 against 29.4). ReAct's advantage is not accuracy alone but groundedness. It had 0% failures from hallucination. In exchange, reasoning errors were 47%, more than CoT's 16%. On the knowledge tasks, the best results came from combining the two.

Misreading 2. "ReAct is a method for training models." The main experiments are all prompting: a frozen PaLM-540B given 1 to 6 examples. Fine-tuning is the supporting experiment of §3.3, and it also shows that small models do not learn ReAct from prompting alone.

Misreading 3. "The thought sentences show the model's actual internal reasoning as it is." The paper lists interpretability and diagnosability as advantages, but it did not separately test whether the written thoughts are really the reasons for the actions (faithfulness). That editing a thought in Figure 5 changes the later actions is evidence that thoughts affect actions as part of the context. That is a different claim from saying the thoughts accurately report the model's internal computation. Faithfulness is a question this paper does not take up, but it is worth raising if you want to rely on the thought sentences as evidence.

Misreading 4. "The more thoughts the better, and at every step." On the decision-making tasks, thoughts are inserted sparsely and the model decides where. ReAct-IM, with dense thoughts, scored below ReAct (53 against 71). ReAct-IM's thoughts were limited to the kind that restates environment feedback.

Misreading 5. "The search ReAct used is a real search engine." It is a deliberately weak API that needs the exact page name and returns only the first 5 sentences or the next sentence containing a string. The scores come from this condition. This paper does not say how the results would change with a strong retriever.

Misreading 6. "ALFWorld 71% is ReAct's performance." It is the value of the best run among six prompts. The average is 57% and the worst is 48%. As Exercise 2 showed, a maximum picked on the evaluation set is biased upward.

Misreading 7. "ReAct invented the agent loop." The paper itself names Inner Monologue as the first work to demonstrate a closed-loop system and says ReAct builds on it. What ReAct claims first is to have shown that a language model combining reasoning and acting works as a closed loop in interactive environments. The Harness survey, too, writes that ReAct "popularized" this loop.

Discussion questions

  1. The trade-off between groundedness and flexibility. In Table 2, ReAct nearly eliminated hallucination while its reasoning errors increased. This is what happens when you enforce a format. In your own work, have you changed the kinds of errors by enforcing a format on a model or on people? On what basis did you decide which errors to reduce and which to accept?

  2. Is the breaking of A2 a defect or a feature? In ReAct, observation text can enter the next action without passing through a thought. This lets it react quickly to changes in the environment. But a sentence someone planted in an observation can enter the action through the same channel. Think ahead to indirect prompt injection in Chapter 15. What do you gain and what do you lose by switching to plan-then-execute (A2 holds)? (Connecting A2 to injection this way is this book's reading. CaMeL, among the side papers of Chapter 15, is one answer.)

  3. If you ran this experiment again. If you were a reviewer, what would you ask the authors to add to Tables 1 and 3? Which is most urgent: the number of questions, the number of repeated runs, standard errors, paired comparisons or the method of choosing prompts? Check your answer in Chapter 18.

Chapter 7 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 7. Tools — Self-Taught Tool Use and a Standard Protocol

The question this chapter answers: how does a model know when to call a tool, and why did the way tools are attached come to need a standard?

Core reading. ① Timo Schick et al., "Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools", NeurIPS 2023. In arXiv v1, 11 pages of main text (two-column layout), 17 with the appendices after the references. ② Two pages of the 2026-07-28 version of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification: Architecture and Server Features — Tools. For why it was made, read Anthropic's announcement (November 25, 2024).

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · NeurIPS 2023 page · No official code (unofficial implementation)

Main specification — MCP specification, 2026-07-28 version · Architecture · Tools · Specification repository · Announcement

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §3.2, Table 7, Table 8 · Harness survey §2.1, §4, Table 1

One-paragraph summary. This chapter looks at tool use from both ends. One end is the model. Toolformer shows GPT-J (6.7B) only a few examples per API, has it insert API calls into web text on its own, actually runs them, keeps only the calls that make the following tokens easier to predict, and fine-tunes on that corpus. No answer labels are used. The model trained this way beat GPT-3, which is 25 times larger, on factual fill-in-the-blank and arithmetic word problems, and fell behind it on question answering. The other end is the harness. MCP is a protocol that fixes "how" an application connects tools. The 2023 paper taught a model to insert [Calculator(400 / 1400) → 0.29] into text; the 2026 specification links an application and a tool server with JSON-RPC messages that carry a name, a description and an input schema. The first is a way of training a model and the second a connection protocol, so the second did not replace the first.

Must read. All of Toolformer §2 (less than two pages) and Figure 2, the three tables in §4.2.1–4.2.3, and the one paragraph of §4.4. If you show only one figure, make it Figure 2. It shows on one page how one of two call candidates is kept and the other discarded. For MCP, Core Components and Design Principles in Architecture, and Protocol Messages and Error Handling in Tools.

Optional reading. Table 9 in Toolformer §5 (how call frequency changes when decoding changes) and Table 10 (filter scores and usefulness as judged by people), and the per-tool heuristics and thresholds in Appendix A. The Stateful Tools section of MCP Tools.

What to cut from the presentation. For Toolformer §4.2.4–4.2.5 (Tables 6 and 7), look only at one sentence of results each. Of the full prompts in Appendix A.2, Figure 3 alone is enough; skip Appendices C and D. Also skip x-mcp-header and the image and audio content items in MCP Tools.

Reading with Chapter 6. ReAct had a model use tools from examples while keeping the weights fixed; Toolformer does it by changing the weights. Set out this contrast at the start of the presentation.

When you quote the numbers. All of Toolformer's scores come from GPT-J 6.7B in the zero-shot condition, with no examples, and the scoring is lenient and differs by task. LAMA counts an answer as correct if the right word is among the first five words; math, if the first number produced is right; question answering, if the right answer is within the first 20 words (§4.2). "SQuAD 33.8" is not exact match. When you quote a number, give the model, the task and the scoring rule with it. The GPT-3 used for comparison is the original davinci, without instruction fine-tuning (footnote 6).

Building intuition

Figure 1 — API calls placed inside text

Figure 1 shows four examples of the model calling an API on its own while continuing a sentence. Inside the brackets is "API name(input) → result", and outside is the original sentence.

The New England Journal of Medicine is a registered trademark of
[QA("Who is the publisher of The New England Journal of Medicine?")
 → Massachusetts Medical Society] the MMS.

Out of 1400 participants, 400 (or [Calculator(400 / 1400) → 0.29] 29%)
passed the test.

The name derives from "la tortuga", the Spanish word for
[MT("tortuga") → turtle] turtle.

The Brown Act is California's law [WikiSearch("Brown Act") → The Ralph M.
Brown Act is an act of the California State Legislature that guarantees
the public's right to attend and participate in meetings of local
legislative bodies.] that requires legislative bodies, like city councils,
to hold their meetings open to the public.

The four examples in Figure 1 of the Toolformer paper. From the top: question answering system, calculator, machine translation and Wikipedia search.

Look at where the calls sit. The division comes right before "29%" is written, and the translation right before "turtle." The paper's point is that this sense of position comes straight out of the training signal. The format resembles Search[Apple Remote] in ReAct (Chapter 6), but there is no thought, and in evaluation the model calls only once per input (§4.2). It is not a loop that looks at an observation and chooses the next action.

The editor's bridge 1 — driver standards like ODBC and JDBC, and MCP

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper or the specification.

Before ODBC and JDBC, an application had to be written separately against each DBMS's own interface. With m applications and n DBMSs, that is m×n sets of connection code. Driver standards cut this to m+n. This is the problem the MCP announcement describes: "Every new data source requires its own custom implementation, making truly connected systems difficult to scale." Lined up, the application is the MCP host, the driver is the MCP server and each connection is an MCP client. Just as driver standards have catalog functions that ask for the list of tables, MCP has tools/list, which asks for the list of tools.

The analogy breaks in two places. The caller of a driver API is a deterministic program, but what chooses an MCP tool is a language model that reads the tool's name and natural-language description and makes a judgment. Anthropic's post on tool design calls tools "a contract between deterministic systems and non-deterministic agents." So the description of an MCP tool is in effect a prompt. Also, a driver that takes SQL sees the query in full, while the MCP specification keeps a server from reading the whole conversation or looking into other servers.

The editor's bridge 2 — a selection rule based on loss reduction

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

For a single candidate call, Toolformer's filter compares two models: one with the API result placed in front and one without it. The difference in (weighted) negative log-likelihood of the following tokens, Li−−Li+, is a log-likelihood ratio, and the call is accepted only when it exceeds the threshold τf. In form, this is the rejection region of a likelihood-ratio test. It is also interesting that there are two control groups. The call has to beat the better of "no call" and "a call made but no result received". The second control is close to a placebo arm. It screens out cases where the question text itself leaks a clue and lowers the loss.

Where it breaks is just as clear. A rejection region is set by the error rate under the null distribution, but the paper writes that it chose τf so that enough examples remain for each tool (§4.1). What this threshold controls is the number of examples left for training. "Accepting" a call likewise decides whether to use it as training data; it does not ask whether the result is true. Section 6 of "The paper in detail" comes back to this with numbers.

The paper has no analogy of its own. But a sentence in §1, giving the reason for choosing self-supervised learning, sets the theme for this chapter. Human annotation is costly, and besides, "what humans find useful may be different from what a model finds useful."

The paper in detail

1. The approach — the model annotates its own data with calls (§2)

Notation for a call. The paper writes an API call as a tuple c=(ac,ic), where ac is the name of the API and ic the input. A call before and after receiving the result r is spelled out as the following text.

e(c)=⟨API⟩ac(ic)⟨/API⟩

e(c,r)=⟨API⟩ac(ic)→r⟨/API⟩

<API>, </API> and → are special tokens (in the formulas the angle brackets are written ⟨⟩). In practice, to avoid enlarging the vocabulary, they were represented by the existing token sequences " [", "]" and "->" (footnote 1). Only two conditions are placed on a tool: its inputs and outputs must both be representable as text, and a few examples of its use must be obtainable (§3).

Three steps to build the data, then fine-tuning. Starting from a plain-text corpus 𝒞={x1,…,x|𝒞|}, steps ①–③ build a corpus 𝒞* with calls inserted, and step ④ fine-tunes on it.

① Sampling API Calls. One prompt P(x) is written for each API (Figure 3 is the one for the question answering tool; two examples are followed by the lines "Input: x" and "Output:"). The probability that model M starts a call at position i is computed as

pi=pM(⟨API⟩∣P(x),x1:i−1)

and positions with pi>τs are kept, using only the top k if there are many. For each remaining position, [P(x),x1,…,xi−1,⟨API⟩] is given as a prefix and up to m calls ci1,…,cim are sampled until </API> appears. Examples that fail to produce </API> are discarded (footnote 2).

② Executing API Calls. All sampled calls are actually executed, and each returns a result ri as a single line of text.

③ Filtering API Calls. This is the heart of the paper. Given a sequence of weights (wi∣i∈ℕ), the weighted cross-entropy loss of the model over the tokens from position i on, with a prefix z placed in front, is defined as

Li(z)=−∑j=inwj−i·logpM(xj∣z,x1:j−1)

and it is computed two ways.

Li+=Li(e(ci,ri))

Li−=min(Li(ε),Li(e(ci,ε)))

ε is the empty sequence. Li+ is the loss with both the call and its result placed in front, and Li− is the smaller of (i) the loss with no call at all and (ii) the loss with the call made but no result given. For a filter threshold τf, only calls that satisfy

Li−−Li+≥τf

are kept. In words, receiving the call together with its result must make the following tokens easier to predict, by at least τf, than "no call" or "a call with no result".

There are two details. When the filter is computed, e(ci,ri) is not inserted at position i but placed in front as a prefix, because before fine-tuning a call in the middle of a sentence is out of line with the pretraining distribution (footnote 3). Then there are the weights. §4.1 uses w~t=max(0,1−0.2·t), wt=w~t/∑sw~s. Working it out, only the five tokens t=0,…,4 receive weight, 1/3,4/15,1/5,2/15,1/15, and everything after is 0 (the editor did this conversion). For a result to count as useful, its effect has to show within the five tokens right after the call. The paper explains that it uses this weighting "to make sure that API calls happen close to where the information provided by the API is actually helpful for the model."

④ Model Finetuning. The remaining calls are inserted at their original positions to make x*=x1:i−1,e(ci,ri),xi:n, and M is fine-tuned on the resulting 𝒞* with the standard language-modeling objective. Apart from the inserted calls, 𝒞* is the same as 𝒞, so the paper's explanation is that the model learns from the same content and additionally learns "when and how to use which tool". At inference time, decoding stops when the → token appears, the API result and </API> are inserted, and decoding continues.

Toolformer's flow drawn in five boxes. Step ① of the text, sampling calls, is split into two boxes, picking positions (1) and sampling candidates (2), so boxes 1–4 are steps ①–③ of the text and box 5 is step ④. Only in box 5 do the parameters change. The editor drew the diagram from §2 and Figure 2 of the paper.

The example in Figure 2. The input is "Pittsburgh is also known as the Steel City", and position i is just before "the Steel City." Candidate ci1 = "What other name is Pittsburgh known by?" receives the result Steel City, gives Li(ci1→Steel City)<min(Li(ci1→ε),Li(ε)), and is kept. The inequality in the figure shows only the direction of improvement. To actually be kept, the difference must be at least τf. Candidate ci2 = "Which country is Pittsburgh in?" receives the result United States, but the inequality goes the other way and it is discarded. The second candidate got a correct answer back and was still discarded. That Pittsburgh is in the United States does not help predict "the Steel City." What the filter asks is not whether the result is true but whether it helps with the next tokens (Misreading 3 below).

2. The five tools and the training data (§3, §4.1, Appendix A)

Tool Implementation Example input Example output
Question Answering Atlas (a retrieval-augmented LM, fine-tuned on Natural Questions) Where was the Knights of Columbus founded? New Haven, Connecticut
Wikipedia Search BM25 over an index of the KILT Wikipedia dump Fishing Reel Types Spin fishing > Spin fishing is distinguished between fly fishing and bait cast fishing …
Calculator A Python script that does only the four arithmetic operations 27 + 4 * 2 35
Calendar Returns today's date, with no input ε Today is Monday, January 30, 2023.
Machine Translation NLLB 600M; the target language is always English sûreté nucléaire nuclear safety

The input and output examples of Table 1 of the paper, combined with the implementation details from §3 and Appendix A.1. Only the beginning of the search output is shown.

Question answering returns only a short answer, while search gives broader information but leaves the model to pick out the part it needs (§3). This difference decides the experimental results later.

Corpus and thresholds. 𝒞 is a subset of the web-crawl corpus CCNet, with texts where calls are likely to be useful picked out in advance by heuristics. For example, the calculator uses only documents containing at least three numbers, and the calendar only documents whose creation date can be extracted from the URL (about 18%) (Appendix A.1). The default thresholds are τs=0.05, τf=1.0, k=5 positions and m=5 candidates per position; for the calculator and translation, which have few target documents, they were loosened to τs=0, k=20, m=10 and τf=0.5 (Appendix A).

API τf=0.5 τf=1.0 τf=2.0
Question Answering 51,987 18,526 5,135
Wikipedia Search 207,241 60,974 13,944
Calculator 3,680 994 138
Calendar 61,811 20,587 3,007
Machine Translation 3,156 1,034 229

Table 2 of the paper. The number of examples with API calls left in 𝒞* for each filter threshold. The unit is examples (texts), not calls.

Fine-tuning uses up to 25,000 examples per API for up to 2,000 steps, and the checkpoint is chosen by perplexity on 1,000 examples of a CCNet development set (§4.1, Appendix B). The choice is not made on downstream task scores, so the design does not peek at the evaluation sets.

3. Experiments — where it wins and where it loses (§4)

Models compared (§4.1).

  • GPT-J: no fine-tuning.
  • GPT-J + CC: a control fine-tuned on 𝒞 with no calls inserted.
  • Toolformer: fine-tuned on 𝒞*.
  • Toolformer (disabled): the same model with the probability of the <API> token fixed at 0.
  • OPT (66B) and GPT-3 (175B): models about 10 and 25 times larger.

The four GPT-J rows read as an ablation design. GPT-J → GPT-J + CC is the effect of extra training, → Toolformer (disabled) the effect of training on data with calls, and → Toolformer the effect of calling at inference time (the editor's arrangement).

Adjusting the decoding. Greedy decoding is used, but a call starts whenever <API> is among the top k tokens (k=10). To prevent a loop of nothing but calls, there is at most one call per input (§4.2). This k uses the same letter as the "top k positions" of §2 with a different meaning, so keep them apart in the presentation.

Table 4 (math word problems ASDiv, SVAMP and MAWPS, scored by the first number produced): Toolformer, at 40.4, 29.4 and 44.0, was far ahead of GPT-3 (14.0, 10.0 and 19.8). Even with calls disabled it is better than GPT-J + CC on ASDiv (14.8 against 9.6). The paper guesses that the model's own math ability improved while it trained on examples containing calls and their results.
