This time it loses to GPT-3. The model called Wikipedia search in 99.3% of the examples. The paper gives two reasons: the search engine is simple and often returned irrelevant results, and Toolformer could not reformulate its query or scan several results. The second is what thought 3 of ReAct in Chapter 6 ("Front Row is not found. I need to search Front Row (software).") did.

The other experiments. On the multilingual question answering task MLQA (Table 6), Toolformer was not consistently better than GPT-J. The paper thinks the extra training on CCNet lowered the scores for some languages. On DATESET in the temporal datasets (Table 7) it was far ahead at 27.3 and called the calendar in 54.8% of the examples. On TEMPLAMA it was also ahead (16.3), but calendar calls were only 0.2%, so the gain came from other tools. Solving it by first asking for the date and then asking again with that date runs into the one-call limit. Perplexity (Table 8) is the same for GPT-J + CC and Toolformer (disabled) (WikiText 10.3, CCNet 10.5), so learning to call cost nothing in language modeling.

4. Model size — a threshold at about 775M parameters (§4.4)

The same method was applied to four GPT-2 models (124M, 355M, 775M and 1.6B parameters) with only three tools (question answering, calculator and Wikipedia search). Figure 4 plots the average scores on the LAMA, math and question answering groups against model size, with calls enabled and disabled, and puts GPT-3 as a horizontal line. The paper writes this.

Figure 4 shows that the ability to leverage the provided tools only emerges at around 775M parameters: smaller models achieve similar performance both with and without tools. An exception to this is the Wikipedia search engine used mostly for QA benchmarks; we hypothesize that this is because the API is comparably easy to use.

It goes on to say that as models grow, their ability to use tools improves too, so that even for the largest model a large gap remains between calls enabled and disabled.

In the figure, the two lines that stay together for small models in the math and LAMA panels separate at 775M, while in the question answering panel they are apart from the smallest model on (the Wikipedia search exception). Values read off the gridlines are not reproduced. The "threshold" means somewhere between 355M and 775M; no value of 775M was separately estimated. Section 6 comes back to this.

The decoding k and "calibration" — §5, Table 9. When the decoding k is set to 0, 1, 3 and 10, the call rate goes from 40.3% (T-REx) and 8.5% (WebQS) at k=1 to 98.1% and 100% at k=10. The paper sees the model at k=1 as "calibrated to some extent". The scores on examples where it decided not to call (44.3, 19.9) are higher than the average when it never calls (34.9, 18.9), so it chooses to call on examples it could not solve alone. Exercise 1 in section 6 checks this with numbers.

5. MCP — a protocol for attaching tools (Architecture, Tools)

From here, 10 minutes go to reading the specification. Where Toolformer dealt with "how a model learns when to call", MCP fixes "in what format an application puts tools in front of a model and runs them".

Why it was made. On November 25, 2024, Anthropic released MCP as "a universal, open standard for connecting AI systems with data sources". What it released first was the specification and SDKs, support for local MCP servers in the Claude Desktop apps, and a repository of MCP servers. Keep in mind when reading that this is a company's post published together with its own products.

Three components. The 2026-07-28 version of the specification defines MCP as a stateless protocol built on JSON-RPC. Every request carries its own protocol version and capabilities. The host is the container and coordinator: it creates clients, enforces security policies and consent requirements, and handles LLM integration and context. A client is created by the host and communicates with exactly one server. A server exposes resources, tools and prompts, and can be a local process or a remote service.

Design principles. Of the four, the third matters for this chapter: "Servers should not be able to read the whole conversation, nor 'see into' other servers". A server receives only the context it needs, and the full conversation history stays with the host. The other three are that servers should be extremely easy to build, that they should be composable with one another, and that features can be added progressively. The client carries capabilities in _meta on every request, and the server announces them in its response to server/discover. A server that exposes tools must declare the tools capability (MUST).

User interaction model. MCP tools are designed to be "model-controlled": the language model finds and calls tools based on the context and the user's prompts. At the same time the specification says "there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations." It is SHOULD, not MUST.

Two messages. The tool list is tools/list and a call is tools/call. Below is a shortened version of the specification's example (the title, icon, cursor and cache fields are dropped, as is _meta, which every real request must include).

// client → server
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list" }

// server → client
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1,
  "result": { "resultType": "complete",
    "tools": [ {
      "name": "get_weather",
      "description": "Get current weather information for a location",
      "inputSchema": { "type": "object",
        "properties": { "location": { "type": "string",
                                      "description": "City name or zip code" } },
        "required": ["location"] } } ] } }

// client → server
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
  "params": { "name": "get_weather", "arguments": { "location": "New York" } } }

// server → client
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2,
  "result": { "resultType": "complete",
    "content": [ { "type": "text",
      "text": "Current weather in New York:\nTemperature: 72°F\nConditions: Partly cloudy" } ],
    "isError": false } }

At the center of a tool definition are its name, a natural-language description and an inputSchema written in JSON Schema. The specification also defines title, icons, outputSchema and annotations, but it does not say which of these the host passes to the model. The specification says the optional annotations must not be trusted unless they come from a trusted server (MUST).

Errors take two paths. Protocol errors such as an unknown tool are returned as JSON-RPC errors; tool execution errors such as API failures or input validation errors are returned as a normal result with isError: true attached, and the specification describes these as containing "actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters". The specification's example, "Invalid departure date: must be in the future. Current date is 08/08/2025.", is an error message written for the model to read, not a person. It even gives today's date so that the next call can be fixed.

State and security. The specification has no protocol-level session, so state between calls is carried by passing an explicit handle returned by a creation tool as an argument to the next call (non-normative guidance). The security section requires servers to validate inputs, control access, rate-limit calls and sanitize outputs (MUST), and recommends that clients ask the user to confirm sensitive operations and validate results before passing them to the LLM (SHOULD). This last sentence is where Chapter 15 starts.

Toolformer and MCP side by side.

Toolformer (2023) MCP specification (2026-07-28 version)
Shape of a call Special tokens in text, <API> a_c(i_c) → r </API> The name and arguments of a JSON-RPC tools/call message
Information about the tool A prompt with a few examples per API (only when generating data) description and inputSchema (the host receives them at run time through tools/list; which of them go into the model's context, and when, is up to the host)
Who decides "when to call" The parameters of the fine-tuned model The model decides, but the specification recommends letting a person refuse (SHOULD)
When tools change Rebuild the data and retrain A list-changed notification; fetch the list again
Failure and security Not addressed (one call only) Return execution errors to the model; validate inputs and results

A table in which the editor picked matching items from the two originals and set them against each other.

The second row is the point of this chapter. In Toolformer, knowledge about tools goes into the parameters θ through fine-tuning. In MCP it lives in the descriptions the host receives from servers and loads into the model's context. Where tools multiply or change, the latter has the advantage, but for that the model must be able to read a description it has never seen and call the tool correctly. The two approaches can be read as a division of labor more than as competitors.

6. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

There are no item counts, with one exception. None of the nine benchmarks in Tables 3, 4 and 5 gives the number of items. LAMA had some examples filtered out, so bringing in the size of the original dataset does not fit either. The only size disclosed is that of DATESET, which the authors built themselves; adding up the counts per template in Appendix Table 11 gives 9,400. Taking this as the number of evaluation items, Toolformer's 27.3% has a Wilson 95% confidence interval of [26.4%, 28.2%], and the disabled model's 5.9% one of [5.4%, 6.4%]. The DATESET difference holds up.

For the rest you can ask the question the other way around. Solving for the number of items at which the difference equals 1.96 standard errors, n=1.962{p1(1−p1)+p2(1−p2)}/(p1−p2)2, as independent samples, SVAMP (Toolformer 29.4 against GPT-3 10.0) needs about 31 items and Google-RE (11.5 against 7.0) about 317. By contrast, the 0.8 percentage points against GPT-3 on TEMPLAMA (16.3 against 15.5), on which the claim that Toolformer "outperforms all baselines" rests, would need about 16,052 items to be told apart from chance (the editor's calculation). With per-item results, a paired comparison would be possible. The variance of a difference is Var(A−B)=Var(A)+Var(B)−2Cov(A,B), so if the two models' correct and incorrect answers on the same items are positively correlated the required number goes down, and if negatively correlated it goes up. Saying the independent-sample calculation is conservative is true only under the assumption of a positive correlation. Since the item counts are unknown, the honest answer is that no judgment can be made.

Figure 4 is five points. The sentence that "the ability to leverage the provided tools only emerges at around 775M parameters" comes from the average scores of five models (four GPT-2 models and one GPT-J, which differs in training data and architecture). The paper does not say it repeated training or evaluation at each size, and there are no error bars, so it is hard to judge from the figure alone whether the split between 355M and 775M exceeds the range of training randomness. The GPT-J point in this figure may also be a different model from the one in Tables 3 and 4. The average of Toolformer's scores is 32.9 in Table 3 and 37.9 in Table 4, yet the vertical axis of the LAMA and math panels in Figure 4 ends at 30, and the rightmost point is inside it too. Since §4.4 says it trained with only three tools, one can read GPT-J as retrained under that condition as well, but the paper does not say so. How to reconcile the two sets of numbers is an open question.

The other two are left for you to calculate as exercises.

Exercise 1 — reading Table 9 as a mixture to check "calibration" with numbers. Below is Table 9 of the paper. All is the overall score, AC the score on the examples where the model decided to call, NC the score on the remaining examples and % the share of examples with a call.

k T-REx All AC NC % WebQS All AC NC %
0 34.9 – 34.9 0.0 18.9 – 18.9 0.0
1 47.8 53.0 44.3 40.3 19.3 17.1 19.9 8.5
3 52.9 58.0 29.0 82.8 26.3 26.5 6.6 99.3
10 53.5 54.0 22.5 98.1 26.3 26.4 – 100.0

Table 9 of the paper.

(a) The overall score should satisfy All=q·AC+(1−q)·NC. Check whether each row is reproduced within rounding error. (b) In the NC examples <API> never made the top k, so the output is the same as with calls disabled (k=0). Use this to work back to the score the called examples would have gotten with calls disabled. (c) Use that value to restate the paper's "calibration" claim.

SolutionSolution

(a) For T-REx, all three rows are reproduced. k=1: 0.403×53.0+0.597×44.3=47.81 (printed 47.8), k=3: 53.01 (52.9), k=10: 53.40 (53.5). Differences of about 0.1 are explained by the rounding error of the four numbers (upper bound about 0.12). WebQS at k=3 also fits, at 26.36. But WebQS at k=1 gives 0.085×17.1+0.915×19.9=19.66, 0.36 away from the printed 19.3, which exceeds the upper bound on rounding error (about 0.10). The paper does not explain this, and the table alone cannot tell which number is off.

(b) Let B be the overall score with calls disabled. Then B=q·X+(1−q)·NC, where X is the "calls disabled" score on the called examples. So X={B−(1−q)NC}/q.

  • T-REx, k=1: X=(34.9−0.597×44.3)/0.403≈21.0. The actual score on the called examples is 53.0, so calling added about 32 points on those examples.
  • T-REx, k=3: X≈36.1. k=10: X≈35.1.
  • WebQS, k=1: X=(18.9−0.915×19.9)/0.085≈8.1. With a call it is 17.1.

(c) At k=1 the model chose to call on examples where on its own it would have scored only 21.0 (T-REx) and 8.1 (WebQS), and the examples where it did not call were easy ones on which it scores 44.3 and 19.9 alone. This is the paper's "calibration" put in numbers. As k grows, the "alone score" of the called examples moves back toward the overall average (34.9), and the small share left over (1.9% on T-REx at k=10) is actually hard (NC 22.5). But the 8.1 for WebQS at k=1 comes from 8.5% of the whole, and with the item count unknown its uncertainty may be large. Also, as seen in (a), one number in this row is off.

Takeaway. A table that prints subset scores together with their shares can be checked for internal consistency with the mixture identity, and it can even recover counterfactual scores that were never printed.

Exercise 2 — reading the filter as a selection rule. (a) What does τf=1.0 mean? Using the fact that the weights are normalized to sum to 1 (section 1), and taking the logarithm to be natural, restate it as "by what factor must the probability of the following tokens grow to pass?" (b) The filter scores in Table 10 and the authors' usefulness judgments are, in order, 5.49 useful (Wiki), 2.11 useful (Calendar), 2.08 useful (QA), 1.59 useful (Calculator), 0.92 not useful (Wiki, "Fast train success"), 0.70 useful (Translation), 0.33 useful (Calendar), −0.02 not useful (Calculator), −0.41 not useful (Calendar), −1.23 not useful (QA). Applying the actual threshold for each tool (0.5 for the calculator and translation, 1.0 for the rest), which remain, and what is the share of useful among them, with an exact 95% confidence interval? Can these ten tell us the filter's precision?

SolutionSolution

(a) The weights wt sum to 1, so Li is a weighted average of the negative log probabilities of the five following tokens. Li−−Li+≥1 means that their weighted geometric-mean probability grows by a factor of at least e≈2.72. The τf=0.5 for the calculator and translation is a factor of e0.5≈1.65. The paper does not state the base of the logarithm, so this conversion assumes the natural logarithm.

(b) Five remain: 5.49, 2.11, 2.08, 1.59 (calculator, at least 0.5) and 0.70 (translation, at least 0.5), and all are useful. The Clopper–Pearson 95% interval for 5/5 is [47.8%, 100%]. One of the five filtered out (0.33, calendar) was useful. The "Fast train success" call (0.92), which the paper gives as an exception, is filtered out at Wikipedia search's actual threshold of 1.0. Even so, these ten cannot tell us the precision. They are examples the authors picked to illustrate, not a random sample; there are only ten; and the judgments are the authors' own. To measure precision you would have to draw calls at random from 𝒞* and have raters who do not know the scores judge them.

Takeaway. A selection rule whose threshold was chosen by yield does not by itself tell you its error rate. To know the error rate you need a random sample with judgments independent of the rule.

7. Limitations the paper states

Toolformer lists five in §7, Limitations.

  • It cannot chain tools. Calls were generated separately for each tool, so the training data has no examples of chaining. TEMPLAMA (§4.2.5) shows the cost.
  • It cannot interact with tools. Uses such as browsing search results or rewriting a query are not possible (the paper gives WebGPT as an example of doing so).
  • It is sensitive to the wording of the input. Whether it calls depends on the exact phrasing of the input.
  • It is sample-inefficient. Even after processing more than a million documents, the useful calculator calls number a few thousand (the calculator row of Table 2: 3,680 at the actual threshold of 0.5). The paper proposes applying the method iteratively as a remedy.
  • It does not take the cost of calls into account. When deciding whether to call, it does not weigh the computational cost, which differs from tool to tool.

One more constraint stated in the body can be added. Call frequency depends heavily on a knob on the harness side, the decoding k. The WebQS call rate is 8.5% at k=1 and 99.3% at k=3 (Table 9). The claim that the model "decides for itself" can also be read as always coming with this knob attached. The arXiv version has no ethics statement. All five tools are read-only, so the risk of changing the outside world did not arise; that risk is handed on to the security section of the MCP specification and to Chapter 15.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

Gorilla (Patil et al. 2024 · NeurIPS 2024). According to the abstract, even GPT-4 gets the arguments of API calls wrong and makes up usage (hallucination), so a LLaMA-based model was fine-tuned for writing API calls. Combined with a document retriever, it is said to keep up when documentation changes and to hallucinate less. Where Toolformer learned "when" to call five simple tools, Gorilla learns which of many APIs to call "with what arguments" and pulls in documentation by retrieval. In supplementing tool knowledge with documentation, it can also be read as a halfway point on the road to MCP's description-based approach (the editor's reading).

HuggingGPT (Shen et al. 2023 · NeurIPS 2023 · Chapter 13 of this book). It does no training. According to the abstract, ChatGPT takes a request, plans the task, picks models by looking at the descriptions of the functions of Hugging Face models, runs the subtasks and summarizes the results. Language serves as "a generic interface". Unlike the main paper, the tools are other AI models, and the basis for choosing a tool is a description loaded into the context, not learned parameters. The structure of dividing work among several models leads on to Chapter 13. This is written only within the scope of the abstract.

Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic 2025). A post on the Anthropic engineering blog. It recommends running agents on evaluation tasks drawn from real work, having an agent analyze those records in turn and fixing the tools, and says a held-out test set was used to avoid overfitting. It gives principles such as building tools around workflows, giving names a namespace and writing descriptions as you would for "a new hire on your team." Toolformer fixed the tools and changed the model; this post fixes the model and changes the tools. It is a prescription drawn from the company's own experience, so read it as design guidance.

TALM (Parisi et al. 2022). The prior work Toolformer singles out with "Perhaps most closely related to our work". According to Toolformer §6, TALM also teaches a calculator and a search engine with a similar self-supervised objective, but was tested only in settings fine-tuned for downstream tasks. The difference is generality: annotating ordinary text with calls without knowing the task.

ReAct (Yao et al. 2022 · Chapter 6 of this book). Toolformer §6 places ReAct on the side of few-shot prompting for tasks where the needed tools are known in advance. In the terms of Chapter 2, ReAct fixed θ and had the model write z, while Toolformer changed θ with no z. ReAct can call many times while looking at observations, but needs human-written trajectories for each task. Toolformer calls once and is done, but needs only a few examples per API.

Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2023 · ICLR 2024 · Chapter 10 of this book). §3.3.3 of the revised AR survey places Self-RAG in the same post-training search box as Toolformer and explains that because it is fine-tuned on a corpus with reflection tokens added, whether to retrieve is learned. In learning "when to ask outside" through special tokens, it pairs with Toolformer's <API>. The difference is who attaches the labels. Going by the survey's explanation, Self-RAG's reflection tokens are attached by a separately trained critic model, while Toolformer's calls are chosen by the model's own loss reduction.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §3.2 — splitting tool use into three boxes

§3.2 of the revised version sums up the core challenge of optimizing tool use as reasoning about "when to use a tool, which tool to select from a library, and how to generate a valid call." These are almost the same three questions as "which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass" in the Toolformer abstract. The survey divides the ways of solving them according to the three optimization targets of Chapter 2: in-context integration (z), post-training integration (θ) and system-level integration (S). Figure 3 pairs three weaknesses of a closed-world LLM (hallucination, outdated knowledge and no ability to compute numbers) with three strengths of tool systems, and these almost coincide with the limitations Toolformer §1 gives as the reason for attaching tools.

The cells in Table 7 where Toolformer and HuggingGPT sit. The cells for this chapter's two methods were checked directly in the table. Below are some of the seventeen rows of Table 7.

Regime Method Stage Learning Tool Strategy Optim. Target
I In-Context Integration ReAct Inference Prompting Interleaved reasoning–action z
II Post-Training Integration Toolformer Post-train Self-sup. + SFT Self-generated API calls θ
II Post-Training Integration ToolLLM Post-train SFT Large-scale API demos θ
III System-Level Integration HuggingGPT System Planner–Exec. Multi-tool coordination S
III System-Level Integration TaskMatrix.AI System Planner Massive API ecosystem S

Some rows of Table 7 of the revised AR survey. The regime names follow the original.

Toolformer is in regime II, "Self-sup. + SFT", with target θ. §3.2.2 gives Toolformer as an example of early work that bootstrapped tool use with SFT, summarizing that models "generate, validate, and retain useful API calls within unlabeled text," then fine-tune on the filtered data. This matches the original. HuggingGPT is in regime III, with target S. §3.2.3 defines this regime as optimizing, with the parameters fixed, the tool library, the orchestration policy and the accumulated record of which tool worked where, across episodes. The HuggingGPT abstract shows only the flow of planning, selection, execution and summarizing for each request, and does not show what it updates across episodes, so this cell can also be read as meaning that it "works on top of a system component, the tool library".

Gorilla appears not in Table 7 but in Table 6, on planning, with target θ (§3.1).

Toolformer is in Table 8 too. In Table 8, which organizes agentic search, Toolformer is listed in the "Post-Training Agentic Search" regime as Sequential · Tool Tokens · APIs, Search · θ, and Self-RAG and WebGPT are in the same box. But post-training is regime II in Table 7 and regime III in Table 8 (Table 8 puts structure-enhanced search in II). In presentation materials, do not write only the Roman numeral; write θ with it. Also, §3.3.3 writes that Toolformer learns when to invoke tools "such as web search or calculators", but the search tool in the original is not web search; it is a BM25 retriever over an index of the KILT Wikipedia dump (Toolformer §3).

The survey's closing paragraph. The Discussion at the end of §3.2 sums up as follows: post-training (θ) steadily improves the validity of calls (correct format and arguments, fewer made-up tools); the system level (S) copes as the tool library grows; and in-context (z) is the option when the tool set is small and fixed or when using an API model with frozen weights. Among the things not yet known it lists whether the ability gained by post-training transfers to tools not seen in training. Toolformer trained with five tools and evaluated with the same five, so it does not answer this question. In an MCP environment, where new tools come in carrying only a description, this is the most practical question. The word MCP could not be found in the body of the revised version. The axis of "how to connect" belongs to the Harness survey.

Matching the notation. Two of Toolformer's symbols share letters with the survey's.

Harness survey §2.1, §4 — the layers of connection

  • The §2.1 timeline. The 2023 entry lists Gorilla, ToolLLM and Toolformer (showing that tool-use capabilities could be "learned or induced") on one line with MCP and A2A (standard interfaces).
  • §4, the tool interface and protocol layer (T). Figure 7 places MCP under protocol standards and Toolformer and Gorilla under tool-augmented training. §4.1 calls MCP "the most visible tool-integration substrate for coding and enterprise agents" and writes that its practical value lies in "ecosystem liquidity" as well as schema-level interoperability: reusing an expanding server catalog instead of writing new connectors. It then classifies the standards by the integration boundary they cross.
Boundary Standard Wire Typed Runtime disc. Long-running
Model ↔ Function Function calling JSON first-class out of scope out of scope
Agent ↔ Capability MCP JSON-RPC first-class first-class partial
Agent ↔ Capability OpenAPI HTTP first-class partial out of scope
Agent ↔ Agent A2A JSON-RPC first-class first-class first-class
Agent ↔ Repo / env AGENTS.md / AGENT.md Markdown out of scope partial out of scope

Table 1 of the Harness survey with the ACP / ANP row removed. The filled, half-filled and empty circles are rendered with the legend's words "first-class support", "partial or convention-level" and "out of scope".

Seen through this table, function calling and MCP do not compete. Function calling is the boundary where the model emits a structured call, and MCP is the boundary where an outside capability is attached to receive and run that call. Toolformer's <API> token can be seen as an early form of learning the first boundary inside the model (the editor's reading). §4.3 writes that tool competence is jointly determined by the training signal, the quality of the interface schema and the runtime selection policy, and that "improving only one component yields limited gains." If Toolformer (parameters), MCP (schema) and the tool-design post (descriptions and evaluation) are read as each taking one component, this chapter comes together in one sentence.

The MCP specification this survey cites is the 2025-06-18 version, and the one this chapter read is the 2026-07-28 version. Checked against the new version, the four cells of the MCP row still read the same. JSON-RPC 2.0 transport, input and output schemas, and runtime tool listing with change notifications are all still there (in the 2026-07-28 version, change notifications moved to a subscriptions/listen stream). Only the basis for long-running work changed. The tasks feature, which came in as experimental in the 2025-11-25 version, became an official extension outside the core specification in the 2026-07-28 version, so looking at the core specification alone it is still only progress notifications and cancellation, hence "partial" (the survey does not give its criteria for each cell; the editor made this comparison). §9.3 also writes that the early MCP specification had no security primitives of its own, and describes a case in which a poisoned tool description alone changed a model's behavior, and a defense that attaches signatures and versions to tool definitions. Chapter 15 picks this up.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "Toolformer was trained on human-annotated tool-use data." All people wrote was one prompt per API with a few examples (§2, Appendix A.2). The model sampled the call candidates, and its own loss reduction decided which to keep. The training data is CCNet web text, not the evaluation tasks (§4.1).

Misreading 2. "Toolformer beat GPT-3 (175B) with 6.7B." It was ahead on LAMA (Table 3), math (Table 4) and DATESET (Table 7). On question answering (Table 5) it was lower on all three datasets (WebQS 26.3 against 29.0, NQ 17.7 against 22.6, TriviaQA 48.8 against 65.9), and on MLQA (Table 6) it did not even consistently beat GPT-J. Note the lenient scoring as well.

Misreading 3. "The filter checks whether the call's result is correct." What the filter looks at is whether receiving the result makes the next tokens of the original text easier to predict. The second candidate in Figure 2 was discarded even though it got a correct answer (United States), and the "Fast train success" call in Table 10 scored 0.92 even though it got information about an unrelated song. The filter is not a fact checker; it is a proxy for "was this useful at this spot".

Misreading 4. "Once a model passes 775M parameters, it knows how to use tools." The claim in §4.4 is an observation from averages over five models, three tools and groups of tasks, with no repeated runs or error bars. Wikipedia search was an exception that helped even the smallest model. It is where the split showed up under these experimental conditions, not a general law.

Misreading 5. "Toolformer is an agent that uses tools many times in a row." In evaluation there is at most one call per input (§4.2), and neither chaining nor interaction is possible (§7). The loop that repeats thought, action and observation belongs to Chapter 6.

Misreading 6. "MCP is a technique for teaching models to use tools". Or: "MCP replaces function calling." MCP is not a training method; it is a communication protocol between host and server. When to call is judged by the model reading the descriptions ("model-controlled"). Table 1 of the Harness survey places function calling at the "Model ↔ Function" boundary and MCP at the "Agent ↔ Capability" boundary, sorting them into roles that do not overlap.

Discussion questions

  1. Whose "usefulness"? Toolformer chose self-supervision on the grounds that people and models may differ in what they find useful, yet in Table 10 the ones judging usefulness were people after all. In your own field (case-law search, looking up statistics, an in-house database), what improves and what becomes risky if tool calls are chosen by "did it help predict the next sentence"?

  2. Should tool knowledge live in the parameters or in the descriptions? Suppose you are connecting an in-house system whose API changes every year. Which is easier to maintain: fine-tuning (θ), or the description and inputSchema sent with every call? What happens to the context when the tools grow to several hundred? Think ahead to Chapter 9.

  3. What it means to "validate" a result. If the result is JSON and there is an outputSchema, schema validation will do. If the result is natural language, like the body of a web page, what should be validated? And what if it contains "ignore the previous instructions"? Check your answer in Chapter 15.

Chapter 8 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 8. Bringing In Outside Knowledge — RAG

The question this chapter answers: what is the simplest probabilistic way to put knowledge that is not in a model's weights into its answers?

Core reading. Patrick Lewis et al., "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks", NeurIPS 2020. 9 pages of main text, 19 with the appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · NeurIPS 2020 paper page · Code (the RAG implementation in Hugging Face Transformers)

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §3.3, §3.3.1, Figure 4, Table 8 · Harness survey §5.5

One-paragraph summary. A pretrained generative model (BART) is given an index that holds 21 million Wikipedia passages as vectors. When a question comes in, the retriever (DPR) pulls out the k nearest passages, and the generator computes the probability of the answer separately for each passage and adds these up, weighted by the retriever's probabilities. Which passage is "responsible" for the answer is left unknown. In statistical terms, it is a mixture model with the document as a latent variable, with the sum cut off at the top k. The paper offers two formulas: RAG-Sequence, in which one document is responsible for the whole answer, and RAG-Token, which can switch documents at every token. The query encoder and the generator are fine-tuned end to end with no labels marking the right document, and the document side is kept fixed. It set the state of the art at the time on four open-domain question answering tasks (the abstract says "three"; on TQA it is best only on the split comparable with T5), and showed that the model's knowledge of the world can be updated just by swapping the index. Today's name "RAG" comes from this paper.

Building intuition

Closed book and open book — Figure 1

The paper divides question answering models into two groups (§4.1). A closed-book model (T5-11B) looks nothing up and generates the answer from its weights alone. An open-book model retrieves documents and, at the time, mostly extracted a span of the answer as it was (extractive: REALM and DPR). RAG stands between them. It retrieves, but it generates the answer.

The paper explains this with two memories (§1). The parameters θ of the generator BART are parametric memory, and the document index that turns Wikipedia into vectors is non-parametric memory. Knowledge in the weights is hard to revise, hard to inspect for its basis and produces hallucinations. Knowledge in the index can be revised directly, and what was fetched can be seen.

Figure 1 draws three tasks side by side: the question "Define 'middle ear'", the claim "Barack Obama was born in Hawaii." (verdict "supports") and the input "The Divine Comedy" for Jeopardy question generation. All three go through the same frame. The input x passes through the query encoder q to become q(x), Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) pulls documents z1,…,z4 out of the index, the generator pθ produces an output for each document, and a "Marginalize" box combines them. The dashed arrow at the top reads "End-to-End Backprop through q and pθ". The training signal reaches only as far as the query encoder and does not touch the index.

One prediction by RAG. The structure of Figure 1 of the paper, with the training scope from §2.4 added. The editor drew the diagram.

The editor's bridge — a mixture model and a query-time join

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

For readers familiar with statistics, the closest thing is a latent class model. When you do not know which class an observation y came from, you sum over all classes: p(y∣x)=∑zp(z∣x)p(y∣x,z). In RAG the classes are documents. There is no label for which document produced the answer, so the document is treated as a latent variable and marginalized out, and maximizing the marginal log-likelihood tilts the prior (the retriever) toward documents that helped with the answer.

For readers familiar with databases, the closest thing is a query-time join. Instead of combining in advance, each time a query comes in you find a few rows in the index and attach them for the computation. Swap the index table and the results change from the next query on. The index hot-swapping experiment in §4.5 is this. The LLM Wiki in Chapter 20 is at the opposite end, corresponding to a materialized view that is computed in advance and kept updated.

The analogy also breaks down. RAG's "classes" number 21 million, the sum is cut to the top k of them, and the cut-off remainder is not measured (Exercise 2). The join is also not an equi-join that finds rows with the same key but an approximate nearest-neighbor search for rows with large inner products, and the result is not a set of rows but a probability-weighted sum.

The paper's own analogy is memory. §5 sees the index as an external memory for a neural network to attend to, and gives as its distinguishing feature that this memory is raw text, so it is human-readable and human-writable.

The paper in detail

1. What it sets out to solve (§1)

What the paper aims at is knowledge-intensive tasks. It defines them as tasks that humans could not reasonably be expected to perform without access to an external knowledge source. Open-domain question answering, fact verification and fact-grounded text generation fall here.

The starting point is hybrid models such as REALM and ORQA, which attach a differentiable retriever to a masked language model. The paper points out that these covered only open-domain extractive question answering, and brings that hybrid memory to the "workhorse of NLP," sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models. Attached to a generative model, it can handle question answering, text generation and classification with the same structure. Also, earlier architectures such as memory networks trained their memory from scratch for each task, while RAG takes both the generator (BART) and the retriever (DPR) pretrained and only fine-tunes them.

2. Two formulas — RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token (§2.1)

Start with the notation. The input sequence is x and the target sequence y; yi is its ith token and N the length of the target sequence. The retriever pη(z∣x) has parameters η and, given a query x, returns a distribution over passages z (truncated to the top k). The generator pθ(yi∣x,z,y1:i−1) has parameters θ and produces the next token from the preceding tokens, the input and one passage. The document is a latent variable. There is no data saying which document is the right one.

RAG-Sequence. One document is responsible for the whole output sequence. For each of the top k documents, the generator computes the probability of the whole output sequence, and these are added up, weighted by the retriever's probabilities.

pRAG-Sequence(y∣x)≈∑z∈top-k(p(·∣x))pη(z∣x)pθ(y∣x,z)=∑z∈top-k(p(·∣x))pη(z∣x)∏iNpθ(yi∣x,z,y1:i−1)

RAG-Token. A different document can be drawn for each target token. For one next token, the per-document distributions are added up with weights, and then the same is repeated for the token after that.

pRAG-Token(y∣x)≈∏iN∑z∈top-k(p(·∣x))pη(z∣x)pθ(yi∣x,z,y1:i−1)

Both formulas reproduce the notation of §2.1 of the paper. The subscript i and superscript N on the product are also as in the original.

The only difference between the two formulas is the order of sum and product. RAG-Sequence takes the product first (a sentence probability for each document), RAG-Token the sum first (a mixture for each token). The first is a sentence-level mixture model, the second a model that picks its mixture component afresh for each token. The paper writes that RAG-Token can draw content from several documents.

Each cell is pθ(yi∣x,z,y1:i−1). The dashed lines show the unit combined in one step. The editor drew the two formulas of §2.1 as a diagram.

For classification tasks the two are the same. If the target class is treated as a sequence of length 1, then N=1 and the order of sum and product no longer matters. This is why the FEVER results are merged into one cell (Table 2, Table 6).

3. Components — the retriever DPR and the generator BART (§2.2–2.3)

Retriever. It uses DPR (Dense Passage Retriever, Karpukhin et al. 2020), a bi-encoder architecture that encodes documents and queries separately.

pη(z∣x)∝exp(d(z)⊤q(x)),d(z)=BERTd(z),q(x)=BERTq(x)

d(z) is the document vector from a BERT-base document encoder, and q(x) the query vector from a BERT-base query encoder. Picking the k documents with the highest prior probability is a Maximum Inner Product Search problem, which can be solved approximately in sub-linear time. The retriever is initialized with DPR's pretrained bi-encoder, which was trained to find documents containing the answers to TriviaQA and Natural Questions questions. Note also that the formula is written with the proportionality sign ∝. Whether it is normalized over all 21 million or renormalized within the top k is not in the text (material for Exercise 2).

Generator. It uses BART-large (the text says 400M parameters). The input x and the document z are simply concatenated. The generator sees one document at a time, and combining several documents is done outside, by marginalization.

Index. The December 2018 Wikipedia is cut into non-overlapping 100-word chunks to make 21 million documents, and a MIPS index is built with FAISS's HNSW approximation (§3). According to Appendix C, loading the index into CPU memory takes about 100GB, or 36GB compressed.

Parameter count — Appendix G. It says the two encoders have 110M each and BART-large 406M, for a total of 626M trainable parameters. This differs from the 400M in §2.3 of the text, and the 626M includes the document encoder, which a parenthesis in the same sentence excludes from training: "although we do not train the document encoder ourselves". Counting only the parameters that are actually updated gives 516M.

4. Training and decoding (§2.4–2.5)

Training. On input–output pairs (xj,yj), the negative marginal log-likelihood ∑j−logp(yj∣xj) is minimized with Adam. There is no direct supervision about which document should be retrieved. Updating the document encoder BERTd as well would require rebuilding the index periodically, as REALM does, which is costly. The paper judged this step unnecessary and fine-tunes only the query encoder BERTq and BART, keeping the document encoder and the index fixed. So on the retrieval side, all training can change is where the query is sent. The generator BART is fine-tuned along with it. The index remains an outside resource unrelated to training. This is why the experiment that swaps out the whole index (§4.5) is possible.

Decoding. At test time argmaxyp(y∣x) has to be approximated, and the two models are in different positions.

  • RAG-Token can be seen as an ordinary autoregressive seq2seq generator. Its transition probability is the following, and it can be plugged straight into a standard beam decoder.

pθ′(yi∣x,y1:i−1)=∑z∈top-k(p(·∣x))pη(zi∣x)pθ(yi∣x,zi,y1:i−1)

The original writes the index of the sum as z and the term inside as zi. Read them as referring to the same document.

  • RAG-Sequence cannot be solved with a single beam search, because its likelihood does not break into a per-token product. A beam search is run for each document to get a set of hypotheses Y; for each document in whose beam a hypothesis did not appear, one more forward pass is run to get its probability, and these are added up weighted by pη(z∣x). This is Thorough Decoding. When outputs are long, |Y| grows, so setting the probability of hypotheses not generated in the beam to pθ(y∣x,zi)≈0 removes the extra computation. This is Fast Decoding.

According to Appendix A, for open-domain QA the test scores were produced with 15 documents for RAG-Token and 50 documents with Thorough Decoding for RAG-Sequence, and decoding was greedy. For MS-MARCO and Jeopardy, both models use 10 documents and a beam size of 4, with Fast Decoding for RAG-Sequence. In training, k∈{5,10} was tried, and the test-time k was chosen on development data (§3).

5. Experimental tasks (§3, Appendix I)

All experiments use a single Wikipedia dump as the non-parametric knowledge source. There are four tasks.

Task Data Input → output Metric Test items (Table 7)
Open-domain QA Natural Questions (NQ) question → answer exact match (EM) 3,611
TriviaQA (TQA) 〃 EM 11,314
WebQuestions (WQ) 〃 EM 2,033
CuratedTrec (CT) 〃 EM 635
Abstractive QA MS-MARCO NLG v2.1 question → sentence answer BLEU-1, ROUGE-L 101,093 (a hidden subset is used for evaluation)
Question generation Jeopardy (SearchQA splits) answer entity → Jeopardy question BLEU-1, Q-BLEU-1, human evaluation 26,849
Fact verification FEVER three-way / two-way claim → verdict label accuracy 10,000 / 6,666

The task descriptions are from §3.1–3.4; the item counts and the MS-MARCO note are from Table 7 in Appendix I.

The generation metrics all compare the model's sentence with a reference sentence and measure overlap; higher is better. BLEU-1 (B-1 in the tables below) is overlap at the level of single words, and ROUGE-L (R-L) overlap based on the longest common subsequence of the two sentences. Q-BLEU-1 (QB-1) is, as the paper explains, a variant of BLEU that gives more weight to getting entities right, and it agrees better with human judgment for question generation (§3.3).

CT and WQ are small, so training on them started from the RAG model trained on NQ. MS-MARCO uses only the questions and answers, not the gold passages attached to each question, so it also contains questions that cannot be answered without the gold passage ("What is the weather in Volcano, CA?"). The human evaluation for Jeopardy is a pairwise comparison that shows a question from BART and one from RAG and asks evaluators to choose on factuality and specificity. Unlike most other methods, FEVER here uses no supervision on the retrieved evidence.

RAG-Token 44.1 55.2 / 66.1 45.5 50.0
RAG-Seq. 44.5 56.8 / 68.0 45.2 52.2

Table 1 of the paper (test sets, EM). For TQA the left value is the standard test set and the right the TQA-Wiki test set. Bold and row grouping follow the original.

Read it in this order.

  1. State of the art on all four tasks. But for TQA only on the split comparable with T5 (the right-hand column); on the standard split DPR (57.9) is above RAG-Sequence (56.8). The paper adds this caveat in parentheses too. According to Appendix D, the standard split is the public TriviaQA Web development split, and TQA-Wiki questions are easier to answer from Wikipedia, so the scores are higher.
  2. The distance from closed book. On NQ, T5-11B scores 34.5 and RAG-Sequence 44.5. According to Appendix G, T5-large (770M parameters), the T5 closest to RAG in parameter count, scored 28.9 on NQ.
  3. Neither special pretraining nor a re-ranker is needed. REALM and T5+SSM use expensive "salient span masking" pretraining. The DPR QA system re-ranks documents with a cross-encoder and pulls out the answer with an extractive reader. RAG does better than these without any of that.

The paper also adds a caveat. The DPR retriever used to initialize RAG's retriever was trained with retrieval supervision on NQ and TriviaQA (§4.1).

Why generation beats extraction. Documents that contain clues to the answer without containing it word for word can still contribute, and an answer can be generated even when none of the retrieved documents contains the right answer. On NQ, the accuracy in such cases was 11.8% (an extractive model would score 0%; the paper gives no denominator).

MS-MARCO (§4.2). RAG-Sequence is 2.6 points above BART on both BLEU-1 and ROUGE-L. In Table 3, for "define middle ear", BART gave the wrong answer "The middle ear is the part of the ear between the middle ear and the nose." (marked "?" in the original).

Jeopardy question generation (§4.3). Here RAG-Token does better than RAG-Sequence, and both beat BART on Q-BLEU-1. The human evaluation was done on 452 pairs produced by BART and RAG-Token.

BART better 7.1% 16.8%

Both good 11.7% 11.8%

This table has two discrepancies. The text says "both RAG and BART were factual in a further 17% of cases," but "Both good" in the table is 11.7%, and 17.7% is the value for "Both poor". And while the factuality column sums to 100.0% (32, 193, 53, 80 and 94 of the 452 pairs), the specificity column sums to 93.0%. The paper explains neither.

Figure 2 — the document posterior that changes with each token. Jeopardy questions often contain two separate pieces of information, and RAG-Token can weave together content from several documents. The paper guesses this is why RAG-Token does better, and gives Figure 2 as an example. The input is "Hemingway", five documents are retrieved, and the generated question is the following.

"The Sun Also Rises" is a novel by this author of "A Farewell to Arms"

The figure draws, for each generated token, RAG-Token's document posterior p(zi∣x,yi,y−i) as a heat map (tokens on the horizontal axis, Doc 1–5 on the vertical). The original does not define y−i separately. Read by convention as "the tokens other than the ith", it is a posterior computed after seeing the whole generated sequence. In RAG-Token the probabilities of later tokens do not depend on zi, so this value equals pη(z∣x)pθ(yi∣x,z,y1:i−1), the retrieval prior times the generation probability of that token, normalized over the documents (the editor's working). The prior pη(z∣x) is the same for every token, but the posterior differs column by column according to which document explains that token well. Document 1 contains A Farewell to Arms (1929), and document 2 the debut novel The Sun Also Rises (1926). Enlarging the figure in the PDF, the darkest cells are document 2 in the "Sun" column and document 1 in the "A" column, where the second title begins. The paper notes that the posterior flattens after the first token of each title is generated. Its hypothesis is that the rest of the title is filled in from parametric knowledge without any particular document.

The authors check this hypothesis with BART alone. Given BART only the partial decoding "The Sun, it continues with "The Sun Also Rises" but repeats the same "The Sun Also Rises" in the second title's place as well; given "The Sun Also Rises" is a novel by this author of "A, it finishes with "A Farewell to Arms". As the paper sums it up, the non-parametric memory guides the generation and draws out knowledge stored in the parametric memory. This interpretation rests on one figure and one example, and how general the flattening is was not measured (Discussion question 1).

FEVER (§4.4). On the three-way task, RAG is within 4.3 percentage points of the best model, a complex pipeline that uses retrieval supervision (72.5 against 76.8); on the two-way task it is within 2.7 percentage points of a RoBERTa model given the gold evidence sentences (89.5 against 92.2). Matching the documents RAG retrieved against the gold evidence documents by title, the top document was a gold document in 71% of cases, and a gold document was among the top 10 in 90%. No denominator is given.

8. Ablations, index swapping and the number of documents (§4.5, Table 6, Figure 3)

Freezing and replacing the retriever. There are two ablations: keeping the retriever fixed during training (Frozen), and replacing the retriever with a fixed BM25 based on word overlap, using its scores as the logits of p(z∣x) (BM25).

The paper's conclusion is that "learned retrieval improves results for all tasks." BM25 did best on FEVER, which the paper guesses may be because FEVER claims are heavily entity-centric and so well suited to word overlap. For the other tasks it writes that differentiable retrieval improves results, "especially for Open-Domain QA, where it is crucial." On NQ, RAG-Token goes from 29.7 with BM25 to 37.8 frozen and 43.5 learned. On CT, by contrast, the difference between frozen and learned is 0.8 points. How far "all tasks" holds up given the sample sizes is examined in section 9.

The MS-MARCO values in this table differ widely from Table 2 (RAG-Token ROUGE-L: 56.2 on dev, 40.1 on test). The paper does not explain the difference, so do not mix numbers from the two tables.

Index hot-swapping. Parametric-only models like T5 or BART need further training as the world changes. The paper built a second index from the December 2016 Wikipedia (the dump DrQA used) and compared it with the December 2018 index. For 82 world leaders who changed between the two dates, it asked the NQ RAG model questions of the form "Who is {position}?" (e.g. "Who is the President of Peru?").

2016 leader as the answer 2018 leader as the answer
2016 index 70% 4%
2018 index 12% 68%

The editor laid out the four figures in the text of §4.5 of the paper as a 2×2 table. The denominator is 82 leaders.

With 82 leaders, each cell can be turned back into whole numbers: 57, 3, 10 and 56. The Wilson 95% confidence intervals are [58.9%, 78.4%] and [57.6%, 77.4%] for the cells where the years match, and [6.8%, 21.0%] and [1.3%, 10.2%] for the mismatched cells, with no overlap at all. Since the same 82 questions were put to both indexes, strictly a paired comparison (McNemar) is needed, but even without per-question results the conclusion is the same. With the 2016 answers as the standard it is 57 against 10, so there are at least 47 discordant pairs, and however the discordant pairs are set, the p value of the exact McNemar test is at most about 4×10−9. Whether the 10 and 3 leaders in the mismatched cells came from old records left in the index or from BART's weights, the paper does not separate.

The number of documents k — Figure 3. In training, there was no significant difference between 5 and 10 documents. The figure has three panels. The left shows NQ exact match by number of documents, the middle NQ retrieval recall (the two learned retrievers, fixed DPR and BM25) and the right MS-MARCO BLEU-1 and ROUGE-L. As the paper describes it, retrieving more documents raises RAG-Sequence's QA score monotonically, while RAG-Token peaks at 10. On MS-MARCO, more documents raise RAG-Token's ROUGE-L and lower its BLEU-1, and the effect is weaker for RAG-Sequence. Values read off the figure's gridlines are not reproduced.

9. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

This paper has denominators. Unlike ReAct in Chapter 6, RAG gives the number of items for each dataset in Table 7 of Appendix I. Treating the two RAG models as independent samples, the standard errors of the differences in Table 1 are as follows.

Task Test items RAG-Token RAG-Seq. Difference (Seq. − Token) SE assuming independence Difference ÷ SE
NQ 3,611 44.1 44.5 +0.4 pp 1.17 pp 0.34
TQA 11,314 55.2 56.8 +1.6 pp 0.66 pp 2.42
WQ 2,033 45.5 45.2 −0.3 pp 1.56 pp −0.19
CT 635 50.0 52.2 +2.2 pp 2.80 pp 0.78

Calculated by the editor from the EM in Table 1 and the item counts in Table 7. TQA uses the standard test set.

Assuming independence, only TQA exceeds two standard errors. The two models were evaluated on the same items, so a paired comparison is possible. The variance of the difference carries a −2Cov(A,B) term (Chapter 7, section 6), so if the two models' per-item correct and incorrect answers are positively correlated, the paired standard error is smaller than this, and if negatively correlated, larger. Which way, and by how much, takes per-item results to know. Exercise 1 estimates the range.

Do the printed percentages fit the denominators? The EM values possible from 635 items are of the form 100k/635, so rounded to one decimal place the value after 49.9 (317 items) is 50.1 (318 items). The CT RAG-Token value of 50.0 in Table 1 cannot come from 635 items, and neither can RAG-Sequence's 52.2 (331 items gives 52.13%, 332 items 52.28%). The REALM 46.8 and DPR 50.6 in the same column, taken from other papers, can be matched. Table 6 makes it plainer. With the dev item counts in Table 7, WQ 362 and CT 134, none of the twelve values (six for WQ and six for CT) can occur. Reduce each denominator by one, to 361 and 133, and all twelve fit. One item may have been dropped from each, or there may be some other reason, but the paper does not explain. Compared with the split table in the DPR paper (the retriever), the item counts in RAG's Table 7 are all larger by 1 (NQ 3,611 against 3,610 and so on), and only the CT test count is given as 635, the same as training, instead of DPR's 694. Setting n=694 turns all four CT values in Table 1 into whole numbers of items. In that case the CT calculations below change to a standard error of 2.68 percentage points and a δ threshold of 8.8%, but the direction of the conclusion is the same. So the CT and WQ calculations in this chapter are approximations.

The "all tasks" of the ablation. Measured the same way, the learned-against-frozen differences in Table 6 split. For RAG-Token, NQ (+5.7 percentage points, 8,758 dev items) and TQA (+4.7) are 6 to 8 times the standard error under independence (around 0.75 percentage points), and WQ (+9.4, 362 items) is 2.6 times. CT is +0.8 percentage points for both models, but with 134 items the standard error is 6.1 points, so it comes to only 0.13 times; RAG-Sequence's WQ (+3.1) is 0.8 times. The observation that BM25 did best on FEVER is also not distinguishable from chance on the three-way task, a difference of 0.6 percentage points (10,000 items, standard error 0.61), and borderline on the two-way task, 1.0 points (6,666 items, 0.49). If the two models' per-item correct and incorrect answers on the same items are positively correlated, a paired comparison makes these ratios larger, so under that assumption these are estimates near the lower bound.

Exercise 1 — two models measured on the same items. (a) Let δ be the share of NQ items on which the two models disagreed (only one got it right). Express the paired standard error of the difference d^=0.004 in terms of δ, and find its value for δ of 5%, 10% and 20%. (b) For the NQ difference to be significant at the 5% level in a paired comparison, how small must δ be? What is the smallest value δ can take? (c) Do the same calculation for CT. (d) In the 452 human-evaluation pairs of Table 4, keep only "BART better" and "RAG better" and run a sign test. What gets in the way when you do the same for the specificity column?

SolutionSolution

(a) On item j, let the two models' correctness be Aj,Bj∈{0,1}. Then Dj=Bj−Aj is one of −1,0,+1, and δ is the share with Dj≠0. Since Var(D)=𝔼[D2]−(𝔼D)2=δ−d2, the paired standard error is

SEpaired=δ−d^2n

With n=3,611 and d^=0.004, it is 0.37 percentage points for δ=5% (difference ÷ SE 1.08), 0.53 for 10% (0.76) and 0.74 for 20% (0.54). These are far smaller than the 1.17 points under independence, but in every case the 0.4-point difference is less than two standard errors.

(b) Solving d^/SEpaired≥1.96 gives δ≤d^2(1+n/1.962)≈1.5%, that is, about 54 or fewer of the 3,611 items. The minimum of δ is |d^|=0.4%. The paper does not publish the per-item agreement rate, so whether δ is below this threshold cannot be known. So whether NQ's 0.4 points is significant in a paired comparison cannot be decided from these data, and 98.5% (1.5% disagreement) should be read only as the threshold at which that decision flips.

(c) For CT, n=635 and d^=0.022, so δ≤8.0% is needed for significance. At δ=5% the difference is 2.49 times the standard error (0.88 percentage points), at 10% 1.76 times, at 20% 1.24 times. The conclusion flips depending on the share of disagreeing items, so the answer is to ask for per-item results. For TQA it is significant as long as δ is 75% or less.

(d) The 7.1% and 42.7% in the factuality column are 32 and 193 of the 452 pairs. The two-sided p value of the exact binomial test is about 3×10−29, and among the pairs with a winner, RAG won 85.8% (Wilson 95% interval [80.6%, 89.7%]). The specificity column is about 76 against 169 pairs, p≈3×10−9. But the specificity column sums to 93.0%, so about 32 pairs are unaccounted for. Even under the extreme assumption that all the missing pairs were "BART better", it is 108 against 169 (p≈3×10−4) and RAG is still ahead, but the error in the table is itself worth reporting. Appendix B says only that the judgments of two poorly performing evaluators were removed; it does not say how many evaluators judged each pair.

Takeaway. Read differences measured on the same items as paired comparisons, and when there are no per-item results, show at what share of disagreeing items the conclusion flips. Check the totals of a table and the denominators of its percentages first.

Exercise 2 — reading marginalization as a mixture model. (a) A toy example with two documents and two output tokens. pη(z1∣x)=pη(z2∣x)=0.5; given document 1, the probability of the first token A is 0.9 and of the second token B (after A) 0.1; document 2 is the reverse, 0.1 and 0.9. Find the probability of the output "A B" with the RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token formulas. (b) If pη is normalized over all 21 million documents and the top k have total probability Mk, what bound is there on the difference between the RAG-Sequence value cut to the top k and the full sum? What happens if you renormalize within the top k? (c) Is there anything the paper reports from which Mk could be estimated?

SolutionSolution

(a) RAG-Sequence multiplies first, for each document. Document 1 gives 0.9×0.1=0.09, document 2 also 0.09, and the weighted sum is 0.09. RAG-Token mixes first, for each token. Both tokens give 0.5×0.9+0.5×0.1=0.5, and the product is 0.25. For an answer whose first part is supported by document 1 and its second part by document 2, RAG-Token gives almost three times the probability. The Hemingway example in Figure 2 has this structure. For an answer that one document supports from start to finish, RAG-Sequence is at no disadvantage. The editor made up this numerical example.

(b) Write the full sum as p(y∣x)=∑all zpη(z∣x)pθ(y∣x,z) and the sum cut to the top k as pk(y∣x). Every term is nonnegative and pθ≤1, so

pk(y∣x)≤p(y∣x)≤pk(y∣x)+(1−Mk)

The cut sum is a lower bound, and the error does not exceed the cut-off prior mass 1−Mk. Renormalizing within the top k, p~k=pk/Mk becomes a mixture model conditional on "the document is in the top k". Then p(y∣x)=Mkp~k+(1−Mk)r, where r is the mixture formed by the remaining documents and lies between 0 and 1, so |p(y∣x)−p~k|≤1−Mk. Either way, the quality of the approximation is set by the tail mass 1−Mk. Fast Decoding (§2.5) is an approximation in the same direction. It sets the per-document probability of hypotheses that did not appear in the beam to 0, so it uses a lower bound on the Thorough Decoding value.

(c) No. The normalization is not in the text, and the probability mass of the top k is not reported. The retrieval recall in the middle panel of Figure 3 measures "is the answer in the top K", a different quantity from Mk. The only indirect evidence is how the scores change as k grows (Figure 3) and the sentence saying there was no significant difference between 5 and 10 documents in training. How well the cut sum approximates the full sum cannot be answered from this paper.

Takeaway. In a mixture model, the order of sum and product is itself an assumption about what counts as one latent cause. Marginalization cut to the top k carries an error up to the tail mass, and if the tail is not measured you cannot know whether the approximation is good.

10. Limitations the paper states

  • How to combine the two memories is an open problem (§6). Whether the two components can be pretrained jointly from scratch, and how best to combine parametric and non-parametric memory, are left for future work.
  • Retrieval collapse — Appendix H. In preliminary experiments on tasks such as story generation, the retriever "collapsed" into retrieving the same documents regardless of the input, after which the generator learned to ignore the documents and RAG performed the same as BART. As possible causes it names the nature of tasks with a less explicit requirement for factual knowledge, or the less informative gradients reaching the retriever because of long target sequences.
  • Questions that need no retrieval — Appendix F. Like REALM, it tried adding one more "null document" and marginalizing over k+1, but this did not help and was dropped. On MS-MARCO, the model was observed learning to always retrieve a particular set of documents for questions unlikely to benefit from retrieval.
  • Evidence extraction for FEVER — Appendix E. FEVER uses a different Wikipedia dump, so the evidence-sentence extraction task was not covered.
  • Knowledge sources and misuse (Broader Impact). Neither Wikipedia nor any other knowledge source can be entirely factual and free of bias. It writes that the misuse concerns raised for GPT-2 (misleading content, impersonation, automated spam and phishing) apply, if to a lesser degree.

One thing the paper does not report can also be noted. The paper does not say whether training and evaluation were run more than once, so the variation from seeds or repeated runs cannot be known. The standard errors in section 9 measure only the variation from sampling items, so small differences, such as which of the two RAG models is better, can also be read as more uncertain than that.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

The list first proposed for the study has no side papers for this chapter. Instead, the chapter contrasts two prior works this paper compares itself with, and the work covered in other chapters of this book. The bibliographic details of the first two were checked in the RAG paper's reference list.

REALM and ORQA (Guu et al. 2020 · Lee et al. 2019). The pair the RAG paper names in §1 as "two recently introduced models" and in §5 as using "a latent variable approach … as in our work." They attached a differentiable retriever to a masked language model but covered only open-domain extractive question answering (§1). REALM updates the document encoder during pretraining, rebuilds the index periodically and uses "salient span masking" pretraining. RAG keeps the document side fixed (§2.4) and generates the answer without that pretraining (§4.1). On NQ, REALM scores 40.4 and RAG-Sequence 44.5.

Closed-book T5 (Roberts et al. 2020). A baseline that generates answers from its weights alone, without retrieval. Its output method is the same as RAG's; only where the knowledge lives differs. On NQ, T5-11B scores 34.5 and T5-11B+SSM 36.6 (Table 1). The bigger difference is updating. A parametric-only model needs further training when the world changes; RAG just needs its index swapped (§4.5).

ReAct and Toolformer (Yao et al. 2023 · Chapter 6 of this book · Schick et al. 2023 · Chapter 7 of this book). Here retrieval is an action the model chooses, or one tool among others. ReAct's search[entity] is a deliberately weak API that returns only the first five sentences (the paper itself says it is significantly weaker than state-of-the-art lexical or neural retrievers), and when, what and how many times to search is decided within its thoughts. Toolformer's Wikipedia search tool is a BM25 retriever, and in the question answering experiments it turned off the question answering tool because the task would become too easy. RAG always retrieves k documents, once per input, before generating. There is no choosing whether to retrieve. In addition, the FEVER "Supervised SoTA" of 89.5 in ReAct's Table 1 cites Lewis et al. 2020 in a footnote, but in RAG's Table 2, 89.5 is the two-way value and the three-way value is 72.5. ReAct's FEVER has three labels, so how to reconcile the two tables is an open question.

Lost in the Middle (Liu et al. 2024 · Chapter 9 of this book). The case study in §5 uses a retriever–reader setup that puts all k retrieved documents into a single prompt. RAG's generator looks at documents one at a time and marginalizes outside, so the problem of "a document placed in the middle of a long context" does not arise in the same form. A document's contribution is set not by its position in the input but by the retrieval probability pη(z∣x) together with the generation probability given that document, pθ(y∣x,z) (this contrast is this book's reading). Saturation as the number of documents grows, and the contrast between the two setups, are examined with numbers in section 6 of "The paper in detail" and in the side papers of Chapter 9.

Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2024 · Chapter 10 of this book). Its introduction names Lewis et al. 2020 and Guu et al. 2020 as conventional RAG (left side of Figure 1), and takes as its problem that they retrieve a fixed number of passages indiscriminately, whether or not retrieval is needed. Self-RAG trains the model to emit reflection tokens so that it retrieves only when needed and evaluates the results itself. It amounts to solving, with separate tokens and training data, the place where the null-document experiment in RAG's Appendix F failed.

LLM Wiki (Karpathy 2026 · preview of Chapter 20 of this book). Of RAG, which retrieves chunks at query time, it writes that "the LLM is rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question. There's no accumulation.", and proposes that knowledge be "compiled once and then kept current, not re-derived on every query." RAG joins at every query; LLM Wiki combines in advance. What the advantage of index swapping and the advantage of accumulating synthesis trade against each other is the subject of Chapter 20.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §3.3 — "traditional RAG" as a reference point

In the first paragraph of §3.3, "Agentic Search", the revised AR survey contrasts agentic RAG, in which an agent governs the entire retrieval–generation loop, with this paper.

Unlike traditional RAG pipelines (Lewis et al., 2020; Huang & Huang, 2024; Yang et al., 2024f) that perform fixed, one-shot retrieval before generation, agentic RAG agents dynamically control when, what, and how to retrieve based on real-time reasoning needs.

Figure 4 draws this contrast. On the left, in the "Traditional RAG System", a query passes through data embedding and a vector database, documents are fetched by "Static Retrieval", and the retrieved document, the user query and the system prompt are combined to produce the answer. On the right, in the "Agentic Search System", an autonomous agent decides "WHEN,WHAT, HOW to Retrieve" and synthesizes the answer through dynamic retrieval, reasoning, Critique & Adapt and tool use.

The survey divides agentic RAG into three branches, in-context (§3.3.1, z), structure-enhanced (§3.3.2, S) and post-training (§3.3.3, θ), matching the three regimes of Table 8. Looking at Table 8 directly, Lewis et al.'s RAG is in none of its cells. Regime I has ReAct, Self-Ask and IRCoT; regime III has Toolformer, Self-RAG, DeepRAG, WebGPT, Search-R1 and others. RAG is the outside baseline that defines agentic search. §3.3.1 introduces reflective retrieval but deliberately states that its best-known instances, Self-RAG and DeepRAG, update θ and so are placed in regime III (Chapter 10).

The survey also cites Lewis et al. on the memory side. §4.2.1 gives dense retrieval methods as examples of traditional systems that treat memory as a passive buffer, and §4.3.3 writes that early search relied on "fixed retrieval heuristics or similarity-based dense retrievers". The preamble of §4.2 states that, in the vocabulary of §2.2, the memory in that section is all system-level (S).

How to read "fixed". This paper fine-tunes the query encoder and the generator, and Table 6 is a result showing that learned retrieval is generally better than frozen retrieval. Read "fixed" as meaning the retriever is not trained and it does not fit; read it as meaning the timing and number of retrievals are set (once per input, before generation, k documents) and it fits. The survey's "fixed, one-shot" can be read as closer to the second meaning. The traditional-RAG box in Figure 4 adds documents to the prompt, which also differs from this paper, which generates separately for each document and marginalizes. Since it is a figure of RAG in general, this can be seen as a difference of scope.

Matching the notation — z overlaps. In this paper z is a document, while zt in the survey and in this book is a reasoning trace (section 6 of Appendix I). "The paper in detail" wrote documents as z to reproduce the original formulas as they are; in this section only, documents are written d instead. The original's d(z) (the document vector) is not used in this section.

RAG paper Notation in this section Place in §2.2 of the revised AR survey
Input x x Observation ot (the user's question)
Document z (latent variable) d Unrelated to the survey's zt. A retrieval result is closer to an observation that goes into the history ht
Retriever pη(z∣x) pη(d∣x) Not an action chosen by the policy π. A fixed procedure run once per input
Generator parameters θ (parametric memory) θ θ
Document index (non-parametric memory) — Part of the system state S (external memory). A mapping that follows the classification in §4.2 of the survey
Fine-tuning the query encoder and generator — The θ mode (post-training)
Index swapping — Changes S, but a person changes it, not the update operator U (Eq. 5)
Marginalization ∑d ∑dpη(d∣x)pθ(y∣x,d) No direct counterpart. Only the shape, marginalizing out a latent variable, is the same

The editor filled in the right-hand column to fit the definitions in §2.2 and §4.2 of the survey.

Seen through this mapping, RAG touches θ through fine-tuning and S through index swapping, and does not touch z. It writes no reasoning traces and does not decide by reasoning whether to retrieve. This is one way to read why the survey put this paper as a reference point outside agentic search. In Chapter 9 and Chapter 10, judgment is added on top of retrieval one layer at a time.

Harness survey §5.5 — retrieval in the long-term memory layer

The Harness survey does not cite Lewis et al. The nearest place is §5.5, "Long-Term: Persistent Memory Systems", which gives "arbitrary recall" — retrieving the most relevant stored memories for a query regardless of when they were created — as the mark of long-term memory. §5.5.3 introduces the "context window plus retrieval store" pattern, and writes that the retrieval-augmented generation survey (Gao et al. 2023) provides the background underpinning the retrieval tier of production memory systems. In the frame of Chapter 3, the index-swapping experiment reads as an experiment that changed only the harness's memory layer while leaving the model as it was (this book's reading).

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "RAG is a technique for pasting retrieved documents into the prompt." This paper's generator sees the input concatenated with one document (§2.3), and adds up the probabilities computed separately for each document, weighted by the retriever's probabilities (§2.1). Putting several documents into one prompt is a variant that became widespread later, and the position effect in Chapter 9 is a problem of that variant.

Misreading 2. "RAG is a method you attach without training." The query encoder and BART are fine-tuned for each task (§2.4). Only the document encoder and the index are kept fixed. Freezing the retriever lowered the NQ score by 5.7 points for RAG-Token (Table 6).

Misreading 3. "The retriever is trained with labels marking the right document." Fine-tuning has no document supervision; it only raises the marginal likelihood of the answer (§2.4). The starting point, though, the DPR retriever, was trained with retrieval supervision on NQ and TriviaQA (§4.1).

Misreading 4. "RAG-Token is better than RAG-Sequence (or the reverse)." RAG-Token was higher on Jeopardy, and RAG-Sequence on MS-MARCO and on NQ, TQA and CT (Tables 1 and 2). But the QA differences mostly lie within the range of item sampling, and under independence only TQA exceeded two standard errors (section 9).

Misreading 5. "The more documents you retrieve, the better." RAG-Token's NQ score peaked at 10 documents, and on MS-MARCO more documents raised ROUGE-L at the cost of BLEU-1 (§4.5, Figure 3). The test settings also differ by task and model: 10, 15 or 50 documents (Appendix A).

Misreading 6. "Using RAG eliminates hallucination." It only reduces it. In the human evaluation, BART and RAG-Token both produced non-factual questions in 17.7% of cases (Table 4). RAG generates answers from parametric knowledge even when the retrieved documents do not contain the answer (NQ 11.8%, §4.1), and that path is not controlled by retrieval.

Misreading 7. "Looking at the retrieval results tells you why that answer came out." In Figure 2, the document posterior flattens after the first token of each title, and the authors infer that BART's weights filled in the rest (the original states this as a hypothesis and cites a single BART-only test as evidence). The retrieved documents do not back every token of the answer. Attribution in Chapter 11 deals with this gap.

Discussion questions

  1. How do the two memories divide the work? In Figure 2, the documents lead the first token of each title, and the authors' hypothesis is that BART's weights filled in the rest. If you used a retrieval-augmented system in your own work, would this division of labor be a strength or a risk? Is there a way to show, in the output, which parts the weights filled in and which parts the documents backed? Think ahead to RARR in Chapter 11.

  2. Does swapping the index change the knowledge? In the index-swapping experiment, the cells where the years were mismatched were not zero either, at 12% and 4%. When old knowledge left in the weights conflicts with a new index, which wins? For material that changes often, such as statutes or company rules, would you choose swapping the index (this chapter) or rewriting a curated wiki (Chapter 20)?

  3. Who decides whether to retrieve? RAG always retrieves. The null document in Appendix F had no effect; instead, on MS-MARCO the model learned to always retrieve a particular set of documents for questions where retrieval is useless. Can this be seen as implicitly learning "not to retrieve"? Compare it with how Self-RAG in Chapter 10 brings this decision out into reflection tokens. This is the question that links the two papers when combining with Chapter 10.
