Chapter 9 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 9. Is More Context Always Better? — Lost in the Middle and Context Engineering

The question this chapter answers: does the answer change depending on where in the context the same information is placed?

Core reading. Nelson F. Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts", TACL vol. 12 (2024). 11 pages of main text, 18 with the appendices (arXiv v3).

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · ACL Anthology (TACL 2024) · Code and evaluation data

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) has no corresponding section (excluded by the criteria in §1.1; only the preamble of §4.2) · Harness survey §5.1–5.3, §5.6–5.7

One-paragraph summary. The model is given one question and k Wikipedia passages. The answer is in exactly one of them. The authors moved that answer document from the very front to the very end, changed k among 10, 20 and 30, and measured accuracy. For most of the six models of 2023, the result was a U-shaped curve: accuracy was highest when the answer document was at the very front or the very end and lowest in the middle. For GPT-3.5-Turbo there were settings in which an answer document placed in the middle gave lower accuracy than giving no documents at all. Models with extended windows drew almost the same curves as the original models, and raising the number of retrieved documents from 20 to 50 lifted accuracy by only a little over 1 to 1.5 percentage points. Where you put something matters as much as what you put in. This is the starting point of the practice now called "context engineering".

Must read. §1 (especially Figure 1 and the last two paragraphs), all of §2.1, the two paragraphs with bold lead sentences in §2.3, all of §5, and §6.3. If you show only one figure, make it Figure 5. Set its three panels side by side and you can see that the valley deepens as documents are added and that the height of the two ends differs from model to model.

Optional reading. Appendix G (the numbers behind Figure 5, material for section 7), Appendix A (unambiguous questions only), Appendix C (distractors in random order), Appendix E (Llama-2 curves by size).

What to cut from the presentation. The lists of related work in §6.1 and §6.2, and the token-count tables in Appendix F (section 3 of "The paper in detail" carries over only the numbers it needs). For Appendices B and D, look at one figure each.

Continuing from Chapter 8. Multi-document question answering is an experiment that isolates the reading step of a retrieval-augmented setup, in which several retrieved documents are concatenated into a single prompt. Its structure differs from the Lewis-style RAG of Chapter 8, which generates separately for each document and marginalizes outside the model (the RAG item in "Side papers" in this chapter). If your group covered Chapter 8 briefly together with Chapter 10, put Figure 3 of the RAG paper (number of documents at test time) back on screen in the first 3 minutes and compare it with §5 of this paper.

When you quote the numbers. The scores are those of mid-2023 models (GPT-3.5-Turbo, version 0613, Claude-1.3 and others) with greedy decoding. The metric is accuracy, counting an output as correct if it contains any one of the annotated answers, and there are 2,655 questions. When you write a number down, give the model, the number of documents and the position of the answer document with it. The drop of more than 20 percentage points refers to the GPT-3.5 models in the 20- and 30-document settings; Claude-1.3's drop is around 5 percentage points.

Building intuition

Figure 1 at a glance

Figure 1 is the curve of a single model, GPT-3.5-Turbo (version 0613). It is given 20 documents, and accuracy is plotted as the document with the answer is moved one slot at a time from the 1st position to the 20th; the red dashed line is closed-book accuracy, with no documents given. The curve is highest at the 1st position, falls steeply over the first few slots, crawls along the bottom around the middle and rises again toward the end. The bottom stretch lies below the closed-book line.

The caption calls the high front "primacy bias" and the high end "recency bias". Values read off the gridlines are not reproduced here. For the same setting, Table 6 in Appendix G gives the numbers at five positions: 75.8% at the 1st, 53.8% at the 10th and 63.2% at the 20th, against a closed-book 56.1% (Table 1).

This experiment is an open-book condition. Even though the passage with the answer sits right there in the input, accuracy differed by more than 20 percentage points depending on where that passage was.

The editor's bridge — factorial experiments and the serial position effect

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

Seen from statistics, §2 is a clean factorial experiment. The factors are the model (6 levels), the number of documents k (10, 20 and 30) and the position of the answer document (1st through k-th), and the response is whether the answer is correct. It is a repeated-measures design that asks the same 2,655 questions under every condition, with the question as the block. The position factor is nested within the document-count factor. The "15th" position in the 20-document setting does not exist with 10 documents, so to compare across document counts you have to convert to relative positions such as "front, middle, end".

Anyone who has studied psychology will think of list-memory experiments. Read people a list of words and have them write down whatever they remember, and they do well on the first and last few words and miss the middle. This is the serial position effect; the advantage at the front is called primacy and the advantage at the end recency.

The analogy also breaks down. In a human free-recall experiment, people recall from memory after the list has gone by. The model in this paper looks for one item while the whole list is still sitting in its input. No time passes, and there is no chance to forget. The same shape of curve does not guarantee the same cause.

§6.3 of the paper builds this bridge itself. The authors write that the U-shaped curve has a connection in psychology known as the serial-position effect (Ebbinghaus 1913, Murdock Jr. 1962): in free recall of elements from a list, people best remember the first and last elements, and the effect plays a role in understanding how humans develop short- and long-term memory. They then add: "Observing a serial-position-like effect in language models is perhaps surprising, since the self-attention mechanisms underlying Transformer language models is technically equally capable of retrieving any token from their contexts." They offer the connection without claiming a common cause.

The paper in detail

1. The question and the design principle (§1)

The input to a language model holds long documents, conversation histories and search results and runs to thousands of tokens. Context windows have grown from 4,096 to 32K and 100K tokens, but how well models actually use those longer windows was not known. That is the authors' starting point.

The criterion fits in one sentence: "If language models can robustly use information within long input contexts, then their performance should be minimally affected by the position of the relevant information in the input context." At the end of §1 the authors put this forward as a new evaluation protocol for long-context models: "to claim that a language model can robustly use information within long input contexts, it is necessary to show that its performance is minimally affected by the position of the relevant information in the input context (e.g., minimal difference in best- and worst-case performance)."

There are two lines of experiment. Multi-document question answering (§2) has the model understand meaning and find the answer in a pile of documents that looks like search results. Key–value retrieval (§3) strips the meaning away and has the model find an identical string among random strings. §4 pokes at three candidate causes, and §5 returns to a real retriever-reader setup to ask how many documents one should put in after all.

2. Design of multi-document question answering (§2.1–2.2)

Task. The input is one question and k documents. Exactly one contains the answer, and the remaining k−1 are distractors that do not. Here is the example prompt from Figure 2.

Write a high-quality answer for the given question using only the provided search
results (some of which might be irrelevant).

Document [1](Title: Asian Americans in science and technology) Prize in physics for
discovery of the subatomic particle J/ψ. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar shared...
Document [2](Title: List of Nobel laureates in Physics) The first Nobel Prize in
Physics was awarded in 1901 to Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, of Germany, who received...
Document [3](Title: Scientist) and pursued through a unique method, was essentially
in place. Ramón y Cajal won the Nobel Prize in 1906 for his remarkable...

Question: who got the first nobel prize in physics
Answer:

The input context of Figure 2 of the paper. The desired answer is "Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen". The original figure puts the document with the answer (Document [2]) in bold. The ellipses are in the original figure.

Note that the question comes at the very end. It becomes a problem again in §4.2.

Data. NaturalQuestions-Open: questions people actually typed into Google search, paired with answers that people extracted from Wikipedia. The authors took the 2,655 questions whose annotated long answer is a paragraph rather than a table or a list. Documents are Wikipedia chunks of at most 100 tokens. The answer document is the paragraph containing the answer from the NaturalQuestions annotation, and the distractors are the k−1 chunks retrieved by Contriever (fine-tuned on MS-MARCO) that are most relevant to the question while containing none of the annotated answers. The distractors are presented in order of decreasing relevance.

A distractor is a passage that resembles the question but has no answer, what information retrieval calls a hard negative. This sets the difficulty of the design.

Two knobs. Position is manipulated by changing only the order of the documents so that the answer document sits where you want (Figure 3), and length by adding or removing documents that do not contain the answer (Figure 4). Turning either knob leaves the desired answer unchanged.

The design of §2.1 and Figures 3–4 of the paper. The position knob moves the answer document within a row, and the length knob changes the number of boxes. The editor drew the diagram.

Metric. An output counts as correct if any of the annotated answers appears in it. It is a lenient metric that checks only whether a string is contained.

Things that could shake the design, and how they were checked. The authors checked three things in footnotes and appendices. A few distractors might contain a reasonable answer (footnote 2), so they reran on a subset of unambiguous questions only (Appendix A). They replaced the distractors with random Wikipedia documents; absolute accuracy went up, but the models still did not use the whole input evenly (Appendix B). And when they shuffled the distractors at random and added "The search results are ordered randomly." to the instruction, the U-shaped curve remained (Appendix C).

Seen from statistics, the last check is a guard against confounding. In the original design, placing the answer document at position j puts the most relevant distractors in front of it. The position effect and the relevance of neighboring documents are entangled, and the random-order condition pulls them apart. The authors state that their whole experimental setup is similar to the needle-in-a-haystack experiments of Ivgi et al. (2023), which place the relevant paragraph either at the beginning or at a random position, but studies "finer-grained changes in the position of relevant information." That remark is not about the random-order check above alone.

Models (§2.2). All use greedy decoding; other decoding methods are left to future work.

Because of cost (footnote 6: more than USD 6,000 for the full set of experiments), GPT-4 (8K) was evaluated only on a random 500 questions in the 20-document setting. Its absolute performance was the highest, but it showed the same U-shaped curve (Appendix D, Figure 15).

Why GPT-3.5-Turbo (4K) is missing from the 30-document table can be seen from the token counts in Table 3 of Appendix F. With the GPT-3.5 tokenizer, inputs with 10, 20 and 30 documents average 1,475.6, 2,946.2 and 4,419.2 tokens, with maxima of 1,960, 3,920 and 6,101 tokens (the paper notes that the Claude-1.3 tokenizer gives the same counts on this data). Even the average 30-document input exceeds the 4K window, and the 20-document input, with a maximum of 3,920 tokens, barely fits. The figure titles' "~2K", "~4K" and "~6K tokens" are closer to the maxima than to the averages.

Drawn from the values printed in Table 6 of Appendix G (20 documents). Only four models are shown; the extended versions (16K and 100K) were left out because they differ from the original models by 0.3 percentage points or less. The horizontal dashed line is GPT-3.5-Turbo's closed-book accuracy from Table 1. The editor drew the diagram.

The paper's two observations. §2.3 summarizes the results in two bold sentences.

  1. "Model performance is highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of its input context." GPT-3.5-Turbo drops by more than 20 percentage points, and "in the worst case," in the 20- and 30-document settings, it falls below its performance without documents (56.1%). The authors read this as meaning that current models cannot effectively reason over their entire context window.
  2. "Extended-context models are not necessarily better at using input context." When the input fits in the windows of both models, their performance is nearly identical. In Figure 5 the curves of GPT-3.5-Turbo and its 16K version almost coincide. In the tables, the two models differ by no more than 0.3 percentage points at the same position, and Claude-1.3 and its 100K version by no more than 0.2.

Reading the tables directly shows more texture than the summary. The "GPT-3.5-Turbo" values in the 30-document setting are, given how the table is built, those of the 16K version, whose closed-book baseline is 56.0%. Drops of more than 20 percentage points appear only in the GPT-3.5 models (20 documents 75.8 → 53.8; 30 documents, 16K, 73.4 → 50.5). For Claude-1.3 and MPT-30B-Instruct, the gap between the highest and lowest points in the 20-document setting is 4.2 and 4.5 percentage points. Which end is higher also differs by model. GPT-3.5 and LongChat are much higher at the front, while Claude-1.3 and MPT are slightly higher at the end in the 20- and 30-document settings. With 10 and 20 documents, LongChat's last position is not higher than its middle (58.5 against 58.9, 55.0 against 55.3), so its curve is more an L than a U. The statistical meaning is taken up in section 7.

Figure 1 plots all 20 positions for GPT-3.5-Turbo, but Figure 5 and Appendix G show only one position in every five. The paper does not say from which set of positions the minimum behind "in the worst case" was taken.

4. A task stripped of meaning — key–value retrieval (§3)

Can a model at least fetch an identical token from its input? §3 is designed as a minimal testbed for that. The input is a JSON object whose keys and values are all random 128-bit UUIDs, and the model must return the value for a given key (Figure 6). Meaning was removed on purpose because linguistic features may be confounders. Position is manipulated through the location of the key to retrieve, length through the number of key–value pairs (75, 140 and 300), with 500 examples per setting.

"Claude-1.3 and Claude-1.3 (100K) do nearly perfectly on all evaluated input context lengths". The other models struggled with 140 and 300 pairs, and GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) and MPT-30B-Instruct were lowest when retrieving a key in the middle (Figure 7). In the 140-pair setting, when the key was at the very front, LongChat-13B (16K) tended to generate code to retrieve the key rather than output the value. Even finding a single exactly matching string is swayed by position.

Two things to add. Looking at the figure, the 300-pair panel of Figure 7 has lines only for Claude-1.3 (100K) and GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K). A 300-pair input averages 14,929.4 tokens (Table 4 in Appendix F) and does not fit in Claude-1.3's 8K window, so "all evaluated input context lengths" should be read as the lengths evaluated within each model's window. And with 500 examples, the standard error near 50% accuracy is about 2.2 percentage points, about 2.3 times that of §2.

5. Why does it happen? — three preliminary investigations (§4)

The authors themselves call these "preliminary investigations".

Model architecture (§4.1, Figure 8). The open models are all decoder-only and attend only to earlier tokens. The encoder-decoder Flan-UL2 was "relatively robust" to position within its 2,048-token training-time window (1.9% between best and worst case) and began to drop in the middle on longer inputs. Flan-T5-XXL behaved similarly. The authors hypothesize that this is because a bidirectional encoder processes each document in the context of the documents that come after it.

Query-aware contextualization (§4.2, Figure 9). Since the question comes at the very end, a decoder-only model cannot see the question while it reads the documents. When the question was placed twice, before and after the documents (query-aware contextualization), all models became nearly perfect on key–value retrieval. GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) was perfect with 300 pairs; without this treatment its worst-case performance was 45.6%. In multi-document question answering, however, it helped slightly only when the answer was at the very front and hurt slightly elsewhere.

Instruction fine-tuning (§4.3, Figure 10). In instruction fine-tuning data the task description usually comes first; could that be what makes models weight the front? The base model MPT-30B showed the same U-shaped curve as MPT-30B-Instruct. Instruction fine-tuning only slightly narrowed the best–worst gap, from nearly 10% to around 4%. The authors add the hypothesis that base models also learn to use long contexts from Internet text seen in pretraining (for example, StackOverflow questions and answers).

In the Llama-2 experiment of Appendix E (Figure 16), 7B showed only recency bias, and the U-shaped curve appeared at 13B and 70B. The 13B base model had a 20-point gap between best and worst, and 10 points after additional fine-tuning; at 70B, fine-tuning barely changed the pattern. The authors hypothesize that earlier work did not see primacy bias because the models it studied were small, under a billion parameters. Only this experiment dropped 20 questions that exceeded Llama-2's 4,096-token window.

6. Does adding more documents help? (§5)

The title of §5 is a question ("Is More Context Is Always Better?", exactly as in the original). The answer is that it depends on the task, because it turns on the marginal value of the added context and on the model's ability to use it. To measure that trade-off, the authors used a retriever-reader setup in which the retriever Contriever fetches the top k Wikipedia documents for each NaturalQuestions-Open question and the language model answers with them included as is in the prompt. Retriever recall and reader accuracy were measured as functions of k. The questions are the subset whose long answer is a paragraph, but the number of questions is not given. Unlike in §2, the top k documents may contain no answer or several.

Results — Figure 11. Retriever recall keeps rising as documents are added (5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50), while reader accuracy flattens much earlier. The text says that going beyond 20 documents adds only about 1.5% for GPT-3.5-Turbo and about 1% for Claude-1.3, while the input length (and thus latency and cost) grows substantially. The directions the authors offer are reranking, which pushes relevant documents toward the front, and ranked list truncation, which retrieves fewer documents when appropriate.

Looking at the figure, the lines that run to 50 documents in Figure 11 are GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K), Claude-1.3 (100K), MPT-30B-Instruct and LongChat-13B (16K), and the Claude-1.3 (8K) line ends at 40 documents. MPT has an 8K window yet is plotted out to 50 documents; extrapolating from the token counts in Appendix F, some inputs may have exceeded its window, but the paper does not explain how this was handled. The comparison out to 50 documents holds only if "GPT-3.5-Turbo" and "Claude-1.3" in the text are read as model families. The paper does not give the numbers in Figure 11 as a table, and this chapter does not reproduce values read off the gridlines.

In the RAG paper of Chapter 8, fetching more documents at test time raised RAG-Sequence's NQ performance monotonically (§4.5, Figure 3). The readers in the two experiments are built differently. "Side papers" returns to this.

7. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper (the three tables of Appendix G, Table 1 and the question count in the text). The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

Each cell rests on 2,655 questions. ReAct in Chapter 6 did not report its question count, so we had to make an assumption. This paper states 2,655 questions in §2.1, and the cells of Appendix G read as accuracies over that full set (only the Llama-2 experiment says separately that it dropped 20 questions). Near 50% accuracy, the standard error of a single cell is 0.5×0.5/2655≈0.97 percentage points, and the half-width of the 95% interval is about 1.9 percentage points. Comparing two cells as if they were independent samples, the standard error of the difference is about 1.37 percentage points. The paper gives neither error bars nor standard errors, but this is enough for a rough sense. The difference between an extended version and its original model (at most 0.3 percentage points) lies within the noise, consistent with the reading "nearly identical", while the 22.0-point gap between the 1st and 10th positions for GPT-3.5-Turbo with 20 documents is 17 times the standard error.

In fact the same questions were asked with only the position changed, so these are paired samples. If the correlation of per-question correctness is ρ, the standard error of the difference shrinks to 2p(1−p)(1−ρ)/n (0.97 percentage points when ρ=0.5), and with per-question results one could use the McNemar test. The independent-sample calculation is conservative only when ρ>0. By the same formula, if ρ<0 the standard error actually grows.

Read as a factorial design. Since this is a repeated-measures factorial design with questions as blocks, one can picture a mixed-effects logistic model like the following, for question q, model m, document count k and relative position r (front, middle, end). The editor set up this model; the paper does not fit it.

logitP(Yqmkr=1)=αq+βm+γk+δr+(βδ)mr+(γδ)kr,αq~N(0,σq2)

Seen this way, Appendix G shows three things. The model × position interaction is large (deep for GPT-3.5, shallow for Claude-1.3, with no rise at the end for LongChat). Summarizing the position effect in a single number erases these differences. The design is unbalanced (the 30-document cell for GPT-3.5-Turbo (4K) is empty, and the two extended-version pairs are in effect the same models). And there is a document-count × position interaction. As Exercise 2 shows, a strict U, with both ends above the middle, appears more often as documents are added.

How would you test the "saturation" of §5? The text says only that going from 20 to 50 documents raised accuracy by about 1.5% (GPT-3.5-Turbo) and about 1% (Claude-1.3), and it does not report the number of questions. Assuming 2,655 questions, a 1.5-point difference between independent samples gives z≈1.09, and the power to detect it is about 19% (80% power would need about 17,400 questions per condition). But "saturates" is a claim that there is no meaningful difference, so a nonsignificant result cannot serve as evidence for it. What is needed is an equivalence test (TOST): fix a tolerance δ in advance and check whether the 90% confidence interval of the difference lies inside (−δ,δ). The upper end of the 90% interval is 3.76 percentage points when ρ=0, 3.10 when ρ=0.5 and 2.51 when ρ=0.8, so with δ=3 percentage points, "saturation" can be claimed only if the correlation between per-question correctness under the two conditions (20 and 50 documents) is fairly high. To test directly whether the retriever finds more but the reader cannot use it, pair the gain in recall with the gain in accuracy on the same questions.

Exercise 1 — testing whether the middle is worse than no documents. GPT-3.5-Turbo scores 53.8% at the 10th position with 20 documents and 56.1% closed-book (Table 6, Table 1). (a) Find the 95% Wilson confidence interval for each value. (b) Treat the two conditions as independent samples and test the difference. (c) Do the same calculation with GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) at the 10th position with 30 documents (50.5%) and its closed-book 56.0%. (d) The text says that "in the worst case" accuracy falls below closed-book. If the true accuracy at every position were the same 55% and the estimate at each position were independent, how far below the true value would you expect the minimum of five positions, and the minimum of twenty positions, to come out?

SolutionSolution

(a) 53.8% gives [51.9%, 55.7%] and 56.1% gives [54.2%, 58.0%]. The two intervals overlap.

(b) The difference is −2.3 percentage points, the standard error about 1.37 percentage points, z≈−1.68 and the two-sided p≈0.092. Treated as independent samples, it is hard to say at the 5% level that it is lower than closed-book. At the 15th position in the same table (55.4%) the difference is smaller, −0.7 percentage points. Setting the per-question correlation at ρ=0.5 shrinks the standard error to about 0.97 percentage points, giving z≈−2.4. The conclusion depends on the pairing information.

(c) The difference is −5.5 percentage points, z≈−4.0 and the two-sided p≈6×10−5. With 30 documents it holds up even without pairing information. The 15th position in the same table (50.9%) also gives z≈−3.7.

(d) The expected minimum of 5 independent draws is about −1.16 in standard normal units, and of 20 about −1.87. With a single-cell standard error of about 0.97 percentage points, even if all true values were equal you would expect the minimum to come out about 1.1 percentage points low over five positions and about 1.8 percentage points low over twenty (when every position is measured, as in Figure 1). That is comparable in size to the observed 2.3-point difference with 20 documents. The 10th position in Table 6, though, was fixed in advance rather than picked as the minimum, so (d) applies to the text's wording "in the worst case".

Takeaway. The single claim that accuracy falls below closed-book with 20 and 30 documents is not supported with the same strength in the two settings. The 30-document case holds up; the 20-document case is on the borderline. When you see "in the worst case," first ask how many it was chosen from (the same structure as "best of 6" in Exercise 2 of Chapter 6).

Exercise 2 — how do you test a U-shaped curve? (a) In Table 6 (20 documents), compute the contrast c=(12,−13,−13,−13,12), that is, "mean of the two ends − mean of the three middle positions", for GPT-3.5-Turbo and LongChat-13B (16K), with its standard error. (b) Is a positive contrast for LongChat evidence of a U-shaped curve? (c) If "U-shaped" is defined as "both the very front and the very end are higher than the middle", both one-sided tests have to pass (an intersection–union test). Taking the middle as the middle position of each table (5th of 10 documents, 10th of 20, 15th of 30), which model × document-count combinations in Appendix G pass at the 5% level (one-sided z>1.645)?

SolutionSolution

(a) For GPT-3.5-Turbo, 75.8+63.22−57.2+53.8+55.43≈69.5−55.5=14.0 percentage points, with a standard error of about 0.84 percentage points and z≈16.8. For LongChat, 68.6+55.02−57.4+55.3+52.53≈61.8−55.1=6.7 percentage points, with a standard error of about 0.86 percentage points and z≈7.8.

(b) No. LongChat's last position is 0.3 percentage points below the middle (55.0 against 55.3, z≈−0.2). The contrast is positive because the very front (68.6%) is so high. A contrast that averages the two ends is positive for an L-shaped curve too. This is why the shape should not be judged by a single contrast.

(c) Calculated with the independent-sample approximation. The extended versions (100K and 16K) get the same verdicts as their original models, so only GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) is kept for 30 documents.

Documents Model Front − middle (z) End − middle (z) Both ends pass
10 Claude-1.3 4.6 (3.4) 1.4 (1.0) No
10 GPT-3.5-Turbo 15.6 (12.5) 1.2 (0.9) No
10 MPT-30B-Instruct 4.0 (3.0) 3.5 (2.6) Yes
10 LongChat-13B (16K) 13.2 (10.2) −0.4 (−0.3) No
20 Claude-1.3 3.1 (2.3) 3.3 (2.4) Yes
20 GPT-3.5-Turbo 22.0 (17.2) 9.4 (7.0) Yes
20 MPT-30B-Instruct 1.5 (1.1) 4.1 (3.0) No
20 LongChat-13B (16K) 13.3 (10.1) −0.3 (−0.2) No
30 Claude-1.3 3.4 (2.5) 4.2 (3.1) Yes
30 GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) 22.5 (17.4) 12.8 (9.5) Yes
30 MPT-30B-Instruct 2.6 (1.9) 5.1 (3.7) Yes
30 LongChat-13B (16K) 14.0 (10.5) 2.2 (1.6) No (borderline)

Counting the extended versions too, 1 of 6 combinations passes with 10 documents, 4 of 6 with 20 and 4 of 5 with 30. If "middle" is replaced by the mean of the inner positions, LongChat with 30 documents passes as well (z≈2.2). Using the pairing would generally make the z values larger, and correcting for multiple comparisons could shake the borderline verdicts (such as the front z=1.9 for MPT with 30 documents).

Takeaway. It can also be read this way. With 10 documents most models are L-shaped, high only at the front; as documents increase to 20 and 30, the end also rises above the middle and the curve becomes a strict U. The shape of the position effect changes with length. The summary in the caption of Figure 5 (highest at the start or end) hides this interaction.

8. Limitations the paper states

The paper has no separate Limitations section. Gathering the reservations scattered through the text gives the following.

  • Decoding. All outputs were produced with greedy decoding, and other decoding methods are left to future work (§2.2).
  • Ambiguity and timing of the data. A few distractors may contain a reasonable answer (footnote 2), and there is a time gap between the retrieval corpus (Wikipedia as of late 2018) and the annotations (Appendix A). The conclusions were the same on the unambiguous subset.
  • Models run only in part because of cost. GPT-4 was evaluated only on 500 questions in the 20-document setting (footnote 6, Appendix D).
  • The causal analysis is preliminary. The authors call §4 a preliminary investigation and present as hypotheses why encoder-decoder models are less sensitive to position (§4.1), how base models learn to use long contexts (§4.3) and why earlier work did not see primacy bias (Appendix E).
  • The answer depends on the task. How much context to include is ultimately specific to each downstream task, and §5 is described as a single case study.
  • The mechanism is not explained. That a phenomenon like the serial-position effect appears even though self-attention can in principle retrieve any token is described only as "perhaps surprising" (§6.3).

Two more things can be read as limitations the paper does not state. The metric checks only whether an answer string is contained, so verbose outputs may be favored; the paper does not analyze output length separately, so it is unknown whether the position effect is entangled with this property. And every experiment is a single question and answer, so the context of an agent, in which tool outputs pile up, is out of scope. The three posts among the side papers fill that gap from the practical side.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

This chapter has three side readings (S15, S13 and S14): one technical report and two company blog posts, one prescriptive and one an account of operations. All three come from experience building the companies' own products and have not been peer-reviewed. Read them as design guidance, not as generalized empirical findings. Added to them are three papers from other chapters of this book.

Context Rot (Hong et al. 2025 · Chroma technical report). Where the main paper manipulated position, this report manipulates length. It fixed task difficulty, increased only the input length and measured 18 models (GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3 and others). Performance fell as inputs grew on variants of needle in a haystack, on LongMemEval conversational question answering (a focused input of about 300 tokens against the full input of about 113k tokens, 306 questions) and on repeated-word copying. The first two were graded by a GPT-4.1 judge calibrated to agree with human judgments more than 0.99 of the time. The results on position differ. Across the 11 needle positions there was "no notable variation in performance for this specific NIAH task", and on repeated-word copying, position accuracy was highest when the unique word was near the beginning. The tasks, model generations and metrics all differ, so it is hard to read this as a refutation of the main paper. The main paper does not appear in the report's references.

Effective context engineering for AI agents (Rajasekaran et al. 2025 · Anthropic blog). A prescription. Citing "context rot", a concept from research in the needle-in-a-haystack line, it tells readers to treat context as "a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns", the model's "attention budget." The guiding principle is to "find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome." For long tasks it gives three techniques: compaction, which summarizes the conversation as the window fills and starts a new window; structured note-taking, which writes notes outside the window and reads them back; and sub-agent architecture, in which sub-agents with clean windows explore and return only a 1,000–2,000-token summary. There are no measurements. It can be read as turning the main paper's §5 finding, that adding more does not help, into a design principle (this book's reading).

Context Engineering for AI Agents: Lessons from Building Manus (Ji 2025 · Manus blog). An account of operations. First, two terms. A KV cache stores the internal computations for the front part (prefix) of an input the model has already processed, so that the next call with the same prefix can reuse them instead of recomputing. The post notes that a difference of even one token invalidates the cache from that point on. USD/MTok is the price in dollars per million tokens. The post calls KV-cache hit rate "the single most important metric for a production-stage AI agent." The ratio of input to output tokens averages around 100:1, and with Claude Sonnet cached input costs 0.30 USD/MTok against 3 USD/MTok uncached, a tenfold difference. So it recommends keeping the front fixed and making the context append-only, and moving large observations out to the file system, keeping only a path or URL in context. The point that touches the main paper directly is todo.md. In tasks that call tools about 50 times on average, constantly rewriting the to-do list is explained as "reciting its objectives into the end of the context", which avoids "'lost-in-the-middle' issues". It turns the measured recency bias to its own use. The main paper's §5 recommends moving relevant documents to the front, but protecting the cache means not touching the front; fixing the front and rewriting what matters at the end is Manus's answer (this contrast is this book's reading).

RAG (Lewis et al. 2020 · Chapter 8 of this book). §1 of the main paper says that multi-document question answering mimics the reading step of retrieval-augmented generation (meaning the common setup of systems like Bing Chat; it does not cite Lewis et al. 2020). But the readers are built differently. RAG's generator processes the input x concatenated with a single document z (§2.3) and marginalizes the probability over the top k documents (5 or 10 in training, §3). The documents are not lined up inside one input, so by the structure of the formula the order among documents does not change the result. The main paper's reader puts all k documents into one prompt, so there is room for a position effect. The results contrast too. In RAG §4.5, retrieving more documents raised RAG-Sequence's NQ performance monotonically; in the main paper's §5, it was nearly flat beyond 20.

MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023 · Chapter 12 of this book). A follow-up that cites the main paper directly and reuses its tasks. §1 cites it as evidence that long-context models do not use additional context effectively, and §3.2 cites its finding of "uneven attention distributions in large context models", better recall at the beginning or end than in the middle, as grounds for doubting approaches that only scale up context. §3.2.1 samples 50 questions from the same retriever-reader question answering and grades them with an LLM judge, and §3.2.2 turns key–value retrieval into nested key–value retrieval, where a value can itself be a key (140 pairs, about 8k tokens, 0 to 4 levels of nesting). The questions differ. The main paper asks how a model uses a fixed window; MemGPT asks what to keep and what to evict when the window fills. When the window is, say, 70% full it inserts a "memory pressure" warning, and at 100% it flushes the queue and leaves a recursive summary (§2.2).

LLM Wiki (Karpathy 2026 · Chapter 20 of this book). A design note. Instead of RAG, which reassembles knowledge from raw sources for each question, it proposes having the LLM build and maintain a cross-referenced markdown wiki in advance. At query time the LLM reads the index file (index.md) first and then drills into relevant pages, and the note says "This works surprisingly well at moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages)". Putting only a few pre-synthesized pages into the context can also be seen as one way to avoid, at query time, the situation of putting dozens of documents in at once and missing the middle. This connection is this book's reading, not a claim of the note itself.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version — why this paper has no slot

The revised AR survey has no section corresponding to this chapter. Its inclusion and exclusion criteria in §1.1 exclude "single-forward-pass prompting without external interaction, pure long-context modeling," and the main paper's experiments are exactly single prompts with no outside interaction. No citation of this paper was found in the body of the revised version.

The preamble of §4.2, on memory, says that rather than merely extending the context window or storing past inputs, research has come to treat memory as an integral component of the reasoning loop. It then says it avoids the term 'in-context memory' and that, in the vocabulary of §2.2, the memory in this section is all system-level (S). §4.2.1 gives MemGPT as one example of treating memory as a passive buffer that addresses the limited context window.

Still, the paper can be placed in the notation of Chapter 2.

Main paper AR survey, revised version, §2.2
Input context (instruction + k documents + question) History ht, or the memory mt that summarizes it and is fed to the model
Question Observation ot
The model's answer External action at (a single final answer, one action)
Position of the answer document No corresponding symbol
Reranking, query-aware contextualization Changing the arrangement of mt outside the model; in the notation, on the side of the system state S

The mapping was compiled by the editor. The main paper does not use this notation.

The fourth row raises one point worth reading. Assumption A1 is πreason(zt∣ht)=πreason(zt∣mt), that is, the assumption that the memory mt is a sufficient statistic of the history. The equation constrains more than "what is in it". It is a condition on the distribution the model actually produces when given mt. What the main paper showed is that, for the same set of documents, answer accuracy varies with their arrangement in the input. If so, A1 may fail for an mt that matches ht only in content, and the arrangement can be read as part of what has to be decided when designing mt. This is the editor's interpretation, not a claim of the survey. Keep it in mind when A1 comes up again in Chapter 12.

Harness survey §5 — the context and memory management layer

Of the seven layers of the Harness survey's ETCLOVG, C (context and memory management) is where this chapter belongs. The head of §5 states the problem of this layer as "give the model exactly the right information at each step, nothing more", and says that with too much, performance degrades in ways that are "measurable, consistent across models, and not fully understood." Figure 8 divides representative work into five cells, and the main paper sits with Context Rot in the "Context Drift and Limits" cell.

  • §5.1 Why context must be engineered. It cites the quadratic cost of self-attention, the main paper's U-shaped curve and the length effect of Context Rot. It summarizes the U-shaped curve as "on multi-document question answering with 20 input documents, accuracy drops by more than 30% when the relevant document sits in the middle of the context, compared to placing it at the start or end", says that it "holds across models, tasks, and context lengths, including models trained specifically on long contexts", and draws the implication that "information placement matters as much as information presence."
  • §5.2–5.3 Context engineering and short-term management. It cites the definition in the Anthropic post (S13) and says that the system prompt, tool definitions, prior turns, tool results and retrieved documents all compete for the same attention budget. As short-term techniques it covers just-in-time retrieval and the KV-cache design rules from the Manus post (S14).
  • §5.6 Long tasks of more than 100 turns. It covers compaction, context isolation through sub-agents, and a decision framework: "pre-load content that is always needed, retrieve just-in-time content that is conditionally needed, compact history when the window approaches saturation, and spawn sub-agents when a subtask requires exploration that would pollute the orchestrator's context." It says that "Context management should be the infrastructure's job, not the agent's."
  • §5.7 Context drift. It distinguishes context rot (a property of a single inference step, in which quality falls as tokens are added) from context drift (a property of a long trajectory, in which behavior moves away from the original intent). Its conclusion is that none of compaction, retrieval or sub-agents prevents drift.

The main paper measured single question–answer exchanges, so in this framework it sits on the side of rot, not drift. The survey's summary has two points to check against the original. The original says "by more than 20%", and computed from Table 6, the gap between the 1st and 10th positions for GPT-3.5-Turbo with 20 documents is 22.0 points absolute and 29.0% relative. The relative drop exceeds 30% for the 16K version with 30 documents (73.4 → 50.5, 31.2% relative), so which number the survey's "accuracy drops by more than 30%" for 20 documents carries over is an open question. And as Exercise 2 shows, most models were L-shaped with 10 documents, and the Claude-1.3 models were nearly perfect on key–value retrieval regardless of position, so "holds across … context lengths" may be read more broadly than the original tables support. The §5.1 sentence "A model rated for 200K tokens may show significant performance loss at 50K." has no citation of its own. The paragraph opens with the experiments of Hong et al. (2025, Chroma's Context Rot report) and refers to that report again in the next sentence, but neither 200K nor 50K appears anywhere in the report's full text (rechecked on October 5, 2026). Read this figure as a sentence whose basis has not been confirmed.

Seen through the definition of a harness in Chapter 3, query-aware contextualization in §4.2 and the reranking that §5 proposes only as a direction are harness-side interventions that leave the model alone and change only the arrangement of the input. Only the first was actually measured, and that intervention made key–value retrieval nearly perfect while barely changing multi-document question answering. It can be read as a case showing that the same intervention can have entirely different effects depending on the task (this is not the paper's explanation).

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "A model with a longer context window uses long contexts better." The second observation of §2.3 refutes this. When the input fits in both windows, the extended version and the original model were within 0.3 percentage points of each other at the same position (Appendix G). A longer window lets you put in more; it does not make the model use what you put in better.

Misreading 2. "If the answer document is in the middle, it is worse than giving no documents." This holds only in some settings of the GPT-3.5 models. Claude-1.3 scores 55.9–57.2% at the middle positions with 20 documents, above its closed-book 48.3%, and even MPT-30B-Instruct's lowest value, 49.0% (30 documents), is far above its closed-book 31.5% (Table 1, Appendix G). The GPT-3.5-Turbo difference with 20 documents (53.8 against 56.1) is also on the borderline of chance (Exercise 1).

Misreading 3. "The U-shaped curve appears symmetrically in every model." GPT-3.5-Turbo and LongChat are much higher at the front, while Claude-1.3 and MPT-30B-Instruct are slightly higher at the end with 20 and 30 documents. With 10 and 20 documents, LongChat's last position is not higher than its middle (Tables 5 and 6 in Appendix G). Llama-2 7B showed only recency bias (Appendix E).

Misreading 4. "Putting the question in front of the documents as well solves it." On key–value retrieval, all models became nearly perfect. On multi-document question answering, it helped slightly only when the answer was at the very front and hurt slightly at other positions (§4.2, Figure 9). Finding a string and finding and using meaning are different problems.

Misreading 5. "Instruction fine-tuning is the culprit behind the front bias." The base model MPT-30B also showed a U-shaped curve, and instruction fine-tuning only narrowed the best–worst gap from nearly 10% to around 4% (§4.3). Llama-2 70B, too, showed similar curves with or without additional fine-tuning (Appendix E).

Misreading 6. "The more retrieved documents, the better." Retriever recall kept rising up to 50 documents, but reader accuracy flattened around 20, and going from 20 to 50 gained a little over 1 to 1.5 percentage points (§5). Establishing this "saturation" statistically requires an equivalence test (section 7).

Misreading 7. "Lost in the Middle and Context Rot measure the same phenomenon." The main paper set length at three levels and manipulated position finely within each; the Chroma report fixed the task and manipulated length. On Chroma's needle-in-a-haystack task there was no notable difference across 11 positions. The model generations (2023 against 2025) and the metrics (string containment against an LLM judge) also differ. §5.7 of the Harness survey sets apart "drift" over long trajectories as distinct from both.

Discussion questions

  1. Reranking or the cache? §5 of the main paper says to push relevant documents toward the front, and Manus says that to protect the KV cache you should not touch the front but only append. Construct a situation where the two prescriptions collide. How would you decide between accuracy and cost? How much of this conflict does the todo.md approach, rewriting what matters at the end, resolve?

  2. How far is it the same as the human serial position effect? §6.3 of the paper offers the connection without claiming a common cause. Can the experience of people missing the middle of long documents (contracts, reports, code reviews) and the model's phenomenon be handled with the same prescriptions (putting a summary up front, repeating the key points at the end)? If not, where do they part ways? Think about it together with the question in Chapter 12 of what to evict when the window fills.

  3. If you designed a new evaluation protocol. The authors proposed an evaluation protocol in which the best–worst gap across positions should be small. But as Exercise 1 shows, the minimum and maximum spread further apart the more positions you measure. If you reported position robustness as a single metric, what would you use (range, variance across positions, a contrast, an intersection–union test)? How would you choose the number of questions and positions? Check your answer in Chapter 18.

Chapter 10 · Core · ★★

Chapter 10. RAG That Decides When to Retrieve — Self-RAG

The question this chapter answers: how do you get a model to decide for itself when to retrieve, and to evaluate the documents it fetched and its own answer?

Core reading. Akari Asai et al., "Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection", ICLR 2024. 10 pages of main text, 30 with the appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · ICLR 2024 paper page · Project · Code

Side paper — CRAG arXiv abstract · Code

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §3.3, §3.3.1, §3.3.3, Table 8 · the Harness survey has no section corresponding to this chapter

One-paragraph summary. Ordinary RAG attaches a fixed number of documents whatever the question, and does not go back to check whether the answer agrees with those documents. Self-RAG fine-tunes a single generator (Llama 2 7B and 13B) to emit four kinds of special tokens itself: whether to retrieve now (Retrieve), whether a fetched passage is useful (ISREL), whether that passage supports the sentence just written (ISSUP) and whether the answer as a whole is useful (ISUSE). The labels for these reflection tokens are inserted into the training corpus in advance by a critic model that distills GPT-4's judgments. At inference time, the probability of the reflection tokens decides whether to retrieve, and the candidate sentences generated for each passage are ranked by a weighted sum of reflection-token probabilities. The weights can be changed at inference time without retraining. On six tasks it generally scored above open models of the same size and above retrieval baselines, and its citation precision was higher even than ChatGPT with retrieval.

If your group skipped Chapter 8. In the first 5 minutes, introduce only the idea of the RAG paper (Lewis et al. 2020): fetch the top k documents, treat them as a latent variable and sum over them (section 6 of Appendix I). The left side of Figure 1 has a different shape. It is drawn as the usual RAG setup that attaches all three documents to a single input and writes in one pass. What the two approaches share, fetching a fixed number of documents every time regardless of the question, is what Self-RAG takes aim at.

When you quote the numbers. The numbers in Table 2 come from fine-tuned versions of the 2023 Llama 2 7B and 13B, given only an instruction with no examples (zero-shot). The metric differs by task. "Accuracy" on PopQA and TriviaQA counts an answer as correct if the gold answer string appears in the generated text (§4.1). Bio uses FactScore, and ASQA uses exact match, ROUGE, MAUVE, and citation precision and recall. When you put numbers in your presentation materials, give the model size, the task and the metric with them. Baselines marked with an asterisk (*) carry numbers reported in other papers, so they are not comparisons run under the same conditions.

Building intuition

Setting the left and right of Figure 1 side by side

The question in Figure 1 is "How did US states get their names?"

Left, ordinary RAG. The retriever fetches three documents: ① "Of the fifty states, eleven are named after an individual person." ② "Popular names by states. In Texas, Emma is a popular baby name." ③ "California was named after a fictional island in a Spanish book." The generator attaches all three and writes in one pass. In the output, "California was named after Christopher Columbus" is marked Contradictory (it conflicts with document ③), and "Texas and Utah, are named after Native American tribe" is marked No information in passages.

Right, Self-RAG. It writes the first sentence and emits Retrieve (Step 1). With the same three documents, it generates the next sentence separately for each document (Step 2). The candidate from document ① is marked Relevant and Supported, document ② Irrelevant, and document ③ Relevant and Partially. In Step 3 it ranks them ① > ③ > ②, chooses ① and starts over from Retrieve. Each sentence of the final answer carries the number of its supporting document.

The bottom row. For "Write an essay of your best summer vacation", RAG still attaches three documents, while Self-RAG emits No Retrieval and writes straight away.

The three scenes correspond one to one with the paper's three concerns. It retrieves when it does not need to (the bottom row). The fetched documents may be useless (document ②). It does not go back to check when the answer conflicts with the documents (Contradictory).

The editor's bridge — screening tests and composite scores

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

The Retrieve token is a screening test. Before an expensive diagnostic test (retrieval), a cheap screening test decides whether the diagnostic test is needed. If the normalized p(Retrieve=Yes) exceeds a threshold δ, the model retrieves (Appendix A.3). Lowering the threshold produces more positives, so fewer cases are missed, but the cost goes up. It has the same form as choosing a cutoff, and Figure 3(c) shows the trade-off. Just as the value of a given cutoff changes when prevalence differs between populations, the loss from retrieving less was small on PubHealth and large on PopQA (§5.2).

The segment score is a multi-criteria composite score. Candidate sentences are scored for relevance, support and utility, and the scores are added with weights (Eq. 4). Anyone who has built a composite index knows the rest. Weights mean something only when read together with the scale of each indicator, and a small change in the weights flips the ranking of some items. That is Exercise 2 in section 8 of this chapter.

The analogy also breaks down. A medical screening test has a ground truth confirmed later (the definitive diagnosis), so sensitivity and specificity can be measured. Self-RAG's question of whether retrieval was needed has no ground truth observable at inference time. Even the labels in training come not from people but from a critic model imitating GPT-4's judgments. And in screening, the person tested and the institution testing are different, whereas in Self-RAG the model that writes the answer grades its own answer.

The paper's own analogy. The authors write that the reflection tokens were inspired by the reward models used in reinforcement learning (§1). Unlike RLHF, though, they do not keep a reward model running during training; the critiques are computed in advance and inserted into the corpus (§3.2.2).

The paper in detail

1. What is the problem? — indiscriminate retrieval (§1)

RAG attaches relevant passages to the input and reduces factual errors on knowledge-intensive tasks. But because it retrieves passages "indiscriminately regardless of whether the factual grounding is helpful", it may "hinder the versatility of LLMs" or pull in off-topic passages. And since the model is not trained to follow the facts in the passages, there is no guarantee that its output agrees with them. The authors have a single generator do three things with special tokens: retrieve only when needed (retrieval on demand), evaluate what it fetched and what it wrote (self-reflection), and use that evaluation to choose its output. The paper does not number its contributions. In the editor's summary there are two. It trains an arbitrary language model by unifying reflection tokens into next-token prediction over an expanded vocabulary, and it makes inference adjustable to hard or soft constraints defined by reflection-token predictions.

2. The four kinds of reflection token (§3.1, Table 1, Appendix A.1)

Formalization. Given an input x, the generator ℳ produces in turn an output y=[y1,…,yT] made of several segments. yt is the token sequence of the t-th segment and contains both text from the original vocabulary and reflection tokens. In the experiments one sentence is treated as one segment. The paper says it can also be applied to units smaller than a sentence (footnote 3).

Type Input Output Definitions
Retrieve x / x,y {yes, no, continue} Decides when to retrieve with ℛ
ISREL x,d {relevant, irrelevant} d provides useful information to solve x.
ISSUP x,d,y {fully supported, partially supported, no support} All of the verification-worthy statement in y is supported by d.
ISUSE x,y {5, 4, 3, 2, 1} y is a useful response to x.

Table 1 of the paper. The original caption: "Each type uses several tokens to represent its output values. The bottom three rows are three types of Critique tokens, and the bold text indicates the most desirable critique tokens. x, y, d indicate input, output, and a relevant passage, respectively."

Retrieve is the retrieval token, and the three below it are critique tokens. The definitions in Appendix A.1 add three things. Continue, the third value of Retrieve, means continuing to use the evidence retrieved earlier, a device for writing several segments from one passage rich in facts. ISSUP follows the concept of attribution and judges how much of the information in the output is entailed by the evidence. ISUSE is a "perceived" utility, judged independently of the retrieved passages (footnote 4), and Appendix A.1 adds that it is also judged "independently from whether it is in fact factual or not." Of the four tokens, ISSUP comes closest to factuality, but what ISSUP checks is whether the given passage supports the output. If the passage itself is wrong, a supported answer is still wrong (Misreading 5).

The first three types are attached to each segment, while ISUSE is attached only once, to the whole output (Appendix A.1). Algorithm 3 in the appendix, which builds the training data, also carries the annotation "(t = T only)". Yet Algorithm 1 for inference predicts ISUSE at each segment, and Eq. 4 also adds the ISUSE score at every time step t. How to reconcile the two descriptions is an open question.

The inference algorithm (Algorithm 1). ℳ looks at (x,y<t) and predicts Retrieve. If Yes, ℛ fetches a set of passages 𝐃, and for each passage d the model runs judge ISREL → generate yt → judge ISSUP and ISUSE in parallel, then ranks the candidates for yt by the three critiques (line 7, §3.3). If No, it writes yt like an ordinary language model and judges only ISUSE. Lines 9–10 use the symbol ℳgen without defining it; read it as the same generator.

Continue, the third value of Retrieve, appears neither in Algorithm 1 nor in the threshold formula of section 4. Both deal only with Yes and No. In the output examples in the appendix, [Retrieve=Continue] appears between segments, which suggests a path for writing the next segment from a passage fetched earlier, but the paper does not say how this value is handled at inference. The diagram below is also a summary that draws only the two branches, Yes and No.

How Self-RAG produces one segment. The editor drew the diagram from Algorithm 1 and §3.3 of the paper. Like Algorithm 1, it draws only the two branches Yes and No and leaves out continue.

3. Training — the critic labels, the generator learns (§3.2, Figure 2, Appendix A.1–A.2)

Two models appear in training: the critic model 𝒞, which attaches reflection tokens, and the generator ℳ, which writes text including the reflection tokens. The key point is that the critic model is not needed at inference time. The critic's only job is to insert reflection tokens into the training corpus in advance (offline), and the generator learns from the resulting corpus to emit reflection tokens itself.

Step 1 — training data for the critic (§3.2.1). Human annotation is expensive, and querying a proprietary model every time raises API costs and diminishes reproducibility. So GPT-4 is given type-specific instructions and examples to attach reflection tokens (the instruction for Retrieve is "Given an instruction, make a judgment on whether finding some external documents from the web helps to generate a better response."), and that knowledge is distilled into an in-house model 𝒞. The text says 4k–20k items per type, but the actual counts in Appendix A.1 are 12,594 for Retrieve (printed as "1,2594" in the original), 11,181 for ISSUP, 19,317 for ISREL and 3,831 for ISUSE. ISUSE falls slightly short of the lower bound in the text. When the authors sampled 20 items per aspect and checked them against GPT-4's judgments, the agreement rates were 95% for relevance, 95% for retrieval necessity, 90% for support and 80% for usefulness (Exercise 1 in section 8).

With the collected data 𝒟critic, 𝒞 is trained with an ordinary conditional language-modeling objective.

max𝒞𝔼((x,y),r)~𝒟criticlogp𝒞(r∣x,y)(1)

r is the reflection token, and the initial model is Llama 2-7B. The condition in the formula has only x,y, but as the table in section 2 shows, ISREL and ISSUP also take the passage d as input. The paper does not explain the difference. Read it as shorthand for including d in the condition depending on the type (the editor's reading).

base LM Retrieve ISSUP ISREL ISUSE
Llama2-7B 93.8 93.5 80.2 73.5
FLAN-3B 85.6 73.1 82.0 72.1

Figure 5 in the appendix of the paper ("Reward prediction accuracy using GPT-4 predictions as ground-truth predictions", %). The text calls this "Table 5", but the label in the PDF is Figure 5, and Table 5 in the appendix is a list of evaluation instructions.

§3.2.1 says the critic achieves "a higher than 90% agreement with GPT-4-based predictions on most reflection token categories", but Llama2-7B exceeds 90% on only two of the four. The wording in Appendix A.2, "In most aspects, our reward model shows higher than 80% accuracy," matches the table. The size of the test set is not given.

Step 2 — training data for the generator (§3.2.2, Appendix A.2). For each segment of an input–output pair (x,y), 𝒞 judges whether retrieval would help. If so, it inserts Retrieve=Yes, ℛ fetches the top K passages, ISREL and ISSUP are predicted and attached for each passage, and ISUSE is added at the end of the output. It is supervised data that imitates the inference process exactly. A passage that is Relevant and Fully or Partially Supported is chosen as the material for the continuation; if there is none, one is chosen at random.

The example on the right of Figure 2 shows the point. The first sentence, "11 of 50 states' names come from person.", is preceded by passage ① ("Of the fifty states, eleven are named after an individual person") and marked Relevant and Supported. The second sentence, "For instance, Louisiana was named after King Louis XIV, and Georgia was named after King George II.", is preceded by the LOUISIANA passage but marked Partially, because the passage says nothing about Georgia. The summer-vacation essay on the left gets only No Retrieval and Util: 5. The original output at the top of the figure says "1 of 50" while the augmented output says "11 of 50", which looks like a typo in the original figure.

Training the generator. On the augmented corpus 𝒟gen it uses the ordinary next-token objective.

maxℳ𝔼(x,y,r)~𝒟genlogpℳ(y,r∣x)(2)

Unlike Eq. 1, ℳ predicts the target output and the reflection tokens together. The retrieved passages (between <p> and </p>) are masked out of the loss, and the set of reflection tokens {Critique, Retrieve} is added to the original vocabulary 𝒱.

Scale and cost. §4.3 says 150k instruction-following input–output pairs. Adding up the eleven datasets in Table 3 of the appendix (five from Open-Instruct and six knowledge-intensive ones including KILT) gives 145,619, which is also the number in the appendix text. The retriever is Contriever-MS MARCO. The authors argue that because they precompute the critiques and train with an ordinary objective, the cost is much lower than PPO, which keeps a reward model running during training (§3.2.2), but there is no experiment measuring cost.

4. Inference — the threshold and segment-level beam search (§3.3, Appendix A.3)

Generating reflection tokens means that knobs appear at inference time. On tasks where factual accuracy matters, retrieve often; on open-ended tasks such as a personal-experience essay, retrieve less and put weight on utility. There are two devices.

Device 1 — the retrieval threshold. Instead of following the Retrieve token as is, the model can retrieve when the normalized probability of Retrieve=Yes exceeds a threshold (Appendix A.3).

p(Retrieve=YES)p(Retrieve=YES)+p(Retrieve=NO)>δ

The denominator in the original formula has an extra p, as in p(p(Retrieve=NO), read here as a typesetting error. The larger δ, the less retrieval. The default is δ=0.2 for most tasks and δ=0 for ASQA, which requires citations, and the authors say they set these values "To encourage frequent retrieval" (§4.3). The defaults lean toward retrieval from the start.

Device 2 — tree decoding guided by critique tokens. Once the model decides to retrieve, ℛ fetches K passages and ℳ produces one candidate for each. A segment-level beam search (beam size B) keeps the top B at each time step and returns the best sequence at the end. The score is the generation probability plus a critique score 𝒮. The paper's notation is reproduced as is.

f(yt,d,Critique)=p(yt∣x,d,y<t)+𝒮(Critique)(3)

𝒮(Critique)=∑G∈𝒢wGstGfor 𝒢={ISREL,ISSUP,ISUSE}(4)

stG=pt(r^)∑i=1NGpt(ri)

stG is the generation probability of the most desirable token r^ of critique type G (for example, ISREL=Relevant), divided by the sum of the probabilities of the NG tokens that the type can take. The original Eq. 3 has one closing parenthesis too many.

The actual calculation in Appendix A.3. In the text, stG stands for "the generation probability of the most desirable reflection token", normalized, but the calculation the appendix gives differs slightly by type.

s(ISREL)=p(ISREL=RELEVANT)p(ISREL=RELEVANT)+p(ISREL=IRRELEVANT)

s(ISSUP)=p(ISSUP=FULLY)S+0.5×p(ISSUP=PARTIALLY)S,S=∑t∈{FULLY,PARTIALLY,NO}p(ISSUP=t)

s(ISUSE)=∑i=15wip(ISUSE=i)S,w={−1,−0.5,0,0.5,1},S=∑t∈{1,…,5}p(ISUSE=t)

ISSUP gives half a point for partial support, and ISUSE is an expected value with scores from −1 to 1 assigned to the five grades. So the three scores have different ranges: ISREL and ISSUP are in [0,1], ISUSE in [−1,1]. The original appendix writes the left side of the ISSUP formula wrongly as s(ISREL), and the normalizing constant S uses the same letter as 𝒮 in Eq. 4, so keep them apart when reading.

The weights are hyperparameters. wG is not learned but set at inference time. To stick closer to the evidence, raise the weight on ISSUP. The defaults are 1.0, 1.0 and 0.5 for ISREL, ISSUP and ISUSE (§4.3). The authors stress that in RLHF the balance among several preferences is usually set by training, whereas Self-RAG does it without additional training. Instead of a weighted sum, a hard constraint can also be used to filter out entirely any candidate that emitted a token such as ISSUP=No support.

Other settings (§4.3). A segment-level beam width of 2, and greedy decoding at the token level. Default retrieval is the top 5 from Contriever-MS MARCO; for Bio and open-domain question answering, 5 more were fetched by web search (Appendix B.2: Google Programmable Search). For ASQA, the top 5 from GTR-XXL provided by the ALCE authors were given identically to all baselines.

5. Experimental setup (§4.1–4.2)

All evaluation is zero-shot, giving only an instruction describing the task with no examples. There are six tasks in three groups.

Group Task Metric Questions
Closed-set PubHealth (public-health fact verification) Accuracy Not given in the paper
Closed-set ARC-Challenge (multiple-choice science exam) Accuracy Not given in the paper
Short-form PopQA (long-tail subset of entities with fewer than 100 monthly page views) Answer included 1,399
Short-form TriviaQA-unfiltered (validation and test split of prior work) Answer included 11,313
Long-form Biography FactScore Not given in the paper
Long-form ALCE-ASQA str-em, ROUGE, MAUVE, citation precision and recall Not given in the paper

Compiled by the editor from §4.1 of the paper. Question counts are given only where printed in the paper's text or appendices.

PopQA and TriviaQA count an answer as correct as long as it contains the gold answer string. It is a metric that can favor writing at length.

Baselines. Without retrieval: Llama2 7B and 13B, Alpaca 7B and 13B (the authors' replication based on Llama2), ChatGPT and Llama2-chat 13B, and CoVE 65B. With retrieval: standard RAG, attaching the top documents from the same retriever; Ret-ChatGPT and Ret-Llama2-chat; perplexity.ai; SAIL and Toolformer, with numbers carried over from their original papers (footnote 6); and Llama2-FT 7B. This model was fine-tuned on the same instruction–output pairs as Self-RAG but without reflection tokens or retrieved passages, with retrieval attached only at test time. It is the control condition that separates whether Self-RAG's gains come from the training data or from the reflection tokens and retrieval.

6. Main results (§5.1, Table 2)

Reading the metrics. Table 2 of the paper puts 10 metric columns in one table. Here the four short-form and closed-set columns and the six long-form columns are split into two tables. Accuracy in the first table is, as seen in section 5, the share of cases where the gold answer string appears in the generated text (PopQA and TQA) or where the chosen answer is correct (Pub and ARC). FactScore in the Bio column of the second table is the share of the small facts a biography is broken into that are supported by the knowledge source, and the original caption classes it as a factuality metric. For ASQA, str-em and ROUGE measure correctness against the gold answers, MAUVE measures fluency, and citation precision and recall measure whether the attached citations support the claims (§4.1, Table 2 caption). All are percentages, and higher is better.

Read the tables in this order.

  1. Among open models, it leads in almost every cell. The paper says it is the best among open models on all tasks (§5.1). ASQA exact match (em) remains an exception: Alpaca 13B with retrieval (34.8) is higher than Self-RAG 13B (31.7).
  2. The difference from the control condition is the key evidence. Against Llama2-FT 7B: PopQA 48.7 → 54.9, PubHealth 64.3 → 72.4, ASQA citation precision 5.0 → 66.9. The authors conclude that the gains do not come from the training data alone.
  3. On some tasks, just attaching retrieval does not help. On PubHealth and ARC, the retrieval baselines are not much better than their no-retrieval counterparts (Alpaca 13B on PubHealth goes 55.5 → 51.1). The authors interpret this as tasks that cannot be solved by copying substrings of the passages.
  4. The largest difference is in citations. Most retrieval baselines have single-digit citation precision and recall, while Self-RAG is in the 60s and 70s. On precision it beats even Ret-ChatGPT (65.1), but Ret-ChatGPT (76.6) is higher on recall.
  5. Against ChatGPT, it depends on the task. It leads on PubHealth, PopQA and Bio and trails on TriviaQA (74.3) and ARC (75.3). The paper says it also beats ChatGPT on ASQA ROUGE, but only 13B (37.0) exceeds ChatGPT (36.2).
  6. Some cells are higher for 7B than for 13B. Bio (81.2 against 80.2) and MAUVE (74.3 against 71.6). The authors' explanation is limited to the factual-precision metric (FactScore on Bio): the smaller model tends to stick to the evidence and write shorter outputs (§5.1). The reversal on MAUVE, a fluency metric, is not explained.

No Retriever is a model trained without retrieved passages, and No Critic a model trained without reflection tokens, always attaching the top 1 document. Among the test-time ablations, Hard constraints retrieves only when Retrieve=Yes instead of using the threshold, Retrieve top1 is standard-RAG-style inference that always uses only the top 1 document, and Remove ISSUP drops only ISSUP from Eq. 4. The paper interprets this as showing that every component matters. The sizes differ from cell to cell. Turning off retrieval costs 20.8 percentage points on PopQA but 0.5 on PubHealth. On ASQA, removing the critic costs 14.0 percentage points and removing ISSUP 1.5. Section 8 asks whether these differences exceed the range of chance.

Changing the weights — Figure 3(b). On ASQA, raising the ISSUP weight raises citation precision and lowers MAUVE (fluency). The authors say this is consistent with prior observations that as generations get longer and more fluent, more claims are not fully supported by citations. It is a concrete case of "inference-time customization". Values read off the gridlines are not reproduced, but it is worth putting the figure on screen to see that the vertical-axis ranges of the two panels differ widely.

Retrieval frequency and accuracy — Figure 3(c). As δ grows, retrieval frequency drops sharply on both tasks. The performance loss is small on PubHealth and large on PopQA, which asks about rare entities. The vertical axis is normalized accuracy, so it cannot be compared directly with Table 2.

Scale of training data — Figure 4(a)–(c). Training separately on 5k to 50k examples, performance generally rises as data grows, with larger gains on PopQA and ASQA citation precision.

S&P checks whether an output is plausible and supported, and cases where Self-RAG predicted irrelevant or no support were excluded.
