8. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

Only two tasks have printed question counts. They are PopQA (1,399) and TriviaQA (11,313). PubHealth, ARC-Challenge, Bio and ASQA have no question count anywhere in the text or appendices, and the CRAG paper also gives only PopQA's 1,399. The metrics of these two tasks are shares of questions answered right or wrong, so the binomial standard error p(1−p)/n applies. Since the comparisons were made on the same questions, the principled analysis is paired (the McNemar test), but without per-question results the two proportions are treated as independent samples. This calculation is conservative when the two models' per-question correctness is positively correlated; with a negative correlation the actual standard error is larger (Chapter 7, section 6).

Task (n) Comparison Difference SE of difference z
PopQA (1,399) Self-RAG 7B 54.9 vs. Llama2-FT 7B 48.7 6.2 1.89 3.3
PopQA (1,399) Self-RAG 7B 54.9 vs. Ret-Llama2-c 13B 51.8 3.1 1.89 1.6
PopQA (1,399) Self-RAG 13B 55.8 vs. Self-RAG 7B 54.9 0.9 1.88 0.5
TQA (11,313) Self-RAG 7B 66.4 vs. Llama2-FT 7B 57.3 9.1 0.64 14.2
TQA (11,313) Self-RAG 13B 69.3 vs. Self-RAG 7B 66.4 2.9 0.62 4.7
TQA (11,313) Self-RAG 7B 66.4 vs. Ret-ChatGPT 65.7 0.7 0.63 1.1

The editor's calculation. Differences and standard errors are in percentage points (pp).

On PopQA the standard error of a single model is about 1.3 percentage points (the Wilson 95% interval for Self-RAG 7B is [52.3%, 57.5%]). The 6.2-point difference from the control condition holds up, while the 0.9-point difference between 13B and 7B cannot be told apart from noise. On TriviaQA, with eight times as many questions, even a 2.9-point difference separates clearly. On the other hand, 7B's 0.7-point lead over Ret-ChatGPT on TriviaQA is within the range of chance (counted with 13B it is 3.6 points and holds up). The claim in §1 that Self-RAG "outperforms retrieval-augmented ChatGPT on four tasks" puts different weight on the TriviaQA cell depending on which size you count.

The ASQA ablation has 150 items. str-em is the mean of a [0,1] value per question, so it is not binomial, but the variance of a [0,1] variable with mean p cannot exceed p(1−p), so the binomial standard error can be used as an upper bound. Near 32.1 that upper bound is about 3.8 percentage points. Because the standard error was taken at its upper bound, the |z| values that come out are lower bounds on the true values. The drop for No Critic (32.1 → 18.1) already has a lower bound of 2.8, so it separates. For Retrieve top1 (lower bound 0.7) and Remove ISSUP (lower bound 0.3), the lower bounds are merely small, so this alone cannot decide whether there is a difference or not. Deciding would need the actual variance of per-question str-em and the covariance between the two conditions. The paper's statement that "removing ISSUP during the beam search results hurts performance on ASQA" can be neither confirmed nor refuted from this table alone. In the PopQA column too, Remove ISSUP (44.1) differs from the reference 45.5 by less than the 1.9-point standard error of the difference, and No Retriever (43.6) is borderline at z ≈ 1.0. The overwhelming cases are turning off retrieval (z ≈ 11.8) and hard-constraint decoding (28.3, a 17.2-point difference, z ≈ 9.6). The paper does not give the number of PopQA questions in the ablation (only ASQA's 150 is stated), so the same 1,399 questions as the main experiment were assumed here.

The other two are left for you to calculate as exercises.

Exercise 1 — how reliable are the reflection-token judgments? (a) In Appendix A.1 the authors sampled 20 items per aspect and checked them against GPT-4's judgments. Convert the agreement rates of 95%, 95%, 90% and 80% into counts and find the 95% Wilson confidence interval for each. (b) Agreement rates do not subtract agreement by chance. For a two-category judgment like ISREL, suppose both judges output Relevant at rate q. For q = 0.5, 0.8 and 0.9, find Cohen's kappa corresponding to agreement rates of 95% and 90%. (c) For five grades like ISUSE, which agreement measure is more appropriate? (d) The human evaluation in Figure 4(d) is said to have been done on "50 samples". Can percentages of 92.5, 95.0 and 85.0 arise from a denominator of 50? Find the denominators they could arise from, and think about what that says.

SolutionSolution

(a) 19, 19, 18 and 16 of 20. The Wilson 95% intervals are [76.4%, 99.1%] for 19/20, [69.9%, 97.2%] for 18/20 and [58.4%, 91.9%] for 16/20. The description "high agreement" is right as a point estimate, but 20 items cannot rule out a true agreement rate in the 70s. Nor can one say that the four aspects differ in agreement; the intervals for 95% and 80% overlap widely.

(b) The probability of chance agreement is pe=q2+(1−q)2, and kappa is κ=(po−pe)/(1−pe).

q pe κ when po=0.95 κ when po=0.90
0.5 0.50 0.90 0.80
0.8 0.68 0.84 0.69
0.9 0.82 0.72 0.44

The more common one category is, the lower the kappa for the same agreement rate. If most passages are relevant (q=0.9), an agreement rate of 90% amounts to a kappa of only 0.44. The paper does not report the marginal distributions, so the actual kappa cannot be calculated, and the q in the table is an assumption. The same goes for the accuracy of the critic model (Figure 5 in the appendix). 80.2% is the score of a classifier that learned nothing, if the majority category makes up 80%.

(c) For five ordered grades, weighted kappa or the intraclass correlation (ICC) is appropriate. Since most disagreements were between adjacent grades, weighted kappa would look better than the simple agreement rate. But in the inference score, 5 counts as 1 point and 4 as 0.5 (Appendix A.3), so disagreement at exactly that boundary moves the score.

(d) 92.5% cannot arise from 50 cases (46.25 cases). Among denominators of 50 or less, the only one at which 92.5% comes out as a whole number is 40 (37/40). 95.0% and 85.0% also cannot arise from 50 cases and need a denominator of 20 or 40. 70.0% and 90.0% can arise from 50 cases as well. Since S&P was measured on what remained after excluding irrelevant and no-support predictions, a denominator below 50 is natural there. But the paper does not explain why even the ISREL and ISSUP agreement rates do not have a denominator of 50. This back-calculation rests on the assumption that the percentages were printed without rounding.

Takeaway. Agreement rates from 20 items have wide intervals. And an agreement rate is not a kappa. An agreement rate reported without the marginal distributions cannot tell whether the judgment was easy or the judges were good.

Exercise 2 — changing the weights flips the ranking. Read the weighted sum in Eq. 4 as a multi-criteria composite score. At the same time step there are two candidate sentences, A and B. The scores below are hypothetical values made up by the editor. A: sISREL=0.9, sISSUP=0.5, sISUSE=0.8. B: sISREL=0.7, sISSUP=0.95, sISUSE=0.2. Assume the generation-probability terms are equal. (a) With the ISREL and ISUSE weights at their defaults (1.0 and 0.5), above what ISSUP weight w does B overtake A? (b) How does the fact that the ISUSE score ranges over [−1,1] while the other two range over [0,1] affect the interpretation of the weight 0.5? (c) How would you design an experiment to measure weight sensitivity systematically?

SolutionSolution

(a) A's score is 0.9+0.5w+0.5×0.8=1.3+0.5w, and B's is 0.7+0.95w+0.5×0.2=0.8+0.95w. They are equal at w=0.5/0.45≈1.11. At the default w=1.0, A (1.80) narrowly leads B (1.75); at w=1.5, B (2.225) leads A (2.05). There are candidate pairs whose choice changes with a small change in the weight. That raising the ISSUP weight in Figure 3(b) moved citation precision and MAUVE in opposite directions can be read as such flips accumulating across the whole output.

(b) Weights have to be read together with scales. ISUSE has a range of 2 while ISREL and ISSUP have a range of 1, so the maximum span of ISUSE's contribution after multiplying by 0.5 (1) equals the span of the other two at weight 1.0 (1). Contrary to the impression that utility gets half the weight, by range it gets the same weight. The first term of Eq. 3, p(yt∣x,d,y<t), also has a scale problem. The generation probability of a whole sentence is a product of token probabilities, so the longer the sentence, the closer it gets to 0. Whether this term is a raw probability, a log probability or a length-normalized value changes its relative weight against the three critique scores completely, and the paper's text does not say. It can be read as meaning that the practical meaning of "weight 1.0" cannot be settled before checking the implementation.

(c) One possible design. Keep a separate development set and vary the three weights on a grid (0, 0.5, 1 and 2 each, 64 combinations), measuring the metrics for each task. Report the Pareto frontier for a pair of metrics (citation precision against MAUVE) and where the defaults sit on it, local sensitivity within ±50% of the defaults, and the per-question agreement of choices between combinations. Choosing among the 64 combinations by looking at the test set would create the best-of-k selection bias of Exercise 2 in Chapter 6, so do the choosing on the development set only. Also compare a scheme that standardizes the three scores before weighting them.

Takeaway. The weights of a composite score cannot be read apart from the scales. And the advantage that the weights can be changed at inference time is verified only when the process of choosing good values is reported.

9. Limitations the paper states

  • Outputs without support still occur. The ethics statement says the model can produce outputs not fully supported by citations, and hopes that explicit self-reflection and fine-grained attribution will help users verify facts.
  • Limits of off-the-shelf retrievers. Retrievers trained on knowledge-intensive tasks were of limited effectiveness for open-ended generation, and performance varies with the Wikipedia dump (Appendix B.2). That is why the December 2020 dump was used for PopQA only.
  • Retrieving less costs something. On PopQA it did (Figure 3(c)).
  • Wobbly judgments of utility. On ISUSE 5 against 4, the critic model, GPT-4 and people all disagree (Appendices A.1, A.2).
  • Scale of training data and output length. The training data was limited to 150k (§5.2), and the cells where 7B beats 13B on factual precision are explained by its tendency to write shorter (§5.1). This can also be read as an admission that the metric is sensitive to output length.

Things the paper does not state are noted too. All are the editor's reading. First, the labels for the reflection tokens are ultimately GPT-4's judgments. Judgments on which GPT-4 is systematically wrong can survive two rounds of distillation, through the critic model and the generator. Second, the model that writes the answer grades its own answer. When people rechecked the model's ISSUP judgments on Bio, 15% disagreed with human judgment (ISSUP 85.0 in Figure 4(d)). Sentences that the self-grading gets wrong still receive citation numbers. Third, for biographies and open-domain question answering, Self-RAG received 5 web-search documents on top of 5 Contriever documents (§4.3). For ASQA the paper says the documents were given "across all baselines for a fair comparison", but whether the web-search documents were also given to the baselines is not clear from this sentence alone. It is a point to check when reading the PopQA, TriviaQA and Bio comparisons in Table 2.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

CRAG — Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (Yan et al. 2024). It does not retrain the generator. A lightweight retrieval evaluator built on T5-large (0.77B) scores the relevance of each question–document pair from −1 to 1, and two thresholds choose one of three actions (§4.2–4.3, Appendix B.3). If even one document is above the upper threshold, the result is Correct: the documents are split into strips and irrelevant strips are filtered out (decompose-then-recompose). If all are below the lower threshold, the result is Incorrect: the documents are discarded, ChatGPT rewrites the question into a keyword query, and the search widens to the web. In between is Ambiguous, which combines the two. The authors say that with only two actions and no Ambiguous, performance was easily swayed by the evaluator's accuracy.

There are three differences from the main paper. In Self-RAG the generator learns the judgment; in CRAG a small model outside does it. Self-RAG makes a candidate for each fetched passage and chooses by rank, and even when it judges a passage useless it does not switch knowledge sources. It does receive 5 extra web-search documents for Bio and open-domain question answering (section 4), but that is a setting fixed in advance per task. CRAG widens to web search when, and because, the evaluator judges all the fetched documents Incorrect. And CRAG looks only at relevance; it does not check whether the generated text is supported by the documents (Self-RAG's ISSUP).

Comparison numbers with Self-RAG (CRAG Table 1). It used the same tasks and the same Contriever retrieval results as Self-RAG. When the generator is Self-RAG's released model (SelfRAG-LLaMA2-7b), Self-CRAG, which adds CRAG to Self-RAG, goes PopQA 54.9 → 61.8, Bio 81.2 → 86.2, PubHealth 72.4 → 74.8 and ARC 67.3 → 67.2. The text does not mention the small drop on ARC. The 6.9-point PopQA difference is about 3.7 times the independent-sample standard error for 1,399 questions (the editor's calculation). Applying the Self-RAG procedure to LLaMA2-hf-7b, which never learned reflection tokens, collapses it to PopQA 29.0 and PubHealth 0.7 (values reproduced by the CRAG authors; Appendix B.5 of CRAG explains that the PubHealth 0.7 includes format failures in which the model could not answer in the True/False format), while CRAG gets 54.9 and 59.5. Some conditions to attach. The Self-RAG rows carry the original paper's numbers, while Self-CRAG was run by the CRAG authors. The evaluator was trained on the rest of PopQA's roughly 14,000 questions (about 12,600) after removing the 1,399 test questions, and was carried over unchanged to the other tasks. The thresholds were set empirically per task (0.59 and −0.99 for PopQA), but on what data is not stated. Running time per example was 0.363 seconds for RAG, 0.512 for CRAG, 0.741 for Self-RAG and 0.908 for Self-CRAG (Table 6, PopQA, generation stage only).

The name collides. "CRAG" is also the short name of a RAG benchmark, CRAG – Comprehensive RAG Benchmark (Yang et al.). The CRAG of this chapter is Corrective RAG.

Active retrieval, FLARE (Jiang et al. 2023). An adaptive retrieval method that Self-RAG cites as prior work. Self-RAG §2 introduces it as a method that adaptively fetches passages during generation on top of a large proprietary model, and CRAG §2 as a method that looks ahead at upcoming content to decide when and what to retrieve. The difference is whether the timing of retrieval is decided by a procedure on top of a model that has not learned it, or by tokens the generator has learned.

RAG (Lewis et al. 2020 · Chapter 8 of this book). The paper that Self-RAG's introduction cites for the conventional RAG on the left of Figure 1. The figure, though, shows three documents attached to one input and written in one pass, whereas the RAG of Lewis et al. treats the top k documents as a latent variable, generates separately for each document and sums (section 6 of Appendix I). Self-RAG makes a candidate for each document and chooses by critique score. This contrast is the editor's summary.

Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023 · Chapter 7 of this book). The two share inserting special tokens into a training corpus and learning them by next-token prediction, and Table 8 of the revised AR survey also puts both in the same cell (θ). Self-RAG §2 describes Toolformer as a model trained to generate API calls for named entities. The difference is what the tokens do. Toolformer's tokens call out to the outside; Self-RAG's critique tokens grade its own output.

RARR and Reflexion (RARR, Gao et al. 2023 · Reflexion, Shinn et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book). The time scale of self-critique differs. Self-RAG critiques each sentence and chooses on the spot. RARR finds evidence for a finished output, attaches attribution and revises unsupported content while preserving the original output as much as possible (RARR abstract). Reflexion leaves a reflection after an episode ends, and §4.1.1 of the revised AR survey classifies this as an update to the system state S. The summary that the unit grows from within a sentence, to after the output, to after the episode is this book's reading.

ReAct (Yao et al. 2023 · Chapter 6 of this book). Both alternate retrieval and generation. What the model emits in between differs. ReAct emits thoughts (Thought) written in natural language; Self-RAG emits segments of the answer along with Retrieve and critique tokens. And ReAct is prompting with examples and does not grade its search results. Table 8 of the revised AR survey puts ReAct under in-context search (z) and Self-RAG under post-training search (θ).

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §3.3 — which of the three regimes?

§3.3 of the revised version divides single-agent agentic RAG into three architectural styles and says that they match the three optimization regimes of Table 8 and the three optimization targets of Chapter 2: in-context agentic RAG (§3.3.1, z), structure-enhanced agentic RAG (§3.3.2, the system state S) and post-training agentic RAG (§3.3.3, θ).

Self-RAG is post-training. The survey goes out of its way to say so. §3.3.1 introduces "reflective retrieval," which retrieves only when necessary, and then says that its two best-known instances (Self-RAG and DeepRAG) do not belong in that subsection. Both change θ by fine-tuning, so they belong in §3.3.3 and in Regime III of Table 8. §3.3.3 repeats it: "Two systems that are often described as prompting methods belong here instead." The reason is that the decision whether to retrieve and the self-assessment are learned rather than drawn out by prompting.

Table 8 column Self-RAG cell
Optimization Regime III Post-Training Agentic Search
Reasoning Structure Reflective
Query / Action Format Reflection tokens
Tool Conditional Search
Optim. Target θ

The Self-RAG row of Table 8 in the revised AR survey. In the same Regime III, the SFT-based group includes Toolformer, DeepRAG and INTERS, and the RL-based group includes WebGPT, Search-R1 and others (§3.3.3).

The point to raise in the presentation is that the name "reflection" and the classification seem at odds. By the name alone, it sounds as if it belongs with the self-reflection of Chapter 11. But the revised version's criterion is what changes. Prompting for reflection at inference time is z; engraving reflection into the weights is θ.

Self-RAG is absent from §4.1.1 (self-reflective feedback). §4.1.1 defines reflective feedback as methods that revise during inference without updating model parameters, and puts Self-Refine, Reflexion and others under the self-reflective type (I-a) and ReAct, PAL and others under the externally grounded type (I-b). The absence of Self-RAG, which changes θ, fits the definition. Looking only at the inference process, though, it resembles I-a, where "the agent is its own critic" and its critique shapes what comes next. A method that uses a learned critique at inference time can also be read as sitting on the boundary of this framework.

Citations elsewhere. §4.2.1 (flat memory) and §4.3.3 (self-evolving search) cite Asai et al. (2023) alongside Lewis et al. (2020) as examples of dense retrieval. That is a different kind of citation from Table 8. The reference list gives Self-RAG as the NeurIPS 2023 instruction-tuning workshop version (titled "Self-rag: Self-reflective retrieval augmented generation").

Mapping the notation. The mapping below is the editor's reading.

Self-RAG paper AR survey, revised version, §2.2
Input x and earlier segments y<t History ht
Calling the retriever ℛ on Retrieve=Yes External action at (a call to the retrieval tool)
Retrieved passage d Observation ot
Weights of the generator ℳ Parameters θ — fine-tuned on the reflection-token corpus
Inference-time weights wG, threshold δ Knobs that adjust search with θ held fixed
Critique score 𝒮, set of critique token types 𝒢, generator ℳ Same letters as, but different meanings from, the survey's S (system state), G (the agent tuple) and M (the memory space)

Read the fourth and fifth rows together and the position becomes clear. The ability to reflect is engraved in θ, and how to use it is set by inference-time weights. The survey puts it in the θ cell based on what was newly acquired.

Harness survey — not applicable

Neither Self-RAG nor CRAG appears in the Harness survey. RAG comes up only in passing, in places such as §5.5.3, as background for the retrieval tier of memory systems. If a connection must be made, a design like CRAG's, which puts an evaluator outside the generator, can be read as placing the judgment on the harness side rather than in the model (Chapter 3). This is this book's reading.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "Self-RAG is a technique for prompting a model to review itself." The generator is fine-tuned on about 150k pairs of a corpus carrying reflection tokens (§3.2.2, §4.3), and that is why the revised AR survey classifies it as post-training (θ) (Table 8). Applying the same procedure to a model that was not trained this way makes it collapse (CRAG Table 1, PopQA 29.0 for LLaMA2-hf-7b).

Misreading 2. "At inference time, a separate critic model attaches the reflection tokens." The critic model 𝒞 is used only to insert reflection tokens into the training corpus in advance. At inference time the generator ℳ emits the reflection tokens itself (§3.1, Training overview).

Misreading 3. "Self-RAG is a way to save cost by retrieving less." The default threshold is 0.2 (0 for ASQA), and the authors say they set it to retrieve frequently (§4.3). In CRAG's measurements, running time per example for Self-RAG (0.741 seconds) is about twice that of standard RAG (0.363 seconds) (CRAG Table 6).

Misreading 4. "The weights wG are learned values." They are hyperparameters set by a person at inference time. The defaults are 1.0, 1.0 and 0.5 (§3.3, §4.3).

Misreading 5. "If ISSUP = Fully supported, the sentence is true." ISSUP checks whether the fetched passage supports the sentence. If the passage is wrong, a supported sentence is wrong too. ISUSE is a perceived utility unrelated to factuality (Appendix A.1). In the human evaluation, the model's ISSUP judgments matched people's in 90.0% of cases on PopQA and 85.0% on Bio (Figure 4(d)).

Misreading 6. "13B is better than 7B on every task." 7B is higher on Bio FactScore and ASQA MAUVE (Table 2). 13B's 0.9-point gain on PopQA is within the standard error for 1,399 questions (section 8 of "The paper in detail").

Discussion questions

  1. Who should decide whether to retrieve? In Self-RAG the generator decides, in CRAG a small evaluator outside, and in ReAct (Chapter 6) a model given a prompt. For a system in your own work (internal search, document question answering), by what criterion would you choose whether to put this judgment inside the model or in the harness? When you swap the model, what changes along with it (the LLaMA2-hf-7b row of CRAG Table 1)?

  2. Can self-grading be trusted? Self-RAG's reflection tokens are GPT-4's judgments distilled twice, and the model that wrote the answer grades its own answer. In human work, why do we separate "self-review" from "third-party review"? This comes up again in Chapter 11.

  3. Who turns the knobs? That the weights and threshold can be changed at inference time is an advantage, but someone has to choose the values. If citation precision and fluency move in opposite directions (Figure 3(b)), which would you weight more in your task? How would you record and verify that choice?

Chapter 11 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 11. Revision and Reflection — RARR and Reflexion

The question this chapter answers: how does fixing a wrong answer "within a single output" differ from fixing it "on the next attempt"?

Core reading. Read two papers.

  1. Luyu Gao et al., "RARR: Researching and Revising What Language Models Say, Using Language Models", ACL 2023. 10 pages of main text (through the limitations and ethics statement), 30 with the appendices.
  2. Noah Shinn et al., "Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning", NeurIPS 2023. 9 pages of main text, 19 with the appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper 1, RARR — arXiv abstract · PDF · ACL Anthology 2023.acl-long.910 · Code

Main paper 2, Reflexion — arXiv abstract · PDF · NeurIPS 2023 presentation page · Code

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §2.2 (Eq. 5), §4.1, Figure 5, Tables 4, 6 and 9 · Harness survey §8.5, §12.3

One-paragraph summary. Neither paper stops once it has produced an output. Each critiques the output and uses the critique to fix it. RARR takes a passage that has already been generated, writes questions to check it, finds evidence with Google Search, makes the smallest edits needed where the passage disagrees with the evidence, and attaches a list of supporting evidence (an attribution report). It is evaluated on two axes: how far the text is backed by evidence (attribution) and how much of the original text it leaves untouched (preservation). When Reflexion fails a task, it writes down in its own words what went wrong, puts that in memory and tries the same task again with the reflection in front of it. The weights do not change. The two differ in the unit they fix. RARR fixes sentences; Reflexion fixes episodes.

Presenter's guide

A 50-minute plan. There are two core papers, so give the first 25 minutes to RARR and the last 25 to Reflexion. The 10 minutes after the presentation are for discussion.

Time Content In the papers

4–12 min RARR's task definition: attribution and preservation, F1AP RARR §2, Figure 1, Eqs. 1–4
12–18 min RARR's method: the research stage and the revision stage RARR §3, Figure 2, Figure 3
18–25 min RARR's results and ablations RARR §5.3 Table 1 and Figure 5, §6.2 Table 2 and Figure 8
25–33 min Reflexion's structure: actor, evaluator, self-reflection, two memories Reflexion §3, Figure 2, Algorithm 1
33–45 min Reflexion's experiments: household tasks, question answering, code Reflexion §4.1–4.3, Figures 3 and 4, Tables 1–3
45–50 min Back to the surveys: Eq. 5 and "Verbal Evolution" AR survey, revised version §2.2, §4.1, Table 9

Must read. For RARR, all of §2, §3, Table 1 in §5.3, and §6.2. If you show one figure, make it Figure 2. It contains the whole process: a passage split into two questions, the evidence for one of them disagreeing, and one date getting fixed. For Reflexion, §3 and Figure 2 (the diagram and Algorithm 1), the results of §4.1 with Figure 3, and Table 1 in §4.3.

Optional reading. RARR Figures 6 and 7 (good and bad revisions) and Appendices A and B. Reflexion Appendix A (Tables 4 and 5), Figure 5 in Appendix B (an actual reflection), B.1 (WebShop) and Appendix D.

What to cut from the presentation. RARR's evaluation guidelines in Appendix C, the full prompts in Appendix D (look only at Figure 13) and §4, Related Work. Reflexion Appendix C.

If your group skipped Chapter 6. Reflexion's actor is ReAct. In the first 3 minutes, point out only that ReAct is a loop that alternates thought, action and observation, and that in the largest failure mode of its HotpotQA failure sample, reasoning errors, many cases were loops repeating the same action (ReAct Table 2).

When you quote the numbers. RARR uses prompting on PaLM 540B, and 150 development and 150 test passages were built for each combination (how many passages went into the human evaluation is not stated). Reflexion uses a different model for each task (GPT-3 for ALFWorld, GPT-4 for programming, and the paper does not say which for the main HotpotQA experiment), and the ALFWorld and HotpotQA figures are cumulative proportions over several attempts. When you write a number down, give the model, the task, the metric and the number of items with it, and say whether it is a single attempt or cumulative.

Building intuition

Why the two go together — the evaluator-optimizer pattern at two scales

The Anthropic post in Chapter 1 lists the evaluator-optimizer as one of its workflow patterns: "one LLM call generates a response while another provides evaluation and feedback in a loop." The post says it fits well when there are clear evaluation criteria, when feedback actually improves the response, and when a language model can provide such feedback. The two papers implement this pattern at different scales. The table below is the editor's arrangement.

RARR Reflexion
What it fixes An already generated passage x The actions of the next attempt
Unit of the fix One factual piece inside a sentence (a date, a name, a number) The plan for the whole episode
Basis of the critique Evidence found by web search The evaluator's success or failure signal + a reflection the model writes
When it fixes Within the same output, once per piece of evidence After an attempt ends, before the next one
What is left A revision y and an attribution report A A few reflections (long-term memory)
Does it need the right answer? No (it looks only at agreement with evidence) Depends on the task ("The paper in detail", sections 6, 7 and 8)
If it fails Sentences it could not fix remain It tries the same task again

The left side follows RARR §3 and Figure 2, the right side Reflexion §3 and Figure 2. The dashed line on the left means "on to the next (query, evidence) pair", the one on the right "on to the next attempt". In RARR, when the agreement model judges that the two agree, the edit is skipped. The editor drew the diagram.

RARR's loop ends when it has gone through all the evidence pairs. It hands back a revision and an attribution report but leaves no memory to pass on to the next input. Reflexion's loop leaves, at every attempt, text to carry into the next attempt.

The editor's bridge — precision and recall, and a verbal version of reinforcement learning

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

RARR is a precision–recall trade-off. Lower a classifier's threshold and recall goes up while precision goes down. In a revision model, the threshold is "how boldly it edits". The bolder it is, the more sentences are backed by evidence (attribution goes up) and the more the original text is damaged (preservation goes down). Delete the original and paste in a retrieved document whole, and attribution becomes 100% (the example in §2.3). That is why the two are combined into a harmonic mean, F1AP, and the paper itself says it is "analogous to how recall and precision are combined in F1".

Reflexion is a verbal version of reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning as described in Chapter 0 updates the policy's weights with the reward received at the end of each episode. Reflexion updates the prompt instead of the weights. It turns a one-bit success or failure signal into a sentence such as "I should have looked for the desklamp first" and attaches it to the input of the next episode. Developers can think of an incident postmortem. Nothing is redeployed; only the document the next responder will read gets longer.

The analogy also breaks down. Precision and recall are two ratios from the same confusion matrix, but attribution and preservation are measured with different instruments (sentence-level AIS judgments and edit distance). A weight update in reinforcement learning changes the whole policy, so its effect can spread to other states (generalization is not guaranteed), while Reflexion's reflections are attached only to the next attempt in the same environment or on the same question.

The papers' own analogies. RARR calls itself "a retrieval-augmented model where retrieval happens after generation rather than before" (§1). The timing of retrieval is the reverse of RAG in Chapter 8. The inspiration came from fact-checking workflows that research and revise claims made by people. Reflexion says that self-reflection acts as "a 'semantic' gradient signal" (§1).

The paper in detail

1. RARR — task definition: attribution and preservation (§2)

The task. The paper defines a new task, Editing for Attribution. The input is a passage x written by some generation model. The output is a revised passage y and an attribution report A, where A is a collection of evidence snippets e1,…,eM that back the content of y. In the example in Figure 1, the original is "The marathon world record is 2:01:39, set by Eliud Kipchoge of Kenya in 2018." The revision changes the record to 2:01:09 and the year to 2022. The report contains "Kipchoge is a Kenyan long-distance runner" from Wikipedia and "Kipchoge shaved 30 seconds … to finish in 2:01:09" from npr.org.

Attribution. The starting point is AIS (Attributable to Identified Sources) of Rashkin et al. (2021). A passage counts as attributed if a generic hearer would affirm the statement "According to A, y". The original AIS gives the whole text 1 or 0. The paper breaks this down to the sentence level. Annotators give an AIS score to each sentence s of y, and the scores are averaged.

AttrAIS(y,A)=avgs∈yAIS(s,A)(Eq. 1)

That is, it measures "the percentage of sentences in y that are fully attributed to A." The evidence in the report is limited to M=5 snippets (inspecting 30 examples showed that 5 were enough). During development the paper uses auto-AIS, approximated with a natural language inference (NLI) model.

Attrauto(y,A)=avgs∈y maxe∈ANLI(e,s)(Eq. 2)

NLI(e,s) is the probability that evidence e entails sentence s, and each sentence is decontextualized before the calculation. Decontextualization fills in pronouns and omitted subjects from the context so that a sentence can be read on its own without the text around it. For example, "He set the record in 2022" would become "Kipchoge set the marathon world record in 2022" before going into the NLI model (the example is the editor's). The paper uses the T5 decontextualization model of Choi et al. (2021) (Appendix B).

Preservation. Intent preservation judged by people, Presintent (1 if fully preserved, otherwise 0), is multiplied by PresLev, measured with character-level Levenshtein edit distance.

PresLev(x,y)=max(1−Lev(x,y)length(x), 0)(Eq. 3)

Prescomb(x,y)=Presintent(x,y)·PresLev(x,y)(Eq. 4)

Lev(x,y) is the minimum number of character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn x into y (each counts as 1). In Figure 1, changing "2018" to "2022" substitutes the last two characters, so it costs 2, and changing "2:01:39" to "2:01:09" costs 1. If the original were 100 characters long, a revision that fixed only these two places would have PresLev=1−3/100=0.97.

Change the intent and the score is 0; keep it and the score is higher the less you edit (the paper notes that this does not capture things worth preserving such as rhythm or wordplay).

Why two axes (§2.3). Optimize attribution alone and an adversarial editor that replaces the input with any retrieved document wins. So the paper reports both and adds their harmonic mean, F1AP. The advantage it claims is that this evaluation needs no "gold" edits, so it can be used for any generation task.

Attribution is not correctness

Footnote 2 of the paper says it deliberately avoids the term "fact-checking": "attribution does not entail correctness." Being attributed to a source does not guarantee that the source is right. This caveat comes back in the peach example of §6.2 and in the ethics statement.

2. RARR — the research stage and the revision stage (§3)

Almost every component is prompting on PaLM 540B (5 to 10 examples per component, temperature 0.7, Appendix D). The only separately trained piece is an existing T5-large model that scores query–evidence relevance.

Research stage (§3.1).

  • Query generation (CQGen). Turns every aspect of passage x that needs checking into a question. Six human-written examples were reportedly enough. To raise diversity and coverage, it samples three times and takes the union of the questions.
  • Evidence retrieval. For each question, Google Search returns K=5 web pages. The pages are cut into candidate snippets with a four-sentence sliding window, ranked with the relevance model Srelevance(q,e), and only the top J=1 is kept per question.

Revision stage (§3.2). The output is initialized as y=x, and the (query, evidence) pairs are processed one at a time.

  • Agreement model. Judges whether y and e imply the same answer to question q. A CoT-style prompt has it first write out the answer implied by y and the answer implied by e, and then give its judgment.
  • Edit model. Runs only when the agreement model judges that they disagree. It is made to point to the span that needs fixing first, and then to write a new y. Edits with an edit distance over 50 characters or over 0.5 times the original length are thrown away (footnote 3), because the editor sometimes drags the whole text toward the evidence.

The examples in Figure 3 look like this (the caption marks blue as input and red as the output the model is to write).

(b) Agreement model (y, q, e) → {0, 1}
You said: Your nose switches ...(same as above)... nasal cycle.
I checked: How often do your nostrils switch?
I found this article: Although we don't usually notice it, during the nasal
cycle one nostril becomes congested … On average, the congestion pattern
switches about every 2 hours, according to a small 2016 study …
Your nose's switching time is about every 2 hours, not 45 minutes.
This disagrees with what you said.

(c) Edit model (y, q, e) → new y
  …
This suggests 45 minutes switch time in your statement is wrong.
My fix: Your nose switches back and forth between nostrils. When you
sleep, you switch about every 2 hours. This is to prevent a buildup of
mucus. It's called the nasal cycle.

Parts (b) and (c) of RARR Figure 3, shortened. The first three lines of (c) are the same as (b) and are left out.

Both prompts are first-person conversation. Before judging, the agreement model sets the two answers side by side ("Your nose's switching time is about every 2 hours, not 45 minutes."), and the edit model points to the place to fix ("This suggests 45 minutes switch time in your statement is wrong.") before writing "My fix". Only one number changed. The example in Figure 2 is the same. From "Millie Inbetween premiered on 24 February 2014 on CBBC." come two questions. The evidence on the premiere date ("the first series premiered on 1 October 2014") disagrees, so the date gets fixed, and the evidence on the channel ("CBBC sitcom") agrees, so the edit is skipped.

Attribution report (§3.3). At the end, an exhaustive search picks at most M=5 snippets that best cover the questions. The criterion is Cover(A,q1:N)=∑i=1Nmaxe∈ASrelevance(qi,e) (RARR's Eq. 5, which is not the same as the AR survey's Eq. 5 later in this chapter).

3. RARR — experimental setup and results (§5)

Three tasks (§5.1). Questions from a dataset are given to a generation model, which writes long answers, and those answers become RARR's input. Each combination has 150 development and 150 test passages. Factoid statements are answers that PaLM 540B and GPT-3 wrote to Natural Questions (NQ) questions; reasoning chains are reasoning they wrote for StrategyQA (SQA) questions; knowledge-intensive dialogue is answers that LaMDA and GPT-3 wrote in QReCC conversations. Table 1 in the main text covers PaLM's NQ and SQA and LaMDA's QReCC; the GPT-3 passages appear only in Appendix Table 5, with automatic metrics only.

Baselines (§5.2). EFEC (Thorne and Vlachos 2021) is a T5 editor fine-tuned to revise given several pieces of evidence at once. To compare editing ability alone, it was fed the evidence RARR had found. LaMDA Research takes LaMDA's three stages (base response → search queries → revised response) and replaces the first with x. For non-dialog tasks an artificial user utterance, "Tell me something interesting.", was inserted.

Scoreboard — Table 1 (AIS and intent preservation are human evaluations; the rest are computed automatically)

Input passages Model auto-AIS (before → after) AIS (before → after) intent Lev comb F1AP

LaMDA 39.5 → 49.9 18.3 → 30.4 26.0 39.6 21.1 24.9

Table 1 of the paper. F1AP is the harmonic mean of AIS after revision and combined preservation. The editor recalculated all nine cells and confirmed that they match the printed values.

Read the table in this order.

  1. On attribution alone, RARR does not win. AIS after revision is highest for EFEC on all three tasks (48.3, 51.7, 48.7).
  2. Preservation decides it. RARR's intent preservation is 90.0 to 95.6%; EFEC and LaMDA range from 6.0 to 40.0%.
  3. F1AP is highest for RARR on all three tasks. The paper writes that RARR is significantly ahead on NQ and SQA, but the main text gives no test.
  4. Attaching evidence without editing leaves attribution at 13.2 to 35.4% (AIS before revision).

One sentence in §5.3 is hard to square with the table. It says that RARR raises attribution "by up to 13% absolute," but the gains in Table 1 are 8.0, 7.0 and 15.1 percentage points in human AIS and 9.3, 7.5 and 10.6 percentage points in auto-AIS. In neither case is the maximum 13.

Figure 5 plots the nine points of Table 1 on a plane with combined preservation on the horizontal axis and human AIS on the vertical axis, over F1AP contour lines. The points sit where the table's values put them. The caption sums it up: "Different models make very different trade-offs between attribution and preservation." EFEC is at the upper left, editing a lot and attributing a lot; RARR is on the right, editing little and attributing somewhat.

Human oracle and how the baselines fail (§6.1). When the authors themselves edited 30 NQ passages until they were 100% attributed, preservation was 88% and F1AP 93.6. In Figure 6, EFEC shortens the same passage ("…submitted its report in 2016.") to one sentence, for 100% attribution and 0% preservation, and LaMDA changes the topic to the minimum wage. RARR changes only 2016 to 2015. The paper adds its own caveat that this comparison is not meant to rank the methods but to show that existing models were not designed for this task.

4. RARR — analysis and ablations (§6)

Strengths and weaknesses (§6.1). A manual look at 40 examples found that in over 80% the questions covered every aspect of the original. Retrieval was good with distinct entities and weak with obvious claims such as "Video games require electricity." Revision was good with entities and numbers, and on NQ it left 90% of the inputs whose AIS before revision exceeded 0.9 untouched. There are failures too. Drawn to the page of MeTV, a rerun channel, it wrongly changed NBC to MeTV (Figure 7d), and after correcting Homer Simpson's fingers from 5 to 4 it left the conclusion "He only need one hand to count to 5." unchanged (7e).

Ablating query generation and the agreement model — Table 2 (automatic metrics, auto-AIS before → after revision)

The F1AP in these two tables is the harmonic mean of auto-AIS after revision and Lev preservation, so it is on a different scale from the F1AP of Table 1 (human AIS and combined preservation). Do not compare the F1AP of the two tables with each other.

  • Remove the agreement model and over-editing appears. It now edits whenever evidence comes in, so Lev preservation drops on all three tasks (89.6 → 82.6, 89.9 → 83.4, 80.2 → 72.0). Figure 8 is an example.
x: The Crown-of-thorns starfish is native to the Great Barrier Reef...The
   starfish was introduced to the Great-Barrier-Reef by ocean currents.
e: [invasivespeciesinfo.gov] Ballast water is one of the major pathways for
   the introduction of nonindigenous marine species...
y: The Crown-of-thorns starfish is native to the Great Barrier Reef...The
   starfish was introduced to the Great-Barrier-Reef by ballast water.

RARR Figure 8.

The evidence says only that ballast water is a major pathway for nonindigenous marine species; it does not contradict the original's claim that the starfish came in on ocean currents. This is a pair the agreement model would have filtered out, and without it an unsupported revision happens. On SQA, removing the agreement model leaves F1AP the same at 60.0. A small rise in attribution and a drop in preservation (89.9 → 83.4) simply cancel out in the harmonic mean.

  • Query = input cannot aim the evidence at the doubtful parts, so attribution barely rises, and on SQA it falls (39.4 → 30.3).
  • Query = sentence gives a similar F1AP (67.8 against 68.1 on NQ). The paper gives two caveats. When Wikipedia is removed from web search, this approach drops more (Table 3, NQ 67.8 → 60.3; full RARR 68.1 → 64.3). PaLM's answers resemble Wikipedia's style, so searching with the sentence itself happened to work well. There is also confirmation bias. Search with "Georgia is called the Peach State, but California actually produces the most peaches." as is, and you get articles that agree, but CQGen asked "Which state produces the most peaches?" and found a more recent article saying South Carolina had overtaken California. The price was a lower F1AP. The paper offers this case as evidence that attribution alone cannot measure correctness.

Preserving usefulness, and side experiments. When a short answer is extracted from the revised text, NQ accuracy goes up by roughly 5%, while on SQA every revision model lowered yes/no accuracy, by up to 2.6% (Figure 9). Appendix A states that the main experiments were run only once and gives the standard deviations of the automatic metrics over three runs on NQ (Attrauto 1.2, PresLev 0.5, F1AP 1.0). Shrinking to 62B costs a lot (Table 4, F1AP 68.1 → 64.4); shrinking only query generation costs less (67.4). The paragraph in Appendix A writes this condition as "64B", while Table 4 writes "qgen 62B".

5. Reflexion — three models and two memories (§3)

Reflexion is made of three models.

  • Actor Ma. Generates text and actions conditioned on observations. It uses CoT or ReAct (Chapter 6), with the memory mem attached as context.
  • Evaluator Me. Gives the trajectory a reward score. For reasoning this is exact match (EM), for decision-making a heuristic, and in some experiments another language model.
  • Self-Reflection model Msr. Takes a sparse reward such as a binary success signal, the trajectory and the memory, and writes specific verbal feedback. A failed agent reasons that some action ai led to the wrong actions that followed, writes that it should have done ai′ instead, and on the next attempt chooses ai′ at that point.

Two memories. The trajectory within an attempt is short-term memory, and the reflections are long-term memory. One reflection accumulates per attempt, capped at a maximum number Ω ("usually set to 1-3"). ALFWorld and HotpotQA keep 3, programming 1. §5 calls this "a sliding window with maximum capacity".

Algorithm 1. From Figure 2(b).

Algorithm 1  Reinforcement via self-reflection
  Initialize Actor, Evaluator, Self-Reflection: Ma, Me, Msr
  Initialize policy πθ(ai|si), θ = {Ma, mem}
  Generate initial trajectory using πθ
  Evaluate τ0 using Me
  Generate initial self-reflection sr0 using Msr
  Set mem ← [sr0]
  Set t = 0
  while Me not pass or t < max trials do
      Generate τt = [a0, o0, . . . ai, oi] using πθ
      Evaluate τt using Me
      Generate self-reflection srt using Msr
      Append srt to mem
      Increment t
  end while
  return

Reflexion Figure 2(b). Subscripts are written on one line.

Two points are worth marking. First, the policy's "parameters" are written θ={Ma,mem}. The weights are fixed and only mem changes. The paper puts this forward as a contribution: it "parameterizes a policy as an agent's memory encoding paired with a choice of LLM parameters." Second, the loop condition "Me not pass or t < max trials", read literally, keeps running to the maximum number of trials even after a pass, and runs forever without one. Given the experimental setup (a cap on attempts), it reads more naturally as "while it has not passed and attempts remain".

The three evaluators in Figure 1. In the figure's "(c) Evaluation" row, decision-making has "Rule/LM Heuristic: Hallucination.", programming has "Self-generated unit tests fail", and reasoning has "Environment Binary Reward: 0", with an "internal / external" marker on the left. This difference, that the source of the signal varies by task, comes back as a classification problem in "Back to the surveys".

6. Reflexion — sequential decision-making: ALFWorld (§4.1)

Setup. The same 134 ALFWorld environments as in Chapter 6. The actor is ReAct, using two of Yao et al.'s example trajectories with GPT-3. The environment reports only task completion, so an evaluator was built separately: a language-model classifier and a hand-written heuristic.

"if the agent executes the same action and receives the same response for more than 3 cycles, or if the number of actions taken in the current environment exceeds 30 (inefficient planning), we self-reflect."

It reflects when the same action gets the same response more than three times (hallucination) or when there are more than 30 actions (inefficient planning). The baseline (ReAct alone) is cut off by the same rule but resets and starts over without a reflection. The memory holds 3 reflections.

Results. ReAct + Reflexion solved 130 of the 134 and kept improving over 12 consecutive attempts. ReAct alone stopped improving between the 6th and 7th attempts. The final value for ReAct alone, which is the reference for §1's "an absolute 22% in 12 iterative learning steps," is not printed as a number.

Figure 3. (a) is the cumulative proportion solved by attempt (three lines: ReAct alone, the heuristic evaluator and the GPT classifier evaluator), and (b) is the share of failure causes (hallucination against inefficient planning). The paper writes that ReAct alone converges near a hallucination rate of 22% with no recovery. Values read off the gridlines are not reproduced here. Two structural facts are worth noting. Both panels are printed with the same title, "(a) ALFWorld Success Rate", and the horizontal axis of (a) runs from 0 to 10 (11 attempts) while the Reflexion lines in (b) run from 0 to 11 (12 attempts). The "12" in the text and the number of points in (a) are off by one.

Analysis. A common failure of the baseline is to believe it is holding an object it has not picked up and carry on with a long trajectory. The paper sees long-term memory helping in two cases: when it points out an early mistake in a long trajectory and proposes a new plan, and when there are many places to search and it searches a room thoroughly across several attempts. Figure 5 in Appendix B shows an actual reflection.

  …
Task: examine the mug with the desklamp.
Trial #1
  …
> go to desk 2
On the desk 2, you see a alarmclock 1, a bowl 1, a mug 3, a pencil 3, and a pencil 2.
> think: Now I find a desklamp (1). Next, I need to use it.
> use desklamp 1
Nothing happens.
  …
Status: Fail
Reflection: In this environment, my plan was to find a mug then find and use a
desklamp. However, the task says to examine the mug with the desklamp. I should have
looked for the desklamp first, then looked for the mug. I noticed that the desklamp
was found on desk 1. In the next trial, I will go to desk 1, find the lamp, then look
for the mug and examine it with the desklamp.
Trial #2
> go to desk 1
  …
> take mug 1 from desk 1
  …
> use desklamp 1
You turn on the desklamp 1.
Status: Success

Reflexion Appendix B, Figure 5, shortened (the environment description, the opening of the first attempt, one repeated action and its observation, and the second attempt's two thought lines and two observation lines are left out; each cut is marked with …).

The first attempt fails at a thought: it believes it has found a lamp at desk 2, where there is none. The reflection does not point out this hallucination. Instead it leaves a lesson about the plan ("I should have looked for the desklamp first") and a fact particular to this room ("I noticed that the desklamp was found on desk 1."). Thanks to that fact, the second attempt finishes in three actions. The second item is a note that is useful only when searching the same room again. This is where the reinforcement-learning analogy breaks down.

7. Reflexion — reasoning: HotpotQA (§4.2)

Setup. Three actors are compared on 100 HotpotQA questions (Figure 4 caption). CoT answers from the question alone (Q→A); CoT (GT) also receives the ground-truth supporting passages Cgt, isolating reasoning ability (Q,Cgt→A); ReAct searches with the Wikipedia API. The success signal between attempts is EM scoring against the right answer, and the memory holds 3 reflections.

Results. Retried at temperature 0.7, none of the three baselines solved any question it had missed on the first attempt. Reflexion kept retrying a question until it failed three times in a row. CoT (GT), even with the supporting passages, "is unable to correctly infer the correct answer for 39% of the questions," and Reflexion raised its accuracy by 14%. The "20% in HotPotQA" of §1 and the opening of §4 appears to be the improvement on the ReAct side of Figure 4(a), but the endpoint values are not printed.

Episodic memory ablation (Figure 4c). The condition that also attaches the reflection was 8% absolute above the condition that attaches only the previous attempt's trajectory (EPM). The paper offers this as support that "refinement-only approaches are not as effective as self-reflection-guided refinement approaches."

With other models — Appendix Table 5 (100 HotpotQA questions)

Model Baseline accuracy Reflexion accuracy
CoT (GT) + text-davinci-003 0.60 0.77
CoT (GT) + gpt-3.5-turbo 0.57 0.71
CoT (GT) + gpt-4 0.68 0.80
ReAct + text-davinci-003 0.30 0.55
ReAct + gpt-3.5-turbo 0.26 0.38
ReAct + gpt-4 0.39 0.51

Table 5 of the paper. The caption says "Pass@1 accuracy", but by the setup in the text the Reflexion column is cumulative over several attempts.

The CoT (GT) baseline of 61% in the text (wrong on 39%) matches none of the rows in Table 5 (0.60, 0.57, 0.68). The paper does not say which model the main experiment (Figure 4) used. Do not mix the numbers from the two places.

Actual reflections (Appendix D). In D.1, the ReAct actor answers with the role of the lead actor Gorden Kaye on the first attempt and is wrong; on the second attempt it searches for Sam Kelly among the cast of Grown-Ups and gets it right. The example in D.4.1 can be read differently. The first attempt says "Jonny Craig has been a member of six bands, … Pete Doherty has been a member of seven bands," answers Pete Doherty and is wrong. The second attempt, with no search tool, writes "After researching, I have found that" and then states that both have been members of seven bands, yet concludes that Jonny Craig has been in more, and is right. On a question that picks one of two, the single bit "the first answer was wrong" settles the right answer. The reflection can also be read as passing on that signal rather than fixing the reasoning. That is not the paper's interpretation.

8. Reflexion — programming (§4.3)

Setup. HumanEval and MBPP are run in Python and in Rust (translated with MultiPL-E), and a new benchmark, LeetcodeHardGym, was built from 40 Leetcode "hard" problems released after GPT-4's pre-training cutoff (October 8, 2022). The evaluator is not a hidden set of reference tests but unit tests the actor writes itself. Tests are generated with CoT, filtered to the syntactically valid ones with an abstract syntax tree (AST), and up to 6 are sampled. Because it does not look at hidden tests, the paper argues that it is eligible to report pass@1 (§2 judges that AlphaCode, Self-Debugging and CodeRL rely on reference tests and so are not). The memory holds 1 reflection.

Scoreboard — Table 1

Benchmark + Language Prev SOTA Pass@1 SOTA Pass@1 Reflexion Pass@1
