HumanEval (RS) – 60.0 (GPT-4) 68.0
MBPP (PY) 67.7 (CodeT + Codex) 80.1 (GPT-4) 77.1
MBPP (RS) – 70.9 (GPT-4) 75.4
Leetcode Hard (PY) – 7.5 (GPT-4) 15.0

Table 1 of the paper. According to the caption, the base strategy is a single code generation sample, and all instruction-based models generate code with no examples. The table gives no number of problems.

Only on MBPP Python is Reflexion below the GPT-4 baseline (77.1 against 80.1). The paper explains why with Table 2.

How well the tests work — Table 2

Benchmark + Language Base Reflexion TP FN FP TN
HumanEval (PY) 0.80 0.91 0.99 0.40 0.01 0.60
MBPP (PY) 0.80 0.77 0.84 0.59 0.16 0.41
HumanEval (RS) 0.60 0.68 0.87 0.37 0.13 0.63
MBPP (RS) 0.71 0.75 0.84 0.51 0.16 0.49

Table 2 of the paper. TP: unit tests pass, solution pass; FN: unit tests fail, solution pass; FP: unit tests pass, solution fail; TN: unit tests fail, solution fail. For Rust, HumanEval is the hardest 50 problems.

These four cells are not the confusion matrix familiar from statistics. In each row, TP + FP = 1 and FN + TN = 1. TP and FP are conditional shares "given that the self-written tests pass", and FN and TN "given that they fail". The FP in the text is P(wrong∣tests pass), 16.3% for MBPP Python and 1.4% for HumanEval Python. Code that passes its tests is submitted at once, so a false positive ships wrong code. A false negative is less harmful in the paper's view, because in the reflection step the agent can decide the test was wrong and keep the code. The same paragraph gives the two base pass@1 values as "82% and 80%", but the Base column of Table 2 is 0.80 for both.

Ablation — Table 3 (GPT-4, HumanEval Rust, the 50 hardest problems)

Approach Test Generation Self-reflection Pass@1 (Acc)
Base model False False 0.60
Test generation omission False True 0.52
Self-reflection omission True False 0.60
Reflexion True True 0.68

Table 3 of the paper.

Reflecting without tests falls below the base (52 against 60). The interpretation is that, unable to judge whether the code is right, it cannot stop early and breaks code that was fine. Tests without reflection equal the base. The paper concludes that "blind trial and error debugging techniques without self-reflection are ineffective on harder tasks such as writing complex programs in Rust." That this is a difference of 4 problems out of 50 is examined in section 9.

With a weaker model (Appendix A). Averaged over 8 runs of HumanEval Python with starchat-beta, both the base and Reflexion scored 0.26 (Table 4). The paper takes the ability to self-correct to be an emergent quality of stronger, larger models.

9. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the two papers. The papers did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn their conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

What F1AP's harmonic mean hides. A harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value. That is the right property for screening out the adversarial editor of §2.3 (attribution 100, preservation 0). There is an opposite extreme too: the "no-edit" approach that changes nothing and only attaches evidence. Preservation is 100 and attribution is the AIS before revision in Table 1, so its F1AP is 52.3 on NQ, 39.4 on SQA and 23.3 on QReCC. RARR's is 57.0, 45.9 and 41.5. On NQ, 52.3 of RARR's 57.0 points are points you get without editing anything. The paper itself makes the comparison ("if we only retrieve evidence to support the original response x without editing, attribution ranges from the low 10s to mid 30s"), so this baseline is already within what the paper says. It just did not put it in the table as a row.

The harmonic mean carries one more hidden assumption: that the two axes weigh the same. Weight attribution more, as with Fβ in information retrieval, and the ranking changes (Exercise 1). And Table 1's F1AP is not the average of per-passage harmonic means but the harmonic mean of two averages (the editor reproduced all nine cells this way). The trade-off within each individual passage does not survive into this number.

Uncertainty in RARR's tables. The main experiment was run once, and Appendix A gives the standard deviations of the automatic metrics over three runs (F1AP 1.0). In Table 2, the F1AP differences between "query = sentence" and full RARR (0.3 on NQ, 1.2 on SQA) lie within this run-to-run variation. There are 150 test passages per combination (it is not stated whether the human evaluation covered all of them, so the calculation below assumes n=150), and only in the pilot phase did three annotators rate the same passages; in the main evaluation each passage was rated by one annotator (Appendix C). No agreement figures are given. A per-passage AIS lies between 0 and 1, so its variance cannot exceed p(1−p), and the standard error of the mean AIS of 43.4 is at most 0.434×0.566/150≈4.0 percentage points.

Reflexion's cumulative curves are survival curves. The vertical axis of Figure 3(a) and Figure 4 is "the share of tasks solved at least once so far". Take the attempt number at which each task is first solved as the event time, and this curve is the cumulative incidence 1−S^(t) of survival analysis, with tasks never solved censored at the last attempt. If survival analysis is new to you, translate the terms like this. S^(t) is "the share of tasks still unsolved after attempt t". Censoring means "the experiment ended and we do not know what came after". Whether a task unsolved within 12 attempts would have been solved on the 13th cannot be known. The hazard is "the share of still-unsolved tasks that get solved on the next attempt". Two things stand out.

First, the attempts are not independent. If every attempt were independent with the same probability p, solving 130/134 within 12 attempts would need only p≈0.254. The first-attempt point in Figure 3(a) is well above that, yet the ReAct-alone curve flattens early. In survival-analysis terms this is frailty. Mixed in are environments the baseline almost never solves, and once the easy environments drop out, the hazard of the remaining group falls to nearly 0. What Reflexion changed is the hazard of that remaining group.

Second, this metric is closer to pass@k than to pass@1. The environment decides success (the completion signal in ALFWorld, EM against the right answer in HotpotQA). As with pass@k in Chapter 17, it means "at least once in k tries". The Wilson 95% confidence interval for 130/134 is a narrow [92.6%, 98.8%]. The question to ask is what it is a confidence interval of.

HotpotQA, 100 questions. For CoT (GT)'s 61% and Reflexion's 75% (61 + 14), the Wilson intervals [51.2, 70.0] and [65.7, 82.5] overlap, and Fisher's exact test treating them as independent samples gives p≈0.048. But they are the same 100 questions, and by the paper's setup the first attempt is the same and the baseline solved nothing more on retry. Then the discordant pairs are 14 to 0, and the exact McNemar p=2×0.514≈1.2×10−4. Whether you use the paired structure turns a borderline difference into a solid one. This calculation rests on the assumption that "the first attempt is the same". The paper gives no per-question results.

HumanEval 91.0. The paper does not give the number of problems. According to AI Agents That Matter (Kapoor et al. 2024, Chapter 18 of this book), 3 of the 164 HumanEval problems have no example tests, so Reflexion was evaluated on 161. Yet 146/161 = 90.68%, 147/161 = 91.30%, 149/164 = 90.85% and 150/164 = 91.46%: with neither denominator does a whole number of problems give 91.0. The paper does not say whether it is an average over several runs. Taking 161 problems and comparing with 80.1 as independent proportions, the standard error of the difference is about 3.9 percentage points and z≈2.8. Kapoor et al. reproduced Reflexion (GPT-4) five times on all 164 problems and got 87.8% on average (86.0–90.9%), while a GPT-4 baseline with no agent structure scored 89.6% (Tables A1 and A7; this was the April 2024 gpt-4-turbo, so the model differs from the original paper's GPT-4). The 80.1 in Table 1 is not a baseline measured at the same time on the same problems. Kapoor et al. conclude: "the question of whether debugging, reflection, and other such 'System 2' approaches [22] are useful for code generation remains open".

Exercise 1 — recalculating F1AP. (a) Compare EFEC and RARR on QReCC with F2=5AP/(4P+A), which weights attribution more (A is AIS after revision, P combined preservation). (b) In Table 2, the F1AP of "no agreement model" on SQA is 60.0, the same as full RARR. What changed underneath, and compared with the run-to-run standard deviations in Appendix A (auto-AIS 1.2, Lev preservation 0.5), which change is larger than the noise?

SolutionSolution

(a) EFEC (A=48.7, P=23.7) gets F2≈40.2 and RARR (A=28.3, P=78.1) gets F2≈32.4. At β=1 RARR (41.5) is ahead, but at β=2 the order flips. "β=2" is often described as "weighting attribution twice as much", but since 1/F2=45·1A+15·1P, the weights inside the harmonic mean are 4 to 1 for attribution over preservation. If you want weights of 2 to 1, use 3AP/(2P+A), that is, β=2. On NQ and SQA, RARR stays ahead even at β=2 (48.0 against 27.9, 36.0 against 14.7). The conclusion "Only RARR has a robust F1AP across all tasks" rests on the choice to weigh the two axes equally. The paper's Limitations section also concedes that the weights may differ by application.

(b) auto-AIS rose by 1.8 percentage points, from 45.1 to 46.9, and Lev preservation fell by 6.5 percentage points, from 89.9 to 83.4, and the two canceled out in the harmonic mean. The drop in preservation is 13 times its standard deviation; the rise in attribution is 1.5 times. The standard deviations in Appendix A were measured on NQ. Assuming the run-to-run variation on SQA is about the same, the change clearly larger than the noise is that "the original got more damaged". If that assumption is wrong, the conclusion could change too.

Takeaway. Two systems with the same summary metric are not the same system. They may sit at different places on the same contour.

Exercise 2 — conclusions from small samples. (a) In Table 3's 50 Rust problems, how many problems are 0.68, 0.60 and 0.52? In the most favorable case, where Reflexion solved every problem the base solved, what is the exact McNemar p for 0.68 against 0.60? (b) What are the Wilson intervals for 15.0% and 7.5% on the 40 LeetcodeHard problems? (c) Suppose Reflexion solved 18 more of the 161 HumanEval problems. If "only the base solved it" is c=0,5,10,20, what is the exact McNemar p?

SolutionSolution

(a) 34, 30 and 26 problems. Even in the most favorable case the discordant pairs are 4 to 0, so p=2×0.54=0.125, and the same holds for the difference between "Test generation omission" and the base (4 problems). The Wilson intervals, 68% [54.2, 79.2], 60% [46.2, 72.4] and 52% [38.5, 65.2], overlap widely. The conclusion that "blind trial and error debugging techniques without self-reflection are ineffective on harder tasks" can be read as hard to support with this one table.

(b) 6 problems and 3. 15.0% [7.1, 29.1] and 7.5% [2.6, 19.9], and even the most favorable paired comparison (3 to 0) gives p=0.25. "Twice GPT-4" is a difference of 3 problems.

(c) p≈7.6×10−6 for c=0, 0.0009 for c=5, 0.005 for c=10 and 0.025 for c=20. With the same net difference, the evidence weakens the more the two get different problems wrong. The paper does not give this number. Nor does it give the source of the 80.1 baseline (Table 1 cites none, and from Table 2's "Base 0.80" and §4.3's "82% and 80%" it reads as a value the authors ran themselves) or per-problem results, so a paired comparison is not possible.

Takeaway. Look for the number of items and the paired structure before the percentages. The big numbers (130/134, 91.0) come from large samples or large differences, but the ablations that carry the conclusions have samples of 50 and 40.

10. Limitations the papers state

RARR (§8 Limitations, §9 Ethics statement).

  • Task definition. Attribution and preservation need not always weigh the same. Self-evident sentences such as "I agree". are penalized too, and how to handle the scope of a claim ("Frozen is a scary movie" against "I got scared watching Frozen") or implicature remains open. An input that is wrong from the start can only be fixed with large changes, which the current metrics penalize heavily.
  • Model. It cannot handle poetry or long documents. It tends to leave unattributed claims in place rather than delete them, and some of those are hallucinations that should be deleted. It is computationally expensive.
  • Ethics. A partially attributed revision should mark the parts that are not attributed. It does not address whether a source is trustworthy (though retrieval can be limited to a corpus the user specifies). It adopts a "permissive" definition under which content counts as attributed if any source supports it.

Reflexion (§1, §5 Limitations, §6 Broader impact, §8 Reproducibility, Appendix B.1).

  • Optimization and memory. Policy optimization done in natural language can also get stuck in local minima. Memory was limited to a sliding window, and the paper names vector embedding databases or SQL databases as future work. §1 concedes that it relies on the ability to self-evaluate (or on heuristics) and has no formal guarantee of success.
  • Limits of test-driven development. Input-output behavior is hard to specify for non-deterministic functions, functions that interact with external APIs, functions whose output varies with the hardware, and parallel or concurrent execution.
  • WebShop (Appendix B.1). With no improvement after four attempts on 100 environments, the experiment was stopped, and the reflections were not useful either. The conclusion is that it cannot solve tasks that need diverse exploration. The caption of Figure 6 says "ReAct + Reflexion fails to significantly outperform ReAct." but gives no test.
  • Impact and reproducibility. The risk of misuse grows with autonomy. On the other hand, the paper sees interpretability improving, since the reflections can be monitored to check intent before a tool is used. It recommends running generated code in an isolated environment.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

This chapter has no designated side papers. Instead it sets the work the two papers compare with directly or cite as prior work against other chapters of this book.

EFEC and LaMDA Research (Thorne and Vlachos 2021 · Thoppilan et al. 2022). RARR's two baselines. EFEC is an evidence-based factual error corrector fine-tuned on Wikipedia sentences; LaMDA is a dialog model trained on human annotations to rewrite its responses with search results. Both were trained on specific data, and neither has a goal of preserving the original text. RARR attaches to any model's output through prompting, takes evidence one piece at a time and has a gate, the agreement model.

AIS — measuring attribution (Rashkin et al. 2021). The source of RARR's attribution metric. How RARR moved it to the sentence level and approximated it with auto-AIS was covered in section 1 of "The paper in detail". The key difference is what is evaluated. RARR measures rewritten text, so attribution alone is not enough, and it added a second axis, preservation (§2.3).

Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023 · the evaluator-optimizer of Chapter 1 of this book). The first prior work Reflexion §2 cites. The same model repeatedly evaluates and fixes its own output. Reflexion judges that Self-Refine is limited to single-generation tasks. The revised AR survey separates the two by what remains. Self-Refine fixes the trace and keeps nothing (z); Reflexion writes its critique into notes that last across episodes (S). Self-Refine is the closest form to the evaluator-optimizer pattern of Chapter 1.

ReAct (Yao et al. 2023 · Chapter 6 of this book). Reflexion's actor; the ALFWorld environments and the example trajectories also come from here. ReAct fixes the next action within one episode by looking at observations; Reflexion fixes the next attempt after an episode ends. Since the largest failure mode in ReAct's HotpotQA failure sample (reasoning errors) included loops repeating the same action (ReAct Table 2 — not the analysis of ALFWorld, where the repetition-detection rule is used), Reflexion's repetition-detection rule can be read as a device that breaks that loop from outside (this book's reading).

Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2024 · Chapter 10 of this book). Critiques itself with reflection tokens during generation, within the same output. It learns to judge whether retrieval is needed, whether a passage is relevant and whether a sentence is supported. It differs from RARR in three ways: during generation or after it, training the critique into the parameters (the revised AR survey classifies it as θ) or prompting a fixed model, and only its own output or any model's output.

MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023 · Chapter 12 of this book). Reflexion's memory is a flat sliding window of 1 to 3 reflections. MemGPT, like an operating system's virtual memory, separates main context inside the window from external context outside it, and the model moves content with function calls. It can be read as one answer to the better memory structure Reflexion names as future work (this book's reading). Table 9 of the revised AR survey lists MemGPT as S under externally grounded (I-b).

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §2.2 — Eq. 5 and "Verbal Evolution"

Of the three optimization targets in Chapter 2, this chapter's share is the system state S. The survey writes that while foundational agents optimize z within an episode, self-evolving agents optimize the system itself across episodes k=1,…,K.

Sk+1←U(Sk,τk,Fk)(Eq. 5)

Sk is the evolvable system state (explicit memories, tool libraries, code), τk the trajectory and Fk the environmental feedback (rewards, execution errors). By the nature of S, it divides self-evolution into Verbal Evolution (written reflections and guidelines), Procedural Evolution (tool and skill libraries, Voyager) and Structural Evolution (the agent's code and architecture, AlphaEvolve). Reflexion is the example of Verbal Evolution: "Methods like Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) update S by synthesizing error logs into linguistic cues that condition future reasoning policies." The mapping is as follows.

Reflexion paper §3 AR survey, revised version §2.2
Trial t Episode k
The attempt's trajectory τt=[a0,o0,…,ai,oi] Trajectory τk
Evaluator score rt=Me(τt) Environmental feedback Fk
Memory mem (the list of reflections sr0,sr1,…) System state Sk
The Self-Reflection model Msr writes srt and appends it to mem Update operator U
Actor Ma (weights fixed) πreason, πexec (θ fixed)
θ={Ma,mem} in Algorithm 1 Symbol clash. The survey's θ means only the model parameters
Memory cap Ω (1–3) Symbol clash. The survey's Ω is the observation kernel

Putting the memory into θ reads as Reflexion's way of saying "we changed the policy", but in the survey's frame that is exactly why Reflexion goes in the S column rather than θ.

Tables 4 and 6 — the same "reflection", different cells

Table 4 reconciles three classifications within the survey (content, mechanism, temporal scope), and its caption singles out Reflexion: "its critique store persists across trials of one task, which makes it S under the primary cut but intra-test-time under the temporal one." The reflections outlast an attempt, so they are S; but they last only while one task is being solved, so in time they are "intra-test-time". The survey has turned into a classification axis the very place where, in "Building intuition", the reinforcement-learning analogy broke down. Table 6, which collects planning systems, lists Reflexion as Sequential (plan structure), Natural Language (plan representation), None (tool) and S (optimization target), and the last paragraph of §3.1.2 contrasts it with Reflect-then-Plan (which refines only within an episode and keeps nothing, so z): "both are 'reflection', and only one of them accumulates."

§4.1, Figure 5, Table 9 — three regimes of feedback

§4.1 divides feedback into three, and Figure 5 contrasts them in three panels: reflective feedback (the model critiques and fixes itself during reasoning), parametric adaptation (feedback is consolidated into the parameters through training) and validator-driven feedback (it sees only a success or failure signal and retries). The first splits again in two. In I-a, self-reflective, the agent is its own critic ("every signal it uses is generated by the model itself"); in I-b, externally grounded, the signal comes from code execution, tools, the environment, a separate verifier or a store. The survey writes that their failure modes differ. Self-reflection can confidently approve a wrong answer, and external grounding helps only as far as the coverage of whatever supplies the signal.

In Table 9, Reflexion is the first row of I-a: Inference stage, "Self-generated critique", update target "Trajectory + episodic notes", optimization target S. Self-Refine, SelfCheckGPT and ASCoT in the same block are all z, so Reflexion is the only S in I-a. ReAct is the first row of I-b (z).

Set beside the experiments, this classification can be read differently. The model writes the content of the reflections, but the signal that triggers reflection is EM against the right answer in HotpotQA (Reflexion's Figure 1 calls it "Environment Binary Reward"), a heuristic that counts environment responses in ALFWorld, and tests run by an interpreter in programming. By the content of the critique it is I-a; by the source of the signal it straddles I-b. How to reconcile the two descriptions is open. Both failures the survey warns of are present in Reflexion. That 16.3% of the MBPP Python code that passed its own tests was actually wrong is the first; that on WebShop a one-bit signal did not reveal the cause of failure is the second. In addition, the third panel of Figure 5 (retrying without reflection) is both Reflexion's ReAct-alone baseline and the retry baseline of Kapoor et al. Reflexion's key comparison reads as I-a against III (this book's reading).

RARR is not in the survey. The editor searched the full text of the revised version and did not find it. Measured against the definitions, it runs at inference time, its signal comes from outside (web evidence), it fixes the output text and it keeps nothing. In Table 9's terms that is "I-b, z". This is not a classification the survey made, and a mismatch remains: the survey's z is a reasoning trace, while RARR fixes the final output.

Harness survey §8.5 and §12.3 — judging the judge

§8.5 divides judgment into three layers: outcome (was the task achieved?), trajectory (was the path efficient and within the rules?) and evaluator (can the evaluator be trusted?). Of the third layer it writes: "The evaluator should be treated as a component under test, not as an oracle outside the system." RARR checks its automatic metric against human judgment (correlation 0.74, biased toward judging non-attributed sentences as attributed, Appendix B), and Reflexion measures the false-positive rate of its own tests in Table 2. Both tested their evaluators, and in both the direction in which the evaluator errs shaped the results. §12.3 mentions Reflexion directly: "Reflexion showed that agents can learn from their own traces in short-horizon settings (Shinn et al., 2023); extending this idea to long-running, multi-session harnesses remains open." Chapter 12 and Chapter 19 are attempts in that direction.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "Text revised by RARR has been confirmed as fact." What it guarantees is attribution, not correctness. Footnote 2 states it flatly: "attribution does not entail correctness." In Figure 7d it was drawn to a rerun channel's page and changed correct text into wrong text, and the ethics statement says it adopted a permissive definition under which content counts as attributed if any source supports it.

Misreading 2. "Reflexion is reinforcement learning that trains the model." The weights do not change. "Verbal Reinforcement Learning" means turning the reward signal into sentences that go into memory. In Algorithm 1's θ={Ma,mem}, only mem changes, and the revised AR survey also classifies Reflexion as S, not θ (Tables 4, 6 and 9).

Misreading 3. "Reflexion corrects itself without knowing the right answer." It depends on the task. The success signal in HotpotQA is EM against the right answer (§4.2). It is not shown the answer, but the fact that it was wrong is judged against the answer and passed on. Only programming fixes without the answer, and the paper says that implementation is eligible for pass@1 (it does not explicitly say the other tasks are not, and the caption of Appendix Table 5 calls the HotpotQA figures "Pass@1" too).

Misreading 4. "Reflexion's success rate on ALFWorld is 97%." 130/134 is the cumulative share of environments solved at least once over several attempts (the "cumulative proportions" of the Figure 3 caption). If the environment does not report success in deployment, do not expect this number.

Misreading 5. "A higher F1AP means a better reviser." It is one choice, equal weights. Edit nothing and you still get 52.3 on NQ, and weight attribution more with F2 and EFEC overtakes RARR on QReCC (section 9).

Misreading 6. "The agreement model is a component that only adds cost." Remove it and Lev preservation falls by 6.5 to 8.2 percentage points on all three tasks (Table 2), and edits happen even on evidence that does not disagree, as in Figure 8.

Misreading 7. "Adding reflection improves any task." The paper has three counterexamples of its own: WebShop (Appendix B.1), the small model starchat-beta (Appendix Table 4), and reflection without unit tests (Table 3, 0.52 against 0.60). The signal has to be reliable, the model strong enough to turn reflections into actions, and the search space not too wide. Grouping the paper's cases into these three conditions is the editor's doing.

Discussion questions

  1. Fix the sentence or fix the next attempt? RARR fixes output that has gone out and learns nothing. Reflexion throws away the output and learns for the next attempt. When an error happens in your work, which do you do (correcting a report, or writing an incident postmortem)? If you used both in one system, what would you put where? (This connects to Chapter 12.)

  2. Who tests the evaluator? Chapter 1 said the evaluator-optimizer pattern fits when the evaluation criteria are clear. Yet 16.3% of the MBPP Python code that passed Reflexion's own tests was actually wrong, and RARR's automatic metric correlated 0.74 with human judgment. How would you test the evaluator itself in your loop?

  3. Attribution against preservation — in what ratio? If you revised a draft contract, a medical information leaflet, marketing copy and customer-service answers with RARR, what would you set β in Fβ to for each? Who should make that choice? (We return to this in Chapter 18.)

Chapter 12 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 12. Memory — MemGPT

The question this chapter answers: when the context window is fixed, who decides what stays and what goes out, and how?

Core reading. Charles Packer et al., "MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems", arXiv preprint (v1 2023-10-12; this chapter read v2, 2024-02-12). 8 pages of main text, 13 with the references and appendix.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · Project page · Code (the successor project, Letta)

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §2.2 (assumption A1), §4.2, Figure 6, Table 10 · Harness survey §5.4–5.5

One-paragraph summary. A language model with a fixed context window is given a memory hierarchy modeled on an operating system's virtual memory. The prompt (main context) is divided into read-only system instructions, a working context that the model rewrites only through function calls, and a FIFO queue where messages pile up in order. Outside the window (external context) sit recall storage, which keeps every message, and archival storage, which holds arbitrary text. As the window fills, a "memory pressure" warning goes in; when it overflows, the front of the queue is evicted and a recursive summary is rewritten. What to keep and what to bring back is decided by the model through function calls. On a task that asks about details of past sessions in a multi-session chat (DMR), accuracy rose from 32.1% to 92.5% with GPT-4, and on nested key–value retrieval only MemGPT with GPT-4 held its performance as the nesting got deeper. Sample sizes are given only for document QA (50 questions) and nested key–value retrieval (30 orderings).
