Building intuition

Three scenes: writing, retrieving and revising memory

Figures 1, 2 and 4 are scenes from a conversation tied together by the name James. The emoji in the original figures (three of them) are left out, and the speaker labels, dates and figure numbers are the editor's layout; the utterances and function calls follow the figures.

[February 7]                                              (Figure 1)
Agent:  How was your day today?
User:   fun my bf james baked me a birthday cake
Agent:  Oh wow, happy birthday!
System Alert: Memory Pressure
        working_context.append("Birthday is February 7")
        working_context.append("Boyfriend named James")

[February 7]                                              (Figure 2)
Agent:  Did you do anything else to celebrate your birthday?
User:   yeah we went to six flags!
        recall_storage.search("six flags")
        Showing 3 of 3 results (page 1/1):
          [01/24/2024] "lol yeah six flags",
          [01/14/2024] "i love six flags been like 100 times",
          [10/12/2023] "james and I actually first met at six flags"
Agent:  Did you go with James? It's so cute how both met there!

[February 14]                                             (Figure 4)
Agent:  How's James doing? Any special plans today?
User:   actually james and i broke up
        working_context.replace("Boyfriend named James",
                                "Ex-boyfriend named James")
Agent:  Sorry to hear that - hope you're OK

The conversations in Figures 1, 2 and 4 of the MemGPT paper, read by enlarging the PDF figures. In the figures, MemGPT is on the left and the user on the right.

The three scenes show three verbs of memory. Figure 1 is writing. Right after a "memory pressure" warning comes in, the model writes the birthday and the boyfriend's name into working context. Figure 2 is retrieving. Six Flags is not in the window, so the model searches recall storage, finds a conversation from about four months earlier ("james and I actually first met at six flags") and weaves it into its reply. Figure 4 is revising. When the relationship changes, it overwrites one line of working context. In all three scenes the model is the one handling memory, and its means is the function call.

The paper's own bridge — virtual memory and paging

This analogy is the backbone of the paper. The abstract says it draws inspiration from "hierarchical memory systems in traditional operating systems which provide the illusion of an extended virtual memory via paging between physical memory and disk", and the title itself casts LLMs as operating systems. The pairs the paper itself draws in §1 and §2 are these.

Operating system MemGPT
Main (physical) memory Main context — the prompt tokens (§2)
Disk External context — recall and archival storage (§2)
Paging overflow data out, retrieving it back via a page fault Moving less important data out of the window; searching for data not in the window and bringing it in (§1)
"an illusion of there being more memory resources than are actually available" "the illusion of an infinite context" (§1)
Interrupts and scheduled jobs User messages, system alerts and scheduled events wake up inference (§2.4, §5)

There is one place where the analogy breaks down, and this chapter keeps coming back to it. An operating system's paging is invisible to applications. When an address is accessed, the hardware detects the page fault and the operating system fetches the page. MemGPT has no such automatic detection, so the model has to notice by itself that "what I need is not in the window now" and search for it. That it often stopped paging through search results before reaching the end in document QA (§3.2.1 — the paper reports only the behavior, not its cause) can be read as related to this difference (the editor's reading).

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

For a database administrator, a buffer pool is closer. Only the disk pages that are needed come up into a fixed-size pool; when the pool fills, a replacement policy picks the pages to evict; and every change is first written to a log (WAL). Then the FIFO queue is a buffer with the simplest replacement policy, recall storage is a log that records everything, and working context is pinned pages. The memory pressure warning resembles the step that writes out modified pages before eviction, except that the model judges what to keep.

The analogy breaks down in two places. A buffer pool is transparent to queries, but in MemGPT the model makes caching decisions directly through function calls. The cache-aside pattern, in which application code reads and writes the cache directly, is closer. And a database does not make summaries of the pages it evicts. No database component corresponds to the lossy compression of a recursive summary, and what it loses is taken up again, in the language of statistics, in "Back to the surveys".

The paper in detail

1. The problem — the window is fixed, and a bigger one does not get fully used (§1, Table 1)

The paper sets up the problem along two lines. On cost: because of self-attention, lengthening the context makes computation time and memory grow with the square of the length. On benefit: beyond the computational problem, there is research (Liu et al. 2023a, that is, Lost in the Middle in Chapter 9) showing that long-context models do not make good use of the added context. So instead of enlarging the window, the paper looks for a way to give the illusion of infinite context while keeping the fixed window.

Table 1 (collected January 2024) shows each model's window size and a rough count of how many messages fit in that window (assuming a preprompt of 1k tokens and about 50 tokens per message). Llama (1) has 2k tokens and 20 messages, GPT-4 at release 8k and 140, GPT-4 Turbo 128k and about 2,600. For a reader in 2026 the numbers are dated, but the question is not. However large the window, if it is finite, someone has to decide "what goes in the window".

2. The memory hierarchy — main and external context (§2, §2.1, Figure 3)

MemGPT divides memory in two. Main context is the LLM's prompt tokens, which the model can see during inference. External context is all information outside the fixed window, and it must always be explicitly moved into main context to reach the model (§2).

MemGPT's memory hierarchy. Inside the dashed line at the top is the fixed-size window (the original figure groups the prompt tokens and the output together), and the three parts other than the output are main context. The two ends at the bottom are external context. The diagram carries over the composition of Figure 3 of the paper and each part's read and write permissions, and follows the original figure's layout. The editor drew the diagram.

Main context is three contiguous sections (§2.1). Together with the two external stores, they are as follows.

Section Who writes it What it holds
System instructions No one (read-only) Control flow, the purpose of each memory tier, how to use the functions
Working context The model, only through function calls Fixed-size unstructured text. In conversation, key facts and preferences about the user and the agent's persona
FIFO queue The queue manager User and agent messages, system messages (memory warnings and the like), function inputs and outputs. The first slot holds a recursive summary of the evicted messages
Recall storage (external) The queue manager (reads through functions) A message database. Every incoming message and every model output
Archival storage (external) The model, through function calls A read/write database storing arbitrary-length text objects

Sections 2.1–2.2 and Figure 3 of the paper, arranged as a table.

The two external stores are different in kind. Recall storage is the record of the conversation, in which the queue manager writes down every message; archival storage is a drawer where the model keeps things aside (in the document-analysis experiments a whole collection of Wikipedia documents was loaded into it). The paper's answer to this chapter's question is already in this table. The system keeps the full record by rule, and the model chooses which parts of it to keep in the window and which to put aside.

3. The queue manager — memory pressure and flushing the queue (§2.2)

The queue manager appends new messages to the FIFO queue, concatenates the prompt tokens to trigger inference, and writes every incoming message and every generated output to recall storage. Messages brought back from recall storage through a function call are appended to the back of the queue.

The queue eviction policy that prevents overflow is also the queue manager's job, and it has two thresholds. When the prompt tokens exceed the "warning token count" (e.g. 70% of the context window), the queue manager inserts a system message into the queue warning of an impending eviction (a "memory pressure" warning). Seeing this warning, the model can move important information in the queue to working context or archival storage. When they exceed the "flush token count" (e.g. 100% of the context window), the queue is flushed. A specific count of messages is evicted from the front (the paper gives the example of that count as "e.g. 50% of the context window", a ratio of token capacity; it reads as enough messages to free about half the window), and a new recursive summary is made from the existing recursive summary and the evicted messages. The evicted messages leave the context but remain in recall storage indefinitely and can be read through function calls. All the percentages are values the paper gives "e.g."

If E(j) is the batch of messages evicted at the j-th flush and s(j−1) the summary up to that point, the recursive summary is

s(j)=Summ(s(j−1),E(j))

The formula is the editor's rendering of the paper's description; the main text does not say which prompt or which model does the summarizing. Readers used to statistics will see the form of a recursive update. Unlike the Kalman filter under a linear Gaussian model, though, a language summary carries no guarantee that information from past data is not lost. The only way to recover a detail dropped from the summary is to search recall storage.

So the answer to "who decides" splits in two. When to evict, and what (from the front of the queue), is decided by the queue manager by rule. What to save before eviction, and what to bring back later, is decided by the model.

4. The function executor and control flow (§2.3–2.4)

Function executor. Data moves between the two contexts through function calls the model generates, and the paper writes that memory edits and retrieval are "entirely self-directed". To make this work, the system instructions include a description of the memory hierarchy and the purpose of each tier, along with the function schemas (with natural-language descriptions). MemGPT parses the output string the model produces, executes the call if the arguments are valid, and returns the result to the model, including runtime errors (for example, trying to add more to a main context that is already full). The paper writes that this feedback lets the system "learn from its actions", but that means the results go into the next prompt, not that the weights are updated. Search results come back page by page (pagination) so the window does not overflow.

Functions that appear in the paper. Neither the main text nor the appendix gives the full list of functions. Collecting the calls that appear in the figures gives the following.

Call Where it appears What it does
working_context.append(text) Figure 1 Adds a line to working context
working_context.replace(old, new) Figure 4 Replaces a line in working context
recall_storage.search(query) Figure 2 Searches recall storage (past messages)
archival_storage.search(query, page=n) Figures 6 and 8 Searches archival storage and turns pages

Taken from the rendered figures. The paper defers the exact function names and the full prompts to the project page (Appendix 6.1).

The prompts in the appendix use names different from the main text ("core memory", conversation_search, "archival memory"). They read as corresponding to working context, recall storage search and archival storage in the main text (the editor's reading). The name "core memory", common today, does not appear in the main text of the paper.

Control flow — events and function chaining (§2.4). Inference is woken by events: user messages, system messages (capacity warnings and the like), user interactions (a login, a finished document upload and so on), and scheduled events that run on a set schedule. The last kind lets it run without the user saying anything. When functions need to be called in succession, as when paging through several pages of search results, it uses function chaining. According to the text of §2.4, if the model includes request_heartbeat=true in its output, inference runs again as soon as the function finishes, and without this flag (a yield) it waits until the next external event. The relevant sentence in the text of §2.4 ("MemGPT will add the function output to main context and (as opposed to pausing processor execution)") is missing a verb and has to be filled in from the caption.

In the language of Chapter 6, function chaining turns the thought–action–observation loop toward memory. §4 of the paper also cites ReAct and notes that MemGPT's model can "plan out loud" when executing functions. But ReAct's actions go out to an external environment, while MemGPT's function calls mostly read and write its own memory.

5. Conversational agents — consistency and engagement (§3.1)

What is measured. Two properties needed by a long-term companion or assistant: consistency, meaning that new facts, preferences and events do not contradict what was said before (the DMR task), and engagement, meaning that it draws on long-term knowledge about the user to tailor its replies (the conversation-opener task). The data is Multi-Session Chat (MSC, Xu et al. 2021), conversations written by human annotators who each play one persona throughout. Each chat has five sessions, and each session has roughly a dozen messages. A new sixth session with a single question–answer pair was created to measure consistency.

DMR — deep memory retrieval (§3.1.1). The user asks a question that explicitly refers back to a past conversation and has a very narrow range of answers. The questions were generated by a separate LLM. The core of the instructions given to that LLM is in Appendix 6.1.3.

Your task is to write a question from user A to user B that test's user B's
memory.
The question should be crafted in a way that user B must have actually
participated in the prior conversation to answer properly, not just have read
the persona summary.
…
Never, ever, ever create questions that can be answered from the persona
information.

An excerpt from the DMR question-generation prompt in Appendix 6.1.3. The spelling (test's) is as in the original.

This prompt forces the questions to ask about details that are only in the conversation record, not in MSC's persona summaries. In the appendix's example, do not ask about the fact that the user likes surfing, which is in the persona, but you may ask that the place they had lunch after surfing was Taco Bell.

Scoring. The generated answers were usually longer than the short gold answers, so ROUGE-L uses recall (R). ROUGE-L measures overlap by the longest common subsequence of the generated and gold answers (a common word sequence that keeps order but may skip words), and recall divides that length by the length of the gold answer. If the gold answer is "Taco Bell" and the generated answer is "We grabbed lunch at Taco Bell", both words of the gold answer appear in order, so R = 1 (the example is the editor's). It looks only at word overlap, so a long answer is not penalized and whether the meaning is right is not checked. Judging meaning is the job of the accuracy column. Accuracy is scored by an LLM judge. The paper cites prior work (Zheng et al. 2023) showing that GPT-4 agrees closely with human raters. One passage of the judge prompt (Appendix 6.1.2) reads as follows.

The generated answer might be much longer, but you should be generous with
your grading - as long as it touches on the same topic as the gold answer, it
should be counted as CORRECT.

An excerpt from the LLM judge prompt in Appendix 6.1.2.

The baseline's conditions. The baseline uses the same LLM without MemGPT and, to mimic the effect of carrying a recursive summary over a long time, sees a lossy summary of the past five conversations. MemGPT has access to the full conversation history but has to bring it in through paginated search. The baseline's preprompt (Appendix 6.1.1) hands over the summary and tells the model to reply only "NO ANSWER" if it lacks the information. The main text does not say who made the baseline's summaries or how, nor whether they are the same as the persona summaries used in question generation. For now, read the two "summaries" as different things.

Model Accuracy ROUGE-L (R)
GPT-3.5 Turbo 38.7% 0.394
+ MemGPT 66.9% 0.629
GPT-4 32.1% 0.296
+ MemGPT 92.5% 0.814
GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% 0.359
+ MemGPT 93.4% 0.827

Table 2 of the paper. The bold was changed by the editor (in the original only the whole GPT-4 Turbo + MemGPT row is bold). Accuracy is the LLM judge's verdict and ROUGE-L is recall. The caption says the questions are about topics discussed in prior conversations (sessions 1–5). The number of questions is given neither in the table nor in the text.

Read the table in this order.

  1. The summary-only baselines score 32 to 39% with all three models. A stronger base model does not raise the score, and among the baselines GPT-3.5 Turbo is actually the highest. This reads as saying that if the answer is not in the summary, a better model cannot get it right. The questions were built to ask about details not in the persona summaries, so the lossy summaries the baselines saw probably missed such details as well. But the paper does not show what was left in the baseline summaries.
  2. With MemGPT, the GPT-4 family goes above 90%. If the original record can be searched, the answer is there.
  3. GPT-3.5 Turbo reaches only 66.9% even with MemGPT. The paper does not explain this gap for DMR. It can be read as the same cause it gives for document QA, GPT-3.5's limited function-calling ability (§3.2.1).

The two arms of this comparison are "the same model seeing only a summary" and "the same model able to search the whole original record". So the differences in Table 2 mix the effect of the memory-management policy (warnings, working context, function chaining) with the effect of access to the original record, and there is no simple RAG baseline that retrieves from the conversation record with the same search tool, so the two cannot be separated. This point does not overturn the conclusion. It only sets the scope of the question the table answers.

Conversation openers (§3.1.2). The model is asked to write a first message that opens the conversation using knowledge built up in past conversations. The paper's logic is that MSC's gold persona is a summary of the knowledge built up in the earlier sessions, so an engaging opener ought to draw on persona items. So the opener is compared with the gold persona (SIM-1, SIM-3) and with the human-written gold opener (the first response of the next session) (SIM-H).

Method SIM-1 SIM-3 SIM-H
Human 0.800 0.800 1.000
GPT-3.5 Turbo 0.830 0.812 0.817
GPT-4 0.868 0.843 0.773
GPT-4 Turbo 0.857 0.828 0.767

Table 3 of the paper. The text says this table gives CSIM scores for MemGPT's openers, in variants that change only the base model, so the three lower rows are MemGPT using each model. The Human row's SIM-H of 1.000 is the human-written opener compared with itself.

This table has no baseline row for an opener written by the same model without MemGPT; the only comparison is with humans. Neither the similarity function nor the difference between SIM-1 and SIM-3 is defined in the text (from the names one might guess one persona item and three, but this needs checking against the original). The text calls it "CSIM" and the table "SIM", so even the names differ.

The paper observes that MemGPT's openers are similar to the human ones and sometimes exceed them, and that they are more verbose than the humans' and cover more persona information. Put the two side by side, and exceeding humans on a metric that is easy to raise by listing many items may mean "copied more of the persona" rather than "more engaging". In fact SIM-1 rises from GPT-3.5 Turbo (0.830) to GPT-4 (0.868) while SIM-H falls from 0.817 to 0.773. The paper also says that storing working context is the key to engagement, but there is no ablation that removes it.

6. Document analysis — multi-document QA and nested key–value retrieval (§3.2)

The paper's concern is that legal and financial documents, for example the annual reports of US public companies (SEC Form 10-K), easily exceed a million tokens, and that real analysis has to cut across several such documents.

Multi-document QA (§3.2.1). This is the retriever-reader task of Lost in the Middle. For questions from NaturalQuestions-Open, a retriever picks Wikipedia documents and a reader LLM answers, and accuracy is measured as the number of retrieved documents K grows. The retriever is the same on both sides (cosine similarity on text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings). MemGPT has all the documents loaded into archival storage (PostgreSQL with pgvector) and searches by itself; the baseline is given the top K and, when there are more than the window holds, truncates the documents to fit. Fifty questions were sampled from NaturalQuestions-Open, the document corpus was a late-2018 Wikipedia dump, and an answer counts as correct only if the LLM judge finds both the answer and the text of the supporting document (Appendix 6.1.5). Figure 6 shows MemGPT finding an answer by paging through results with page=2.

The results are the curves of Figure 5. The paper's description comes down to the following.

  • The fixed-window baselines are roughly capped by the retriever's performance. If the retriever does not surface the gold document, they have no way to see it, and the gold document often appeared outside the first dozen retrieved results. As K grows, documents have to be truncated, the gold snippet drops out and accuracy falls.
  • MemGPT can query archival storage several times and turn pages, so the number of documents it can use is not tied to the window. In the figure MemGPT is a horizontal line that does not vary with K. Since it has no K condition, the line reads as a single measured value drawn across (the editor's reading). MemGPT with GPT-4 and with GPT-4 Turbo gave the same result (caption).
  • But MemGPT often stopped paging before going through the whole database, and MemGPT with GPT-3.5 dropped sharply because of limited function-calling ability.

The caption sums up: "MemGPT's performance is unaffected by increased context length." Values read off the gridlines are not reproduced, and the paper gives no table of numbers either. From the shape of the lines, there are stretches where the GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-4 baselines come close to MemGPT's horizontal line (GPT-4 peaks near K = 10 and then falls, while the text says it "continues to improve"), so "you do not need to choose K" may be a more accurate summary of this figure than "it is always much better".

Nested key–value retrieval (§3.2.2). The synthetic key–value task of Lost in the Middle (keys and values are both 128-bit UUIDs) is modified so that a value can itself be a key. It is a task that requires several hops (multi-hop). The number of UUID pairs is fixed at 140, which is about 8k tokens, the window length of the GPT-4 baseline. The nesting level varies from 0 (the first value is not a key) to 4 ("4 total KV lookups are required to find the final value"), and 30 different orderings of the positions of the first key and the nested keys were sampled.

System Alert: Archive Storage Upload Complete
User:   Find the value for key 831…ea5
        archival_storage.search("831...ea5")
        Showing 1 of 1 results (page 1/1):  "Key: 831…ea5, Value: 5b8…4c3"
        archival_storage.search("5b8...4c3")
        Showing 2 of 2 results (page 1/1):  "Key: 5b8…4c3, Value: f37…617",
                                             "Key: 831…ea5, Value: 5b8…4c3"
        archival_storage.search("f37...617")
        Showing 1 of 1 results (page 1/1):  "Key: 5b8…4c3, Value: f37…617"
Agent:  f37…617

The trajectory in Figure 8 of the paper, taken from the rendered figure. The UUIDs were already shortened in the original figure.

The last search returns only the line that has f37...617 as its value, so it is not a key. So the agent stops and answers. This is the behavior called for by the instruction in Appendix 6.1.6: "DO NOT STOP SEARCHING UNTIL YOU VERIFY THAT THE VALUE IS NOT A KEY."

The results (Figure 7 and the text) are these. GPT-3.5 drops to 0% accuracy at nesting level 1 right away (its main failure is returning the first value as is), and GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo fall in the same way, reaching 0% at level 3. MemGPT with GPT-4 was unaffected by the nesting level. MemGPT with GPT-4 Turbo and with GPT-3.5 did better than the baselines but began to drop at level 2 because they did not perform enough lookups.

In this section the paper does not agree with itself in a few places. They are worth pointing out in the presentation.

  1. Range of nesting levels. The text says the level was varied from 0 to 4, but the horizontal axis of Figure 7 runs from 0 to 3. There are no results for level 4.
  2. How levels are counted. If level 0 is one lookup, level n is n+1 lookups, but the text describes level 4 as "4 total KV lookups". The caption of Figure 8 calls 831→5b8→f37 "two nesting levels", but by the definition of level 0 it is level 1.
  3. Where the key–value pairs are. The text says MemGPT with GPT-4 succeeds "by accessing the key-value pairs stored in main context repeatedly via function queries", but in Figure 8 the pairs are in archival storage.
  4. Text and figure. The text says MemGPT with GPT-3.5 begins to drop at level 2, but in Figure 7 that line has already fallen sharply at level 1 (read from the shape of the line, not from gridline values).

7. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

Sample sizes. Of the four experiments, sample sizes are printed only for multi-document QA (50 questions) and nested key–value retrieval ("30 different ordering configurations" — whether per level is not stated). DMR (Table 2) and conversation openers (Table 3) give no number of questions, no number of repeated runs and no standard errors.

Table 2 — narrowing the denominator from the numbers. If accuracy is "number correct ÷ number of questions", then with n questions the only possible values are of the form k/n. Checking whether all six values, printed to one decimal place, could come from the same n, the smallest such n is 411, and round numbers like 100, 200 or 500 do not work (Exercise 1). If the six values are results of running the same question set once each, there are at least 411 questions; if not, they are averages over several runs or the denominator differed by model (for example, questions dropped for format errors). The paper does not say which.

Taking n=411 and treating the two groups as independent (if right and wrong answers on the same question are positively correlated across the two conditions, this calculation errs on the conservative side; see Chapter 7, section 6), the standard error of the difference is about 3.3 percentage points for the GPT-3.5 Turbo pair, about 2.6 for the GPT-4 pair and about 2.7 for the GPT-4 Turbo pair, and the differences are 8.4, 22.8 and 21.9 times those. These are not differences chance can explain. What to ask of Table 2 is not "is it significant?" but the design questions of the previous section. What could the baseline see, how lenient was the judge, and what were the questions built to target?

Multi-document QA — the resolution of 50 questions. Near an accuracy of 0.5, the standard error with 50 questions is 0.5×0.5/50≈0.071, and the Wilson 95% interval for 25/50 is [0.37, 0.63]. The half-width at a single point is 0.13, so two independent curves that are less than about 0.2 apart at a point are hard to tell apart from that point alone. Since the same 50 questions are used in every condition, this is a paired design, and per-question results would allow a sharper look.

Table 3 has no number of questions, no spread and no baseline, so there is nothing to calculate.

Exercise 1 — the hidden denominator of Table 2. (a) Find the smallest n for which all six accuracies are values of k/n for the same n, rounded to one decimal place. Why do n=100,200,500 not work? (b) With n=411, find the Wilson 95% confidence intervals for the GPT-3.5 Turbo baseline and for MemGPT. (c) This is a paired comparison on the same questions, but there are no per-question results. How far does the p value of the McNemar test move depending on the number of discordant pairs? Would the conclusion have wavered if there had been only 50 questions?

SolutionSolution

(a) Going up from n=10 and checking, for each value p, whether there is an integer k with |100k/n−p|≤0.05, the first n is 411. The numbers correct are 159, 275, 132, 380, 145 and 384 (for example, 159/411 = 38.69%). With n=100 only whole percentages come out; with n=200 the spacing is 0.5 percentage points, so only 92.5% fits; with n=500 the spacing is 0.2 percentage points, so only 93.4% fits (38.7% falls between 193/500 = 38.6% and 194/500 = 38.8% and cannot come out).

(b) The Wilson interval for 159/411 is [34.1%, 43.5%] and for 275/411 [62.2%, 71.3%]. The two intervals are far apart.

(c) Let b be "only MemGPT correct" and c "only the baseline correct"; then b−c≈0.282n. The p value is smallest when c=0 and largest when c is at its maximum possible value (n×min(0.387,1−0.669)≈0.331n). Calculated with the exact binomial test, p<0.01 in every case at n=411 or n=100, but at n=50 the p value would move from about 0.0001 to 0.06. The more the two methods get different questions right, the less clearly they may separate. For the GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo pairs (around 60 percentage points), p<0.001 in every case even at n=30.

Takeaway. Even when a table gives no number of questions, the printed digits carry information about the denominator. And in a paired design without per-question results, a p value can be stated only as a range, not as a single number.

Exercise 2 — can 30 orderings support "unaffected"? (a) What is the 95% confidence interval (Clopper–Pearson) for the true accuracy when 30 of 30 are correct? When 0 are? (b) Suppose MemGPT with GPT-4 gets 30/30 at level 0 and has true accuracy q at level 3. What is the power of Fisher's exact test at q=0.9,0.8,0.7? (c) Design a test of the multi-document QA curves (Figure 5) that makes use of the fact that the same 50 questions are used across K values and methods.

SolutionSolution

(a) The Clopper–Pearson 95% interval for 30/30 is [0.884, 1] (the lower bound is 0.0251/30). For 0/30 it is [0, 0.116], and the "rule of three" approximates the upper bound as 3/30=0.10. Even with all 30 correct, a true accuracy around 88% cannot be ruled out.

(b) Approximated with 4,000 Monte Carlo runs, the power is about 0.07 at q=0.9, about 0.57 at q=0.8 and about 0.92 at q=0.7. Even if the true accuracy has fallen to 90%, the test almost never catches it. The word "unaffected" is more accurately read as "no drop was observed over 30 orderings". Conversely, the baselines' change from near 1.0 down to 0 is large enough to see with 30. The text does not say whether the 30 orderings were the same for every method (whether the design is paired).

(c) One design. Let YqK∈{0,1} record whether question q was answered correctly under condition K. These are repeated measures on the same question, so in a mixed logistic regression with the question as a random intercept, logitP(YqK=1)=αq+f(K), let f be a quadratic in logK and test whether the quadratic term is negative. This tests curvature only. To say "it rises and then falls within the range of K tested", you also have to check that the estimated peak lies within that range and the signs of the slopes on either side of it (for differences between conditions themselves, the nonparametric Cochran Q test). Compare MemGPT and the baseline with McNemar tests on the same question pairs at each K, and correct for multiple comparisons. Fifty questions are few. Estimating with the McNemar approximation the number of questions needed to detect a 10-percentage-point difference at significance level 0.05 and power 0.8 gives about 76 when 10% of pairs are discordant, about 155 at 20% and about 312 at 40%. Even this design cannot answer the effect of the retriever. Only by recording the retrieval rank of the gold document for each question can you directly test the explanation that "the baseline is capped by the retriever".

Takeaway. When you see "no difference" or "unaffected", ask about power first. Not seeing a difference in a small sample is not evidence that there is none.

8. Limitations the paper states

There is no separate limitations section. Collecting the statements scattered through the experiments and the conclusion gives the following.

  • Limits of the retriever. Because of embedding-similarity search, document QA is hard for every method, and the gold document often appeared outside the first dozen retrieved results (§3.2.1).
  • It stops paging early. In theory it could find the right answer even with a poor ranking, but in practice it often stopped before going through the whole database (§3.2.1). This can be read as the price of a design in which page faults do not happen automatically.
  • The base model's function-calling ability. MemGPT with GPT-3.5 dropped sharply on document QA and did best with GPT-4 (§3.2.1). On nested key–value retrieval too, MemGPT with GPT-4 Turbo and with GPT-3.5 did not perform enough lookups (§3.2.2). Even with the same architecture, the ability of the model managing memory decides performance.
  • Future work (§5). Applying it to other domains, integrating memory-tier technologies such as databases or caches, and refining the control flow and memory-management policies.

The paper has no ethics statement, and it does not discuss how scenes like Figure 1, which remembers a birthday and a romantic relationship, meet privacy, or what happens when memory is contaminated. An indirect prompt injection paper from the same year (Greshake et al. 2023) demonstrated, in a chat app with a key–value store attached as long-term memory, an attack injected in one session that was stored in memory and reinfected a new session (Figure 8, "Persistence"). A reading is possible in which a memory the model writes and reads by itself is also a long-lived attack surface (Chapter 15).

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

Generative Agents (Park et al. 2023). A social simulation that releases 25 agents into a town resembling The Sims (UIST '23). Experience accumulates in the memory stream, a list of natural-language records. The retrieval score is a weighted sum of three components (§4.1). Recency is an exponential decay over the game hours since the memory was last retrieved (decay factor 0.995); importance is a score from 1 to 10 assigned by the LLM when the record is created; relevance is the cosine similarity between the embeddings of the query and the record. The three are min–max scaled to [0,1] and added as score=αrec·recency+αimp·importance+αrel·relevance, with all the α set to 1 in the implementation. When the summed importance of recent events exceeds 150, a reflection is made (two or three times a day), and reflections also go into the memory stream and become material for further reflection (§4.2). Where it parts from MemGPT is who decides. Here a fixed scoring function decides what goes into the window at every action; in MemGPT the model decides whether to search and with what. Generative Agents §4.1 chooses retrieval over summarization on the grounds that summarizing all experience makes the responses bland. The evaluation applied TrueSkill and the Kruskal–Wallis test to ranking data from 100 evaluators. TrueSkill is a rating method that extends chess's Elo rating to contests among many players; from ranking results it estimates each condition's latent skill as a normal distribution N(μ,σ2). The μ below is the mean of that estimated distribution, not an average accuracy or score (§6.5; the full architecture's μ=29.89 against μ=21.21 for the condition with memory, planning and reflection all removed, H(4)=150.29, p<0.001). This contrasts with MemGPT, which reports no tests.

A bridge from the editor — the retrieval score and exponential smoothing

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

Recency 0.995Δt has the same form as the weights in exponential smoothing (EWMA), and its half-life is ln0.5/ln0.995≈138 game hours (about 5.8 days) (the editor's calculation). Because Δt is measured from the last retrieval, a memory that is taken out often does not age. This is the same principle as LRU in a buffer pool. And because the reference for min–max scaling is the candidate set at that moment, even with all the weights at 1 the actual influence of each component is set by how widely it is spread among the candidates.

MRAgent (Ji et al. 2026). An ICML 2026 paper whose title is its claim: memory is reconstructed, not retrieved. It distinguishes a passive policy that selects memory units from the query alone, {v(1),…,v(T)}=πp(x), from an active policy that selects the next unit conditioned on the evidence gathered so far, v(t)=πa(t)(x,S(t−1)) (§2.1), and builds memory as a Cue–Tag–Content graph over which the LLM expands and prunes paths (§3–4). The abstract reports improvements of up to 23% over strong baselines on LOCOMO and LongMemEval. MRAgent does not use MemGPT as a baseline, but by its definition MemGPT's function chaining (in Figure 8 it looks at a value and decides the next search term) can also be read as an active policy. Then the difference between the two is the structure of memory: flat text with vector search against a graph that exposes associative paths through tags. MRAgent's S(t) (the evidence gathered) and Z(t) (the active set) mean something different from the AR survey's S and Z.

Voyager (Wang et al. 2023 · Chapter 20 of this book). A lifelong-learning agent that explores Minecraft and builds up skills without human intervention. According to the abstract, it consists of an automatic curriculum, a skill library of executable code, and iterative prompting that feeds in environment feedback, execution errors and self-verification; it queries GPT-4 as a black box and needs no fine-tuning. If MemGPT stores "what happened" (messages, facts), Voyager stores "how to do it" (executable procedures). The idea meets us again in WikiSkill in Chapter 20 (a framework that evolves skills together with a persistent knowledge base).

Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book). The trajectory history is short-term memory and the reflections are long-term memory, with long-term memory capped at a maximum of Ω (usually 1 to 3) (§3). The limitations section suggests extending this sliding window to a vector embedding database or an SQL database. Reflexion's memory is a few lines of lessons used when retrying the same task, cut off by the number of attempts. MemGPT's memory is the whole record of a conversation that never ends, cut off by token pressure, and what is cut still remains outside the window.

RAG (Lewis et al. 2020 · Chapter 8 of this book). A retriever picks the top K documents and a generator marginalizes over them as latent variables. MemGPT §4 says its external memory builds on this line of retrieval-augmented work, and singles out FLARE (Jiang et al. 2023), in which the model decides when and what to retrieve. The fixed-window baseline in document QA is exactly the setup that inserts the top K once. The difference is who takes the initiative. In RAG the system retrieves once in a fixed way; in MemGPT the model decides the search terms, the number of searches and the paging.

Lost in the Middle (Liu et al. 2024 · Chapter 9 of this book). The paper showing that performance is highest when the relevant information is at the beginning or end of the input and drops sharply in the middle. MemGPT uses it as evidence that "enlarging the window alone does not work" and takes two tasks from it (Kevin Lin of UC Berkeley is on the author lists of both papers). Yet MemGPT did not separately measure position effects within its own main context.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version — assumption A1 and memory

In the formalization of Chapter 2, the history is ht=(o≤t,z<t,a<t) and mt∈M is an internal memory state that summarizes the history. §2.2 of the survey states the second of its three assumptions like this.

(A1) Memory sufficiency. πreason(zt∣ht)=πreason(zt∣mt), i.e., mt is a sufficient statistic for ht. This is an assumption made by systems, not a property of the setting. Section 4.2 surveys the mechanisms built to make it approximately hold, and the long-horizon failures discussed there are failures of A1.

Placed in this frame, MemGPT maps as follows.

MemGPT AR survey, revised version §2.2
The whole conversation record (all of it is in recall storage) History ht
Main context (system instructions + working context + FIFO queue) Memory state mt∈M
Recursive summary, working-context edits Updates to mt
Archival storage (outlasts sessions) System state S
Memory function calls These do not go out to the environment, so they are closer to internal operations that modify mt than to external actions at (the editor's interpretation). Messages sent to the user are at

On top of this mapping the editor places one reading. It is not something the MemGPT paper or the survey said.

Working context and the recursive summary can be read as devices that try to approximate a sufficient statistic. A sufficient statistic is a summary that reduces the sample without losing information about the parameter, the way the sample mean alone is enough when estimating the mean of a normal distribution. The recursive summary s(j)=Summ(s(j−1),E(j)) is an attempt to do this in language. But sufficiency holds only once you fix "for what". A sample mean sufficient for the mean is not sufficient for the variance. In a conversation, the "for what" is the questions still to come, and at the time of summarizing those are unknown.

DMR was built to target this weakness. The question-generation prompt forbade questions that can be answered from the persona summary. If the baseline's "lossy summarization of the past five conversations" were the same as that persona summary, A1 would be broken by design, but since the paper does not say how the baseline summaries were made, one cannot go that far. What can be said is this. The questions ask about details that summaries easily drop, and the summary-only baselines stopped at 32 to 39%. MemGPT won not by making a summary that holds A1 better but by keeping open a way back to the original record ht (recall storage search) when the summary falls short. When the search results are appended to the queue, the next memory state mt+1 holds the pieces needed for the present question. The strategy is to build, as needed, "a memory state sufficient for the question now" instead of "a summary sufficient for every future question". In statistical practice, this means keeping the raw data rather than only summary tables, and re-tabulating when a new question arrives.

The survey says that the long-horizon failures discussed in §4.2 are failures of A1, but about the only statement in §4.2 that deals with failures directly is a sentence in §4.2.1 saying that flat stores rely on fixed heuristics and adapt poorly to tasks such as long-term planning.

The cells where MemGPT sits in the tables. The revised version puts MemGPT in three tables and lists its optimization target as S in all three.

Table Cell Description
Table 4 (reconciling the self-evolution vocabularies) Verbal Evolution · Memory (§4.2) · inter-test-time Same row as A-Mem and Reasoning Bank
Table 9 (feedback) I-b externally grounded feedback · Inference stage Feedback source "Retrieved memory", update target "Persistent memory"
Table 10 (memory systems) I. Flat Memory Stores · Inference-time Stored content Text, memory type Factual

The caption of Table 10 treats memory as the paradigm case of S: a store that persists across episodes is system-level even when θ is frozen and every entry is placed in the prompt. Figure 6 likewise divides memory into flat memory stores, structured representations (graph and multimodal) and post-training control, and says that the first two change S and only the third changes θ.

There are also passages in the survey that read differently from the MemGPT paper. §4.2.1 gives "cache-inspired designs like MemGPT" as an example of a passive buffer, alongside dense retrieval and the modules of LangChain and LlamaIndex, and writes that such approaches usually only augment the prompt without affecting internal reasoning. Set against MemGPT's emphasis that memory edits and retrieval are entirely self-directed, it is open whether this classification is by storage structure or also assesses the mode of control. It is worth discussing together with MRAgent among the side papers.

The cells of the side papers. Though they deal with memory, Generative Agents and Voyager are not in Table 10. Generative Agents is not cited in the revised version. Voyager appears in Table 4 (Procedural Evolution — S is a library of executable tools and skills), Table 9 (I-b, update target the skill library, S) and Table 12 (the self-evolution cell for embodied agents, §6.3.2).

Harness survey §5.4–5.5 — the implementation layer

Section 5 of the Harness survey divides memory by time horizon. The short term is the current window, the mid term is session state and persistence across runs, and the long term is stores that outlast sessions.

  • §5.4, the mid term. The simplest technique is a notes file such as NOTES.md, read at the start of each run and updated before the context is cleared. The survey gives the example of Claude playing a Pokémon game for thousands of steps and carrying on through its own notes even after compaction. In externalizing working memory it points the same way as MemGPT's working context, and its limitation is that information only flows forward to the next run and is not retrieved from an indexed store.
  • §5.5, the long term. The first entry is MemGPT as "OS-inspired tiered memory." The survey judges that this paper made explicit the connection between agent memory and operating-system memory that underlies most later long-term memory systems. The second entry is Generative Agents' observation, reflection and retrieval, and Figure 8 places the two side by side in the "Long-Term Persistent Memory Systems" cell.

There are two places to read against the original. The survey writes that, like an operating system, MemGPT gives the illusion of a long context through "transparent memory management", yet the sentence just before says it gives the model function calls to page information in and out explicitly. MemGPT's paging may be transparent to the user, but it is not transparent to the model. And the survey writes that the ablations of Generative Agents showed the contributions of observation, reflection and retrieval each, but the ablation conditions in §6.2 of the original paper remove observation, reflection and planning.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "MemGPT is a technique for enlarging the context window." The window stays as it is. The goal is to give the illusion of infinite context while using a fixed-window model (§1). The paper itself writes that long-context research enlarges the main memory (§4).

Misreading 2. "As in an operating system, the memory you need is brought in automatically." There is no counterpart to a page fault. The model has to decide what to search for, and in document QA it often stopped before paging all the way through the search results (§3.2.1). What is automatic is only the opposite direction: the queue manager's eviction (§2.2).

Misreading 3. "Conversation pushed out of the window survives only as a summary." The original text of evicted messages remains in recall storage indefinitely and can be read through function calls (§2.2). The DMR results come from this access to the original.

Misreading 4. "MemGPT learns as it talks with the user." The weights do not change. In §2.3, "learn from its actions" means that execution results go into the next prompt. The AR survey also lists the optimization target as S, not θ (Tables 4, 9 and 10).

Misreading 5. "Table 2 is evidence that MemGPT beats RAG." DMR's baseline is the same model seeing only a summary, with no retrieval, and there is no RAG baseline that retrieves from the conversation record with the same search tool.

Misreading 6. "In the conversation-opener task, MemGPT wrote more engaging openers than people." Table 3 measures only similarity to the persona and to the human opener; it has no human ratings of engagement, no baseline row and no number of questions. The paper's own observation that the openers are more verbose and cover more of the persona (§3.1.2) may have pushed the similarity up.

Discussion questions

  1. What rules should decide and what the model should decide. In MemGPT, rules (FIFO, thresholds) decide when and what to evict, and the model decides what to put aside and what to bring back. If you attached a memory hierarchy like this to a system at your work, which decisions would you leave to rules and which would you entrust to the model?

  2. Trust the summary, or keep the original? Assumption A1 is the assumption that memory is a sufficient statistic for the history. On what kind of question, months later, does an organization that kept only meeting summaries part ways with one that also kept full transcripts? Weigh the cost of keeping the original and the cost of finding it again against the "knowledge compiled in advance" of Chapter 20.

  3. The risk of memories that last. Look at two axes separately. On retention the two systems are alike. MemGPT keeps every message in recall storage indefinitely, and Generative Agents' memory stream also maintains a record of all experience ("a comprehensive record", §4). On retrieval priority they part ways. Generative Agents lowers the score of memories not taken out for a long time exponentially; MemGPT takes them out only when the model searches. A low priority is not deletion. What benefits and risks does an agent that never forgets bring the user? Think about it alongside the demonstration in which a memory, once contaminated, reinfects the next session (Chapter 15).

Chapter 13 · Core · ★★

Chapter 13. Working Together — MetaGPT

The question this chapter answers: why do errors spread when several agents are chained together, and how does the standard operating procedure (SOP) of a human organization stop them?

Core reading. Sirui Hong et al., "MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework", ICLR 2024. 9 pages of main text, 29 with the appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · ICLR 2024 proceedings · Code

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §2.2, §5.1–5.2, §5.4 · Harness survey §2.1, §6.3

One-paragraph summary. When several language-model agents are set to talk to one another, facts get twisted as the words pass back and forth, and a slip at an early stage becomes the premise of the later ones. The authors call this "cascading hallucinations caused by naively chaining LLMs" and prescribe the standard operating procedures (SOPs) that human companies have refined over a long time. Modeled on a software company, the system has five roles — product manager, architect, project manager, engineer and QA engineer — and each role must hand over documents in a fixed format (requirements document, system design, task list, code). The documents are not exchanged in conversation but published to a shared message pool, and each role subscribes only to the documents it needs. The engineer writes code, then runs unit tests itself and fixes the code. With GPT-4, this setup reached pass@1 of 85.9% on HumanEval and 87.7% on MBPP, and on a software-development task set the authors built themselves it produced more executable code than ChatDev. That comparison, though, rests on 7 tasks, and the role ablation on 2.

Presenter's guide

A 50-minute plan. The 10 minutes after the presentation are for discussion.

20–25 min Executable feedback §3.3, Figure 2 right

45–50 min Back to the surveys: the cell MetaGPT sits in and the confounds the survey points out AR survey, revised version §5.2.1, Table 11, §5.4

Must read. The abstract and §1, all of §3 (3 pages), the dataset and metrics paragraphs of §4.1, Figure 4, Table 1 and Table 3. If you show only one figure, make it Figure 3. On one page it shows which formatted documents the five roles pass along, starting from the one line "Make the 2048 sliding tile number puzzle game". Next, enlarge one message on the left of Figure 2.

Optional reading. Appendix B (a demo of the execution), Table 4 in Appendix C.2 (executability by task), Table 5 (comparison of backends), Table 7 (HumanEval results from five runs of GPT-4), Appendix D (limitations and ethics). If you also present the statistical reanalysis, be sure to look at Table 4 and Table 7. The reanalysis in section 6 starts from them.

What to cut from the presentation. §2, Related Work (the "Side papers" section stands in for it), Appendix A.2 (an introduction to the authors' own platform), the full code in Appendix B, Figures 11 and 12. In Table 9, look only at the average row.

If your group skipped Chapter 1 and Chapter 6. In the first 5 minutes of the presentation, go over prompt chaining and orchestrator-workers from Chapter 1 and ReAct's thought–action–observation loop from Chapter 6. MetaGPT reads fastest as a fixed prompt chain with a ReAct-style agent placed on each link.

When you quote the numbers. The HumanEval and MBPP scores are the values printed above the bars in Figure 4, and the backend is the GPT-4 of 2023. The SoftwareDev comparison (Table 1) uses 7 of the 70 tasks, and the role ablation (Table 3) is an average over 2 tasks. Executability is a score of 1 to 4 assigned by people. When you quote a number, give the number of tasks and the scoring method (automatic or human) with it.

Building intuition

The telephone game — the paper's own analogy

The paper explains the weakness of collaborating in natural language alone with the telephone game ("the telephone game (or Chinese whispers)", §3.2). After a few rounds of passing it on, the original information may be quite distorted. §1 gives an example of the idle chatter exchanged in role-playing frameworks.

"Hi, hello and how are you?" – Alice (Product Manager); "Great! Have you had lunch?" – Bob (Architect).

In the authors' view, chatter like this raises the risk of hallucination. The prescription is the way human companies work: every employee follows a strict and streamlined workflow, and every handover must comply with established standards. In the abstract's words, MetaGPT "encodes Standardized Operating Procedures (SOPs) into prompt sequences for more streamlined workflows, thus allowing agents with human-like domain expertise to verify intermediate results and reduce errors."

Figure 1 — a human team's SOP beside MetaGPT

The diagonal on the left of Figure 1 is a human team's development SOP (Planning → Requirement Analysis → Architectural Design → System Design → Coding → Testing → Acceptance Check). In the middle are MetaGPT's agents. The Product Manager produces the requirement document, the Architect the system design, the Project Manager the tasks and the Engineer the code, and the QA Engineer passes the result to the acceptance check. On the right are the stages from 1/5 Define to 5/5 and two human interventions. At the start a one-line requirement goes in ("Write a classic and simple Flappy Bird game."), and at the end the boss makes the acceptance check and payment ("Pretty good ! I can directly use the interface and keyboard to play Flappy Bird." — the space before the exclamation mark is in the figure). People appear only at the start and the end, and the agents' SOP fills everything in between.

The editor's bridge — the approval chain and publish–subscribe

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

Think of the assignment-of-duties chart in a government office or a company. Each person has set duties and set forms to file, and documents flow in one direction along the approval chain. The drafter writes on the prescribed form, and the reviewer first checks whether the blanks on the form are filled in. Information that would vanish if passed on by word of mouth survives because the form has a box for it. MetaGPT's role profile (name, profile, goal, constraints) corresponds to the chart of duties, the document format for each role to the approval form, and the order of the five roles to the approval chain.

Developers and database administrators can think of publish–subscribe in a message queue instead. A producer does not call each recipient; it publishes a message to a topic, and consumers subscribe only to the topics they care about. Producers and consumers need not know about each other, so there are fewer connections. MetaGPT's shared message pool corresponds to the broker, and subscription by role profile to topic subscription.

The bridge from statistics is multiplication. If there are five stages and each is right with probability 90%, independently, the probability of being right all the way through is 0.95≈0.59 (calculated again in section 6).

The analogies also break down. In a human approval chain, the reviewer sends documents back. MetaGPT's flow mostly runs one way, and the only loop that goes back is the engineer's execution feedback (at most 3 retries). The paper does not explain whether the "Anything Unclear ?" marks in Figure 3 work as a device for asking back to an earlier stage. A message queue guarantees delivery and order, but MetaGPT's subscription is only a device for picking "what is of interest". The multiplication analogy rests on the assumption that stage errors are independent and are not corrected. When the same model plays every role, the errors become correlated, and a later stage sometimes fixes an earlier stage's error.

The paper in detail

1. The problem — what happens when you chain naively (abstract, §1)

The abstract states the problem in one sentence.

Solutions to more complex tasks, however, are complicated through logic inconsistencies due to cascading hallucinations caused by naively chaining LLMs.

The paper does not define or measure this phenomenon. The existence of the problem is presented through the telephone-game analogy and the example of chatter, and the experiments measure the effect of the prescription (the SOP). Section 6 comes back to this point.

The grounds in §1 are the experience of human organizations. SOPs support task decomposition, outline each member's responsibilities and set standards for intermediate outputs. A product manager in a software company writes a Product Requirements Document (PRD) with a standardized structure. What the paper gives as the difference from earlier work (CAMEL, ChatDev) is these structured outputs: MetaGPT requires agents to produce intermediate outputs such as requirements documents, design artifacts, flowcharts and interface specifications.

The name meta-programming. The authors use meta-programming as "programming to program" and distinguish it from meta-learning (§1). The idea is that a group of agents takes a one-line requirement and delivers a program, doing everything from requirement analysis to debugging. It does not change how programming itself is done. The experiments in the main text were run on a fixed SOP.

What it claims as contributions. The three items at the end of §1: a multi-agent framework with role definition and message sharing; the integration of SOPs and a novel executive feedback mechanism (a 5.4% absolute improvement on MBPP); and state-of-the-art performance on HumanEval and MBPP. §1 also says that "MetaGPT achieves a 100% task completion rate" in its experiments, but nowhere in §4 is this "task completion rate" defined, nor is it said what was counted or how.

2. Role specialization and workflow (§3.1, Figures 1 and 3)

Five roles. §3.1 defines five roles in the software company: Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager, Engineer and QA Engineer. Each role gets an agent profile with four fields: name, profile, goal and constraints. A real one is at the top right of Figure 2.

Name        Alex
Profile     Engineer
Goal        Write elegant, readable,extensible, efficient code
Constraint  The code you write should conform to code standard like PEP8,
            be modular,easy to read and maintain

The "Agent Profile" box at the top right of Figure 2 of the MetaGPT paper. The missing spaces after commas are as in the original figure.

Each role is also given its own context and skills. The Product Manager uses a web search tool, and the Architect and Project Manager use a diagram tool (labels attached beside the roles in Figure 2; the tool box at the bottom left holds only the web search, debugging and diagram tools, and the Engineer has no tool label). That the Engineer executes code is stated in the text of §3.1. And all agents follow ReAct-style behavior (§3.1 cites Yao et al. 2022 from Chapter 6). Each agent monitors the environment, that is, the message pool, and when it spots an important observation such as a message from another agent, uses it to trigger an action or to finish the job.

Workflow. The paper says that, following the SOP of software development, all agents work in a sequential manner. The "Action" column is the name written at the top right of each box in Figure 3, and the outputs come from the text of §3.1 and Figure 3.

Order Role Action (Figure 3) Receives Produces
1 Product Manager WritePRD The user's one-line requirement PRD: Product Goals, User Stories, Competitive Analysis and a Competitive Quadrant Chart, Requirement Analysis, Requirement Pool (with priority labels — only P0 in Figure 3, up to P1 in the demo in Appendix B)
2 Architect WriteDesign PRD System design: file list, data structures, interface definitions, program call flow (sequence diagram)
3 Project Manager WriteTasks System design Task List, Shared Knowledge, Logic Analysis (the role of each file)
4 Engineer WriteCode Task list and the earlier documents Code files
5 QA Engineer WriteCodeReview Code Test cases and code quality review

The example in Figure 3 starts from one line put in by a person, "Make the 2048 sliding tile number puzzle game". The Product Manager's box has one line of thought ("Think: The boss requires the creation of 2048 sliding title number puzzzle game." — "title" for "tile" and "puzzzle" are as printed in the figure) along with product goals, user stories, competitive analysis, a quadrant chart and the requirement pool. The Architect thinks "For this project, we will use Pygame, an open-source library designed for making video games with Python." and produces a class diagram, the program call flow and a file list. The Project Manager turns these into a task list and a logic analysis for each file, the Engineer starts writing the Game class in game.py, and the QA Engineer reviews code quality. At the bottom, a person plays the finished game on the keyboard.

Look closely at the figure. The first product goal of the Product Manager is "Create a web-based 2048 game that is easy to play", but the Architect decides to use Pygame, and "web" does not appear again in the Architect's box. Within what the figure shows, the requirement that the game be web-based dropped out at the design stage. The paper does not discuss this, but it can be read as an example that a requirement from an earlier stage can drop out at the next stage even when structured documents are exchanged. The demo in Appendix B is similar. The user input is a GUI app for drawing ("write a python3 GUI app such that you can draw an image with it"), but the "Original Requirements" in the PRD is a color meter that outputs RGB values ("The boss requires a Python3 GUI color meter that outputs the RGB values when it moves."), and the file list in the system design and the Project Manager's task list also differ from each other. Documents from different runs may have been pasted together, but the paper does not explain.

3. Structured communication and publish–subscribe (§3.2, Figure 2 left)

The communication protocol in §3.2 has two parts.

Structured communication interfaces. Most multi-agent frameworks communicate in unconstrained natural language. Citing the telephone game, the paper sets a schema and format for each role and has each role produce its outputs in that format. For the Architect, these are the system interface design and a sequence flow diagram. In the paper's words, "agents in MetaGPT communicate through documents and diagrams (structured outputs) rather than dialogue. These documents contain all necessary information, preventing irrelevant or missing content."

Enlarge one message on the left of Figure 2 and you see five fields.

content:          {Architect: Implementation appro...}
instruct_content: "Data structures and in ..."
cause_by:         WriteTasks
sent_from:        ProjectManager
send_to:          Engineer

The message box inside the "Shared Message Pool" on the left of Figure 2 of the MetaGPT paper. The ellipses are in the original figure. The editor aligned the field names.

From the database side, this is one row of a message table. Because cause_by is an action name, a subscriber can pick messages by "which action produced it" as well as by "who sent it". In the figure, this message names the Engineer in send_to and also goes into the "subscription" box on the Engineer's side. The text does not explain how addressed delivery and subscription are used together.

Publish–subscribe mechanism. The Architect and the Engineer both need to look at the PRD. Passing information one-to-one each time, as earlier work did, complicates the communication topology. So the paper introduces a shared message pool through which all agents exchange messages directly. Agents publish structured messages to the pool and read other agents' messages transparently. There is no need to ask other agents for information and wait for their answers.

Giving all information to everyone leads to information overload. So there is a subscription mechanism. Agents choose the information to follow based on their role profiles, and in the implementation an agent "activates its action only after receiving all its prerequisite dependencies." The Architect mainly looks at the Product Manager's PRD and pays less attention to documents from the QA Engineer.

MetaGPT's communication protocol. Solid lines are publishing, dashed lines subscription. The five roles do not call each other but go through one pool. The editor redrew the diagram from §3.2 and the left of Figure 2. In the original figure, four roles (Architect, Project Manager, Product Manager, QA Engineer) and the Engineer surround the pool.

Count the connections against the case where every role can talk to every other directly (an undirected complete graph): one-to-one connections among N roles come to N(N−1)/2 pairs (10 pairs for five), and going through the pool gives N connections between the roles and the pool. Real conversational setups do not have every pair talking, so this compares maximums, and it counts connections, not the messages that pass along them. The calculation is the editor's; the paper says only that one-to-one communication complicates the communication topology.

4. Executable feedback (§3.3, Figure 2 right)

The paper itself says that the SOP and structured documents were not enough: "Our first MetaGPT implementations overlooked certain errors during the review process, due to LLM hallucinations (Manakul et al., 2023)." The paper's diagnosis is that the code review and self-reflection introduced by earlier work are non-executable, and so they have trouble ensuring that the code actually runs and is correct at run time. So after the initial code generation it added executable feedback.

The procedure is this. The Engineer writes code based on the original PRD and design. It then writes and executes the corresponding unit test cases and receives the results. If they are satisfactory, further development tasks begin; otherwise it debugs the code before resuming programming. This loop continues until the test passes or a maximum of 3 retries is reached. The Engineer accumulates its own execution and debugging history in memory and uses it to improve the code. The right of Figure 2 draws this loop. It writes game.py while looking at the PRD, system design and code retrieved from memory; if execution fails, it goes back through Debug; if it succeeds, it adds the code to the history.

Restated in the language of Chapter 11, the Engineer's evaluator is the executor. Instead of the model judging the code it generated, the environment (the Python interpreter) decides. But the one writing the test cases is the same Engineer. If the tests share a misunderstanding with the code, both can pass while being wrong. The paper does not discuss this possibility. The Reflexion paper takes up the same problem head-on ("Side papers").

5. Experiments (§4, Appendix C)

Datasets. Two public benchmarks and one of the authors' own (§4.1).

Dataset Size Contents Metric
HumanEval 164 handwritten programming tasks Function specifications, descriptions, reference code and tests pass@1
MBPP 427 Python tasks Core concepts and standard library features, automated tests pass@1
SoftwareDev 70 tasks (7 representative tasks chosen at random for the comparisons) Mini-games, image processing, data visualization and so on The five metrics below

pass@k follows the unbiased estimator of Chen et al. (2021). If n samples are generated for each problem and c pass the tests, pass@k=𝔼problems[1−(n−ck)/(nk)]. The paper does not say how many samples (n) were generated for each problem.

SoftwareDev has five metrics. (A) Executability: rated by people from 1 to 4 ("'1' is for non-functional, '2' for runnable but imperfect, '3' for nearly perfect, and '4' for flawless code"). (B) Cost: running time, token usage and expenses. (C) Code statistics: number of code files, lines of code per file, total code lines. (D) Productivity: token usage divided by lines of code (lower is better). (E) Human revision cost: the number of manual code corrections, for things like package import errors and incorrect class names. Typically each correction involves up to 3 lines. The paper does not say how many evaluators there were or whether they knew which system's output they were rating.

Code-generation scores — Figure 4. The values printed above the bars. "—" marks a slot with only a dash and no bar.

Method HumanEval pass@1 (%) MBPP pass@1 (%)
AlphaCode (1.1B) 17.1 —
Incoder (6.7B) 15.2 17.6
CodeGeeX (13B) 18.9 26.9

The values printed above the bars in Figure 4 of the paper. The bars were told apart by the legend (HumanEval sky blue, MBPP purple). The figures for Incoder, CodeGeeX and others are as reported by Dong et al. (2023) (§4.1), and GPT-4's 67.0 is the value from the OpenAI technical report (Appendix C.2).

Without executable feedback, the two benchmarks drop by 4.2 and 5.4 percentage points. This is the executable-feedback ablation of §4.4. HumanEval and MBPP are tasks that write a single function, and the text does not explain what the division of labor among five roles did here. §4.1 says only that the prompts were slightly modified to align with response format requirements.

The paper reads the table as saying that adding roles "consistently improves both revisions and executability." Revisions do fall monotonically, but executability does not. The setup with the Project Manager instead of the Architect (2.0) is lower than the one with the Architect (2.5), and it has the most lines of code.
