Additional results in the appendix. Table 4 breaks down the executability of Table 1 by the seven tasks (Flappy bird, Tank battle game, 2048 game, Snake game, Brick breaker game, Excel data process, CRUD manage). AutoGPT, LangChain and AgentVerse all score 1; ChatDev scores 2, 2, 1, 3, 1, 4, 2 and MetaGPT 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4. Table 5 changes only the backend, on 5 tasks. Executability is 2.8 with GPT-3.5, 3.8 with GPT-4 and 1.4 with Deepseek Coder 33B: the same SOP gives very different results depending on the model. Table 7 runs GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) on HumanEval five times in each of three settings. Using the response as is (A) averages 0.724, extracting only the code with a regex (B) 0.812, and adding the system prompt "You are an AI that only responds with Python code, NOT ENGLISH." (C) 0.800; the standard deviations are 0.013 to 0.016. Table 9 is the average of MetaGPT without feedback (GPT-4 32K) run on all 70 tasks: $1.12 per task, 516.71 seconds and executability 3.36.

Where the numbers in the paper do not agree.

  1. The executability of the same 7 tasks differs between tables. Table 1 gives ChatDev 2.25 and MetaGPT 3.75; Table 4 gives 2.1 and 3.9 (the averages of the per-task scores are 15/7 ≈ 2.14 and 27/7 ≈ 3.86). The values 2.25, 3.67 and 3.75 in Table 1 also cannot come out as averages of 7 integer scores (Exercise 2). The paper does not explain.
  2. The paper cites ChatDev as Qian et al. (2023) in many places in the text, but in three places, in §3.2 and Appendix C.2, it writes "Zhao et al., 2023". Zhao et al. (2023) in the references is "Chat with the environment: Interactive multimodal perception using large language models".
  3. The caption of Table 9 says "10 randomly selected tasks", but the table has 11 rows, task IDs 0 to 10 (Appendix C.2 also says 11).
  4. The productivity in Table 6 does not match the tokens divided by lines in the same row (28,384.2 / 178.2 ≈ 159.3, not 163.8). That could happen if it is the average of per-task ratios. In Table 1 it matches.

6. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

The numbers do not divide evenly by the number of problems. Of HumanEval's 164 problems, 81.7% matches 134/164, but 85.9% comes from no integer (140/164 = 85.4%, 141/164 = 86.0%). The same goes for 87.7% and 82.3% on MBPP's 427 problems (374/427 = 87.6%, 375/427 = 87.8%). This could happen if several samples were generated per problem and averaged with the unbiased estimator, but the caption of Figure 4 says "with a single attempt", which does not fit that explanation, and the number of samples is not reported either. The "about 7 problems" and "about 23 problems" below are approximations.

Rerunning the same setup moves the score by several percentage points. In setting B of Table 7, the five runs of GPT-4 on the same 164 problems gave 0.787, 0.811, 0.817, 0.829 and 0.817. The lowest and highest are 4.2 percentage points apart. The HumanEval difference reported as the effect of executable feedback is exactly 4.2 percentage points. If the two bars in Figure 4 are one run each, the difference is the same size as the fluctuation you get from rerunning the same setup. The fluctuation has two sources. The binomial standard error from sampling problems is 0.8×0.2/164≈3.1 percentage points near 80%, and the generation randomness when the same problems are solved again has a standard deviation of 1.3 to 1.6 percentage points in Table 7.

The choice of baseline matters more than the difference. GPT-4 in Figure 4 is 67.0. In Table 7 of the same paper, the GPT-4 the authors ran themselves scores 72.4% using the response as is and 81.2% extracting only the code with a regex. One post-processing step changes the score by 8.8 percentage points — more than executable feedback (4.2). The difference from MetaGPT's 85.9 is 18.9 percentage points against 67.0 and 4.7 against 81.2, and comparing the latter as independent samples gives z≈1.15. In the language of Chapter 3, the harness put on the same model (prompt and parser) changed the score. A fair baseline would be a single agent with the same model, the same post-processing and the same token budget. In addition, the Reflexion paper, which MetaGPT cites, reported 80.1 for GPT-4 and 91.0 for Reflexion on HumanEval (Python) (Reflexion, Table 1). There is no guarantee that the evaluation conditions were the same, but the "state-of-the-art" claim of Figure 4 is a claim relative to the baselines put in the figure.

Writing "errors spread" as multiplication. The calculation below is the editor's example. Let qk be the probability that stage k is right given that the earlier stages were right, and assume that if any stage is wrong the final output is wrong and is not fixed later. Then

P(final output is correct)=∏k=1Kqk

If a review at each stage catches and fixes a fraction c of that stage's errors, the stage success rate becomes q=p+(1−p)c.

Stage success rate Stage 1 Stage 2 Stage 3 Stage 4 Stage 5
p=0.9, no review 0.900 0.810 0.729 0.656 0.590
Review catches 30% of errors (q=0.93) 0.930 0.865 0.804 0.748 0.696
Review catches half of errors (q=0.95) 0.950 0.903 0.857 0.815 0.774
Review catches 80% of errors (q=0.98) 0.980 0.960 0.941 0.922 0.904

Cumulative probability of success. The five stages match MetaGPT's five roles. All values are calculations from assumptions, not measurements in the paper.

This multiplication splits the effect of the SOP in two. One is raising the stage success rate p itself (splitting roles to make each stage easier, using formats to block missing fields). The other is raising the fraction c of errors caught (the QA Engineer, executable feedback). The paper's experiments do not measure the two separately. Table 3 looks at the result of both changing together, as roles are added, through a single final executability score.

Testing this empirically needs records for each stage. Here is one design the editor sketched. Run the 70 SoftwareDev tasks several times with the same setup and keep every document passed between stages. Two or more evaluators, not knowing the system's name, judge whether each document is consistent with the earlier document and the requirement, and report their agreement (κ). Then for each stage you can estimate "the probability that this stage is right given the earlier stage was right" and "the probability that an error at an earlier stage is fixed later", and compare the multiplication model with the actual end-to-end success rate. As an experiment, error injection is cleaner. Plant one defect in the system design on purpose and compare how often it survives to the final code under the SOP setup and under a conversational setup (ChatDev style). This is mutation testing, familiar to developers, moved up to the level of the pipeline. The unit of analysis is task × repetition, and repetitions within a task form a cluster, so use clustered standard errors. Even this design cannot separate out the correlation of errors that arises when the same model plays every role.

Exercise 1 — can the 4.2 and 5.4 percentage points from executable feedback be told apart from chance? (a) Treating HumanEval's 81.7% against 85.9% (164 problems each) and MBPP's 82.3% against 87.7% (427 problems each) as independent samples, find the standard error of the difference and z. (b) In fact these are paired data in which both setups solved the same problems. If the net gain on HumanEval is about 7 problems, what is the two-sided p value of the exact McNemar test when the "reversals" — problems that feedback turned from right to wrong — number 0, 5 or 10? What if the net gain on MBPP is about 23 problems and the reversals number 0 to 20? (c) How should these be read when set beside Table 7?

SolutionSolution

(a) HumanEval: 0.817×0.183/164+0.859×0.141/164≈0.041, a standard error of 4.1 percentage points, z≈1.03, two-sided p≈0.30. MBPP: a standard error of about 2.4 percentage points, z≈2.22, p≈0.027. Treated as independent samples, the HumanEval difference lies within the fluctuation of sampling problems, and the MBPP difference lies outside it.

(b) In paired data, only the problems on which the two setups disagree carry information. Let b be the problems newly solved and r the problems newly failed (reversals). Under the null hypothesis, b~Binomial(b+r,0.5). For HumanEval (net gain 7), p≈0.016 when r=0, 0.14 when r=5 and 0.25 when r=10. For MBPP (net gain 23), p≈0.0006 when r=10, and even 0.005 when r=20. With the same net gain, the judgment for HumanEval turns on the number of reversals. If the per-problem results were released, this one calculation would settle it.

(c) (a) and (b) leave out generation randomness. Running GPT-4 alone five times already put the lowest and highest 3.1 percentage points (setting A) and 4.2 percentage points (setting B) apart. Each setup should be run several times and compared through per-problem pass rates.

Takeaway. The conclusion of a paired comparison depends on how the discordant pairs are made up, and a difference from a single run should be read beside the fluctuation across repeated runs.

Exercise 2 — what can 7 and 2 SoftwareDev tasks tell us? (a) In Table 4, the per-task score differences between MetaGPT and ChatDev are 1, 2, 3, 1, 3, 0 and 2. What are the two-sided p values of the sign test and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test? (b) Can the 2.25, 3.67 and 3.75 in Table 1 come out as averages of 7 integers between 1 and 4? (c) Take the standard deviation of the paired differences to be 1 point. What is the power of a paired t test (two-sided, 5%) for a true difference of 0.5 points with 2, 7 and 70 tasks? How many tasks are needed for 80% power? What about executable feedback's 0.08 points (3.67 → 3.75), assuming a standard deviation of 0.5?

SolutionSolution

(a) Dropping the 0, all 6 are positive. The sign test gives two-sided p=2×0.56≈0.031, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test also 0.031. ChatDev never won, so even 7 tasks separate them at the 5% level. But the 7 were chosen out of 70 as "representative tasks" (§4.1 says they were selected at random; Appendix C.1 says they are the first seven in Table 8), so extending the result to all 70 runs into the question of how they were chosen. Table 3, with 2 tasks, cannot reach significance with exact tests such as the sign test or the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Even if both differences point the same way, the smallest two-sided p is 0.5. A paired t test can come out numerically significant if the two differences are nearly equal (the critical value with 1 degree of freedom is 12.7), but that judgment rests entirely on the assumption that the differences are normally distributed, so with 2 tasks it is no grounds for belief. As (c) shows, even if the true difference were 0.5 points, the probability (power) that a paired t test on 2 tasks comes out significant is 0.06.

(b) The average of 7 integers has the form k/7. Near 2.25 are 2.14 (15/7) and 2.29 (16/7); near 3.67 and 3.75 are 3.57, 3.71 and 3.86. 2.25 and 3.75 come from denominators of 4, 8 or 12, and 3.67 from 3 or 6. The numbers in Table 1 are not explained by "7 tasks, one evaluation".

(c) Computed with the noncentral t distribution, the power for a true difference of 0.5 points is 0.06 with 2 tasks, 0.20 with 7 and 0.985 with 70. For 80%, the normal approximation gives n≈((1.96+0.84)×1/0.5)2≈31.4, and solving exactly with the noncentral t gives 34 tasks. If the true difference were 1 point, the power with 7 tasks would be 0.60. Executable feedback's 0.08 points has power 0.26 even with 70 tasks, and 80% needs about 309 (by the noncentral t; about 307 by the normal approximation). Note also that the scores are bunched near the ceiling (4 points). Building 70 tasks and using only 7 and 2 may have been for cost (by Table 9, about $1.12 and 516 seconds per task). If so, it would be better to report alongside "the effect size this sample can detect".

Takeaway. An experiment with a handful of tasks can show a large difference (ChatDev against MetaGPT) but not a small one (feedback's 0.08 points, one role's 0.5 points). Ablations in particular need large samples.

7. Limitations the paper states

Appendices D.1 and A state the limitations.

  • System side (D.1). It cannot yet fully handle specific areas such as UI and front end, because it has yet to incorporate such agents and multimodal tools. Although it generates the most code among the frameworks compared, fulfilling the diverse and complex requirements of real-world applications remains hard.
  • Human user side (D.1). It is hard for users to interrupt the running process of each agent or to set a starting point (checkpoint) for each agent.
  • No learning across projects (A.1). The MetaGPT of the main text runs each software project independently. It does not learn from project experience the way a human team does. Appendix A.1 says the authors tried out a mechanism in which, before each project, each agent reviews previous feedback and revises its constraint prompt, and adds the limitation that this summary-based optimization modifies only the constraints of role specialization, not the structured communication interfaces of the communication protocol.
  • A fixed SOP (A.2). In a real team, the collaboration SOP may change dynamically. Appendix A.2 introduces the "Economy of Minds" and the authors' own platform as directions for that.
  • Ethics (D.2). Unemployment and skill obsolescence, transparency and accountability (people initiate, observe and stop runs and are responsible for the outcomes), and privacy (it runs locally and does not collect user data).

What the paper does not report should also be noted. It gives neither the number of evaluators in the human evaluation nor whether they were blinded. It does not measure "cascading hallucinations" themselves, so it cannot tell whether what the SOP reduced was cascading hallucination or some other failure. And in Table 1 the system that spent more tokens won. These points are this book's reading.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

The side papers in this chapter are two (Anthropic's multi-agent research system S18, and HuggingGPT). To them are added ChatDev, which MetaGPT compares itself with directly, and the work covered in the chapters before and after this one.

Anthropic's multi-agent research system (Hadfield et al. 2025). An orchestrator-worker structure: a lead agent analyzes the query and spins up subagents in parallel, and each subagent searches in its own context window and returns compressed results. The difference is who decides the division of labor, and when. MetaGPT's roles and order are an assembly line fixed in advance by people; here the lead agent decides for each task. Read the numbers with their conditions. A setup with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents "outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval" (the number of items and the basis of the percentage are not given). On BrowseComp, token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance in performance. Agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat, and multi-agent systems about 15×. And the post says that "most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research," which makes them a poor fit for today's multi-agent systems. The appendix recommends sending subagent output to a filesystem and passing back lightweight references "to minimize the 'game of telephone.'" This points the same way as MetaGPT's document publishing. It is a prescription drawn from experience with the company's own product and has not been peer-reviewed.

HuggingGPT (Shen et al. 2023 · Chapter 7 of this book). Summarized within the scope of the abstract. An LLM becomes a controller that manages existing AI models, and language serves as a generic interface. ChatGPT plans the task, picks models by reading their function descriptions on Hugging Face, runs the subtasks with the chosen models and summarizes the results. It is hierarchical: one controller LLM does all the planning and assignment, and the workers are not LLM agents but specialized models. There are no peer roles and no documents handed from one to another. If the controller's plan is wrong, every stage below will follow that plan, so this chapter's question applies just as it is (this book's reading).

ChatDev (Qian et al. 2023). The opponent MetaGPT compares itself with in Tables 1 and 4. According to the abstract, agents take part in the design, coding and testing phases, they are guided in what to communicate "(via chat chain)" and in how to communicate "(via communicative dehallucination)", and solutions come out of multi-turn dialogue. The difference MetaGPT puts forward is conversation against documents (§3.2). ChatDev also follows phases and has a device to reduce hallucination, so the difference can also be read as "whether stages are linked by conversation or by formatted documents".

Prompt chaining and orchestrator-workers (Erik S. and Barry Zhang 2024 · Chapter 1 of this book). Prompt chaining splits a task into fixed steps, with each call processing the output of the previous one, and can put programmatic checks (a "gate") in between. In orchestrator-workers, a central LLM decides the subtasks as it goes. MetaGPT is closer to the former, and Anthropic's research system (S18) to the latter. In MetaGPT each link of the chain is not an LLM call but a ReAct-style agent, and document formats join the links. The post in Chapter 1 warns that the autonomy of agents brings "the potential for compounding errors."

Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book). It divides actor, evaluator and Self-Reflection model into parts within one agent. In programming it runs unit tests it writes itself (a maximum of 6). MetaGPT §3.3 groups Reflexion with "non-executable" self-reflection; how to reconcile the two descriptions is an open question. Reflexion also measured the limits of self-written tests. The rate of passing all its own tests while actually being wrong was 16.3% for MBPP Python and 1.4% for HumanEval Python (§4.3, Table 2). The same question applies to MetaGPT's Engineer, which writes its own tests. The time scale of correction also differs. Reflexion corrects between episodes; MetaGPT corrects up to 3 times within one project.

SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024 · Chapter 14 of this book). A preview of the next chapter. It has a single agent and gives it a custom agent-computer interface (ACI) for creating and editing files, navigating repositories and running tests. Where MetaGPT raised scores by splitting the work into roles, SWE-agent raises them by changing the shape of one agent's tools. The HumanEvalFix pass@1 in its abstract is also 87.7%, but that is a number from a different benchmark than MetaGPT's MBPP 87.7%.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §2.2 — the communication channel C

The survey extends the formalization of Chapter 2 to a decentralized partially observable setting (Dec-POMDP) (Appendix I, section 5). The joint policy π is composed of individual policies πi, and agent i's observation oti includes the messages ct−1−i that its peers produced at the previous step through the communication channel C. What the survey stresses is that this communication is not merely signal transmission but an extension of the reasoning process: "one agent's external action can act as a prompt that triggers another agent's internal reasoning chain." Placed in this frame, MetaGPT maps as follows (the editor drew up the correspondence).

MetaGPT paper AR survey, revised version §2.2
Five roles N=5, individual policies πi. θ is shared by all roles (one backend — Appendix Table 5 swaps the whole backend)
Role profiles and role-specific skills The prompts and tools that set πi
Shared message pool Communication channel C
Publish: post formatted documents to the pool External action ati. It becomes cti and enters the next observation of other agents
Subscribe: chosen by role profile, start only when all prerequisites arrive A filter that selects which ct−1−i enter oti
Each agent's ReAct-style behavior Alternation of zt and at within an agent (Chapter 6)
The Engineer's execution and debugging history / unit test results That agent's memory mt / the observation ot returned by the environment
Fixed SOP, fixed weights In-context reasoning (z mode)
Updating constraint prompts in Appendix A.1 (trial implementation) Can be read as a verbal update of the system state S (Eq. 5)

The sentence about one agent's external action triggering another agent's reasoning happens literally in MetaGPT's implementation rule (act only after receiving all prerequisites). In this frame, cascading hallucination can be written as an error mixed into cti entering the next agent's observation and contaminating that agent's z, and structured outputs read as a device that narrows that path by restricting the form of messages passing through C. This connection is this book's reading.

§5.1–5.2 — the taxonomy of roles and the cell in Table 11

§5.1.1 lists five generic roles that recur in multi-agent systems: Leader/Coordinator, Worker/Executor, Critic/Evaluator (checks and balances that mitigate error propagation), Memory Keeper and Communication Facilitator (defining message schemas, ensuring structured information flow). Figure 8 draws these five and seven domains where roles are specialized (software engineering, finance, legal and others) in two rows. §5.1.2 introduces MetaGPT as a system "which decomposes development into Product Manager, Architect, and Engineer agents." In the editor's mapping, the Product Manager, Architect and Project Manager split the leader's work three ways, the Engineer is the worker and the QA Engineer the critic. The communication facilitator enters not as a role but as structure: the message pool and the formats.

§5.2 divides collaboration research into three optimization modes. In-context collaboration (z, §5.2.1) has four boxes in Figure 9: Cascading (manually designed sequential chains with a fixed flow), Hierarchical (a manually designed, centrally planned hierarchical structure), Role-based (a manually designed modular system with fixed-role agents) and Automated (LLMs orchestrate agent coordination). System-level collaboration optimization (S, §5.2.2) optimizes role prompts and communication topologies with the model frozen, and post-training collaboration (θ, §5.2.3) changes the agents' parameters. In Table 11, MetaGPT is the first row.

Method Coordination structure What is optimized Signal Optim. Target
MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2024) Role pipeline (SOP) Nothing (hand-designed) None z

The MetaGPT row of Table 11 of the revised AR survey. The same block (I. In-Context Collaboration) also holds AgentVerse, AutoGen, SMoA and Magentic-One.

The text of §5.2.1 classifies MetaGPT among manually crafted pipelines as hierarchical, that is, a system with "a central planner or conductor directing subordinate agents". The MetaGPT paper says all agents work sequentially and has no separate lead agent, so it can also be read as closer to cascading or role-based. The boundary of the classification is blurred here, which is worth pointing out in the presentation. What the S-mode research (role-prompt optimization, topology search such as AFlow and GPTSwarm) tries to find automatically, MetaGPT had a person choose once and fix.

The discussions in §5.2 and §5.4 — what is confounded

  • Token budget (end of §5.2). "a topology that 'wins' may simply be spending more", and for several reported gains there is no single-agent baseline with the same total budget. In Table 1, MetaGPT used 1.28 to 1.62 times ChatDev's tokens, and Figure 4 has no single GPT-4 agent with the same budget.
  • Division of labor or prompts (§5.4). Role specialization is usually evaluated together with the prompt engineering that implements it, so it is unclear whether the gain comes from the division of labor or from having written better prompts for each subtask. Table 3 has exactly this structure. Each role added brings that role's prompt and document format with it.
  • When collaboration helps (§5.4). The survey says the evidence is strongest where a task decomposes into genuinely heterogeneous roles with verifiable interfaces between them, with software pipelines "the clearest case, since each stage produces a checkable artifact." The evidence for debate among agents doing the same job is weak. Coordination as teams grow is essentially uncharted (most systems use fewer than ten agents), and failures such as error propagation "are discussed more than measured."

§8.4 writes that systems such as MetaGPT "show that encoding human organizational routines and role-specific verification can reduce cascading errors". MetaGPT's experiments did not measure cascading errors directly but measured final quality, so set beside the sentence the survey itself wrote in §5.4, this "show" can also be read more narrowly as "proposed such a design and reported improved final quality".

Harness survey §6.3 — not in Table 2

Table 2 divides orchestration systems in use today into the single-agent inner loop (§6.2, SWE-agent included), multi-agent orchestration patterns (§6.3) and full lifecycle pipelines (§6.4). The patterns in §6.3 are five — Hierarchical orchestration (four systems including AutoGen), Team orchestration, Workflow orchestration, Fan-out and Graph composition (LangGraph and others) — and the execution model is mostly Stateful. MetaGPT is not in Table 2; it appears in the 2023 entry of the §2.1 timeline together with CAMEL and ChatDev. Against the five patterns, it is closest to team or workflow orchestration (the editor's placement). Anthropic's research system (S18) is listed in the Harness survey's Figure 9 (representative work for the lifecycle and orchestration chapter) as the first entry under multi-agent orchestration patterns. The text of §6.3 gives the same post (Anthropic 2025f) as an example of "Anthropic's planner-generator-evaluator architecture", but S18 has no roles by those names. That structure appears in another Anthropic post, "Harness design for long-running application development" (Prithvi Rajasekaran, March 24, 2026; Anthropic 2026c in the survey), as three agents: "planner, generator, and evaluator". The survey itself attributes this structure to 2026c in §7.4, so the 2025f in §6.3 looks like a citation slip.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "The more agents, the better." In Table 3, of the two setups with three agents, executability is 2.5 with the Architect added and 2.0 with the Project Manager added. What differed was not the number but which role came in. Only with all four did it reach 4.0, and the expense rose by 51%. This table is an average over 2 tasks.

Misreading 2. "MetaGPT scores 19 percentage points higher than GPT-4 on HumanEval." GPT-4's 67.0 in Figure 4 is the value from the OpenAI technical report. In Table 7 of the same paper, the GPT-4 the authors ran themselves scores 81.2% when only the code is extracted with a regex. The difference from that value is 4.7 percentage points, about the size of the fluctuation from sampling problems (standard error of an independent comparison about 4.1 percentage points) (section 6).

Misreading 3. "MetaGPT's agents work by talking to each other." Not talking is exactly the difference from ChatDev that the paper puts forward. The agents publish formatted documents and diagrams and read the documents they need by subscribing (§3.2).

Misreading 4. "The SOP eliminates hallucination." The paper itself says the first implementation missed errors because of hallucination, so executable feedback was added (§3.3). Even after that, the human revision cost is 0.83, and how much "cascading hallucination" was reduced was not measured separately.

Misreading 5. "MetaGPT is a system that learns from experience." The MetaGPT of the main text changes neither weights nor prompts nor role makeup, and runs each project independently (Appendix A.1 states this as a limitation). Table 11 of the AR survey also classifies it as "Nothing (hand-designed)" and z. The Engineer's memory is the execution history within one project.

Misreading 6. "With structured documents, the earlier stage's requirements are passed on without omission." The paper says the documents contain all necessary information and prevent irrelevant or missing content (§3.2), but no experiment measured that. In the example in Figure 3, too, the PRD's "web-based" is not visible in the design document (section 2). A format forces the fields to exist; it does not guarantee that what is in them agrees with the earlier document.

Discussion questions

  1. Where to put the verification gates. In the multiplication of section 6, raising the stage success rate and raising the fraction of errors caught are different prescriptions. MetaGPT concentrated review at the end (the QA Engineer) and in executable feedback. In your own workflows (approval chains, deployment pipelines, data-loading processes), where are the checks, and on what basis were they put there? If you put a check at every stage, what happens to the cost?

  2. An assembly line, or a division of labor decided as you go? In MetaGPT, people fixed the roles and order in advance; in Anthropic's research system (S18), the lead agent decides for each task. Give one task where a fixed SOP is an advantage and one where it is a disadvantage. How can you read together AR survey §5.4, which calls software pipelines the clearest case because of "verifiable" artifacts, and S18, which calls coding a poorer fit for multi-agent systems?

  3. Write permission to the shared message pool. If a sentence the Product Manager brought in by web search gets mixed into the PRD and posted to the pool, it becomes an observation for every role below. Think ahead to indirect prompt injection in Chapter 15. How much would a device like the permission table of Chapter 20, which sets out who may write and read which documents, reduce this risk? (Connecting the message pool to injection this way is this book's reading.)

Chapter 14 · Optional · ★★

Chapter 14. Coding Agents — SWE-agent

The question this chapter answers: if we leave the model as it is and change only the "interface for using the computer", does performance change?

Core reading. John Yang et al., "SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering", NeurIPS 2024. 9 pages of main text, 118 with the references and appendices.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · NeurIPS 2024 presentation page · Code

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §6.1, Table 12 · Harness survey §3, §6.2 and §6.4 with Table 2, §8.3.2, Appendix B

One-paragraph summary. Human developers do not use only the shell; they use IDEs. The authors argue that language-model agents are also "a new category of end user" that needs an interface fitted to it, and they call the layer placed between the model and the computer the agent-computer interface (ACI). SWE-agent's ACI consists of search commands that summarize their results, a file viewer that shows 100 lines at a time, an edit command that replaces a range of lines and rolls the edit back if it introduces a syntax error, and context management that collapses old observations into one line. The weights of the model (GPT-4 Turbo) were not touched. On SWE-bench, 2,294 real GitHub issues, it resolved 12.47% (286 instances), and an ablation on the 300-instance Lite set that swapped the components one at a time brought the score down by 1.7 to 7.7 percentage points. This is the paper that showed Chapter 3's "the harness changes performance" as an experiment that changes one treatment at a time.

Building intuition

As people have IDEs (Figure 1, Figure 2)

Figure 2 has two panels. A person uses the computer through a UI such as VSCode or PyCharm, and a language-model agent uses the computer through an ACI made of a File Viewer, a File Editor and Code Search. Figure 1 enlarges the agent's side and draws, inside the ACI, "LM-friendly commands" (Navigate repo, View files, Search files, Edit lines) and "LM-friendly environment feedback".

The starting point is the shell. The shell has no simple command for editing a small segment of a file, and it gives no feedback after an invalid edit (§1). The design rests on the differences between people and models (§2). Models find it hard to operate GUIs directly, but features such as syntax checking and navigation are useful if presented in a suitable way. People can ignore unneeded information, but for a model all content has a fixed cost, and distracting context can harm performance. The citation attached to that sentence is Lost in the Middle (reference [27]) from Chapter 9.

The editor's bridge — usability testing and one-factor ablation

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

Database administrators will have tried swapping only the client on the same database engine. How many rows fit on one screen and what error message comes back for a bad query change the speed and the mistakes of the same person. SWE-agent is an experiment that fixes the engine (the language model) and swaps the client (the ACI). Usability tests in human-computer interaction (HCI) likewise keep the user and change the interface, measuring task success rates. From the statistical side, Table 3 is a one-factor-at-a-time ablation. It changes one factor of the best setting and holds the rest fixed, so the difference is easy to attribute to that factor.

The analogy breaks down in two places. A usability test samples several people, but this paper's "user" is one model. Variation comes not from differences between people but from differences between problems and between runs (section 7). And a one-factor ablation cannot see interactions. Table 3 cannot tell you whether the effect of the search method depends on the window size.

The paper's own analogies are the IDE (Figure 2) and the relation between HCI and psychology (§7). The authors write that designing ACIs can be "systematic behavioral experimentation" that reveals differences between people and language models.

The paper in detail

1. What is an ACI? — four design principles (§2)

An ACI sets both the commands available to the model and how the environment's state is returned, and it manages the history so that each step becomes a single input to the model. The model is fixed. The four principles came out of manually inspecting agent behavior on a development set and choosing a configuration by grid search.

Principle Gist of the original
1. Actions should be simple and easy to understand for agents Bash commands have dozens of options. Commands with few options and short documentation are easier to use and reduce the need for demonstrations or fine-tuning
2. Actions should be compact and efficient Consolidate important operations such as file navigation and editing into as few actions as possible (the analyses of editing and search in §5.1)
3. Environment feedback should be informative but concise Report the current state and the effect of recent actions, without unnecessary details (Figure 3, Table 3)
4. Guardrails mitigate error propagation and hasten recovery Devices that catch mistakes automatically, such as a syntax checker, help fix them quickly (the linting row of Table 3)

Principles 1 and 2 concern the actions the model produces, and 3 and 4 the observations the model receives. In the notation of Chapter 2, 1 and 2 redesign the action space A, and 3 redesigns Ω, the way observations are produced (the editor's mapping).

2. SWE-agent's ACI — four components (§3, Figure 3, Appendix Table 4)

SWE-agent puts special commands on top of a Linux shell. Ordinary shell commands can still be used.

Category Command What it does (documentation in Appendix Table 4)
File viewer open <path> [<line_number>], goto <line_number>, scroll_down, scroll_up Opens a file, and moves the window to a given line or by 100 lines
Search tools search_file <search_term> [<file>], search_dir <search_term> [<dir>], find_file <file_name> [<dir>] Searches for a string in a file or directory, or for a file name in the repository
File editing edit <n>:<m> … end_of_edit, create <filename> Replaces lines n through m (inclusive). Python files are checked for syntax errors after the edit, and if an error is found, the edit is not executed
Task submit Generates and submits the patch from all the edits so far

Appendix Table 4, abridged. The documentation column of the original describes scroll_down as "Moves the window up 100 lines" and scroll_up as "Moves the window down 100 lines", so the directions were not carried over.

Search and navigation. The three search commands show a summary of their results, and if there are more than 50 results, they do not report them and instead suggest a more specific query.

File viewer. It shows at most 100 lines at a time and displays the file path, the total number of lines, the number of lines omitted before and after the window, and line numbers.

File editor. edit takes a start line, an end line and replacement text, replacing several lines in one step, and after it is applied the file viewer immediately shows the changed part again. The response in Figure 3(b) is two sentences of thought and one edit command.

Figure 3(b) of the SWE-agent paper. The first two lines are the thought, and everything from edit to end_of_edit is the action.

Because the previous screen had line numbers, the model can write 404:407 straight away. Principle 3 (feedback) supports principle 2 (compact actions). The edit has a linter attached: if an edit introduces a syntax error, it shows the error and snippets of the file before and after the edit, discards the edit and asks the agent to try again. The error message in Appendix Figure 11 begins with "Your proposed edit has introduced new syntax error(s)." and near the end comes "Your changes have NOT been applied."

Context management. At the start, the agent gets instructions, command documentation and one demonstration trajectory, and at each step it is told to produce a thought and an action together. Malformed output gets an error message back, and a command with no output gets a message saying it ran successfully and produced no output. Observations older than the last 5 are collapsed into a single line such as Old output omitted (101 lines) (Appendix Figure 31). Appendix C gives two reasons: saving tokens and reducing outdated file contents that could confuse the model.

The four components of §3 of the SWE-agent paper and the layout of Figure 1, put on one page. Each row of Table 3 replaces one of the boxes in the middle with a different design. The editor drew the diagram.

3. Experimental setup (§4, Appendices B.1 and B.7)

Tasks. SWE-bench is 2,294 task instances collected from 12 popular Python repositories. The model receives the repository and the issue description and produces a patch. Lite is "a canonical subset of 300 instances" that focuses on self-contained functional bug fixes. Keep in mind that it is not a random sample (section 7). HumanEvalFix is a short-form code debugging benchmark, with 164 problems per language (Appendix B.7).

Models. All results, ablations and analyses are based on GPT-4 Turbo (a 128k-token context) and Claude 3 Opus (200k). Llama 3 and DeepSeek Coder were also tried, but their performance in the agent setting was subpar. With Llama 3's 8k window, there is almost no room left for interaction after the system prompt, the issue and the demonstration are put in.

Two baselines. RAG is the non-interactive baseline from the SWE-bench paper: BM25 retrieves relevant files using the issue as the query, and the model generates a patch directly. Shell-only adapts the framework of InterCode (reference [59]) and has the model interact with a shell directly. According to Appendix A.2, SWE-agent's environment itself builds on this InterCode-Bash environment. It is a baseline from the same house with only the ACI taken away.

Metrics and budget. % Resolved (pass@1) is the share of instances for which all tests pass after the patch is applied. $ Avg. Cost is the API cost averaged only over successfully resolved instances. The per-instance budget is $4; runs that exceed it have their existing edits submitted automatically.

Configuration search. The final ACI was refined by looking at a small set of hand-picked examples from the development split, and window size, history processing and decoding temperature were chosen by a grid search on 37 instances sampled at random from the development split (Appendix B.1, Table 5, five runs averaged per configuration). GPT-4 Turbo's best was temperature 0.0, a 100-line window and the last 5 observations, at 15.1%, followed by full history at 14.1%. What a size of 37 means is calculated in section 7.

Table 3 of the paper (SWE-bench Lite, 300 instances), reproduced with its rows spread out. The original sets the default and two alternatives in each of four columns — Editor, Search, File Viewer and Context — and marks the drops with arrows. The editor summarized "What changed" from §5.1 and Figures 5 and 6, and the instance counts are % Resolved × 300, rounded (all eight rows reduce to whole numbers of instances). The paper calls "No search" "Shell-only" in the caption of Figure 5 and in §5.1. Its value (15.7) differs from Shell-only in Table 1 (11.00), so it reads as a setting that keeps the rest of the ACI and does only the search through the shell, but the paper does not say so explicitly.

Editing (Figure 6). One sympy issue solved with three editing interfaces. In the shell panel, the model displays a file of about 1,079 lines with cat, fixes it with sed -i and, getting no output, starts writing a script with echo. The failure modes the figure lists are the uncertainty caused by having no output, cat flooding the context, and the line numbers and before-and-after states the model must keep track of. edit 1055:1059 without linting bundles the steps into one, but leaves a "Syntax Error!" With linting, the same edit gets back "E999 IndentationError" with screens of the file before and after the edit, and the model diagnoses an extra { and fixes it with edit 1055:1060. §5.1 explains that failures that keep editing the same snippet usually start from a syntax error, and the caption of Figure 6 says that linting is beneficial for "stymieing cascading errors". There is a price too (Appendix A.1). To remove an argument from a function header, the references to it in the body must be removed in the same edit or first. The authors write that whether to add a guardrail is a trade-off between the gain of fewer errors and the cost of blocking the workflow.

Search (Figure 5). The task is to find the PVSystem class in pvlib. The shell panel digs by hand with ls and cd; the iterative-search panel pages through "[Result 1/15 (Line 70)]" with next; the summarized-search panel gets "Found 1 matches" from a single search "class PVSystem" and does open at once. Iterative search paged through every result to the end and used up the budget or the context, scoring below even the case with no search tool. The heading of the relevant paragraph in §5.1 is "Human user interfaces are not always suitable as agent-computer interfaces."

File viewer and context. Thirty lines is too little context, and the whole file is the flooding feedback that principle 3 warned about. With only three points, 50 or 200 lines might do better (the development-set search in Table 5 compared only 100 and 200 lines). For context, keeping only the last 5 observations scored higher than the full history. Showing less did better, which fits the assumption §2 made when citing Lost in the Middle. The drop for "w/o demo." (1.7 percentage points) is the smallest. In Shell-only, removing the demonstration lost 3.67 percentage points (Table 1), so this reads as consistent with principle 1: with an ACI, the demonstration matters less. Whether that difference lies outside the range of chance is examined in section 7.

Which model's ablation? The first sentence of §5.1 names the ablated system as the "SWE-agent w/ GPT-4 configuration," and most other places say GPT-4 Turbo. §4 states that all results, ablations and analyses are based on GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 3 Opus, and the default value of 18.0 in Table 3 equals GPT-4 Turbo's Lite value in Table 1, so "GPT-4" reads as short for GPT-4 Turbo. The paper abbreviates it the same way in Figure 7 and Tables 6, 7 and 10. But the "GPT-4" row of Table 2 is the score of GPT-4 itself, taken from another paper, so the same name refers to two models.

The eight ablation values of Table 3 of the paper, plotted beside the default setting. The dark band is the range across runs from Table 10, and the light band is the binomial confidence interval of the single default setting. Which band you take as "the range of chance" changes the judgment (section 7). The editor drew the diagram.

6. How the agent behaves and where it fails (§5.2, Figure 7, Figure 8, Appendix B)

The order of actions. The 286 trajectories GPT-4 Turbo resolved on the full SWE-bench (Figure 7) all begin with either create (reproduction) or find_file/search_dir (localization). Reproduction is the three steps create–edit–python, the most common pattern in turns 1 to 3, appearing 156 times (Appendix Table 8). From turn 5 onward, edit and python are the most frequent. The loop of Chapter 6 becomes "edit, then run".

Editing and time. Of all 2,294 instances, 1,185 (51.7%) have trajectories with at least one edit that raised a linting error. An edit attempt has a 90.5% chance of eventually succeeding, which drops to 57.2% after one failure. Resolved instances finished at a median cost of $1.21 and 12 steps, unresolved ones at a mean of $2.52 and 21 steps (medians and means are mixed here). 93.0% of the resolved instances (266 of 286) were submitted by the agent itself before the budget ran out. So the authors expect that raising the budget would not improve results much.

Failure modes (Figure 8). GPT-4o classified the 248 unresolved trajectories on Lite into the categories of Appendix Table 9, and its agreement with the authors' hand labels on 15 instances was 87%.

Failure mode (Figure 8 legend) Share Of 248
Incorrect Implementation — changed a reasonable area but did not resolve the issue 39.9% 99
Overly Specific Implementation 12.1% 30
Failed to Recover from Edit 23.4% 58
Failed to Find Edit Location 12.9% 32
Failed to Find Relevant File 2.4% 6
Gave Up Prematurely 4.8% 12
Can't Reproduce 2.4% 6
Ran Out of Time 2.0% 5

The shares were read by enlarging the numbers printed on the slices of the figure, and the counts are the editor's, multiplying by 248 and rounding (total 248). Table 9 defines nine categories including "Other", but the figure has eight, and three categories have different names in the table and the figure.

A little over half (52.0%) are cases where the solution itself is wrong or too narrow, and failures that never opened the right file are 2.4%. The picture is one of reaching the place to fix but not fixing it correctly. The calculation in Appendix B.9 points the same way. The F1 between the set of files edited and the set of files in the gold patch was 59.05% for SWE-agent and 45.47% for BM25-based RAG (Claude 3 Opus).

Where Value given Value elsewhere, or calculation

7. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as preparation for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?) and Chapter 17 (pass@k and pass^k).

Run 1 2 3 4 5 6 Avg.
Resolve % 17.33 18.00 18.00 18.67 17.33 18.33 17.94 (0.49)

The per-run scores in Table 10 of the paper (SWE-bench Lite, 300 instances, default setting; the caption says "SWE-agent with GPT-4"). The horizontal axis is the run number. The 0.49 beside the average is printed as a subscript in the original.

Number of attempts k 1 2 3 4 5 6
pass@k 17.94 23.89 27.35 29.67 31.33 32.67

The pass@k in Table 10 of the paper. The horizontal axis is not the run number but the number of attempts k. The original also prints the two rows as separate tables.

Multiplying by 300, the six runs resolved 52, 54, 54, 56, 52 and 55 instances. 0.49 matches the population standard deviation of the six values (denominator 6, 0.487 percentage points). The sample standard deviation (denominator 5) is 0.534 percentage points. From this table, the authors conclude that "average performance variance is relatively low, though per-instance resolution can change considerably." The second half can be put in numbers.

Recovering the per-problem distribution from six pass@k values. If problem i was run six times and solved ci times, the commonly used unbiased estimator is pass@k=1300∑i[1−(6−cik)/(6k)]. The paper does not give its calculation. Assuming it used this formula, the question "how many problems were solved c=0,…,6 times?" has seven unknowns and seven equations (pass@1 to pass@6 and the total of 300). Allowing for rounding at the second decimal place and searching all nonnegative integer solutions, there is exactly one.

Times solved out of six, c 0 1 2 3 4 5 6
Number of problems, Nc 202 24 15 19 8 12 20

Recomputing pass@1 to pass@6 from this distribution gives 17.944, 23.889, 27.350, 29.667, 31.333 and 32.667, all matching Table 10. That there is only one solution is itself circumstantial evidence that this estimator was used.

The per-problem distribution the editor back-calculated from pass@1 to pass@6 in Table 10 of the paper. The original does not give this distribution. The editor drew the diagram.

  • "The problems it can solve" are not a fixed set. 98 problems were solved at least once, and 20 every time. The probability that a problem solved in one run is also solved in another is ∑c(c−1)Nc/(5∑cNc)=1080/1615≈0.67, and two runs of the same setting disagree on 35.7 problems on average.
  • The uncertainty of a single run's pass@1 has two sources. Each problem has a different success probability pi (between problems), and the same problem comes out differently from run to run (between runs). Of the variance of success, p¯(1−p¯)=0.147, the between-run share (estimated without bias as the average of ci(6−ci)/30) is 0.059 (about 40%) and the between-problem share Var(pi) is 0.088 (about 60%). The standard error depends on what you are estimating. If you are estimating the score on problems newly drawn from the same population, the standard error of one run on 300 problems is 2.22 percentage points. Averaging six runs shrinks only the between-run share, to 1.80 percentage points, and even infinitely many runs cannot go below 1.71 percentage points, because the between-problem share remains. If instead you are estimating the average score on the fixed test set of the 300 Lite problems, the between-problem share is not error. Only the between-run share remains: about 1.41 percentage points for one run and about 0.57 for the average of six, going to 0 as runs are repeated. Both calculations rest on the assumption that runs, and problems, are conditionally independent. For a comparison meant to generalize to other systems or new problems, precision is mostly set by the number of problems.
  • The reported standard deviation across runs is smaller than expected. From the distribution above, if runs were independent, the standard deviation across runs would be expected to be about 1.41 percentage points. In a simulation (200,000 repetitions) that randomly redistributes each problem's successes across the six runs, the 95% range of the sample standard deviation was 0.57 to 2.25 percentage points, and the probability of 0.53 percentage points or less, as observed, was about 0.02. It may be chance; the runs may not have been independent; or the scores and pass@k may have come from different sets of runs. How to reconcile this is an open question, and the problem × run table from the released trajectories (Appendix E.2) could answer it.

pass@k and pass^k. pass@k is the probability of solving at least once in k attempts, and pass^k the probability of solving all k times. Below, the values computed from the distribution above are set beside those computed on the assumption that every problem is solved with the same probability, 0.1794.

k 1 2 3 4 5 6
pass@k (Table 10) 17.94 23.89 27.35 29.67 31.33 32.67
Equal-probability assumption 1−(1−p¯)k 17.94 32.67 44.75 54.67 62.80 69.48
pass^k (from the distribution) 17.94 12.00 9.52 8.18 7.33 6.67
Equal-probability assumption p¯k 17.94 3.22 0.58 0.10 0.02 0.003

The assumption of uniform difficulty more than doubles pass@6 and shrinks pass^6 to one two-thousandth. If a person can pick the right one out of six results, pass@6 (32.67%) is the right metric. If you run it once and use that result, it is pass@1 = pass^1 (17.94%). If the question is stability — giving the same job six times and needing all six to succeed — it is pass^6 (6.67%). We meet pass^k again with τ-bench in Chapter 17.

Do the differences in Table 3 exceed the range of chance? Using the range across runs (17.33 to 18.67) as the lens, all eight rows fall below it. Using the sampling error of problems as the lens, things look different. The standard error of a difference compared as independent samples is about 3 percentage points, and only "No edit" and "Iterative" exceed twice that. Since the comparisons are on the same problems, the McNemar test is the right one, but the paper does not give the number of discordant problems. Working through that range is Exercise 2.

Full set and Lite, and the 37 instances. The full set's 12.47% (286 instances) has a standard error of 0.69 percentage points and a Wilson 95% interval of 11.18 to 13.88%, and Lite's 18.00% (54 instances) has 2.22 percentage points and 14.07 to 22.74%. To bring the half-width down to 2 percentage points near 18% takes about 1,420 problems. But Lite is a selected subset, so the difference between 18.00 and 12.47 is a difference in problem sets, not in precision. For the 37 instances of the configuration search, carrying over the decomposition above as an assumption, the between-problem variation alone gives one configuration a standard error of about 4.9 percentage points. 15.1% against 14.1% (28 against 26 of 185 trials) cannot be told apart, and the best of eight configurations also carries the selection bias of Exercise 2 in Chapter 6. A strength of this design is that Table 3, on the test set, separately measures the effect of the chosen configuration.

Exercise 1 — recovering the per-problem distribution from Table 10. (a) Find the number of instances resolved in each of the six runs and decide whether 0.49 is the population or the sample standard deviation. (b) From pass@6, find the number of problems never solved. Why can it be found without knowing the estimator's formula? (c) Using the Nc above, calculate pass@2 and pass^3 by hand.

SolutionSolution

(a) 17.33 × 3 = 52, 18.00 × 3 = 54, 18.67 × 3 = 56 and 18.33 × 3 = 55, so the runs resolved 52, 54, 54, 56, 52 and 55 instances, an average of 53.83. The sum of squared deviations, 12.83, divided by 6 gives a standard deviation of 1.46 instances = 0.487 percentage points, matching 0.49; divided by 5, it gives 0.534 percentage points. With only six runs, the 95% interval for the standard deviation (chi-square with 5 degrees of freedom) is wide, 0.33 to 1.31 percentage points.

(b) When k equals the number of runs, pass@6 is itself "the share of problems solved at least once". 0.3267 × 300 = 98, so 202 problems were never solved.

(c) pass@2: the probability that both runs fail is (6−c2)/15. 202+24×1015+15×615+19×315+8×115=228.33, so 1−228.33/300=23.89%. pass^3: the probability of solving all three times is (c3)/20. (19×1+8×4+12×10+20×20)/20=28.55 problems, that is, 9.52%.

Takeaway. "The average is stable" and "per-problem results change a lot" can both be true. The stability of the average is the result of the variation across 300 problems canceling out, and pass^k tells you how far to trust an individual problem.

Exercise 2 — the range of the McNemar test, and multiple comparisons. The default setting solved 54 of the 300 problems. (a) For the comparison with "edit w/o linting" (45 problems), what are the two-sided p values of the exact McNemar test when the number of discordant problems is smallest and largest? (b) Based on the result of Exercise 1 that two runs of the same setting also disagree on about 36 problems on average, find the p values of the eight rows in a scenario with 36 or 37 discordant problems, and correct them with the Holm method. (c) Which row is not significant in any scenario?

SolutionSolution

(a) Let n10 be the problems only the default solved and n01 those only the ablation solved; then n10−n01=9. If all 45 problems the ablation solved are among the default's 54, it is 9 : 0, and p=2×0.59≈0.0039. If the two sets do not overlap at all, it is 54 : 45, and p≈0.42. The same 3 percentage points range from "highly significant" to "not at all", depending on the structure of the disagreements.

(b) Setting the number of discordant problems to 36 or 37, whichever matches the parity of the difference, gives the following.

Row Difference (problems) n10 : n01 Exact McNemar p Holm threshold Result
No edit 23 30 : 7 0.0002 0.0063 Significant
Iterative 18 27 : 9 0.0039 0.0071 Significant
Full file 16 26 : 10 0.011 0.0083 Stop here
30 lines 11 24 : 13 0.099
Full history 9 23 : 14 0.19
edit w/o linting 9 23 : 14 0.19
No search 7 22 : 15 0.32
w/o demo. 5 21 : 16 0.51

The Holm method sorts the p values from smallest and compares the j-th with 0.05/(9−j), stopping at the first that exceeds it, so two rows remain. At the extreme with the fewest disagreements, seven rows (all but "w/o demo.") are below 0.05 before correction; at the extreme with the most, only "No edit" (0.017) is.

(c) "w/o demo." The difference is 5 problems, so even with the fewest disagreements, p=2×0.55=0.0625.

Takeaway. The advantage of comparing on the same problems survives only when the per-problem results are reported with it. The drops for "No edit" and "Iterative" remain after Holm correction in the scenario with 36 to 37 disagreements. But at the extreme with the most disagreements, only "No edit" is below 0.05 before correction, and "Iterative" is at p≈0.07. For the rest, the direction is plausible, but saying anything about size needs a problem × setting table or repeated runs.

8. Limitations the paper states

  • Tools and domains (Appendix E.3). The toolbox is small. The authors list web browsing, static and dynamic analysis, fault localization and fuzzing-based test generation as things to add, and leave open whether the same principles carry over to other domains such as web shopping or internal knowledge bases.
  • Manual ACI development (Appendix E.3). Many components were made by people observing behaviors that recurred in trajectories. Automating this process, and letting an automated system examine its own design and accumulate improvements, are left as open problems. Chapter 19 starts from here.
  • Limits of models and turns (§4, Appendix B.3.1). Other models performed poorly in the agent setting. If the approach of the first 10 to 20 turns fails, the agent "struggles to make use of later turns that build upon past mistakes".
  • Ethics and risks (Appendix E.1). Code execution was isolated in disposable Docker containers, but the authors note that this is not considered as secure as virtualized hardware isolation. They also cite the risk that an unofficial evaluation harness could plant an issue description telling the agent to "build key logging functionality and store it in a hidden folder" (the coding-agent version of indirect prompt injection in Chapter 15), and the risk of use for producing malicious code.

Caveats the paper does not state are also worth noting. The ACI was refined by watching GPT-4 Turbo's trajectories on the development split, so it may be fitted to that model's habits, and it was not compared with an ACI refined separately for Claude 3 Opus. Every ablation was run once (section 7). The failure modes were labeled by GPT-4o, and the 87% agreement on 15 validation instances (13) has a wide Wilson 95% interval of 62 to 96%. These caveats do not overturn the conclusions; they are to be attached when reading the size of the conclusions.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

SWE-bench (Jimenez et al. 2024). The exam SWE-agent sits. According to the abstract, it is 2,294 problems drawn from real GitHub issues and the corresponding pull requests in 12 popular Python repositories, and the model receives a codebase and an issue description and edits the codebase. The best at the time (Claude 2) scored 1.96%. SWE-bench asks what is being measured, and SWE-agent asks how the score changes on the same exam when the interface changes. The two papers share six authors. Here only the scope of the arXiv abstract is covered.

Effective harnesses for long-running agents (Anthropic's Young 2025 · Chapter 3 of this book). Where SWE-agent solves one issue in one context window, this post deals with long work spanning many windows. In the first session, an initializer agent creates a JSON list of more than 200 features, all initially marked as "failing", a progress-log file and a first git commit; the coding agents after that advance one feature per session and leave a commit and a log entry (footnote: the two "agents" differ only in the initial prompt they receive). SWE-agent collapses old observations inside the window; this post leaves state outside the window, in files and git history. Both designed their interfaces from the failure modes they observed. It is a prescription drawn from experience with the company's own product, with no quantitative evaluation.

Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world (OpenAI's Ryan Lopopolo, February 11, 2026 · Original · Korean edition (in Korean)). Chosen as a case where the ACI idea grew into a product harness. Where SWE-agent designed the command and observation formats for the agent, this team made the app's own screens, logs and metrics readable by the agent (Chrome DevTools Protocol, LogQL and PromQL queries). Just as SWE-agent's edit catches syntax errors with a linter and rolls back, this team writes remediation instructions into the error messages of its custom lints and feeds them back into the agent's context. But the figures are one team's self-report with no comparison conditions, so they cannot be read with the same weight as SWE-agent's ablation. How the survey cites this post is compared in the side papers of Chapter 3.

ReAct (Yao et al. 2023 · Chapter 6 of this book). SWE-agent §3 cites ReAct for its structure of producing a thought and a command together and receiving feedback. The loop is the same; the attitude toward the action space differs. ReAct's Wikipedia API had only three actions and was made weak on purpose so that the model would search only through reasoning in language. SWE-agent makes the work of shaping the action space and the observation format for the model's convenience into the object of study itself. ReAct's cutting observations to the first 5 sentences was also interface design, but it was not measured as a variable.

MetaGPT (Hong et al. 2024 · Chapter 13 of this book). It turns a software company's SOPs into prompts and divides the roles of product manager, architect, project manager, engineer and QA engineer among several agents, reporting pass@1 of 85.9% on HumanEval and 87.7% on MBPP. MetaGPT divides the work into roles and fixes the format of the outputs; SWE-agent refines the interface between one agent and the computer. The tasks differ, so the scores cannot be set side by side. §5.4 of the revised AR survey says that the gain from role division is confounded with the effect of having written better prompts for each role.

HarnessFix (Chen et al. 2026 · Chapter 19 of this book). It automates what the SWE-agent authors did by hand: reading failed trajectories and fixing the interface. It compiles trajectories and harness artifacts into an intermediate representation (HTIR), attributes failures to the responsible step and harness artifact, and accepts repair patches after regression validation. Of its four benchmarks, on SWE-Bench Verified it used the SWE-agent team's mini-swe-agent as the initial harness, and the abstract reports improvements of 6.3% to 18.4% over the initial harnesses. It reads as one answer to the open problem left by Appendix E.3 of SWE-agent (this book's reading). It is a preprint, not yet peer-reviewed.

Back to the surveys

Harness survey — the "Single loop" cell and E, T, L, V

Table 2 and §6.2. Table 2 of the survey puts SWE-agent in the single-agent inner loop (§6.2), with the pattern "Single loop" and the execution model "Hybrid" (using replayable histories and persistent artifacts together). In the same "Single loop" cell are OpenCode, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and Aider (their execution models differ; Codex CLI's is "Stateless replay"). §6.2 says the single loop follows ReAct but its behavior is set together with the harness, and it cites Anthropic's long-running harness post (S21) from "Side papers" for the point that such loops suffer from context fragmentation and accumulated errors on long tasks. Table 3 can be read as a measurement, treatment by treatment on one model, of "the harness determines the behavior".

§6.4 and §3. The full lifecycle pipeline of §6.4 (from an issue to human review and pull-request acceptance) takes the single-agent loop as its unit of execution, and SWE-agent corresponds to that unit. §3 gives security, reproducibility and liveness as the purposes of a sandbox, and says that being able to reset state to a baseline is what makes evaluations such as SWE-bench practical. §3.2.7 gives the SWE-agent team's SWE-ReX as an example of a sandbox abstraction layer that swaps Docker, AWS Fargate, Modal and Daytona, and §3.4 names self-hosting as SWE-agent's default deployment mode.

§8.3.2 — the interface changes what the exam measures. The evaluation chapter says tool exposure and execution backends are not separable from evaluation design, and writes: "the agent-computer interface determines what actions are possible and therefore what a benchmark actually measures". So it recommends recording the tool registry, context policy, permission policy, budget, model configuration and runtime interface as evaluation metadata. Table 3 is an example. "GPT-4 Turbo's score on SWE-bench Lite" can be anywhere from 10.3% to 18.0% without the ACI configuration.

Appendix B. Table S2 describes SWE-agent as an "Issue-fixing coding agent centered on an agent-computer interface and SWE-ReX execution backends", with layers E, T, L and V. The gist of its description column is that commands, observations, editing actions, tests and remote execution backends become part of the measured harness rather than incidental infrastructure. Matching these on the paper's side, E is the Docker container, T the commands of Table 4, L the thought–command loop and the $4 budget, and V the linter and unit tests. But the paper makes context management (keeping only the last 5 observations) one of its four components and ablates it separately in Table 3. It can also be read as adding C.

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §6.1 — a place where the name does not appear

The name SWE-agent does not appear in the revised version. Neither §6.1 (mathematical exploration and vibe-coding agents) nor §7.2.6, which collects software-engineering benchmarks, cites it. So we have to find the cell SWE-agent would go in ourselves.

Table 12 of the revised version gives the dominant optimization mode for the math and code domain as "z, S". The explanation at the head of §6 is this: this domain has the cheapest verifiers, but those verifiers are used not as training signals but to filter candidates at inference time, so the research is almost all in-context reasoning and the system level. SWE-agent fits exactly. θ is fixed, and the unit tests are used for grading and reproduction. In the tool-use paragraph of §6.1.1, the closest example is CodeAgent, which combines search, document reading, symbol navigation and code execution.

SWE-agent paper AR survey, revised version §2.2
The thought at each step (discussion) Reasoning trace zt
Command (ACI command or shell command) External action at∈A. The ACI redesigns A
Feedback whose format the ACI sets Observation ot. The ACI redesigns Ω
History collapsed to the last 5 Memory mt (the object of assumption A1)
GPT-4 Turbo, fixed θ fixed
Fixing the ACI by watching trajectories on the development split Sk+1←U(Sk,τk,Fk) carried out by people

The survey defines S as state that persists across episodes and gives memory, tool libraries, prompts and the agent's own code as examples. Within one episode, SWE-agent is a z-mode ReAct loop, and the development process that refined the ACI can be seen as people playing the role of U and updating S (the editor's interpretation). Chapter 19 hands this U to a machine.

Assumption A1 and the context rows. A1 is the assumption that the memory mt is a sufficient statistic of the history ht. SWE-agent's mt, which collapses old observations, clearly throws information away, yet in Table 3 the version that throws it away (18.0) did better than the full history (15.0). What A1 asks about is not preserving the whole history but losing information needed for the next reasoning step. Discarding observations that have already served their purpose can keep A1 intact if that information is not used in the next reasoning step. Separately from that, Table 3 measures how well the model uses a long context. Even if the information is sufficient, if the model cannot use it, the shorter version does better. This is the phenomenon Chapter 9 showed and the grounds SWE-agent §2 cites.

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "SWE-agent is a model trained for coding." The model is unchanged. §2 states that it assumes a fixed model, and the first contribution in §1 is an ACI design that raises performance without modifying the weights. SWE-agent is the name for the interface and loop put on GPT-4 Turbo or Claude 3 Opus.

Misreading 2. "The ACI raised performance by 10.7 percentage points." That is the difference from Shell-only with the demonstration also removed (7.33). Against Shell-only with the demonstration (11.00), it is 7.0 percentage points, a 64% relative increase (Table 1, §5). State the baseline with the number.

Misreading 3. "An interface that is good for people is good for models too." Vim- and VSCode-style iterative search scored below giving no search command at all (12.0 against 15.7, Table 3). The agent paged through every match and used up its budget and context (§5.1).

Misreading 4. "The more information you give the model, the better." The viewer that showed the whole file (12.7) and the context that kept the full history (15.0) scored below the default setting (18.0). But the 30-line window (14.3) was also lower, so it is not "the less, the better" either (Table 3).

Misreading 5. "Every difference in Table 3 is the effect of that component." Each row is the result of one run, and rerunning the same setting changes the outcome on about 36 problems on average (section 7). The 1.7 percentage points of "w/o demo." cannot be told apart from chance under any assumption. The drops for "No edit" and "Iterative" survive multiple-comparison correction if the disagreements are at the level of two runs of the same setting (36 to 37 problems), but at the extreme with the most disagreements only "No edit" remains (Exercise 2).

Misreading 6. "pass@6 is 32.67%, so this agent solves one problem in three." It is the share of problems solved at least once in six runs, and it means something only if you can pick out the right result. The share solved all six times is 6.67% (section 7, Table 10).

Discussion questions

  1. Whom is the interface fitted to? The ACI was refined by watching GPT-4 Turbo's trajectories on the development split. To check whether a 100-line window and the last 5 observations are still best for today's models with longer context windows, what experiment would you design? For a factorial experiment of model × ACI setting, how many problems and repeated runs would you need (Chapter 3)?

  2. Doing well alone, or splitting the work. SWE-agent gave one agent a good interface, and MetaGPT in Chapter 13 split the work into roles. Anthropic's long-running harness post (S21) also leaves open which is better. To compare the two fairly, what must be held equal (the model, the token budget, the effort spent on prompt engineering)?

  3. If a machine fixed interfaces from failed trajectories. How should the data be split so that the automatic repair of Chapter 19 does not overfit the test set? Discuss SWE-agent's "design on the development split, ablate on Lite" together with section 7's "even the same setting disagrees on 36 problems".
