Must read. In Kapoor: the list of contributions in §1, §2.2–2.3 and Figure 1, §3.2 and Figure 2, the first four paragraphs of §4, the beginning of §5 and Table 1, §5.1, and the five root causes in §6. In Miller: all 14 pages. If time is short, Equations 1–4, §3.3, Equation 7 and Equation 9. The one figure is Kapoor Figure 1, the one table Miller Table 5.

Optional reading. Kapoor Appendices A (Table A1, Figure A1 with error bars), B (Table A3, Figure A6 with the break-even point), D (NovelQA, Table A5) and E (Tables A6 and A7). Miller Appendices A (derivation of Equation 4), B (derivation of Equation 9) and C (the clustered version of sample size).

What to cut from the presentation. Kapoor §1.1 (the definition of an agent), the individual rows of Table A4 in Appendix C (the aggregate in Table 1 of the main text stands in for them) and the checklist.

When combining with Chapter 17. Make S29 the core reading ② of Chapter 17 and read only §2 and Figure 1. Of Miller, introduce only the Galleon table from "Building intuition" and Equations 2 and 7. If your group does not hold this chapter, put Kapoor Figure 1 in the side papers of Chapter 17.

If your group skipped Chapter 6, Chapter 14 and Chapter 17. Every number needed for the exercises is written into the problems.

When you quote the numbers. Kapoor's costs are measured at April–May 2024 prices, and the paper itself says the conclusions change if prices change. Miller's Tables 1, 2, 3 and 5 are fictional numbers, and only Table 4 is real. Note this distinction, along with the number of questions.

Building intuition

Same table, different conclusions — Galleon and Dreadnought

Miller starts with two hypothetical models (§1). To choose a model for coding and math, you run three benchmarks and get the following table.

Eval Galleon Dreadnought Difference
MATH 65.5% 63.0% +2.5%
HumanEval 83.6% 87.7% −3.1%
MGSM 75.3% 78.0% −2.7%

Miller Table 1. Hypothetical data from two fictional models, given the names of real benchmarks. Dreadnought's HumanEval score appears as 86.7% in Tables 2 and 5, and the difference of −3.1% also matches 86.7%. The 87.7 in Table 1 reads as a typo. The "Difference" column is written in % as in the original, but its unit is percentage points.

On its face, Dreadnought won two of three. The conclusion Miller reaches at the end of §4 is different. Taking into account the number of questions (5,000, 164 and 2,500) and the cluster structure (MGSM translates the same problems into several languages), and comparing question by question on the same questions, the only significant difference is Galleon's lead on MATH. In Miller's words, the differences on HumanEval and MGSM "are indistinguishable from statistical noise." From these data you cannot say that Dreadnought won those two, or that it lost them. The numbers in the table stay the same. Only the way of reading them changed.

The editor's bridge — survey sampling and the efficient frontier

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

Miller's framework takes the same stance as the superpopulation model of survey sampling theory. Benchmark questions are a sample from all the "questions that measure this skill", and a leaderboard score is a sample mean. DROP, with several questions attached to one passage, is cluster sampling; comparing two models on the same questions is a paired t-test; and deciding the number of questions is sample-size design.

Kapoor's Pareto curve resembles the mean–variance efficient frontier of portfolio theory. Cost replaces risk and accuracy replaces expected return, and the shape — the boundary of points not dominated by any other point — is the same. The reasons for drawing the boundary convex differ. Kapoor (footnote 2) gets convexity from the fact that invoking two agents with probabilities p and 1−p mixes expected cost and expected accuracy linearly, producing points on the segment between them. A portfolio frontier bends because, when two assets are held in one portfolio, the variance does not mix linearly, because of the covariance term.

The analogy also breaks down. Benchmark questions are not drawn at random; their makers wrote them. Miller's super-population is an assumption made knowing this ("hypothetical, infinite, unseen"). The mixing strategy, too, lies on the segment only in expectation.

As for the papers' own analogies, Miller writes that assuming a super-population lets us jump "through the looking glass" of the specific questions to the underlying skill, and he titles his section on temperature "Don't touch the thermostat!" Kapoor §1.1 also remarks that a thermostat would qualify as an agent under traditional definitions.

The paper in detail

1. Looking only at accuracy lets cost grow without limit (Kapoor §1–§2)

§1 sums up five contributions: controlling for cost (§2), jointly optimizing cost and accuracy (§3), the different needs of model developers and downstream developers (§4), shortcuts in benchmarks (§5), and the lack of standardization and reproducibility (§6). This chapter follows the same order.

Accuracy can be bought (§2.1). Calling the model several times and taking a majority vote raises accuracy, and more so when there is a signal to check correctness. In the AlphaCode work the paper cites, accuracy went over 15% with 1,000 retries and over 30% with a million (counted as correct if one of the top 10 answers is right). Coding tasks come with example tests, so you can simply resample until one passes.

The experiment (§2.2). The authors reran two agents from the HumanEval leaderboard that had released code, plus Reflexion, which is not on the leaderboard (footnote 1) — LDB (debugging by checking execution step by step), LATS (tree search) and Reflexion (Chapter 11) — and set simple baselines beside them. These were GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 alone (zero-shot); Retry, which at temperature 0 calls the model again up to five times when an example test fails (output is not deterministic even at temperature 0, Appendix A.1); Warming, which raises the temperature 0 → 0.3 → 0.5 across attempts; and Escalation, which starts at Llama-3 8B and moves up through GPT-3.5 and Llama-3 70B to GPT-4. The original HumanEval has example tests for only 161 of its 164 problems, so they used the version modified by the LDB paper, and ran everything five times and averaged.

Kapoor Appendix Table A1. Means of five runs, with minimum–maximum in parentheses. An asterisk marks a combination the original paper did not evaluate. For LDB, the parentheses give (code-generation model, debugging model). The maximum for LDB (Reflexion, GPT-3.5) is printed as "0.91.5" in the original and is given here as 91.5.

Results (§2.3). First, there is no significant accuracy difference between Warming and the best agent (93.2 against 93.3). The authors write that they are not aware of any paper proposing a new agent on HumanEval that compares it with baselines like these. Second, costs differ by almost two orders of magnitude. Reflexion and LDB cost over 50% more than Warming, and LATS over 50 times more (134.50 ÷ 2.45 ≈ 55). In the table, LDB (GPT-4, GPT-3.5) costs USD 2.19, less than Warming, so the numbers work only if this "LDB" is read as the two versions that debug with GPT-4 (USD 6.36 and 7.26). Third, Escalation is more accurate than LDB (GPT-3.5) at less than half the cost (85.0 against 80.2, USD 0.27 against 0.63). Hence the paper's conclusion that the belief that "System 2" techniques such as planning, reflection and debugging raised accuracy is untested and an open question. It adds the caveat that such techniques may be useful on harder tasks such as SWE-bench.

"Accuracy alone cannot identify progress because it can be improved by scientifically meaningless methods such as retrying."

The Pareto frontier. The main text (§2.3) defines the frontier as the points for which no other agent has "significantly" better performance on both dimensions simultaneously, while Appendix A.1 defines it as the points not dominated in mean cost and accuracy. The first looks at uncertainty, the second only at point estimates. Computed from the means in Table A1, six points are non-dominated (GPT-3.5, Escalation, GPT-4, LDB (GPT-4, GPT-3.5), Warming and LDB (GPT-4)), and four remain on the convex frontier: GPT-3.5 → Escalation → Warming → LDB (GPT-4). This matches the dashed line in Figure 1. GPT-4 alone drops out because it lies below a strategy that mixes Escalation and Warming (the example in footnote 2).

Kapoor Figure 1 redrawn from the numbers in Appendix Table A1. The original figure breaks the horizontal axis to fit in LATS (GPT-4); here it is changed to a log scale. The dashed line is the convex frontier the editor computed from the means in Table A1, and it joins the same four points as the dashed line in the original figure (on a log axis, the line between points is not the path of a mixing strategy). The editor drew the diagram.

The money spent per problem solved. Dividing total cost by the number of problems solved gives 2.45/(0.932×164)≈ USD 0.016 for Warming, USD 0.0019 for Escalation and USD 0.93 for LATS (GPT-4). To solve one problem, LATS spends about 58 times what Warming does (the editor's calculation).

What do the error bars measure? Appendix Figure A1 draws 95% intervals from the five runs using the t distribution. The same 164 problems were run five times, so these bars contain only how much the answers to the same problems wobble, not the wobble from redrawing the problems. We come back to this in section 11.

2. Optimizing cost and accuracy together (Kapoor §3)

Cost splits into a fixed cost, paid once to choose the configuration (prompt, examples, temperature), and a variable cost, paid on every run in proportion to tokens. The more an agent is used, the more the variable cost dominates, so it pays to spend more up front to find a design that keeps its accuracy with shorter prompts.

The experiment (§3.1). A multi-hop question-answering agent built with DSPy is run on HotPotQA. "Accuracy" here is not answer match but whether all the ground-truth supporting documents were retrieved. Optimization used 100 training examples and evaluation used 200. There are five designs, and joint optimization uses Optuna to solve two objectives together: raise accuracy and cut the number of tokens in the examples (the search covers per-module temperatures, the number and choice of examples, and whether to include formatting instructions).

Results (§3.2). At similar accuracy, joint optimization cut the variable cost by 53% for GPT-3.5 and 41% for Llama-3-70B (from the table, 54–55% and 42–43%). For the break-even point, the main text says "after 1,350 tasks", and the caption of Figure A6 says 1,332 runs for Llama-3-70B and 1,275 for GPT-3.5. Computing the break-even against DSPy few-shot from Table A3 gives about 1,330 and 1,279 runs, which matches the caption; the 1,350 in the main text reads as a rounded figure.

What "maintaining accuracy" means. For 200 questions at accuracy near 0.6, the binomial standard error is 3.5 percentage points. For Llama-3-70B, the 2.1-point difference between joint optimization (0.601) and few-shot (0.622) lies within it. "Maintaining" means that no difference was found; showing that the two are the same takes an equivalence test (TOST) with a preset margin (this book's reading). The paper, too, notes in the caption of Figure A5 that the error bars reflect only the variation within the test set, and not the variability from optimization and resampling.

3. Model developers and downstream developers need different things (Kapoor §4)

Model evaluation is a scientific question. You want to know whether a change in data or architecture raised accuracy, so parameter count or compute is a better axis than dollar cost, which varies over time and across companies. Downstream evaluation is an engineering question. It decides what to buy and use, and cost itself is the construct being measured. Here proxies mislead. Mistral released a figure showing cost by number of active parameters, but as of June 2024, Mixtral 8x7B cost twice as much as Llama 2 13B on Anyscale. The prescription is to report input and output token counts along with dollar cost, so that anyone can recompute.

The NovelQA case (§4.1, Appendix D). A benchmark that feeds in the full text of a novel (from 50,000 to over a million words) and asks all of that novel's questions (5 to 100) at once. Its cost structure differs from real use, where questions are asked one at a time. In the reevaluation (one run), RAG and long context had the same accuracy, 67.89 and 67.81. Total cost the NovelQA way was USD 52.80 against USD 99.80, but asking one question at a time made the cost ratio about 21.86 (Table A5). That is a tenfold misjudgment. The accuracy difference of 0.08 percentage points is far smaller than the binomial standard error for about 2,300 questions (about 1 percentage point), and since the questions are tied to 88 novels, the clustered standard error of section 7 is larger still.

4. Shortcuts in benchmarks (Kapoor §5)

Agent benchmarks usually have a few hundred questions. If you know the test questions, you can write them directly into the agent, so overfitting is a more serious problem than training-data contamination, and in principle a lookup table could score 100%. So a holdout is needed, private if possible. The principle is that "the more general the intended generality of the agent, the more the held-out set should differ from the training set".

Level of generality What should be held out Num. benchmarks with appropriate holdouts
Distribution-specific In-distribution samples 1 / 1
Task-specific Out-of-distribution samples 3 / 6
Domain-general Tasks 1 / 8
Fully general Domains 0 / 2

Kapoor Table 1. The authors' classification of 17 benchmarks. A holdout was counted as appropriate if one actually exists at the appropriate level or the benchmark designers indicate intent to create one (Appendix Table A4).

In total only 5 of 17 have an appropriate holdout (Table A4 caption: 7 have no holdout and no plan for one, and of the 10 that have one, only 5 are at the right level). Among the benchmarks in this book, ALFWorld is domain-general, but its holdout is new games within the same six task types, so the level does not match; GAIA is fully general, but it is unclear whether its 300-question holdout comes from a different distribution; and WebArena has no holdout.

WebArena and STeP (§5.1). WebArena has 812 tasks on clones of six websites. The top agent on the leaderboard, STeP (35.8%), was more than double the best baseline in the original paper and over 10 percentage points ahead of the next-best agent, and part of the secret was hardcoding policies that solve specific tasks. For a task that navigates to a Reddit user's profile, for example, it appends /user/user_name to the base URL. If the site changes (drift), this breaks, and if an agent calls policies dozens of times for one task, then, in the paper's words, "The overall probability of failure compounds quickly." Even if each call succeeds 99% of the time independently, 30 calls give 0.9930≈0.74 (the same form as pass^k in Chapter 17; the editor's calculation). The paper grants that STeP's design makes sense given its developers' goals. The problem is the downstream developer who reads that number as accuracy on real web tasks.

§5.2 points to a bias in the other direction too. Evaluation is bunched at the two ends, chatbot answers (MMLU) and agents with no supervision, yet in a study it cites, simple feedback alone raised GPT-4's performance on challenging programming problems from 0% to over 86%. Without a holdout, evaluation tilts toward overestimation; leaving out human intervention tilts it toward underestimation.

5. The lack of standardization and reproducibility (Kapoor §6)

The paper defines reproducibility as "that the code and data accompanying a paper should be enough to reproduce the results that it reports", and names five root causes. (1) Evaluation scripts do not fit the agent's design or have bugs, so each developer writes their own. (2) Benchmarks built for language models are repurposed. Three HumanEval problems have no example tests, so Reflexion and LATS dropped those problems and LDB added examples, yet PapersWithCode puts them all on one leaderboard. (3) Evaluation is expensive, so confidence intervals are rare. SWE-bench has over 2,000 problems, and with a cost limit of USD 4 per task, a single run can cost over USD 8,000. In the authors' reproductions, many reported scores were above the maximum of five runs, and some reported baselines were below the minimum. (4) Errors in interacting with the environment. The assumption that tasks are independent, so their order does not matter, breaks with WebArena's limit on Reddit posts. (5) With no standard, bugs creep in. LATS and STeP marked some failed tasks as correct and evaluated with some tasks left out (1 and 8). The fourth is a case of a broken independence assumption between questions, and it overlaps the fifth. Below is part of a log from the STeP authors (Appendix Listing 2).

"objective":  "Find a subreddit focused on topics related to city Pittsburgh,
               and post my question, \"places for new drivers to learn driving\" there",
"action":     "stop [N/A]",
"reason":     "… an error message is displayed stating, \"You cannot post more.
               Wait a while before trying again.\" This means the action to post
               the question cannot be completed at this moment …",
"done": true, "reward": 1.0, "success": 1.0, "num_actions": 12

The STeP trajectory log from Kapoor et al. §5.1. The url and observation fields are left out for length; the ellipses mark the editor's omissions.

The agent judged that it could not post because of the posting limit and stopped, yet its reward and success are 1.0. According to Table A6, this limit affected 2 of the 129 Reddit tasks in the original paper's evaluation and 30 in the STeP evaluation.

The agents' reported scores are generally higher than the reproduced ones, and the GPT-4-alone score reported in the LDB paper (75.0) is far below the reproduction (89.6). The tilt runs toward lower baselines and higher proposed methods. According to Appendix E.1, LATS was graded on only part of the hidden tests, which inflated its accuracy by 3 percentage points. §6 leaves a standardized agent evaluation framework as future work, and the first author released HAL (Kapoor et al. 2025) the following year.

6. Questions are a sample — independent questions (Miller §1–§2.1)

The abstract's diagnosis is that evaluations are experiments, but the literature on evaluations has largely ignored the literature from other sciences on experiment analysis and planning. Results mark the best score in bold without testing it for significance; Chatbot Arena's Elo confidence intervals and the Llama 3 report are the rare exceptions. There are five recommendations (§1): compute standard errors with the Central Limit Theorem; use clustered standard errors for questions drawn in groups; reduce variance by resampling and with next-token probabilities; compare two models through question-level paired differences; and use power analysis to see in advance whether an eval can test the hypothesis.

Formalization. Suppose n questions are drawn independently from a super-population, and split the score on question i as si=xi+ϵi. xi is the mean conditional on question i being drawn (the conditional mean), and σi2=Var(ϵi) is the conditional variance, the amount the answer wobbles when the same question is asked again. The target of inference is μ=𝔼[s]=𝔼[x], and the standard error of μ^=s¯ comes from the Central Limit Theorem.

SEC.L.T.=Var(s)/n=(1n−1∑i(si−s¯)2)/n(1)

SEBernoulli=s¯(1−s¯)/n(2)

CI95%=s¯±1.96×SEC.L.T.(3)

Equation 2 is the case of 0/1 scores. Two practical points follow. Unless the sampling scheme is complicated, bootstrapping is unnecessary. And the Llama 3 report used Equation 2 even for fractional scores such as F1, which Miller says will "tend to be conservative" (too wide). The editor's explanation: when scores lie in [0,1], the variance computed with denominator n cannot exceed s¯(1−s¯). Equation 1 divides by n−1, so for 0/1 scores it is actually n/(n−1) times larger than Equation 2. With a few hundred questions the difference is negligible. As a reporting format, Miller recommends giving the number of questions and the standard error in parentheses.

Eval # Questions Galleon Dreadnought
MATH 5,000 65.5% (0.7%) 63.0% (0.7%)
HumanEval 164 83.6% (3.2%) 86.7% (3.0%)
MGSM 2,500 75.3% (0.9%) 78.0% (0.9%)

Miller Table 2. Fictional models and numbers.

Checking with Equation 2, MATH is right, and MGSM's Dreadnought comes out at 0.83% (rounded, 0.8), 0.1 percentage points off the 0.9 in the table. For HumanEval, Equation 2 gives 2.9 and 2.7 percentage points, but the table has 3.2 and 3.0. For 0/1 scores, Equation 1 is 164/163≈1.003 times Equation 2, which gives only 2.90 and 2.66 points, so this correction does not explain the gap. It reads as a slip made while choosing the fictional numbers.

7. Questions drawn in groups — clustered standard errors (Miller §2.2)

DROP, QuAC, RACE and SQuAD attach several questions to each passage, and MGSM translates the same problems into several languages. The questions were drawn together, so Equation 1 is not a consistent estimator. Write si,c for the scores within cluster c, and assume clusters are independent:

SEclustered=(SEC.L.T.2+1n2∑c∑i∑j≠i(si,c−s¯)(sj,c−s¯))1/2(4)

The triple sum holds the cross terms within clusters. It is a "sliding scale": if scores within a cluster are perfectly correlated, each cluster acts as a single observation, and if they are uncorrelated, it behaves like Equation 1. Appendix A derives it by plugging X=1n and Ωc=ucuc′ (ui,c=si,c−s¯) into the sandwich estimator (X′X)−1(∑cXc′ΩcXc)(X′X)−1 for a regression with only an intercept. Removing the diagonal terms from the result ∑c∑i∑jui,cuj,c/n2 gives Equation 4. It is the single-intercept case of the cluster-robust variance. The reporting format is to give the number of clusters too (Table 3, fictional). The real values are in Table 4.

Exercise 1 — ALFWorld's 134 games, "best of 6" and six task types. Table 3 of ReAct in Chapter 6 reports the success rate on 134 unseen games broken down into six task types. There are six prompts per type.

Method Pick Clean Heat Cool Look Pick 2 All
Act (best of 6) 88 42 74 67 72 41 45
ReAct (avg) 65 39 83 76 55 24 57
ReAct (best of 6) 92 58 96 86 78 41 71

Three rows from ReAct Table 3 (%). The ReAct paper does not give the number of games per type.

(a) The number of games per type, nc, is not in the paper. Under the conditions that each cell is "an integer k divided by nc and rounded" and that ∑cnc=134, find every possible combination, and in each combination weight and add the per-type best values. How do they compare with "All", 71 and 45? (b) If one type has 20-odd games and a success rate near 60%, how much higher than the average would you expect the best value to come out even if the six prompts were in fact the same? (c) Assume the combination (24,31,23,21,18,17), and for a hypothetical single run obtained by rounding the ReAct average row (successes 16,12,19,16,10,4, total 77), find the standard error by Equation 1, by Equation 4 treating type as a cluster, and as a stratified standard error treating type as a stratum. (d) Which of the three is right? Answer by connecting to Kapoor Table 1 in section 4.

SolutionSolution

(a) There are 12 combinations that satisfy the twelve cells of the two best-of rows, and in every one the weighted sum of the per-type best values is 73.9–79.8% for ReAct and 63.5–68.0% for Act. "All" — 71% (95 games) and 45% (60 games) — does not come out. The per-type cells are values with the best prompt chosen separately for each type, while "All" is the value of the single best run. If you read the per-type cells as the performance of one system, selection bias enters every cell. The paper does not say this separately.

(b) The standard error for one type is 0.6×0.4/22≈ 10 percentage points, and the expected maximum of 6 standard normals is about 1.27, so the expected inflation is about 13 percentage points (10–15 points per type with the combinations above). The table's "best − average" values are 27, 19, 13, 10, 23 and 17 points. Part is real differences between prompts, part is selection bias.

(c) The success rate is 77/134 = 57.5%.

Method Standard error
Equation 1 (independent questions) 4.29 percentage points
Equation 4 (task type = cluster) 8.22 percentage points (1.92 times Equation 1)
Stratified (task type = fixed stratum) 3.90 percentage points

Stratified is ∑c(nc/n)2p^c(1−p^c)/nc. Depending on whether you treat the differences in success rate between types (24–83%) as chance or as structure, the answers differ by more than a factor of two.

(d) The question decides. If the six types are all the tasks of interest, type is a fixed stratum and 3.9 points is right. If you want the agent to handle new types of household tasks too, type is a cluster drawn from "a population of types", and there are only six clusters. In Kapoor's terms, a domain-general benchmark should hold out tasks, but ALFWorld's holdout is new games within the same six types (Table A4). In that case the standard error computed from the six type success rates is 9.3 points, and the half-width of the t interval with 5 degrees of freedom is 24 points. With few clusters, Equation 4 itself is unstable. The paper by Abadie et al. that Miller cites is titled "When Should You Adjust Standard Errors for Clustering?"

Takeaway. The question decides between cluster and stratum. For a "best of k" row, check first whether it is one system.

8. Two ways to reduce variance, and one thing not to do (Miller §3)

By the law of total variance, the variance of μ^ splits into the variance of the conditional mean, which comes from choosing questions, and the mean conditional variance, which comes from the answers wobbling on the chosen questions.

Var(μ^)=Var(s)/n=(Var(x)+𝔼[σi2])/n

Raising n shrinks both. Var(x) is a property of the super-population and stays as it is. What can be worked on is 𝔼[σi2], and there are two ways.

Resampling (§3.1). Sampling the answer K times per question and averaging gives Var(si)=σi2/K. Once 𝔼[σi2]/K≪Var(x), increasing K further will have "little effect" on the standard error. The variance keeps shrinking, but each reduction shrinks as 1/K. If scores are 0/1 and difficulty is x~U[0,1], then Var(x)=1/12, 𝔼[σi2]=1/6, and Var(μ^∣K)=Var(μ^∣K=1)×(1+2/K)/3. The reduction is 1/3 at K=2, 1/2 at K=4 and 5/9 at K=6, with a limit of 2/3. Pooling the K×n answers into one sample to compute the standard error is wrong. The K answers to the same question are themselves a cluster.

Next-token probabilities (§3.2). For a multiple-choice eval answered in the first token, use the probability pi of the correct token as the score, which makes ϵi=0. In the uniform example the variance drops by 2/3. This path is not open to agents that write out their thinking and call tools.

Don't touch the temperature (§3.3). Lowering the temperature changes the model's behavior, and it only shifts reducible variance into irreducible variance or injects bias. In a single-token true/false eval with xT=1~U[0,1], at T=0 you get xT=0=1{xT=1>0.5}, and the variance of the conditional mean triples from 1/12 to 1/4. With xT=1~U[1/3,1], the mean moves from 2/3 to 3/4 and the variance grows about fivefold, from 1/27 to 3/16. The original describes the second case as "a Bernoulli distribution with p = 1/4", but since the mean is 3/4, it has to be read as the probability of a 0. The recommendation is two-pronged. If next-token probabilities can be used, compute the standard error from the expected score per question; otherwise compute it from per-question means over a sufficient K. Either way, leave the temperature alone.

ReAct's main experiments in Chapter 6 used greedy decoding, that is, temperature 0. And Kapoor Appendix A.1 notes that output is not deterministic even at temperature 0. Temperature 0 does not even remove the conditional variance.

Exercise 2 — running SWE-agent six times (SWE-agent Appendix Table 10). SWE-agent (GPT-4) from Chapter 14, run six times on the 300 problems of SWE-bench Lite, resolved 17.33, 18.00, 18.00, 18.67, 17.33 and 18.33% (mean 17.94; the original table attaches 0.49 as a subscript — this chapter writes it ±0.49), and pass@1–6 are 17.94, 23.89, 27.35, 29.67, 31.33 and 32.67%. The paper says that average performance variance is relatively low, though per-instance resolution can change considerably.

(a) What standard deviation is ±0.49? (b) If trials are independent, pass@k=1−𝔼[(1−pi)k]. Use pass@1 and pass@2 to find Miller's Var(x) and 𝔼[σi2]. (c) What are the standard errors for K=1,3,6,∞? (d) If the runs were independent, what should the standard deviation of the per-run resolve rate be?

SolutionSolution

(a) The resolved problems are 52, 54, 54, 56, 52 and 55 (total 323). The standard deviation is 0.489 with denominator 6 and 0.536 with denominator 5, so ±0.49 is the value with denominator n.

(b) Since pass@2=2𝔼[p]−𝔼[p2], we get 𝔼[p2]=2(0.1794)−0.2389=0.1199, and

𝔼[σi2]=𝔼[p(1−p)]=0.1794−0.1199=0.0595,Var(x)=0.1199−0.17942=0.0877

The sum, 0.1472, is exactly p¯(1−p¯). pass@2 splits the total variance of a binary score into two pieces. The variance from sampling answers is 40%.

(c) At K=1, 0.1472/300=2.22 percentage points; at K=3, 1.89; at K=6, 1.80; and the limit is 0.0877/300=1.71 points. At K=6, 𝔼[σi2]/K is 11% of Var(x), and adding runs without end would shrink the standard error only 0.09 points further, from 1.80 to 1.71. Whether to stop here is decided by weighing the cost of one run against the target precision. What dominates the uncertainty is the number of problems, 300, and even the mean of six runs has a 95% half-width of 3.5 points.

(d) It should be 𝔼[σi2]/n=0.0595/300=1.41 percentage points. The observed value is a little over a third of that. Solving pass@1–6 in integers gives a solution, matching within 0.005 points, in which the problems solved 1 to 6 times out of six number 24, 15, 19, 8, 12 and 20 (total 98). In 20,000 simulations that fix these counts and assign the successes to runs at random, the standard deviation averaged 1.22 points, and values of 0.49 or below occurred about 2% of the time. The runs are too even for independent trials. It could be chance, or there could be dependence between runs or between problems. The paper's information cannot tell them apart (this book's reanalysis).

Takeaway. "The mean is stable across several runs" does not mean the estimate is precise. The variance from redrawing the problems does not shrink however many runs you add.

9. Comparing two models — unpaired and paired (Miller §4)

Unpaired comparison (§4.1). The score difference of two models, μ^A−B=μ^A−μ^B, gets the standard error SEA−B=SEA2+SEB2.

CIA−B,95%=μ^A−B±1.96×SEA−B(5)

zA−B=μ^A−B/SEA−B(6)

Miller writes that these equations can be used on scores reported separately for the two models, even when they were evaluated on different random subsets. The premise is that the two estimates are independent and target the same population of questions. If the subsets overlap or were drawn from different distributions, the equations cannot be used as they stand. The paired comparison (§4.2) uses the difference on the same question, sA−B,i=sA,i−sB,i.

SEA−B,paired=Var(sA−B)/n=(1n−1∑i(sA−B,i−s¯A−B)2)/n(7)

Miller takes the two models' residuals ϵA,i and ϵB,i to be uncorrelated ("recognizing that the cross-model residuals are uncorrelated") and obtains the following. The assumption holds if each model's answers are sampled separately, but if the two share an execution environment and wobble together on a question for the same reason (the same tool outage, the same cache), it has to be examined separately.

Var(μ^A−B,paired)=(Var(sA)+Var(sB)−2Cov(sA,sB))/n=Var(μ^A−B,unpaired)−2Cov(xA,xB)/n

If the two models agree even a little on which questions are easy, the variance shrinks. Miller calls this a "free" reduction in variance, and notes that with just the standard errors and the correlation it can be computed as SEA−B,paired=SEA2+SEB2−2SEASEBCorr(sA,sB). With clusters, it is Equation 4 applied to the difference scores.

SEA−B,paired,clustered=1n(∑c∑i∑j(sA−B,i,c−s¯A−B)(sA−B,j,c−s¯A−B))1/2(8)

One number in the worked example. If the two models' scores are uniform on [0,1] with correlation 0.5, then Var(sA)=Var(sB)=1/12 and Cov=1/24. The original says the variance falls by 1/3, "from 1/6 to 1/9", but by the equation above it is 1/6−2/24=1/12, a reduction by half. This 1/9 carries over into the power example of §5 (section 10).

How Galleon and Dreadnought end.

MATH Galleon Dreadnought +2.5% (0.7%) (+1.2%, +3.8%) 0.50
HumanEval Galleon Dreadnought −3.1% (2.1%) (−7.2%, +1.0%) 0.64
MGSM Galleon Dreadnought −2.7% (1.7%) (−6.1%, +0.7%) 0.37

Only on MATH does the interval avoid 0. Checking with the correlation formula, MATH gives 0.7 and MGSM gives 1.74 with the clustered standard errors of Table 3, both matching. Exercise 3 — GAIA's scores by level (GAIA Appendix Table 4). GAIA in Chapter 17 splits 466 questions into three levels and reports the average of three runs for the API models.

Method Level 1 (146 questions) Level 2 (245 questions) Level 3 (75 questions)
GPT4 9.1 ± 2.5 2.6 ± 0.6 0
GPT4 Turbo 13.0 ± 2.1 5.5 ± 1.4 0
GPT4 + plugins (picked by a person) 30.3 9.7 0
Human annotator 93.9 91.8 87.3

Only the scores from GAIA Appendix Table 4 (%). The table does not say what ± is.

(a) Test GPT4 Turbo against GPT4 at Level 1 (3.9 percentage points) and at Level 2 (2.9 points) as unpaired comparisons. (b) In a paired comparison, how high would the correlation of question scores have to be for the Level 1 difference to be significant at 5%? What is the maximum possible correlation at these marginal proportions? (c) How many questions would it take to catch 3.9 points with 80% power (ρ = 0, 0.5, 0.7)? (d) If ±2.5 is the standard deviation of three runs, what is the 95% interval for its true value? (e) What does 0/75 at Level 3 say? (f) Recompute the abstract's "humans 92%, GPT-4 with plugins 15%".

SolutionSolution

(a) The standard error of the difference is 3.66 percentage points, z=1.06, p=0.29. Level 2 gives z=1.63, p=0.10. Unpaired, neither separates.

(b) About 0.71. The correlation of two binary variables is at its maximum when Turbo gets right every question GPT4 got right (Covmax=min(pA,pB)−pApB), which is about 0.82. It is possible, but it takes strong agreement. Without per-question results it cannot be checked.

(c) Setting the σ2 terms of Equation 9 to 0 and ω2=vA+vB−2ρvAvB (v=p(1−p)) gives about 1,010, 511 and 312 questions. The minimum detectable effect with 146 questions is 10.3, 7.3 and 5.7 points.

(d) Assuming the three results came independently from a normal distribution, (m−1)S2/σ2 (m=3) for the sample variance S2 follows a chi-square distribution with 2 degrees of freedom. Inverting this, the 95% interval for the true standard deviation is [1.3,15.7] percentage points. Three runs tell you almost nothing about the standard deviation. If 2.5 points were the true value, it would require 𝔼[σi2]=0.0252×146≈0.091, but for binary scores this cannot exceed p¯(1−p¯)=0.083. Either ± is something else, or it came out large by chance.

(e) The 95% upper bound is 4.8% by Clopper–Pearson and 4.0% by the rule of three. Read it not as "0%" but as "probably below 5%".

(f) The levels are strata. Weighting by the number of questions gives (30.3×146+9.7×245)/466=14.6% for GPT4 with plugins and 91.7% for people, matching the abstract.

Takeaway. Each stratum has a different number of questions and so a different power, and a "0" is read together with the sample size. A paired comparison requires per-question results to be published.

10. Power — how many questions to tell them apart? (Miller §5)

The inputs are the significance level α, the power 1−β and the minimum detectable effect δ, and we set

ω2=Var(xA)+Var(xB)−2Cov(xA,xB),σA2=𝔼[σA,i2],σB2=𝔼[σB,i2]

zp is the (1−p) quantile of the standard normal. If answers are sampled KA and KB times in a paired analysis, the number of independent questions needed is

n=(zα/2+zβ)2(ω2+σA2/KA+σB2/KB)/δ2(9)

and if the number of questions is fixed, it is solved the other way.

δ=(zα/2+zβ)(ω2+σA2/KA+σB2/KB)/n(10)

The original prints zβ in Equation 10 as zB. The derivation in Appendix B is the standard one that eliminates the threshold from two z scores at the same threshold under the null and alternative hypotheses.

Two worked examples and one number. With σ2=0 and ω2=1/9, catching δ=0.03 with α=0.05 and β=0.20 takes n≈969, so Miller recommends at least 1,000 questions for a new eval. With σA2=σB2=1/6 and n=198, raising K from 1 to 10 shrinks the minimum detectable effect from 13.2% to 7.5% (recomputed: 13.3% and 7.6%). Both examples use ω2=1/9 (the first "following the conditions described in Section 4.2", the second with the conditions of §3.1 plus a correlation of 0.5), but as section 9 showed, either set of conditions gives 1/12. Plugging in 1/12 gives n≈727 and minimum detectable effects of 12.9% and 6.8%. The sense of scale in the recommendation stays the same. With clusters, replace ω2 and σ2 with clustered versions in the form of Equation 8, estimated cluster by cluster from earlier data with K≫1 (Appendix C).

A sense of scale for agent benchmarks. With 300 problems and a success rate near 18%, the minimum detectable effect at 80% power is 2.802×0.18×0.82/300≈8.8 percentage points for an unpaired comparison, and 6.2 points even for a paired comparison with correlation 0.5. That is a design number, asked before setting up the experiment. Whether an observed difference is significant is judged separately by the standard error of that difference; under the same conditions the significance threshold is 1.96×SE, that is, 6.1 points unpaired and 4.3 points paired. A difference of 1–2 points falls short of the threshold either way, and even if the true difference is 2 points, the chance that this benchmark catches it as significant is only 10–15% (the editor's calculation).

Exercise 4 — ReAct against CoT, 27.4 against 29.4 (ReAct Table 1). In Table 1 of ReAct in Chapter 6, HotpotQA EM is 27.4 for ReAct and 29.4 for CoT. The same questions were solved by PaLM-540B with greedy decoding, and the number of questions is not given. The GPT-3 comparison in the appendix (Table 5) used 500 questions drawn from the validation set.

(a) Assume 500 questions and test as an unpaired comparison. (b) In a paired comparison with correlation ρ = 0, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7, what is the minimum detectable effect, and how many questions are needed for 2.0 points? (c) If 50 questions had discordant answers, what is the p of McNemar's exact test? (d) In Table 5, PaLM-540B ReAct is 29.4. What does that say?

SolutionSolution

(a) Standard error 2.85 percentage points, z=0.70, p=0.48, minimum detectable effect 8.0 points.

(b) With the σ2 terms set to 0, the minimum detectable effects are 8.0, 6.7, 5.6 and 4.4 points, and the questions needed for 2.0 points are about 7,976, 5,584, 3,989 and 2,394. It takes thousands of questions to tell them apart.

(c) With b the questions only CoT got right and c those only ReAct got right, b−c=10 and b+c=50, so b=30, c=20, and the exact test gives p=0.20 (keeping the difference at 10 questions, the number of discordant questions cannot be odd, so 74 gives 42 against 32 with about 0.295, and 76 gives 43 against 33 with about 0.302 — both 0.30 to two places). The information lies only in the discordant questions.

(d) 29.4 is the value on a random 500 questions, and 27.4 reads as the value on a different, unstated set (Chapter 6 points this out). The same method and model moved 2.0 points with only the question set changed, and that is the same size as the difference separating ReAct and CoT in Table 1. It is a scene where Miller's Var(x)/n becomes visible.

Takeaway. For a table with no question count, compute the minimum detectable effect from an assumed question count first, to see what size of difference the table was built to catch. Ranking is judged separately, by the standard error and confidence interval of the observed difference. A difference smaller than the minimum detectable effect can still come out significant. But in such a table, a small difference that is not significant is no evidence of "no difference".

11. Reading the two papers together — what do Kapoor's error bars measure?

Kapoor's five-run t intervals come from the same 164 problems, so they reflect only Miller's 𝔼[σi2]/n side. Dividing Warming's range of 1.8 points by the expected-range constant for a sample of 5 (about 2.33) gives a between-run standard deviation of 0.77 points and a 95% half-width of 2.78×0.77/5≈0.96 points. The binomial standard error that includes sampling the problems is 1.97 points, with a 95% half-width of 3.9 points, about four times wider. The 0.1-point gap between Warming and LDB (GPT-4) cannot be detected with either bar. Kapoor's conclusion, too, is that there is "no significant accuracy difference", not that the two are the same. To say they are the same, you would first set an allowable difference and run an equivalence test (TOST), as section 2 showed. But to say that Retry (92.0) and Warming (93.2) differ, you have to include the sampling of problems, and since they solved the same 164 problems, a paired comparison could narrow the interval. The answer lies in per-problem results that were not published. Put the two papers together and Kapoor says what to put on the axes and what to leave out, while Miller says what bar to draw at each point. Whether a point is on the Pareto frontier, too, should be judged by whether it is "significantly" dominated (this book's reading).

12. Limitations the papers state

Kapoor et al. (Appendix G). Cost-controlled evaluation and joint optimization rely on current pricing, so the results change if prices change (hence the web app they released). They could not cover every task environment and agent. They did not analyze other costs such as environmental impact, annotation labor or maintenance. The main text has caveats too. More sophisticated joint optimization would far surpass their own method (§3), NovelQA was run only once because of cost (Appendix D), and evaluations with human intervention are expensive and depend on the skill of the people involved (§5.2).

Miller. There is no limitations section. He draws the lines himself: he does not judge the qualitative merits of evals (§1), the super-population is hypothetical (§2), and the examples are fictional except Table 4. Equations 1–10 assume independent draws of questions (by cluster), so environments where the order of execution changes the result, like WebArena's posting limit, or settings where a model is tuned by repeatedly submitting to the same test set, can also be read as lying outside this framework.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness (Yunbei Zhang et al. 2026 · Chapter 3 of this book). A position-paper preprint; this chapter covers it only as far as the arXiv abstract. It argues the "Binding Constraint Thesis": when frontier models of comparable capability are compared on long-horizon tasks, the harness governs performance more than the model, so current evaluation misattributes harness-level gains to model improvements. It offers a formalization that treats the harness as the controller of a closed loop, evidence that harness-induced variance can exceed model-induced variance and even reverse rankings, and a harness disclosure standard with a variance decomposition protocol. Comparing the arXiv author list with page 1 of the Harness survey shows that all six authors (Zhang, Wang, Ge, Xu, Hamm and Reddy) are authors of the survey. If Kapoor says to control for cost and Miller for sample size, this paper says to separate the treatment variable (model or harness). Kapoor's Retry and Warming can be read as treatments that keep the model and change only the harness.

ReAct's best of 6 (Yao et al. 2022 · Chapter 6 of this book). It reports ALFWorld success rates as the best of six prompts, and as Exercise 1 showed, the per-type cells are values chosen separately for each type. Kapoor judges that ALFWorld's holdout is not at the right level.

SWE-agent's six runs (Yang et al. 2024 · Chapter 14 of this book). The "cost limit of USD 4 per task" that Kapoor gives as an example of evaluation cost is this paper's setting. Even so, Table 10, released after six runs, is a rare piece of repeated-run data (Exercise 2).

GAIA and pass^k (Mialon et al. 2023 · Chapter 17 of this book). GAIA has levels as strata and reports the average of three runs (Exercise 3). pass^k in Chapter 17 is pk when trials are independent, the same calculation as Kapoor's remark in §5.1 that the overall probability of failure compounds quickly.

HarnessFix (Mengzhuo Chen et al. 2026 · Chapter 19 of this book). It diagnoses and fixes harness flaws from failed trajectories, and accepts a patch only after checking on a held-out validation set that it does not break tasks that were already solved (regressions). Performance is the mean of three independent runs, and against the baselines it reports p=2.4×10−4 to 4.9×10−4 from one-sided paired sign tests on the repeated-run outcomes (RQ1 in §V.A, the test on the comparisons in Table IV). The smallest p of a sign test is 2−m, when all m pairs fall on one side, and 2−12=2.44×10−4, 2−11=4.88×10−4. This reads as all 12 pairs — four benchmarks × three runs — favoring HarnessFix. The unit of the test is not a question but "benchmark × run". This arithmetic is the editor's.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version §7.3 — what benchmarks cannot yet tell us

§7.3 names five interacting issues. The survey does not cite the two main papers, but the correspondence is clear.

Issue in §7.3 Content In this chapter
Contamination Benchmarks built from public sources are also in pretraining corpora. It is rarely measured, and when it is, usually by string overlap Kapoor §5 sees overfitting by writing in the questions as more serious
Reproducibility of live environments Benchmarks on the open web drift, so two numbers months apart cannot be strictly compared The drift in Kapoor §5.1, the posting limit in §6
Validity of LLM judges Judge scores are sensitive to the judge model, version and prompt, and favor their own family Outside both papers. In Miller's framework, the judge's randomness adds to σi2 (this book's reading)
Single-run reporting The quotation below Miller §3, Kapoor §6, Exercise 2
Scarcity of long-horizon and multi-session evaluation Every benchmark is a single session, so S-based methods that pay off only across sessions are evaluated with S reset Outside both papers. Chapter 12 and Chapter 20

"single-run numbers without variance remain the norm, and reported gaps between systems are frequently smaller than the run-to-run spread of either."

The last paragraph of §7.3 holds the survey itself to the same standard. Comparisons in the literature are confounded, since backbone, tools, retrieval corpus and token budget change along with the treatment, so instead of rankings the survey says it will name the confounds. Kapoor's cost control and S32's harness disclosure read as demands to separate out two of them, the token budget and the harness.

Mapping the notation. Placing Miller's notation in the frame of Chapter 2 gives the following (the editor's mapping).

Miller Revised AR survey §2.2
Question i One task in environment E (the starting condition of one episode)
Score si The reward R of that episode (1 for success, 0 for failure)
Conditional mean xi The expected reward that πθ and the system state S produce on task i
Conditional variance σi2 Sampling in πreason and πexec, plus the randomness of transitions T and observations Ω
Resampling K K episodes of the same task
μ The expected reward over the task distribution, that is, the objective J(θ) reduced to a one-step reward

Then S32 says that "xi depends on the harness as well as on θ", and Kapoor's levels of generality become a question of "over which task distribution μ is defined".

Harness survey §8.4.3, §11.1, §11.3 — evaluation is part of the harness too

  • §8.4.3 Cost, latency and resource tracking. It says to report the cost of achieving quality along with the quality, and to show a success–cost–latency frontier instead of ranking by success rate alone, giving Kapoor's follow-up HAL as an example. The Pareto curve of Kapoor §2 has become one stage of the evaluation process.
  • §11.1 The cost–quality–speed trilemma. It says that more faithful environments and deeper evaluation raise quality but add cost and latency, so production systems cannot treat quality as a scalar objective. Miller's resampling sits inside this too. Running K times costs K times as much, and as in Exercise 2, once 𝔼[σi2]/K drops below Var(x), each additional run costs the same while the standard error it removes keeps getting smaller.
  • §11.3 The harness coupling problem. It says that because the layers are coupled, agent scores cannot be cleanly attributed to the model without specifying the surrounding controller, and cites "Zhang et al., 2026c" (S32).

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "A lead of 1–2 points on the leaderboard means a better system." Look at the number of questions first. With 300 problems and an 18% success rate, a difference must exceed 6.1 points unpaired, and 4.3 points even paired with correlation 0.5, to be significant (section 10). Warming's 93.2 and LDB (GPT-4)'s 93.3 on the 164 HumanEval problems are two points whose difference could not be detected. Saying they are the same takes a separate equivalence test (section 11).

Misreading 2. "We ran it several times and drew error bars, so all the uncertainty is captured." Bars from rerunning the same questions capture only 𝔼[σi2]/n and leave out Var(x)/n (Miller §3, caption of Kapoor Figure A5). SWE-agent's between-run standard deviation was 0.5 percentage points, while the standard error including the sampling of problems was 1.8–2.2 points (Exercise 2).

Misreading 3. "Setting the temperature to 0 removes the noise from evaluation." The variance of the conditional mean grows, or the target of estimation changes (threefold and fivefold in Miller §3.3). Besides, output is not deterministic even at temperature 0 (Kapoor Appendix A.1).

Misreading 4. "With 10,000 questions, compute the standard error with 10,000." DROP's clustered standard error was 3.05 times the naive one (Miller Table 4), and the effective sample of its 9,622 questions comes to roughly a little over 1,000 (section 7).

Misreading 5. "If two models' confidence intervals overlap, there is no difference." In Miller Table 2, the individual 95% intervals for MATH, [64.1, 66.9] and [61.6, 64.4], overlap, but the unpaired z of the difference is 2.5 and the paired interval is (+1.2, +3.8) (Table 5). Judge by the standard error of the difference.

Misreading 6. "Kapoor et al. claim that complex agent designs are useless." They say only that the usefulness of System 2 techniques was not demonstrated on HumanEval, and they note that such techniques may be useful on harder tasks (§2.3). The demand is to report simple baselines and cost together.

Misreading 7. "Parameter count or compute can stand in for cost." In model evaluation, yes; in downstream evaluation, proxies mislead (the Mixtral example in Kapoor §4). Report dollars and token counts together.

Discussion questions

  1. Your own leaderboard. At work, what do you look at to choose a model, prompt or version? Sort Miller's five recommendations into those you could apply tomorrow and those you cannot because of cost. For the ones you cannot, which vertex of the Harness survey's §11.1 trilemma are you sacrificing?

  2. What are benchmark questions a sample of? GAIA's questions were written by people and checked by two others; 68% were valid as they were, and the rest were fixed or removed (GAIA Table 3). Can they be seen as a random sample from a super-population? If you take the benchmark itself as the population, what does a standard error mean? Think about it together with Kapoor's levels of generality and the "cluster or stratum" of Exercise 1.

  3. If you corrected comparisons that do not disclose the harness with an experiment. In a factorial design of three models × three harnesses to test S32's thesis, what are the experimental unit and the cluster, and how many tasks are needed (Equation 9)? What model would you use to split the variance into model, harness and interaction? Take it together with ETCLOVG in Chapter 3 and the regression validation in Chapter 19.

How this was checked. On October 5, 2026, the section, equation and table numbers and the figures were checked against the PDFs of the two main papers (both arXiv v1; Kapoor has only v1 on arXiv) and their text extractions. Kapoor Figures 1 and 2 were read by rendering PDF pages 4 and 6, and the redrawn figure in this chapter was drawn from the numbers in Table A1, not from the figure's gridlines. The numbers from ReAct, SWE-agent, GAIA and HarnessFix, §7.3 and §9 of the AR survey, and §8.4.3 and §11 of the Harness survey were checked in each PDF. Authors, publication status and licenses follow the bibliographic details in Appendix III, and the abstract and authors of S32 and the arXiv numbers and titles of LDB, LATS, HAL, Madaan and Card were checked the same day on the arXiv abstract pages. The calculations were done by the editor in Python (scipy and numpy) from the printed numbers. Standard errors and z tests use the normal approximation, McNemar uses the exact binomial test, the upper bound for 0/75 uses Clopper–Pearson, the interval for the standard deviation uses the chi-square distribution, and the expected inflation of the maximum uses a Monte Carlo approximation. The numbers of ALFWorld games per type were found by enumerating every combination that satisfies the integer conditions, and the per-problem resolution counts of SWE-agent were solved as integer solutions of pass@1–6 and used in 20,000 simulations.

Chapter 19 · Core · ★★

Chapter 19. Fixing the Harness from Failed Trajectories — HarnessFix

The question this chapter answers: when an agent fails, how do we tell "the model's fault" from "the harness's fault", and how do we decide what to fix?

Core reading. Mengzhuo Chen et al., "From Failed Trajectories to Reliable LLM Agents: Diagnosing and Repairing Harness Flaws", arXiv preprint (2026, cs.SE). The main text ends at the top of page 11, and with the references it runs to 13 pages. There are no appendices. The procedures for data collection, classification and annotation, and the model settings, are deferred to the authors' website.

Links to the originals

Main paper — arXiv abstract · PDF · Code (no conference page)

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview): no corresponding section (§8.5 is the closest) · Harness survey §7, §8.5, §12.3

One-paragraph summary. When an agent fails, the usual response is to keep changing the prompt or the harness until the score goes up. This paper reverses the order. It puts the failed trajectory and the harness code into one representation (HTIR) and first finds which step is responsible for the failure and which file or function of the harness produced that behavior. It groups recurring diagnoses into "flaw records," builds patches only within the scope of predefined repair operators, and accepts a patch only when, on held-out validation tasks, the target flaw goes down and there is no unacceptable regression (the value of that limit is not in the paper). The list of operators came from about 57,780 development records in 30 public agent repositories. With GPT-5 mini, the task completion rate on four benchmarks rose 6.3 to 18.4 percentage points over the initial harness. It is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and the test tasks number 34 to 100 per benchmark.

Presenter's guide

A 50-minute plan. The 10 minutes after the presentation are for discussion.

Time Content In the paper
0–5 min The question and the intuition: not one of three payment requests was created, yet the agent said it was done Figure 3
5–13 min The motivational study: where in the seven layers were the harness flaws of real repositories? Later part of §I, §II-B, Tables I and II, Figure 1
13–28 min The method: an intermediate representation that lines up trajectory and implementation → diagnosis → scoped repair → regression-aware validation and memory §III, Figure 2
28–38 min Experiments: RQ1–RQ4 §IV, §V, Tables III–VII
38–45 min The statistician's eye: what does zero regressions tell us? (Exercise 2 only) Section 6 of "The paper in detail", Exercise 2
45–50 min Back to the surveys Harness survey §7, §8.5, §12.3

In 38–45 min, do only one calculation: parts (a) and (b) of Exercise 2, which show that on Terminal-Bench, with 17 validation tasks, the regression rate could be as high as 63% even when zero regressions are observed. The rest of section 6 (the rough standard errors, the sign test, McNemar, the cluster effect in Figure 1, causal attribution), Exercise 1 and the six items of "Side papers" are for participants to study on their own before or after the presentation.

Must read. The later part of §I (the paragraphs on the three challenges and the list of contributions), §II-B with Figure 1, all of §III (keep Figure 2 open beside it), §IV-B and §IV-D (the task splits and the number of runs), and the tables of §V. If you show only one figure, make it Figure 2.

Optional reading. All of Table II, §VI Discussion with Table VIII, and the "Trace Analysis, Failure Attribution" paragraph of §VII.

What to cut from the presentation. Do not walk through the field definitions of §III-A line by line. Look at the example boxes side by side with Figure 3. Skip the list of self-improving agents in §VII.

If your group skipped Chapter 3. In the first 5 minutes, introduce the seven ETCLOVG layers with Table I, and cut "Back to the surveys" to 3 minutes.

When combining with Chapter 20. Put HarnessFix in place of the optional reading WikiSkill in Chapter 20, and split the 50 minutes as follows. The gist gets 15 minutes (0–15 min: intuition 3 minutes, three layers, three operations and two files 9 minutes, why it works 3 minutes), HarnessFix 15 minutes (15–30 min: the Figure 3 case 5 minutes, §II-B and Figures 1–2 10 minutes), and the synthesis activity 20 minutes (30–50 min). On the gist side this shrinks the 0–22 min stretch of the presenter's guide in Chapter 20 to 15 minutes. On the HarnessFix side, look only at the overview of the four stages through Figure 2, and skip the details of §III, the experiments (§IV–§V) and section 6 of this chapter.

When you quote the numbers. The score is the task completion rate (TCR), averaged over three runs on the test tasks. The paper writes the gains in "%", but as the note to Table IV makes clear, they are percentage points. When you write a number down, give with it the benchmark, the number of test tasks, the task model (GPT-5 mini by default) and what it is compared with (the initial harness H0 or another baseline).

Building intuition

Figure 3 — did the model get it wrong, or the harness?

The case the paper carries to the end is one AppWorld task. The instruction is to split the last three Amazon orders among the user and three roommates, create one Venmo payment request per roommate, and set the note to "Amazon Purchases".

The trajectory in Figure 3 of the main paper, with the two links drawn by the example boxes of §III-A added on top. The editor drew the diagram.

At S4 the model sends the payment request three times but leaves out a required argument, the recipient's email. Up to here it is the model's mistake. At S5 the API calls fail, the execution code swallows the errors, and the environment returns "Execution successful". At S6 the harness's completion guard looks only at that "success" and lets the task-completion function be called. The evaluator expected three payment requests, and not one was created.

Whose fault is it? If the model had not left out the argument, if the error had been exposed, or if the completion guard had demanded evidence of an effect, any one of these alone would keep the trajectory from ending as it did. The repair specification the paper sketches targets the last two. It leaves the model weights alone and puts "require artifact/state effect evidence before complete_task" and "expose API-error evidence" into the harness's execution routine (execute() → task_completed()) (§III-C — the actual patch and whether it was accepted are not reported). The symptom and the cause sit at different places in the trajectory, what produced the cause is harness code that does not appear in the trajectory, and there is more than one way to fix it. The whole concern of this paper is in this one case.

The editor's bridge — root-cause analysis, regression tests and causal attribution

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

For developers, the closest thing is an incident postmortem. You trace back from the symptom through logs and distributed traces to the first bad state and the code location that produced it, and after the fix you add a reproduction test to the regression suite and deploy only if the existing tests do not break. The trajectory is the distributed trace, a link is a parent–child relation in the trace, an implementation anchor is the file and line number in a stack trace, a flaw record is a bundle of incident tickets with the same root cause, and regression-aware validation is the pre-deployment regression test.

For readers at home with statistics, it is the problem of causal attribution for a multi-factor failure. If, as in the case above, the failure happens only when all three flaws are present, the question "what percentage of this failure is the observability layer's fault?" has no single answer. As in the sufficient-component cause model of epidemiology, each of the three is a cause whose removal alone makes the failure disappear, so the shares by cause add up to more than 100%. The Shapley value takes every order in which the flaws could be fixed and averages each flaw's marginal contribution to removing the failure. In this case, whatever the order, the first flaw fixed removes the failure and the other two have nothing to add, and the three flaws are in symmetric positions, so each gets one third. Which to choose is settled by the decision "what are we going to fix?"

The analogy also breaks down. A postmortem ends with a reproduction test when the incident reproduces deterministically (incidents that reproduce erratically because of concurrency or external services exist in traditional software too). For agent trajectories, that kind of incident is the default, and each run differs. So the paper collects many failures and fixes only flaws that recur (§III-B 2). Passing or failing a regression test is also probabilistic. Section 6 of "The paper in detail" works this out.

The paper's own analogy is the contrast with traditional software (§I). There, business logic is written into the control flow, so a failure can be traced straight to a code location. An agent's behavior is set at run time by model inference, so failures show up on the trajectory.

The paper in detail

1. The problem — what is hard (§I)

The paper splits existing approaches into two lines. Runtime supervision and correction bypass the problem or suppress errors for a while, and leave the harness flaw in place. Outcome-driven optimization changes prompts or workflows by looking at final scores, but does not first find where in the trajectory the responsibility lies, so the changes are broad, indirect or poorly scoped. What the paper puts forward instead is diagnosis-driven repair, and that path has three challenges.

  1. The evidence is fragmented. It is spread across multi-step interactions, tool calls, natural-language reasoning and environment responses.
  2. Runtime and implementation are not aligned. The trajectory holds behavior at run time; the harness holds static artifacts such as code, prompt templates, tool specifications and configuration files.
  3. Fixing one thing breaks another. In agents, the dependencies between runtime behavior and harness mechanisms are not explicit, so regressions are harder to anticipate than in traditional program repair.

The four stages of the method answer them one by one: HTIR for 1, implementation anchors for 2, and scoped repair and regression-aware validation for 3. In the paper, "harness repair" means modifying editable artifacts and does not include updating the base model's parameters (§II-A). In the notation of Chapter 2, it fixes θ and changes the system state S.

2. The motivational study — where were the harness flaws? (§II-B, Table I, Figure 1, Table II)

Data. The paper uses the seven ETCLOVG layers of the Harness survey (Chapter 3) as a vocabulary that connects runtime evidence to what needs repair (Table I). To count real flaws by these layers, it collected about 57,780 issues, pull requests, commits and release notes from 30 popular open-source agents. Whether a record was harness-related was judged by an LLM-based analysis agent and validated by people (example annotation → agent classification → manual inspection → strategy refinement → a final sampled audit). Harness-related records number 26,174, about 45.3% (26,174 ÷ 57,780 = 45.30%, which checks out), and all 30 repositories have them. The detailed procedure is deferred to the website.

Distribution by layer — Figure 1. The flaws were divided among the seven layers in the same way.

Layer Responsibilities (Table I of the paper) Share (Figure 1b)
Lifecycle and Orchestration Controls agent execution flow: think-act-observe loops, retries, task-state management, multi-agent coordination, and termination 25.4%
Tool Interface Governs how agents discover, describe, select, and invoke tools, including schemas, documentation, and error feedback 21.5%
Observability Records traces, logs, tool calls, errors, and cost information well enough to diagnose failures and monitor behavior 18.1%
Context and Memory Determines what the model sees at each step: context window, session state, summaries, retrieved evidence, and persistent memory 13.2%

Table I and Figure 1(b) of the paper. The shares are the numbers printed inside the figure (summing to 100.0%); counts by layer appear neither in the figure nor in the text. Figure 1(a) gives 45.3% harness-related and 54.7% unrelated.

The paper makes three observations. Flaws appear in all seven layers. Lifecycle, Tooling and Observability are the most frequent, and 29 of the 30 agents showed flaws in these three layers. Lifecycle flaws were more common in long-running systems, and verification flaws in benchmark-facing harnesses. So repair has to deal with several layers, not one prompt.

There is something to check. The center of the donut says "Harness related records" and the label below says "Distribution of Harness Flaws", so it is unclear whether the denominator is records or flaws. And this is less a frequency of flaws than a distribution of the change records developers left, as classified by an LLM (the editor's reading).

The three operators chosen for Figure 3 (verification-gated finalization, effect-evidence completion guarding, API-error and state-delta logging) appear in this table as they are. The reason for fixing the list in advance is that free-form editing raises the risk of unstable edits, architectural breakage and broad regressions (§II-B 3, §III-C).

3. The method — four agents, four stages (§III, Figure 2)

HarnessFix is four LLM agents. The trace abstraction agent builds HTIR from the raw trajectory and the harness artifacts; the diagnosis agent attributes failures to steps and layers and groups them into flaw records; the repair agent maps flaw records to operators and builds patches; and the validation agent checks whether a patch reduces the flaw within scope and without regressions.

Figure 2 of the main paper, condensed. The dashed line is the statement in §III-D that "Accepted records provide implementation examples for similar future flaw records", while rejected records "help prevent future iterations from proposing the same ineffective change." The editor drew the diagram.

3.1 HTIR — an intermediate representation that lines up trajectory and implementation (§III-A)

HTIR (Harness-aware Trace Intermediate Representation) is the raw trajectory "compiled" once into a form suited to diagnosis. It has five components.

TraceStep. One recoverable execution step (a model call, a tool-mediated action, a final submission) is one node. It holds a sequence number and the full request and response messages, with three annotations attached: (a) role (information acquisition, tool invocation, artifact editing, validation, orchestration decision, final submission), (b) execution status (success, failure, timeout, blocked), and (c) artifact/state effect (no observable external effect, read-only, artifact change, environment or application state change, mixed, unknown, with details). The decisive clue in Figure 3 is the mismatch between (b) and (c). S5 has the status "success" but the effect "no observable external effect".

Data-flow links. These connect what information in a later step's model input came in from earlier steps, disappeared or was transformed. The reason is that many harness flaws arise when evidence, constraints or error messages are lost, go stale or are summarized wrongly. The agent looks at the earlier steps together with the harness code that assembles the input (memory assembly, tool descriptions, prompt templates), and catches both explicit reuse, such as copying, and semantic reuse with different surface wording.

Data-flow link: S3 → S4
  source id: S3 (API documentation)
  target id: S4 (payment request)
  source span:
    ... create_payment_request API docs ...
    args: amount, description, user_email, ...
    user_email: email of payment receiver
    required fields include user_email ...
  target span:
    ... create_payment_request(amount=54.0,
    description=Amazon Purchases, ... )
    body={amount, description, ...}
  reuse relation: semantically reused

The example box of §III-A 2 of the paper.

Through this link, the fact that the user_email required by the documentation is missing from the request body becomes "observable". But the amount in this box is amount=54.0, while the description of S4 in Figure 3 says the request was called three times with "amount=117.6". The paper does not explain why the amount differs between two figures of the same case.

Control-flow links. These connect why the harness moved from this step to the next. They match the observed transition to the harness's execution logic (continue, retry, delegate, validate, finalize, terminate) and record the triggering logic and condition. The example in §III-A 3 records the triggering logic of the S5 → S6 link as "completion guard" and the condition as "status=success", and points out that the logic lives in execute() -> task_completed() of appworld_agent/core.py.

Implementation anchors. Links only describe what happened at run time; they do not say where in the harness the behavior was produced. Anchors are the bridge. Using signals such as tool names, template references and validator events as clues, they locate artifacts (a path and line range, a prompt or schema identifier). In the case, the S3–S4 link is tied to the prompt file and initialization function of AppWorld's official simplified ReAct code agent. The ReAct loop of Chapter 6 returns here as an object of repair.

Layer mapping. The anchored evidence is compared with the responsibility criteria of Table I and mapped to layers. This is decided per trajectory, not per file, and one step can map to several layers. In the case, S6 maps to Lifecycle and Verification, and S5, which swallowed the errors, to Observability.

3.2 Flaw diagnosis — failure attribution and flaw consolidation (§III-B)

Failure attribution. The diagnosis agent takes four steps. ① It locates the symptom from the external evaluation result and the final step, ② follows links backward to pick candidate responsible steps — a stage the paper calls "deliberately broad", ③ for each candidate, checks whether it formed, propagated, failed to expose, failed to constrain or failed to validate the failure-relevant information, and chooses the final responsible steps, and ④ assigns the layers of those steps. The result is one diagnosis record per trajectory (attribution result, failure signal, harness diagnosis). Separating ② from ③ is the same arrangement as putting a confirmatory test responsible for precision after a screening test responsible for recall (the editor's reading).

Flaw consolidation. "Single failed executions can be accidental." So the diagnosis records from many tasks are indexed by layer, and only those that overlap in layer and point to the same flaw in root cause and evidence are merged into a flaw record. One flaw record is the unit of repair.

3.3 Scoped repair — operators and the repair specification (§III-C)

The artifacts a diagnosis points to are usually core logic such as orchestration or context construction, so letting the agent edit them freely carries a high risk of regression. Two layers of constraint are therefore applied. First, candidate operators are retrieved from Table II by the flaw record's layers and filtered by root cause; the one that most directly targets the responsible step becomes the primary operator, and those that expose evidence or modify adjacent mechanisms become auxiliary operators. Next, the chosen operators are bound to this flaw and this harness in a "flaw-specific implementation contract," the repair specification.

Repair specification
  target and scope:
    flaw record          = completion accepted without artifact/state effect
    implicated layers    = Lifecycle, Verification, Observability
    selected operators   = verification-gated finalization;
                           effect-evidence completion guarding;
                           API-error and state-delta logging
    representative diagnoses = ...
  edit constraints:
    allowed artifacts    = appworld_agent/core.py; execution-result instrumentation
    forbidden artifacts  = task data/oracles, validation/test labels, public APIs
  required behavior:
    expose API-error evidence
    require artifact/state effect evidence before complete_task()
      e.g., PaymentRequest records

The example box of §III-C 2 of the paper.

The "forbidden artifacts" include task data and oracles, and validation and test labels. The paper places this list under edit constraints. So what the specification blocks is the route of raising the score by editing the answers or the grader. Whether there is a separate mechanism that also keeps the repair agent from reading the answers is not stated in the paper. This connects to the discussion of benchmark shortcuts in Chapter 17.

3.4 Regression-aware validation and harness repair memory (§III-D)

A candidate patch passes two gates. Pre-validation checks whether the diff follows the specification and passes syntax and static-analysis checks. Validation-set assessment checks, on held-out validation tasks, whether the target flaw went down and whether there are no unacceptable regressions on tasks the original harness solved. A patch is accepted only if it achieves the target improvement and stays within the regression limit. The value of that limit is not given in the paper.

Accepted or rejected, the outcome is kept in harness repair memory: the specification, a diff summary, the validation results, the tasks that regressed and a natural-language description of the conditions under which the repair applies. Accepted records become implementation examples for similar flaws, and rejected records keep the reason (pre-validation failure, insufficient improvement, excessive regression) to prevent the same wasted effort. In shape it resembles the reflection memory of Chapter 11, but what accumulates here is a history of harness changes, and the reader is the repair agent.

4. Experimental design (§IV)

Research questions. RQ1 performance and token efficiency, RQ2 accuracy of diagnosis, RQ3 contribution of the design elements (ablation), RQ4 whether a repair obtained with one model works for other models.

Benchmarks and initial harnesses. For each benchmark, one initial harness H0 was set as the starting point, and the sampled tasks were split at random into training, validation and test sets.

Benchmark Initial harness H0 Sampled / total tasks Training / validation / test
GAIA (open-ended research QA) open-deep-research 150 / 166 (questions with public ground truth) 60 / 30 / 60
SWE-Bench Verified (repository-level software repair) mini-swe-agent 250 / 500 100 / 50 / 100
AppWorld (stateful application automation) official simplified ReAct code agent 225 / 750 90 / 45 / 90
Terminal-Bench 2.0 Verified (terminal-based command-line workflows) Harbor Terminus-2 85 / 89 34 / 17 / 34

§IV-B of the paper, arranged as a table.

Metric and runs. The task completion rate (TCR) was averaged over three independent runs (§IV-D). So each printed value should be a fraction whose denominator is "number of test tasks × 3", and on checking, all the values in Table III fit that grid (GAIA 43.3 = 78/180, Terminal-Bench 17.6 = 18/102).

Baselines. Human-designed harnesses (GAIA: DeepResearchAgent and MiroFlow; SWE-Bench: OpenHands and Trae-Agent; AppWorld: FullCodeRefl, IPFunCall and CUGA; Terminal-Bench: OpenCode and OpenHands), and four automated baselines that fix an agent from observed executions: GEPA, reflective prompt evolution (Agrawal et al.); SCOPE, memory-guided prompt evolution; ReCreate, which turns trajectories into task-domain scaffolds; and Meta-Harness, which optimizes harness code from prior versions, scores and trajectories (Lee et al. 2026, reference [47] of the main paper).

Setup. By default every agent runs on GPT-5 mini, and four other models (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen3.5 Plus, Gemini 3 Pro) were also run. The gold standard for RQ2 is 20 failed test trajectories per benchmark on which three annotators marked the responsible step, cause, anchor, layer and operator. For RQ4, the GAIA harness repaired with GPT-5 mini was put on the four models unchanged.
