The reading in §VI goes like this. GEPA, SCOPE and ReCreate edit only a narrow slice, and Meta-Harness touches all seven layers but its search is untargeted, so it costs many tokens. The layers repaired differ by benchmark. On GAIA they were Tool Interface and Observability (missing API configuration, unsupported document formats), on AppWorld Tool Interface, Lifecycle, Verification and Governance (argument validation, exposing errors, refusing completion before the effect), and on Terminal-Bench Context and Memory, Lifecycle, Verification and Governance.

One point does not fit. The specification example in 3.3 put the Observability layer and "API-error and state-delta logging" into the AppWorld case, but in the AppWorld column of Table VIII, Observability is "not edited." How to reconcile the two statements is an open question.

6. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

It uses only the numbers printed in the paper. The paper did not do this analysis, and the aim is not to overturn its conclusions. It is an exercise in how the same numbers can be read through a statistician's eye. It doubles as review for Chapter 18 (can we trust the scores?).

The test tasks number 34 to 100. Even averaged over three runs, the unit of the sample is the task. Repetition only reduces the randomness within a task; it does not reduce the variation that comes from which tasks were drawn. Treating the GPT-5 mini row conservatively as two independent proportions, the standard error of the difference is 9.0 points on GAIA, 7.0 on SWE-Bench, 7.3 on AppWorld and 10.0 on Terminal-Bench, and the gains are 2.05, 1.71, 0.86 and 0.89 times those. A paired analysis reduces the standard error when the two harnesses' per-task results are positively correlated (when they solve or miss the same tasks together). Without per-task results, neither that correlation nor how much it would reduce the error is known. The differences of 2.6 to 5.0 points against Meta-Harness are a third to a half (0.30 to 0.56 times) of the standard errors above.

The sign-test p values are powers of 2. The reported endpoints, 2.4×10−4 and 4.9×10−4, equal 0.512=2.44×10−4 and 0.511=4.88×10−4 after rounding. In a one-sided sign test, if all n pairs fall on one side then p=0.5n, so this can be read as "four benchmarks × three runs = 12 pairs (11 after dropping a tie), all on HarnessFix's side". If so, the test says only "it won all 12 times" and says nothing about the size of the difference, and the three runs on the same tasks are not independent pairs either. But the human-designed baselines are compared on only one or two benchmarks, so at the level of runs there would be 3 to 6 pairs and a minimum p of 0.125 to 0.016, and "p<0.001 against every baseline" could not come out. The unit of pairing is an open question.

Table V is 80 trajectories. The Wilson 95% interval for Full HTIR's step accuracy of 68/80 is [75.6%, 91.2%], and for the raw trace's 44/80 it is [44.1%, 65.4%]. Since this is a comparison on the same trajectories, the McNemar test is the right one, but the number of discordant pairs is not given. A range can still be found. Let b be the number that only HTIR got right and c the number only the raw trace got right; then b−c=24 and 0≤c≤12, and the exact McNemar p runs from 1.2×10−7 to 7.2×10−4, solid in every case. The last step (62 → 68, b−c=6), by contrast, gives p of 0.031, 0.24 and 0.36 when c is 0, 6 and 12. The gain from adding anchors and layer mapping is not settled with 80 trajectories.

The effective sample of Figure 1 depends on within-repository correlation. Treating the records as independent, the 95% half-width for Lifecycle's 25.4% is 0.53 points. But the records are clustered in 30 repositories (about 872 on average). The paper gives no data to estimate the within-repository correlation ρ, so assume a value. If ρ is 0.05, the design effect is 1+871×0.05≈44.6, the effective sample about 587 records and the half-width 3.5 points, and the 3.9-point difference between Lifecycle and Tooling is only 1.4 times its standard error (about 2.8 points). If ρ is near 0 this shrinkage is small, and the larger ρ, the larger it is. Misclassification by the LLM classifier comes on top.

Flaw attribution is a problem of causal attribution. For a failure like Figure 3, which happens only when three flaws are present together, "what percentage is which layer's fault?" has no single answer. HarnessFix sidesteps this. It maps one step to several layers and measures layer judgments by macro-F1 (the original gives only the metric name). But "fixing which layer makes the failure disappear?" is a counterfactual question that can be answered only by intervening. The ablation in Table VI is an intervention that removes HarnessFix's components, not one that fixes flaw layers one at a time. Running a factorial experiment on the same task set that switches the three operators of one flaw record on and off in 23 combinations would let you estimate the main effects and interactions by layer separately (the editor's suggestion).

Exercise 1 — looking again as a paired comparison. Treat the average of three runs as if it were one run. (a) Terminal-Bench, GPT-5 mini: 6 of 34 tasks → 9. In the most favorable case, where HarnessFix solves all 6 of H0's and 3 more, what is the exact McNemar p? (b) GAIA: 26 of 60 tasks → 37. What is p when (HarnessFix-only successes b, H0-only successes c) = (11, 0), (13, 2), (15, 4), (17, 6)? (c) To detect the 2.6-point difference against Meta-Harness on SWE-Bench Verified with a paired design (two-sided α=0.05, power 0.8), how many tasks are needed? Answer for discordant-task shares of 10%, 20% and 30%.

SolutionSolution

(a) With b=3 and c=0, under the null hypothesis b~Binomial(3,0.5), so the one-sided p=0.125 and the two-sided is 0.25. Even under the most favorable assumption it cannot be told apart from chance.

(b) The two-sided p values are 0.00098, 0.0074, 0.019 and 0.035 in turn. With the same difference, the more of H0's solved tasks are missed, the weaker the evidence.

(c) Putting d=0.026 into n≈(z0.975ψ+z0.8ψ−d2)2/d2 gives about 1,159, 2,320 and 3,481 tasks for ψ=0.1,0.2,0.3. Under these assumptions, even using all 500 tasks of SWE-Bench Verified the power is only about 0.45, 0.25 and 0.18, and with the 100 test tasks the paper used it is lower still. Unless the discordant share is far below 10% or the difference larger, telling 2.6 points apart at the target power with this one benchmark is hard.

Takeaway. The difference in means alone cannot settle a paired comparison. The numbers of newly solved and newly missed tasks have to be reported together, and the latter is the size of the regression itself.

Exercise 2 — the power of regression validation. The validation sets are 30 tasks for GAIA, 50 for SWE-Bench, 45 for AppWorld and 17 for Terminal-Bench. Assuming H0's completion rate equals that on the test set (GPT-5 mini), H0 solves about 13, 23, 17 and 3 validation tasks. (a) If a patch independently breaks each previously solved task with probability q, what is the probability of observing no regression at q=0.05,0.1,0.2? (b) After observing zero, what is the exact 95% upper bound on q? (c) What does the fact that runs are stochastic add?

SolutionSolution

(a) The probability of zero regressions is (1−q)k (k is the number of validation tasks H0 solves).

Benchmark k q=0.05 q=0.1 q=0.2
GAIA 13 0.51 0.25 0.055
SWE-Bench Verified 23 0.31 0.089 0.006
AppWorld 17 0.42 0.17 0.023
Terminal-Bench 2.0 3 0.86 0.73 0.51

On Terminal-Bench, even a patch that breaks 20% of previous tasks has a one-in-two chance (0.51) of showing no regression at all in this validation. Acceptance also requires the target improvement and the pre-validation checks, so this is not the probability of passing the whole gate.

(b) The one-sided 95% upper bound 1−0.051/k gives 20.6% for GAIA, 12.2% for SWE-Bench, 16.2% for AppWorld and 63.2% for Terminal-Bench (with the two-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound, 24.7, 14.8, 19.5 and 70.8%). "No regression" means "the regression rate could be as high as 12% to 63%".

(c) False regressions. Regardless of the patch, a task solved once can be missed on the next run. A strict limit rejects good patches because of noise, and a loose one lowers the power of (a) further. A mechanism is needed that runs tasks several times to define "tasks that were reliably solved". The paper gives neither the value of the regression limit nor the number of repetitions on the validation set.

Takeaway. "Passing" a regression test is not proof that there is no regression. It is a statement that no regression of this size was seen, and the validation set sets that size.

7. Limitations the paper states

This paper has no Limitations or Threats to Validity section. Gathering the statements scattered through the text gives the following.

  • Detailed procedures are kept outside the text. The data collection and classification procedures were put on the website "due to space limitations" (§II-B), and the annotation and metric details and model settings without a reason (§IV-D). From the text alone, the accuracy of the classifier, the agreement among annotators and the prompts of the repair agent cannot be checked.
  • A single failure can be accidental. So only recurring flaws are fixed (§III-B 2). This also means rare flaws are out of scope.
  • Fixing one thing can break another. The paper names this itself as the third of its three challenges (§I). Regression-aware validation is the countermeasure.
  • The transfer effect is smaller than the original effect (§V-D).
  • It is early-stage research. The conclusion calls the work an "early effort" (§VIII).

If the editor may add, it can also be read this way. There is only one H0 per benchmark, so whether the same size of gain appears for a harness that is already well tuned is unknown. The human-designed harnesses were presumably each tuned for different models, yet all were run with GPT-5 mini, so that comparison may mix in the fit between harness and model (the point of S32 in Chapter 18). And this paper is a preprint, and a bibliographic check found it is not on the ICML 2026 list of accepted papers.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

The observability and evaluation chapters of the Harness survey (Li et al. 2026 · Chapter 3 of this book). The main paper's layer classification came from here. §7 covers trace collection and reliability engineering, and §8.5 the stage that attributes failures to harness layers. The difference is prescription against method. The survey prescribes turning trajectories into "layer-specific engineering feedback", and the main paper automates that with HTIR, flaw records and repair specifications and measures it in numbers. AgentFixer, which §7.4 of the survey introduces, is a study that attached 15 validation tools to IBM's CUGA, and CUGA appears in Table IV of the main paper as a human-designed baseline for AppWorld (41.1%).

Anthropic's harness for long-running agents (Young 2025). A case of people fixing a harness by hand. When the agent was asked to build a web app across many context windows, it tried to do everything at once and ran out of context, declared the job done once it saw progress, and marked features complete without testing. The fix was to keep a JSON list of over 200 features, all initially marked "failing", and a progress file, and to let the agent change a feature to passing only after testing it end to end. Declaring completion too early is in the same family as the completion-guard flaw of Figure 3 (the editor's reading). The difference is the diagnostician and the evidence. Here an engineer diagnosed by observation, and there is no numerical comparison.

SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024 · Chapter 14 of this book). Figure 8 automatically classified, with GPT-4o, the 248 trajectories GPT-4 Turbo failed to resolve on SWE-bench Lite into nine categories (agreement with the authors' labels 87%). 52.0% were incorrect or overly narrow implementations, and 23.4% were failures to recover from failed edits. The difference is the axis of classification. These categories are symptoms of behavior, and the interpretation that carried them over to the harness was done by people. The device people built that way is the editing linter guardrail, and removing it drops the score from 18.0% to 15.0% (Table 3). HarnessFix automates the interpretation that goes from symptoms to layers and implementation locations.

Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book). It learns from failure too, but what it fixes is different. In Reflexion, after a failure the model writes a reflection, keeps the most recent one to three in memory (the original's Ω is "usually set to 1-3") and uses them on the next attempt at the same task. HarnessFix collects failures from many tasks, fixes the harness code and measures the effect on unseen test tasks. Both fix θ and change S, but Reflexion is closer to Verbal Evolution, where S is text, and HarnessFix to Structural Evolution, where S is code (the latter classification is this book's reading).

The critique of comparisons without harness disclosure (Zhang et al. 2026 · Chapter 18 of this book). The abstract puts forward the "Binding Constraint Thesis": for long-horizon tasks across models with "comparable frontier capability," the harness "is often a stronger determinant of agent performance than the model it wraps." It reports that harness-induced variance can substantially exceed model-induced variance, "including cases of model ranking reversal", and calls for a disclosure standard and variance decomposition. In Table III of the main paper too, repairing the harness for each model swaps first and second place on GAIA (Gemini 3 Pro 69.4 against Claude Sonnet 4.5 66.7 → 83.9 against 84.4) and third and fourth place on SWE-Bench. But those differences are 0.5 to 0.6 points, far smaller than the standard errors. Read together, the more automatically harnesses are fixed, the greater the need to state "on which harness was this score measured?"

LLM Wiki (Karpathy 2026 · Chapter 20 of this book). A preview of the next chapter. It keeps a schema document that sets out the wiki's structure and procedures (something like CLAUDE.md), periodic health checks (Lint) and an append-only work log (log.md). The schema document is a harness artifact, the health check is the work of the observability and verification layers, and the work log sits where the repair memory sits (this book's reading). The difference is what gets fixed. HarnessFix fixes the harness; the agent in LLM Wiki fixes knowledge.

Back to the surveys

Harness survey §7, §8.5, §12.3 — the general account and its automation

§7 Observability and operations (O). §7.1 covers trace collection that records LLM calls, tool calls and context assembly as span trees, together with its standards, and §7.4 covers reliability engineering. The failure taxonomies in §7.4 (MAST's 14 failure modes of multi-agent systems, and AgentErrorTaxonomy, which treats error propagation, where one root cause spreads to later decisions, as the bottleneck) share a lineage with the main paper's concern that "symptom and cause sit in different places". §7.5 gives, as a way to close the gap between observability and evaluation, automatically generating regression test cases from production failure traces, and the main paper's regression-aware validation and repair memory are one implementation of it. In light of the "harness-as-assumption" principle in the same section (every component encodes an assumption that the model cannot do something on its own, and goes stale as models improve), Table VII can also be read as showing that devices that patched GPT-5 mini's weaknesses were less needed by stronger models (the editor's reading).

§8.5 Stage 4: multi-level judgment and failure attribution. Judgment is made at three levels — outcome, trajectory and evaluator — and the diagnosis asks where among the model, tool interface, context, execution environment, orchestration loop, benchmark specification and evaluator a failure started. The main paper carries out §8.5.2's "trajectory evaluation turns benchmark results into layer-specific engineering feedback" as written. What is missing also shows. The survey says to put the evaluator itself under test (§8.5.3), but HarnessFix's seven layers have no benchmark specification (the V layer of Table I includes final output evaluation, so one cannot say "there is no evaluator"). Which layer a failure caused by a wrong grader would go to is not settled.

§12.3 Diagnosing failures from trajectories. Going beyond evaluation centered on final scores, the survey proposes "trace-native evaluation", which makes the trajectory the primary object from which outcome scores, trajectory quality, failure attribution and regression tests are all computed. As grounds it cites LangChain's 2026 survey: 89% of teams use observability tools, but only 52.4% run offline evaluations. The main paper is one answer to this open problem. Whether three runs and a sign test are enough to deal with the variance of single-run pass rates, which the same section points out, can also be read differently in light of section 6.

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version — no corresponding section

The revised AR survey has no section corresponding to this chapter, and the word "harness" does not appear in its text (only "Harnessing" in the titles of references). There are three nearest places.

§8.5 Verification of Agent Behavior. The open problem that validators give output verification but not process verification, so outcome-level evaluation misses "right answer, wrong process" failures. Figure 3 is its mirror image. The harness trusted only a process signal, "Execution successful", and did not check the outcome.

§2.2 system update (Eq. 5). Harness repair is system-level optimization that fixes θ and changes S. The revised version does not cover HarnessFix, so the mapping below is this book's reading.

Main paper AR survey, revised version, §2.2
The base model's parameters are not updated (§II-A) θ fixed
Harness artifacts (code, prompt templates, tool specifications, configuration) The evolvable system state S. In the survey's classification, closest to Structural Evolution, where S is the agent's code or architecture
Failed trajectories Trajectory τk
Evaluator report, execution errors Environmental feedback Fk
Diagnosis → scoped repair → regression-aware validation The update rule U in Sk+1←U(Sk,τk,Fk)
A repair round k. The survey's k is an episode number; one HarnessFix round is a batch that pools failures from many episodes

The attribution problem in §8.2. The survey points out that responsibility for a failure is split between two channels, gradient updates to θ and writes to S, and names as something the field lacks "evaluation protocols that hold θ fixed while varying only the accumulated state, so that the two channels can be measured separately". HarnessFix's experiments fix θ and change only the harness, and Table VII fixes the harness and changes the model. They can be read as a partial example of such a protocol (this book's reading).

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "HarnessFix reduces failures by fixing the model." It does not touch the base model's parameters (§II-A). In Figure 3 too, what the repair specification targets is not the model's missing argument but the harness's execution routine that hid that mistake and finalized prematurely (the actual patch and whether it was accepted are not reported).

Misreading 2. "The abstract's 6.3–18.4% improvement is the range across all models." It is the range of the GPT-5 mini row. Across all of Table III it is 5.9 to 18.4. The "%" means percentage points (the note to Table IV). Read as a relative improvement, Terminal-Bench's 17.6 → 26.5 becomes a rise of over 50%, and the impression changes a great deal.

Misreading 3. "p<0.001, so it is clearly better than every baseline." The endpoints of the reported p values equal those of a sign test where 12 pairs (11 pairs) all fall on one side, and a sign test says nothing about the size of the difference (section 6). The 2.6 to 5.0 points against Meta-Harness are smaller than the standard errors for 34 to 100 test tasks (section 6).

Misreading 4. "Figure 1 is the frequency with which harness flaws actually occur." It is the share of development records from 30 public repositories as selected and classified by an LLM (§II-B). Counts by layer and classification accuracy are not in the paper. The records are clustered by repository, so the effective sample is smaller than the number of records, and how much smaller depends on the within-repository correlation (in the assumed calculation of section 6, about 587 records when ρ=0.05).

Misreading 5. "Each failure has one responsible layer." One step can map to several layers (§III-A 5), and the flaw record of Figure 3 lists three layers. §8.5.4 of the Harness survey also says that attribution is rarely a single-label classification problem.

Misreading 6. "A diagnostic accuracy of 85% is human level." It is the rate of agreement with gold labels made by three annotators (80 trajectories). Agreement among the annotators is not in the paper, and the 45–52% of existing techniques is a figure from other papers on other data (§V-B).

Discussion questions

  1. The model's fault or the harness's? In Figure 3, the model left out an argument, the execution code swallowed the error and the completion guard trusted only the status value. Which of the three would you fix first? Which kinds of failure suit having the model write reflections, as in Chapter 11, and which suit fixing the harness code? In your work, is there an incident recorded as "human error" that was really a flaw in the procedure?

  2. If you set the regression limit. With 17 validation tasks, even a large regression is missed (Exercise 2). Would you choose "miss none of the previously solved tasks", "net improvement just has to be positive" or "an upper bound on the number of missed tasks", and how many times would you run the validation set? Recall the power analysis of Chapter 18.

  3. Leaderboards in an era of automatic harness repair. If the harness can be fixed automatically for each model, on which harness should "model A is better than B" be measured to be fair: the same initial harness, a harness each optimized for itself or a published standard harness? Discuss it with the call for harness disclosure in Chapter 18 and the schema document of Chapter 20 side by side.

Chapter 20 · Core · ★★★

Chapter 20. Synthesis — LLM Wiki, an Agent That Compiles Knowledge

The question this chapter answers: if, instead of retrieving at every query, we organize knowledge in advance and let it accumulate, how are the parts we have seen so far rearranged?

Core reading. ① Andrej Karpathy, "LLM Wiki", GitHub Gist, April 4, 2026. One markdown file, about 1,950 words of English. ② (optional) Liyan Tang et al., "WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution", 2026 preprint. 14 pages of main text, 28 with the appendices.

Links to the originals

Main sources — LLM Wiki gist · WikiSkill arXiv abstract · WikiSkill PDF

Surveys — Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version (OpenReview) §8, §9 (with §2.2 Eq. 5 and §2.4 Table 5) · Harness survey §2.3, §3–§9 (all seven ETCLOVG layers)

One-paragraph summary. Most use of LLMs with documents takes the form of RAG, so when a question arrives that needs five documents synthesized, the synthesis is redone from scratch every time. Karpathy's gist proposes reversing the order. When a source comes in, the LLM reads it and integrates it into a markdown wiki. It revises entity pages and topic summaries, flags where the source contradicts old claims and adds cross-references. The knowledge is "compiled once and then kept current". The structure is three layers (raw sources, wiki, schema), three operations (ingest, query, lint), and a catalog with an append-only log. The optional reading, WikiSkill (a 2026 preprint), applies the same idea to an agent's execution experience and reports that accumulating a wiki without ever rolling it back raised scores in skill evolution. This chapter fills in a single table showing how the parts seen over twenty chapters are rearranged inside this one system.

Presenter's guide

A 50-minute plan. The 10 minutes after the presentation are for discussion.

5–17 min Three layers, three operations, two files The gist's "Architecture", "Operations", "Indexing and logging"
17–22 min Why it works, and what this piece does not say The gist's "Why this works", "Note"
22–30 min (Optional) WikiSkill — compiling experience into a wiki WikiSkill abstract, §1, Figure 2, §5.1 and Table 3
30–50 min Synthesis activity: mapping LLM Wiki onto the seven ETCLOVG layers "Back to the surveys" in this chapter, Harness survey §2.3

The side papers and §8–9 of the AR survey come out when filling in cells during the synthesis activity. If time runs short, cut WikiSkill.

Must read. The whole gist (20 minutes). If you show only one figure, make it the concept diagram in section 2 of "The paper in detail" (the gist has no figures).

What to cut from the presentation. The tool settings in the gist's "Tips and tricks", WikiSkill §4.2.2 (transfer across models), Tables 4 and 5, Appendix D.

If your group skipped Chapter 3. In the first 5 minutes of the presentation, show the table of layer definitions from Chapter 3 (survey §2.3), and cut WikiSkill by that much.

When combining with Chapter 19. In this chapter, do only the whole gist and the synthesis activity, and skip WikiSkill. Shrink the gist stretch (0–22 min in the table above) to 15 minutes and give the 15 minutes after it to HarnessFix. The split by stretch is in the "When combining" item of Chapter 19.

When you quote the numbers. The gist's "A single source might touch 10-15 wiki pages" and its statement that the index works "at moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages)" are the author's experience of use, not experimental results. WikiSkill's numbers are averages over three evolution runs, with particular 2026 models, on five benchmarks of 85 to 280 test items each. Quote them with the model, benchmark and number of items, and say that the paper is a manuscript not yet peer reviewed.

Building intuition

Searching again every time against organizing in advance

The gist starts from one sentence. In RAG, "the LLM is rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question. There's no accumulation." If a question asking for the synthesis of the same five documents comes yesterday and again today, the system finds the fragments and pieces them together both times, and yesterday's synthesis disappears into the chat history. LLM Wiki keeps that synthesis as a file. The time at which the work is done moves from query time to the time a source is added. This is why the gist calls the wiki "a persistent, compounding artifact."

The editor's bridge — materialized views, ETL, codebooks

A bridge from the editor

The analogy below is meant to help understanding. It is not a claim of the paper.

It is a choice familiar to database administrators. When heavy join queries come in often, you either use an ordinary view that joins at every query, or create a materialized view that computes the result in advance and refreshes it when the base tables change. RAG is the first path, LLM Wiki the second. The price is the cost of refreshing and the risk that the view goes stale. The gist's ingest is the refresh, and lint's "stale claims that newer sources have superseded" is the search for a stale view. Broadened to the data warehouse, it is ETL: extract from the source (the raw layer), transform by rules (the schema) and load into the store (the wiki).

For readers at home with statistics, codebook management is close. You leave the raw data as it is, write variable definitions and coding rules in the codebook, and keep a change history every time a rule changes. The schema document corresponds to the codebook, and the append-only log file to the change history. Just as coding rules are refined together with the coders, the schema too is something "You and the LLM co-evolve this over time".

The analogy also breaks down. A materialized view is a deterministic function of the base tables, so recomputing it tells you whether it is right. LLM Wiki's compilation is lossy summarization; running it again on the same sources does not produce the same pages, and judgments such as what to emphasize go into it. A wrong page cannot be caught by recomputation. That is why the raw layer is left immutable, and it is where the operational problem at the end of this chapter (errors in the summary layer pass verification) arises.

The gist's own analogies are two. One is "Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase." The other is the Memex Vannevar Bush envisioned in 1945, a personal knowledge store with associative trails between documents. The gist holds that the part Bush could not solve was "who does the maintenance", and that the LLM takes it on.

The paper in detail

1. The problem — RAG rediscovers every time ("The core idea")

The gist calls itself an "idea file". It is written so that, pasted into the user's coding agent, the agent builds an implementation together with the user.

The first paragraph's summary of RAG is as we saw in "Building intuition" ("Nothing is built up."). The gist writes that NotebookLM, ChatGPT file uploads and most RAG systems work this way. This is a description from experience of use, not a quantitative comparison, and section 7 designs a way to measure the actual difference.

The alternative is that the LLM "incrementally builds and maintains a persistent wiki". The wiki is a collection of interlinked markdown files that sits between the user and the raw sources. When a new source comes in, the LLM does not just index it but integrates it into the existing wiki. It revises entity pages ("updating entity pages"), rewrites topic summaries, flags where the new source contradicts old claims ("noting where new data contradicts old claims") and strengthens or challenges the evolving synthesis.

Division of labor. Sourcing, exploration and asking good questions are the person's job, and the "grunt work" of summarizing, cross-referencing and bookkeeping is done by the LLM. As uses it lists cumulative work such as personal records, research over months, reading a book and an internal company wiki.

2. Three layers ("Architecture")

The structure of the gist's "Architecture", "Operations" and "Indexing and logging" on one page. The two boxes at the bottom are the two special files kept inside the wiki. The editor drew the diagram.

Layer The gist's definition Who writes it
Raw sources The user's curated collection of source documents (articles, papers, images, data files). "These are immutable" — the LLM reads from them but never modifies them. "This is your source of truth." The user adds them
The wiki A directory of LLM-generated markdown files. Summaries, entity pages, concept pages, comparisons, an overview, a synthesis "The LLM owns this layer entirely." The user reads it
The schema A document that tells the LLM how the wiki is structured, what the conventions are and the workflows for ingest, query and lint (e.g. CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, AGENTS.md for Codex) The user and the LLM refine it together

The three paragraphs of the gist's "Architecture", arranged as a table.

The layer the gist stresses most is the schema. "This is the key configuration file — it's what makes the LLM a disciplined wiki maintainer rather than a generic chatbot." In the terms of Chapter 3, the schema is part of the harness. It leaves the parameters alone and changes behavior through text read every session. Calling the raw layer the "source of truth" means, conversely, that the wiki is not the standard of truth. It is like not deleting the raw data and keeping only the summary tables.

3. Three operations ("Operations")

Ingest. The LLM reads a new source, discusses the key points with the user, writes a summary page, updates the index and related pages, and appends a line to the log file. "A single source might touch 10-15 wiki pages." The author prefers to ingest sources one at a time and guide what to emphasize, and says to write that procedure into the schema.

Query. The LLM finds and reads the relevant pages and answers with citations. The sentence the gist marks in bold as "The important insight" is this: "good answers can be filed back into the wiki as new pages." If a comparison you asked for or a connection you discovered is put back into the wiki rather than buried in the chat history, exploration also accumulates as knowledge. That querying also grows the wiki is the second point where it parts from RAG.

Lint. Periodically, have the LLM health-check the wiki. There are six items: contradictions between pages, stale claims that newer sources have superseded, orphan pages with no incoming links ("orphan pages with no inbound links"), concepts mentioned but lacking their own page, missing cross-references, and data gaps that could be filled with a web search. As the name lint from software suggests, it is the work of regularly paying down the debt that builds up as the wiki grows. Placed in the distinction of Chapter 1, the skeleton of the procedure for the three operations is a workflow set by the schema, while which pages to revise and which contradictions to flag are decided by the model.

4. The catalog and the log ("Indexing and logging", "Optional: CLI tools")

As the wiki grows, it needs a way to find things. The gist keeps two special files that answer different questions.

index.md log.md
Character content-oriented chronological
What it holds A link and one-line summary per page, organized by category When ingests, queries and lint passes happened
Updated On every ingest "append-only" — entries are only added
Use Read first at query time, then drill into pages A timeline of how the wiki evolved; shows what was done recently

The two paragraphs of the gist's "Indexing and logging", arranged as a table.

The gist writes that the index works surprisingly well at "moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages)" and avoids the need for embedding-based RAG infrastructure. If each entry in the log file starts with a consistent prefix (for example ## [2026-04-02] ingest | Article Title), one line, grep "^## \[" log.md | tail -5, shows the last five entries.

The next section ("Optional: CLI tools") matters. As the wiki grows, "you want proper search", and as an example the gist gives a local search engine (qmd) that combines hybrid BM25/vector search with LLM re-ranking. It attaches both as a command-line tool and as an MCP server (Chapter 7). LLM Wiki does not do away with search. The object of search changes from fragments of raw sources to organized pages, and reading the index replaces search only while the scale is small.

5. Why it works, and what this piece does not say ("Why this works", "Note")

The gist's explanation is cost. The tedious part of maintaining a knowledge base is not the reading or the thinking but the bookkeeping. "Humans abandon wikis because the maintenance burden grows faster than the value." LLMs don't get bored, don't forget to update a cross-reference and can touch 15 files in one pass. So, the gist says, the cost of maintenance becomes "near zero." Put in statistical terms, the claim is that both the value of the wiki and its maintenance cost grow with the number of pages, and the LLM flattens the cost curve. There are no data measuring the two curves. The phrase "near zero" reads as a statement about people's working hours; it does not address token costs or the cost of correcting wrong updates.

"Note" pins down the nature of the piece. "This document is intentionally abstract." The directory structure, schema conventions, page formats and tooling are all optional and modular. "The document's only job is to communicate the pattern." So LLM Wiki is not a system that makes performance claims but a design pattern, and this chapter looks at which parts of the previous nineteen chapters the pattern overlaps with and what is missing.

6. (Optional) WikiSkill — compiling an agent's experience into a wiki (WikiSkill §1–§3, §4.2, §5.1)

The problem. An agent skill is a reusable module that packages instructions, scripts and resources into one directory (§1). Recent studies do "skill evolution": running an agent on training tasks, analyzing the trajectories and refining the skills. WikiSkill points out that these methods do not keep what has been learned as "a separate, evolving knowledge representation", so the insights are scattered across optimization histories, and, citing the gist, it asks whether an agent's experience too can be compiled into persistent, compounding knowledge.

Three layers. The workspace is split into three layers (§3.1, Figure 2).

Layer What it holds Label in Figure 2
Raw Layer All execution trajectories of the training tasks (reasoning, tool calls and outputs, final answers). Immutable Permanent, Write Once
Wiki Layer Pattern pages by failure mode and success strategy, an index, an evolution log (logs.md), a skill-impact tracking file (skill-impact.md) Compounding, Never Reset
Skills Layer For each skill, SKILL.md (the body) and PURPOSE.md (the wiki pattern that gave rise to the skill) Reversible, Conditional Update

WikiSkill §3.1 and Figure 2 arranged as a table. The label inside the figure is "Skill Layer"; the caption and §3.1 say "Skills Layer".

Four steps. One iteration passes through four components (§3.2, Algorithm 1).

  1. The Inference Agent solves training tasks with the skills put whole into the system prompt, and the trajectories pile up in the Raw Layer. The execution agent has no access to the wiki.
  2. The Wiki Maintainer samples up to 8 trajectories (up to 5 failures and 3 successes, each cut to 15,000 characters) (Appendix C), extracts the root causes of failures and the strategies of successes, creates or revises pattern pages as patches, and then updates the index and the evolution log.
  3. The Skill Proposer, in the ReAct style (Chapter 6), starts from the wiki index, the skill-impact file and a summary of successes and failures, reads the pages and trajectories it needs, and makes a proposal Pk aimed at one skill.
  4. Gating and Rollback evaluates the candidate on the validation set.

Before the formula, a note on notation. Here S is the skill set (it shares only the letter with the survey's system state S — see the mapping table in "Back to the surveys"). Applying the proposal Pk to the previous skill set Sk−1 gives the candidate Sk′; the trajectories from running the candidate on the validation set are 𝒯val,k, and their score is ℛ(𝒯val,k). ℛbest starts from the validation score of the empty skill set and is updated to the candidate's score each time a candidate is accepted (§3.2.4).

Sk←{Sk′if ℛ(𝒯val,k)>ℛbestSk−1otherwise(WikiSkill Eq. 4)

The candidate is accepted only when the validation score beats the best so far; otherwise the skills are rolled back. But "the wiki Wk is never rolled back" (§3.2.4). Whatever the outcome, the outer harness programmatically appends the proposal's diff, the validation score and the acceptance decision to the skill-impact file, and the paper calls this "an objective, ground-truth audit trail". In the case in Figure 3, a proposer that saw the record of a rejected abstract skill won acceptance at the next iteration with a concrete rule, "Never Return an Item to Its Origin Location".

What is the same as the gist and what differs. The immutable raw sources, the index and chronological log, and a wiki revised by patches are the same. They part at the third layer. The gist's third layer is rules read by the maintainer (the schema); WikiSkill's third layer is procedures read by the execution agent (the skills). WikiSkill's wiki is an intermediate product for the proposer, and part of it (the impact file) is written by the harness. It amounts to not entrusting the model with the judgment record that must not be wrong (this book's reading).

Main results — the average column of Table 1. The comparison spans five benchmarks (LiveMath, mathematics; SealQA, web search; SpreadSheet, spreadsheet manipulation; OfficeQA, long-document question answering; ALFWorld, text-based embodied household tasks) and five models. Every method starts from an empty skill set, and the score is the average test performance of the three skill sets obtained by running the whole evolution process three times (§4.2).

Model No skill Trace2Skill EvoSkill SkillOpt WikiSkill
Qwen-3.5-4B 26.2 32.1 33.7 35.2 38.5
Qwen-3.5-9B 29.9 36.7 42.3 40.2 47.4
Qwen-3.6-27B 39.4 47.3 53.3 50.7 63.3
Gemma-4-31B 41.3 45.8 43.4 49.1 54.9
Gemini-3.5-Flash 49.5 55.6 56.1 55.9 68.1

Only the average (Avg.) column over the five benchmarks, from Table 1 of the paper. For values by benchmark, see the original. Bold marks the row maximum, which differs from the original's significance marking.

The test sets have 124 items for LiveMath, 85 for SealQA, 280 for SpreadSheet, 172 for OfficeQA and 134 for ALFWorld, and the validation sets 10 to 40 items (Appendix Table 6). Significance is judged by a paired bootstrap that resamples the test items 1,000 times (Appendix C).

  • WikiSkill has the highest average for all five models and is 3.3 to 12.0 points above the strongest competing method (§4.2.1; recomputing from the table gives the same). But in the average column for Qwen-3.5-4B, SkillOpt's 35.2 and WikiSkill's 38.5 are both in bold, so by the paper's paired bootstrap that 3.3-point difference is not significant.
  • Against no skill, it is higher in 23 of the 25 model–benchmark cells, equal in 1 (Gemini-3.5-Flash on ALFWorld, 85.9 — the validation score was already 100% before evolution, so there was no evolution) and lower in 1 (Qwen-3.5-4B on OfficeQA, 28.5 against 30.2). This is the abstract's "most model-benchmark settings" (the cells were counted by the editor).
  • In the Qwen family, the gain grows with size: +12.3 points for 4B, +17.5 for 9B and +23.9 for 27B.

One note on notation. §1 writes these gains as "12.3%, 17.5%, and 23.9%", and §5.1 writes the ablation result below as "(+15.0%)," but computed from the tables they are all percentage points (38.5 − 26.2 = 12.3). §4.2.1 writes the same value as "+12.3 points". Reading them as relative increases is wrong.

Ablation — who should see the wiki? (§5.1, Table 3). Using Gemini-3.5-Flash alone, wiki access for the execution agent and for the skill proposer is switched on and off separately. When the proposer's access is switched off, the wiki maintainer is also removed, so the wiki does not accumulate.

Execution agent's wiki access Skill proposer's wiki access LiveMath SealQA SpreadSheet OfficeQA Average
(no skill) 33.0 29.4 50.5 48.6 40.4
yes no 43.8 42.0 44.4 51.0 45.3
no no 51.3 38.4 49.9 55.2 48.7
yes yes 64.8 42.8 80.2 55.6 60.9
no yes (default) 72.6 44.7 76.6 60.7 63.7

Table 3 of the paper. The values in bold in the original are LiveMath 72.6, SealQA 44.7, SpreadSheet 80.2, OfficeQA 60.7 and the average 63.7. ALFWorld is left out because Gemini-3.5-Flash already had a validation score of 100% before evolution (§4.2).

There are two conclusions. First, giving the proposer the wiki raises scores a great deal. With the execution agent's access off, the average rises from 48.7 to 63.7, with large gains on LiveMath (51.3 → 72.6) and SpreadSheet (49.9 → 76.6). Second, when the execution agent was also given the wiki, the observed average fell from 63.7 to 60.9, and LiveMath from 72.6 to 64.8. By the rough calculation in Exercise 2(b) of section 7, the 95% interval for the average difference contains 0, so only the direction is suggested. The paper offers the cause as a hypothesis, with "We hypothesize": if the execution agent gets task-solving knowledge from the wiki rather than from the skills, its trajectories become less informative for skill development.

The second conclusion connects to the synthesis activity. If the paper's hypothesis is right, showing organized knowledge in advance to the side that produces the trajectories used to diagnose what to fix blurs the diagnosis. In that case it has a structure similar to the principle of independent verification, which says not to give the reviewer the author's reasoning (this connection is this book's reading). Meanwhile, in the second row (only the execution agent has access) the wiki maintainer is removed and the wiki does not accumulate, and the paper does not explain what the execution agent read. How to read this row is an open question.

7. Rereading with a statistician's eye

This section is a reanalysis done outside the paper

The gist has no numbers. The first part is an exercise in designing what would have to be measured to test the gist's claims empirically (a study-design exercise), and the second part is a short reanalysis using only numbers printed in WikiSkill. It is not an analysis the originals did, and the aim is not to overturn their conclusions. It reuses the tools of Chapter 18.

The gist is a design pattern that makes no performance claims (section 5). Still, testing the pattern's advantages needs a comparative proposition, so this book sets up one hypothesis: "a wiki compiled in advance is better than RAG that retrieves at query time". "Better" mixes accuracy, citation accuracy, the delay until a new source is reflected in answers, and cost, and the four can move in opposite directions. Compiling in advance lowers the cost per query but raises the cost of ingesting, and a stale wiki increases the delay. The design has to ask "under which conditions is what better?"

Exercise 1 — design an experiment comparing compilation with retrieval at query time. Compare LLM Wiki and RAG with the same set of raw sources and the same model. Write down the treatment and control, the outcome measures, the unit of the sample and a rough size, the confounders, and what this design still cannot answer.

SolutionSolution

Treatment and control. The treatment is a gist-style wiki (revise pages each time a source is ingested; at query time go from the index into pages), and the control is RAG that chunks and indexes the same raw sources. Match the model, context window, query prompt and token cap per query. A third arm, "wiki + retrieval over raw sources", lets you tell whether the wiki replaces RAG or complements it. The gist itself says to add search as scale grows, so the third arm is closest to practice.

Outcome measures. Accuracy (binary per question), citation accuracy (whether the cited source actually supports the claim in the raw source — the attribution of Chapter 11. In the wiki arm too, count it correct only when it traces back to the raw source. If wiki pages are accepted as citations, errors in the summary layer pass), update delay (the number of sources from ingesting a source that changes the right answer until the new answer first appears), and cost (measure ingest and query tokens separately and estimate the break-even number of queries).

Unit and size of the sample. The unit is "question × knowledge time point". Ingest the raw sources in chronological order, stop at about 8 time points, and at each one put the same questions to both arms. It is a paired comparison with binary outcomes, so the McNemar test. If 30% of questions get discordant answers from the two arms and the difference in accuracy is 10 percentage points, about 234 items are needed at a 5% significance level and 80% power (155 with 20% discordant, 940 with a 5-point difference). Since questions cluster within time points, with 30 items per time point and an intraclass correlation of 0.05 the design effect is 1+29×0.05=2.45 (the clustered standard error of Chapter 18). Then about 234×2.45≈573 pairs are needed. Eight time points × 30 items (240 pairs) is not enough; with 30 items per time point, about 20 time points are needed. If you keep to 8 time points, the effective sample cannot exceed 8/0.05=160 however many items you add. There is one more correlation. If the same questions are asked again at every time point, the results also cluster by question (crossed clustering of time point and question), so decide first whether to use new questions at each time point or repeat the same ones, and fit the analysis model to that choice.

Confounders. Corpus size (the gist says the index is enough up to about 100 sources, so cross size with the treatment), how often contradictions occur (the wiki's advantage is likely larger in fields where sources often disagree), question type (a factual question about one document against a synthesis across several — whether the type changes the effect is the core of the design), human involvement (mixing wikis people revised with wikis only the LLM wrote makes two treatments), and feedback from queries (if good answers are filed back into the wiki, earlier questions change the conditions of later ones, so either do not file back evaluation questions or make filing back a separate treatment).

What this design still cannot answer. Whether errors in the wiki accumulate over months, and the understanding people gain by reading the wiki, are not captured by accuracy. If the right answer changes over time, the grading key has to be rebuilt for each time point (Appendix A.2 of ReAct, seen in Chapter 6, where an out-of-date dataset answer made a right answer count as wrong). And §7.3 of the revised AR survey writes that every benchmark the survey tabulates is confined to a single session. Multi-session evaluation of this kind has to be built from scratch.

How solid is WikiSkill's ablation result? There are no per-item results, so treat the two configurations as independent samples and approximate with binomial standard errors. Since the comparison is on the same items, a paired analysis could shrink the standard errors. On the other hand, the variation among the three evolution runs enters neither this approximation nor the paper's bootstrap, which resamples only the test items (Appendix C). The paper itself acknowledges that with validation sets of 10 to 40 items the gating decisions are noisy (Appendix B). The approximation carries errors in both directions.

Exercise 2 — measure the size of the two conclusions. (a) For the effect of the proposer's wiki access with the execution agent's access off (48.7 → 63.7), approximate the difference, standard error and 95% interval for each of the four benchmarks and for their average. (b) Do the same calculation for the effect of the execution agent's wiki access when the proposer sees the wiki (63.7 → 60.9). (c) On SealQA, with 85 test items, what is the smallest difference between two configurations near 60% accuracy that can be detected with 80% power? (d) How should the values in bold in Table 3 be read?

SolutionSolution

For each benchmark SE=p1(1−p1)/n+p2(1−p2)/n, and the standard error of the difference in the four-benchmark average is 14∑bSEb2 (matching the paper's practice of averaging benchmarks with equal weight).

(a) The effect of the proposer's wiki access.

Benchmark (test items) Difference (pp) Standard error Difference/SE
LiveMath (124) +21.3 6.0 3.5
SealQA (85) +6.3 7.5 0.8
SpreadSheet (280) +26.7 3.9 6.8
OfficeQA (172) +5.5 5.3 1.0
Four-benchmark average +15.0 2.9 5.1

The 95% interval for the average difference is [9.2, 20.7], far from 0 even under a conservative approximation. But the effect is concentrated in LiveMath and SpreadSheet.

(b) The effect of the execution agent's wiki access (with access minus without).

Benchmark Difference (pp) Standard error Difference/SE
LiveMath −7.8 5.9 −1.3
SealQA −1.9 7.6 −0.3
SpreadSheet +3.6 3.5 +1.0
OfficeQA −5.1 5.3 −1.0
Four-benchmark average −2.8 2.9 −1.0

The 95% interval for the average difference is [−8.4, 2.8], which contains 0, and on SpreadSheet the direction is reversed. Under the condition where the proposer does not see the wiki (the second and third rows), the execution agent's access also points the same way, −3.4 percentage points on average. Reading it as "the direction is suggested but the size is not settled" fits the sample better.

(c) The minimum detectable difference for an independent comparison is (z0.975+z0.8)2p(1−p)/n=2.80×2×0.6×0.4/85≈21 percentage points. It is about 17 for LiveMath (124 items), about 15 for OfficeQA (172) and about 12 for SpreadSheet (280). Even if a paired comparison reduces it, a difference of a little over 2 points on SealQA cannot be told apart with this design.

(d) The caption of Table 3 gives no rule for the bold marking. Applying the rule of the Table 1 caption and Appendix C (when several are bold, they are not significantly different from the best) as it stands, the fact that only SealQA's 44.7 is bold would mean it differs significantly from 42.8. That is 1.9 points on 85 items, a difference of fewer than two items. Reading it as a column-maximum mark is more natural, but the paper does not say, so it remains open.

Takeaway. In the same table, one conclusion (give the proposer the wiki) is solid and the other (do not give it to the execution agent) shows only a direction. Quote them together with the conditions: one model, four benchmarks, three evolution runs.

8. Limitations the paper states

The gist. It has no section on limitations, and "Note" states that it is intentionally abstract. There are reservations here and there. Batch ingestion means working "with less supervision", and for a company wiki there is "Possibly" a human review loop. The scale at which the index works has an upper limit. The workaround for not being able to read markdown with images in one pass, viewing the images separately, is described as "a bit clunky" ("Tips and tricks").

WikiSkill. The Limitations section lists four. (1) Because skills were put whole into the prompt, retrieval and triggering of skills, which matter as skills multiply, were not evaluated. (2) The strict gate that accepts only proposals that raise the validation score filters out proposals that are neutral now but could enable gains later. (3) Pattern pages, evolution logs and proposal diffs only accumulate, and there is no automated mechanism to prune the wiki. (4) Tasks that span hundreds of actions or several hours were not covered.

The third limitation applies to the gist too. Lint finds stale claims, but there is no policy for what to delete. It is the point that §2.4 Table 5 of the AR survey records as a caution for the S mode: "an eviction and validation policy is required, not optional". Both pieces can also be read as detailed on how to accumulate and silent on how to discard.

Side papers — how they differ from the main paper

The studies below implement, in different forms, the idea of "accumulating knowledge or experience in a persistent external store". They differ in what they accumulate, who reads it and when it is computed.

Agent Skills (Zhang et al. 2025). A post on Anthropic's engineering blog. A skill is a directory holding instructions, scripts and resources, and its design principle is progressive disclosure. At first only the names and descriptions of all skills go into the system prompt; when a skill looks relevant, the body of SKILL.md is opened, and files referenced within it are opened only when needed. The post says real work requires "procedural knowledge and organizational context." The contrast that LLM Wiki accumulates "what is known" and skills accumulate "how to do it" is this book's summary. Skills can bundle code to run deterministically, and the post also warns that untrusted skills should be audited before installation (Chapter 15).

Voyager (Wang et al. 2023 · Chapter 12 of this book). A lifelong-learning agent that explores Minecraft without human intervention and keeps adding skills. The components in its abstract are an automatic curriculum, an "ever-growing skill library of executable code", and iterative prompting that improves programs using environment feedback, execution errors and self-verification; it calls GPT-4 as a black box and needs no fine-tuning. The difference is how things are checked. Voyager's skills are code, so they can be run, and whether they are right is checked by the environment feedback and execution errors from running them and by self-verification (the three signals the iterative prompting above uses). That a run ended without errors is not on its own taken as achieving the task. A wiki page has no executor, so finding where it is wrong requires checking it against the raw sources. The revised AR survey gives Voyager as an example of Procedural Evolution, where S is a library of executable skills (§2.2).

RAG (Lewis et al. 2020 · Chapter 8 of this book). For each query it retrieves the top k documents and attaches them to generation. Only the index is prepared in advance, and synthesis happens at query time. One caution. Lewis et al.'s RAG fine-tunes the query encoder and the generator, so by the AR survey's criteria it belongs on the θ side (the survey itself cites this paper only as traditional RAG that performs "fixed, one-shot retrieval" and does not place it in the three regimes — Appendix I, section 4). The RAG the gist talks about is closer to a product-style file upload that does not touch the weights. Keep them apart so as not to compare different things under the same name.

MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023 · Chapter 12 of this book). Like paging in an operating system, it moves information into and out of the context window (abstract). In MemGPT the model puts memories in and takes them out during the conversation; in LLM Wiki a separate operation tends the store as documents that people can also read.

RARR (Gao et al. 2023 · Chapter 11 of this book). It finds external evidence (attribution) for a generative model's output and post-edits unsupported content while preserving the original output as much as possible (abstract). In LLM Wiki this happens when citations are attached to answers and when lint looks for contradictions. The difference is what things are checked against. RARR checks against retrieved original evidence, while LLM Wiki's lint compares pages with each other. If every page came from the same wrong summary, no contradiction shows up.

WikiSkill's comparison methods — EvoSkill (Alzubi et al. 2026), Trace2Skill (Ni et al. 2026), SkillOpt (Yang et al. 2026). According to the summary in WikiSkill's Appendix D.1, EvoSkill revises skills with failure trajectories and a flat history of proposals, Trace2Skill with parallel patches from success and error analysts, and SkillOpt edits one large skill document through a six-stage pipeline. All three share the loop of trajectory analysis → skill revision → validation and keep what they have learned in the history or in the skill document. WikiSkill keeps it separately in a wiki that is never rolled back. The description is limited to the scope of WikiSkill's summary.

Back to the surveys

Agentic Reasoning survey, revised version — what does it optimize?

Seen through the three optimization targets of Chapter 2, LLM Wiki does not touch the weights θ, and search over z within a query is not its main work either. What it changes is the system state S that persists across sessions: the wiki and the schema. Ingest is one application of the update operator in the survey's Eq. 5.

Sk+1←U(Sk,τk,Fk)(AR Eq. 5)

LLM Wiki · WikiSkill AR survey, revised version, §2.2 Note
The wiki (including the index and log) and the schema System state S (θ fixed) The survey's examples of S include explicit memories and prompts

Mapped to the notation of §2.2 of the revised AR survey. The mapping is the editor's arrangement; the survey does not cover LLM Wiki or WikiSkill.

Placed under assumption A1, the reason for not deleting the raw layer can be formalized. Reading only the wiki at query time assumes that the wiki holds all the information needed to answer the next query, that is, that the wiki is a sufficient statistic for all the sources read. That a summary discards information does not by itself break this assumption. If what was discarded is not used by future queries, sufficiency holds. It breaks when a question not foreseen at summary time needs the discarded information, and in a wiki, where the questions cannot all be known in advance, such a question will come sooner or later. When you notice the break, the ht to go back to is the raw layer.

The cells of the table. In the survey's Table 3 (the 3-layer × 3-mode grid), LLM Wiki reads as sitting in the self-evolving layer × S cell ("Reflective note stores, episodic and semantic memory, skill libraries"). The wiki at query time can also be seen as the "structured retrieval substrates" of the foundational layer × S cell. That one system's two faces are split across two cells is this book's reading.

The prescription of §2.4 Table 5. The S mode is recommended for "Repeated tasks in a fixed domain; no GPU access", because cost amortizes across episodes and the state can be inspected, edited and audited. The caution is "Stale or wrong entries accumulate; an eviction and validation policy is required, not optional". A personal research wiki fits these conditions exactly, and lint answers the first half of the caution (validation). The second half (eviction) is empty, as we saw in section 8.

§8 open problems. The introduction to §8 writes that once state survives across episodes, attribution, verification and auditing no longer end within one episode. LLM Wiki is the real-world instance of this sentence.

§8 section The survey's statement In LLM Wiki (this book's connection)
§8.2 long-horizon interaction and attribution The memory write that caused a failure may have been committed dozens of episodes earlier and may have been correct when it was written. There is neither an operational definition of a "harmful write" nor an evaluation protocol that holds θ fixed and varies only the accumulated state When a page written wrongly months ago makes today's answer wrong, how do you find the cause? The design in section 7 is "θ fixed, evaluation that varies only the state"
§8.5 verification of behavior There is output verification but no process verification. What most needs verification is what has the longest reach, namely entries written to S One page affects every later query. Lint and source verification fill this place
§8.7 governance Auditing requires provenance for every write and the ability to replay a run against a reconstructed state. "Almost no current system provides this." The append-only log, the immutable raw sources and the git version history the gist says you get for free are a partial answer

§9 conclusion. "z buys immediate deployability at a recurring per-call cost; S buys amortization and auditability at the cost of state hygiene; θ buys serving efficiency at the cost of flexibility and of a training budget." Product-style RAG stands on the side that pays again for every query; LLM Wiki stands on the side that spreads the cost but takes on state hygiene. Since the S mode needs only inference access, it is "the mode most practitioners can actually use." The same section points out that the mechanisms of S pay off only across sessions, yet nearly every benchmark resets state before then. That is why LLM Wiki's gains cannot yet be measured. The survey ends by saying to ask this of any new system: "what, exactly, does it optimize?" LLM Wiki's answer is S, and that S includes the schema that people revise together with the model.

All ETCLOVG layers of the Harness survey — synthesis activity (20 minutes)

Bring back the seven layers of Chapter 3: E execution environment, T tools, C context, L lifecycle and orchestration, O observability, V verification, G governance. As the caption of Figure 3 says, E, T, C and L are the structural pillars of the harness, and O, V and G are monitoring, evaluation and constraints across the whole system (§2.3).

The components below come from the gist, WikiSkill, and a generalized form of the knowledge store the editor actually uses. From the third source, only the form of the structure and rules was carried over; contents, file names and numbers were not. No sample repository was built.

Points to note by layer.

  • E. The gist presupposes an execution environment but says nothing about it. Yet "raw sources are immutable" can be enforced here. If the raw folder is made read-only, the rule becomes a permission of the E layer; otherwise it stays a promise in the schema (G). This is the coupling between layers that §10 of the survey describes.
  • C. §5.3 of the survey writes that Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md at session start and opens only the files it needs, when it needs them, with glob and grep. The gist's query (from the index into pages) works this way. The structured notes of §5.4 (leave a note file and read it again on the next run) are a small form of LLM Wiki.
  • O. Measured against the fields §9.5 of the survey requires of a replayable audit record (trace identifier, acting principal, tool calls, policy decision and version, execution result, cost, integrity hash), one line of the gist's log holds only some of them.
  • G. §9.4 of the survey counts it as an advantage that a deployment-time constitution is a declarative file separate from code, so it can be read, edited and compared (diffed), and gives YAML files as the example. A natural-language schema is a looser form. The survey's open challenge, "Tooling to validate that a constitution is internally consistent (e.g., no contradictory allow/deny rules) … appears limited in the current ecosystem", applies even more directly to a natural-language schema.

(a) The emptiest layer. E. Considering that an agent that reads outside documents uses a shell (Chapter 15), it is not something to leave blank.

(b) Code or promise? Immutable raw sources, the permissions table and the source-verification rules are sentences in the schema, so they depend on whether the model follows them. What code enforces is roughly the automated checks, hidden-text scanning, version history, and WikiSkill's gate and impact-tracking file. That WikiSkill has the harness write the judgment record can be read as a design conscious of this distinction.

Discussion material — three problems that arise in operation. For each, discuss which layer's problem it is and which chapter's parts could prevent it.

  1. Overwriting by concurrent sessions. When two sessions of the same kind edit the same file at the same time, the one that writes later erases the one before. This is the lost update of databases. An append-only log holds up, and the index header, which replaces a whole line at a time, is weak. A permissions table distinguishes only kinds of agent; it cannot distinguish two sessions of the same kind. An L-layer answer is optimistic locking. When reading, remember the file's version (a version number or modification time); when writing, check that the version is unchanged and write in one atomic step; and if another session has edited it in between, do not write, but reread, merge and retry. If there is a gap between checking and writing, rereading alone cannot prevent lost updates (compare it with the shared message pool of Chapter 13).
  2. Errors in the summary layer pass verification. An error introduced in a summary passes a verification that checks against that summary, and a lint that compares pages with each other, unchanged. Verification has to be done against the raw data, and an independent reviewer should not be given the author's reasoning. This is in the same family as RARR checking against original evidence and WikiSkill hiding the wiki from the execution agent (this book's reading). The process verification of AR survey §8.5 belongs here.
  3. General knowledge buried in work products. A report for a particular task contains knowledge that holds independently of that task, but if it is not moved into the wiki it is buried along with the task when the task ends. This is the gist's advice to file good answers back into the wiki, seen from the side of work products. When, and by whom, is it judged "knowledge to promote to the wiki"?

Common misreadings

Misreading 1. "LLM Wiki does away with RAG." The index is enough only up to about 100 sources and a few hundred pages; beyond that, "you want proper search", and the gist recommends a hybrid search engine ("Optional: CLI tools"). What goes down is repeating, at every query, a synthesis that has already been organized. The synthesis a new question requires is still done at query time, and good answers are filed back into the wiki (query, section 3). Search remains, and its object changes from fragments of raw sources to organized pages.

Misreading 2. "LLM Wiki is the name of a particular folder structure and tool." "Note" says the directory structure, schema conventions, page formats and tooling are all optional. What is shared is the pattern: three layers, three operations, and the separation of index and log.

Misreading 3. "Once there is a wiki, the raw sources can be deleted." The gist defines the raw sources as "immutable" and as "your source of truth." The wiki is a lossy summary, and the raw sources are the standard for checking whether it is wrong and for recompiling it. WikiSkill too treats execution trajectories as "Permanent, Write Once".

Misreading 4. "The person does nothing." The person just does not write the wiki directly; they choose sources, set the direction of analysis, ask good questions and think about what it all means ("Why this works"). The schema too is refined by the person and the LLM together.

Misreading 5. "Since it was compiled in advance, the wiki is verified knowledge." It is a summary that does not produce the same pages even when the same sources are ingested again. That is why lint exists, and AR survey §2.4 Table 5 also lists the accumulation of stale or wrong entries as a caution for the S mode.

Misreading 6. "WikiSkill demonstrated that LLM Wiki is better than RAG." What WikiSkill measured is performance in skill evolution, and the reader of the wiki is the skill proposer, not an agent that answers questions. No experiment comparing a wiki with RAG on question answering appears in either piece. WikiSkill is a manuscript before peer review, and its key ablation comes from one model and four benchmarks.

Misreading 7. "The more people and agents see the wiki, the better." In WikiSkill Table 3, showing the wiki to the execution agent lowered the average from 63.7 to 60.9. The reanalysis in section 7 suggests only a direction, but it is clear that "who sees what" is a design variable.

Discussion questions

  1. What to compile in advance and what to compute at query time. When designing a materialized view, you weigh read and write frequency, refresh cost and tolerance for staleness. In your own work materials (regulations, case law, internal documents, research notes), what is your criterion for dividing what to organize into a wiki from what to look up with RAG as needed? What do the results of Chapter 8 and Chapter 9 add?

  2. Who should not see the wiki? WikiSkill hides the wiki from the execution agent, and independent verification hides the author's reasoning from the reviewer. If you designed the evaluation of Chapter 17, what would you not show the evaluating agent? How far is this the same as blinding in statistics?

  3. If this book were made into an LLM Wiki. If the original PDFs of the twenty chapters are the raw layer, what goes into the summary layer, the wiki layer and the schema? How would you fill the layer that was empty in Exercise 3 (E) and the promises written only in prose? If you applied the failed-trajectory analysis of Chapter 19 to running the wiki, what would you need to record?

Further study

  • The rest of the originals. The gist's "Tips and tricks". WikiSkill §4.2.2 (transfer of skills between models — cases where skills made by a small model hurt a large one), §5.2–5.3 and Figure 3, and Algorithm 1 in Appendix A.
  • Originals and code. The LLM Wiki gist was written to be pasted into your own coding agent, and doing that is the most direct exercise. Start with a few public papers, without company materials or personal information. As of October 4, 2026, WikiSkill has no code link (per Appendix III). Voyager has released its code and prompts.
  • Reading on in the surveys. AR survey, revised version, §4.2 (memory, Table 10), §7.3 (the lack of multi-session evaluation). Harness survey §5.4–5.5, §9.4–9.5, §10–12.
  • Within this book. Chapter 3 (the seven layers), Chapter 8 (retrieval at query time), Chapter 11 (checking against original evidence), Chapter 12 (hierarchical memory and Voyager), Chapter 15 (outside documents entering the wiki), Chapter 19 (failed trajectories).

After finishing this book. The twenty chapters were arranged in the order of adding parts, one at a time, to an augmented LLM. In the first half, the model started from writing out its thinking (Chapter 4 and Chapter 5) and acting while observing (Chapter 6), and gained tools and outside knowledge (Chapter 7 to Chapter 10). Then it revised against sources (Chapter 11), split memory into tiers (Chapter 12), worked in teams (Chapter 13) and moved on top of code repositories (Chapter 14). The second half covered the attack surface those parts opened (Chapter 15), alignment (Chapter 16), evaluation (Chapter 17 and Chapter 18) and fixing the harness from failures (Chapter 19).

In LLM Wiki, these parts appear again in the order of the work. When sources are ingested, the synthesis RAG did at query time is done ahead of time, and the result accumulates in a wiki that makes MemGPT's external memory readable by people too. When questions are asked, that wiki is searched. Lint turns RARR's attribution and the metrics of the evaluation chapters on the wiki itself. The schema and permissions table that tie all this work together correspond to the harness's governance. And readers can build this system on their own computers tomorrow. Build it, and the questions of this book come back: what does it optimize, who should see what, and can we trust the results?
